en: The "Preface to the Brief Outline for Contemplating the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*" uses topical outlines (*ke*) to divide the scripture; this is a practice established from antiquity. Formerly, when Dharma Master Dao’an divided the scriptures into three sections, his contemporaries criticized him for dissecting the meaning of the sūtras.
When the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Bandhuprabha arrived, it indeed divided the entire scripture into three sections, just as he had done. At that time...

He then sighed in admiration, finding it a most elegant synthesis. For each scripture has its own fundamental principles; this *ke* (classification) extracts those essential outlines and brings them to life, enabling the reader to grasp the core significance.
It is intended that one may realize the meaning beyond words and enter into awakening, thereby discarding the trap and the snare.
This is by no means a mere piecemeal dissection or an exercise in arbitrary speculation. Later scholars of the exegetical tradition, however, remained ignorant of this "meaning beyond words."
Each relied upon their own views and proliferated their doctrines, thereby incurring the fault of slandering the Dharma and leaving students with no way to follow.
This is truly what is meant by "losing one's sheep on many paths. Now, the *Laṅkāvatāra* takes the ultimate truth beyond words as its primary tenet;
it does not involve the lips or mouth. Furthermore, how could it be entered through discursive thought and conceptual discrimination? And as for that which...
I have categorized and structured this work because the scriptural text is concise and archaic, its underlying logic profound and hidden; without finding the proper gateway, one cannot enter.

Therefore, I have specifically extracted its essential framework so that one may understand the origins of the questions and answers, harmonize them into a single thread, and perceive them clearly within the mind and eyes.
I hope that one may forget words to grasp the meaning, rather than regarding the written word as an obstacle; this is not a matter of mere conjecture.
This [text] already constitutes a superfluous teaching. Those who awaken hereafter must by no means regard it as deficient and further add to its doctrines;
otherwise, they will incur the grave sin of slandering the Dharma.

On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment during the first month of summer in the Wuli (1618) year of the Wanli era, the Śramaṇa Deqing inscribed this brief outline of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* upon the walls of the Qingmen fortress in Wuyang.

Record of the Contemplation on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra;
annotated by the Ming Dynasty Haiyin Śramaṇa Śākya Śīla Deqing.
The record states: The old commentary says that *Laṅkā* is the name of a mountain; here it is translated as "Inaccessible.

It is also said to be the name of a city, because on the summit of the mountain lies the city of the Yakṣa King. The mountain is situated on the shore of the Southern Sea. *Abhaya-tara* (or *Abhayatara*) means "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
*Ratna* signifies "precious" or "valuable," used here as a general metaphor for this scripture. Thus, it is the "Inaccessible Unsurpassed Precious Scripture. It is not [the name of a person].
Master Shou said: "The realm of self-awakened noble wisdom cannot be fabricated by false knowledge; therefore, it is said that one 'cannot go there.
A mani-jewel that reflects colors cannot be compared to worldly treasures; therefore, it is called 'unsurpassed.
This implies that at this place where one cannot go, there exists this unsurpassed treasure. However, even this does not fully capture the truth. The *Huayan lun* states: "The World-Honored One..."
He was preaching the Dharma within the city of Laṅkā on the summit of Mount Malaya in the Southern Sea.

That mountain is five hundred *yojanas* high and overlooks the great ocean; there is no path by which to ascend it. The city is composed of various jewels, its radiance outshining the sun and moon, and it has no gate through which to enter.
Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are capable of ascending there. This represents the Dharma of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*).

"Gate! Only by having neither cultivation nor realization can one ascend. This teaching is indeed so. When I, the fool, resided at Mount Wutai, I once encountered a Brahmin master from the country of Khotan.
His hair was over ten feet long; he did not speak of his age, only saying that he had entered this land for more than thirty years.
He was refined in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), well-versed in the vehicles of the teachings (*śāsana*), and skilled in local dialects. I, the fool...
I requested that he reside with me in an araṇya for three years.

During our conversations, whenever there were Sanskrit terms already clarified in the sūtras, I would occasionally ask him to test his knowledge of them; everything he explained accorded perfectly with the ancient translations.
When I inquired about the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Master was startled and said, "Is this sūtra also found here? This is something that cannot be spoken of."
"This is a Dharma that cannot be grasped. The King of my land treasures it. He then asked how many fascicles there were.

I replied, "The transmitted version consists of four fascicles. The Master smiled and said, "What you have brought is but a fraction of the whole. This sutra has forty fascicles; what you have is only one-tenth.
Furthermore, when I probe the essential purport of the scripture, every word elucidates the transcendence of mind and intellect."
The realms of consciousness cannot be fully described. [A questioner] asked, "Where is Mount Laṅkā located?
The Master said, "This mountain is in the South Sea of the country of India. He asked again, "Why is it named Laṅkā? The Master said, "Laṅkā is the name of a precious gem;
its shape is octagonal, yet when viewed, it appears perfectly round, and its substance is extremely solid. It does not...
It can be pierced; it constantly emits radiance and is the most supreme treasure in the world. Thus, *abhatara* means "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) in this language.
Because the mountain consists entirely of this treasure, the mountain is named after that treasure; hence it is called Mount Laṅkā-abhatara-ratna.
On the summit of the mountain is a city, which is naturally formed of this treasure and has no gate through which one may enter.
However, it is currently occupied by a yakṣa king and ghost-king. The Buddha preached this sūtra within the city atop this mountain;
thus, the sūtra is named after its location. Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asked, "Can people reach this mountain? The Master replied, "People cannot reach it."

Because this mountain is narrow at its base and broad at its summit, whenever the sky is overcast with dark clouds or the waves surge violently, the form of the mountain becomes even more distinct and its radiance grows ever more intense.

However, when the sea is as still as a mirror and the sky is clear and cloudless, such that the sea and sky become one color, the mountain then disappears from view. Nevertheless, there are monks in that land who practice meditation.
He walked along the seashore, intending to enter meditative observation (vipaśyanā) by gazing out at it. This follows the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*.
According to the words of this Indian master, the mountain is named after its substance, while the sūtra is named after its location; there is profound significance in this.

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that within the "Inconceivable Assembly" (*Acintya-pariṣad*), he taught the dhāraṇī-wisdom of dependent origination according to others (*paratantra-pratītyasamutpāda-dhāraṇī-jñāna*), which is called...
The *laṅkā* (Lanka) in "Lankā-rāja-vijñāna" likely expresses the Dharma by way of its location; furthermore, its profundity and mystery are evident.

Yet, the teachings speak of an ocean of wisdom (*jñāna-samudra*), an ocean of nature (*prakṛti-samudra*), an ocean of awakening (*bodhi-samudra*), and an ocean of mind (*citta-samudra*). As for the "ocean of jewel-luminous emptiness," this sutra calls it the "ocean of the storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna-samudra*).

Moreover, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is metaphorically likened to an ocean, and nirvāṇa is likewise likened to an ocean; mountains are also used as metaphors, and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are similarly likened to mountains—let alone the yakṣas.
It is said that "fearful ghosts" are those who fly through the air and devour living beings.
Yet, our Buddha specifically dwelt in this Yakṣa King’s City on the Jewel Mountain within this ocean to preach this sutra, thereby manifesting the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
That which is expounded in this sutra consists of the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness;

it is the method for contemplating reality as it is. Its purport is subtle indeed. Why is this? As the sutra says: "The ocean of the storehouse-consciousness abides eternally, stirred by the winds of objective realms."
Great waves surge through the dark abyss, never ceasing for a moment. Thus, the ocean of wisdom has no inherent nature; through the awakening to delusion, it becomes the state of an ordinary person.
The profound and tranquil ocean of the mind transforms into the ocean of karma of birth and death. This is the wondrous mind of precious luminosity.
It transforms into the illusory and false body and mind of the eight consciousnesses and five aggregates; thus, the jewel has eight facets.
Although the mountain is five hundred yojanas high, it is occupied by the yakṣas of afflictions and birth-and-death.
Yet, when the clouds thicken into a pitch-black night, or when the waves surge in tumultuous confusion, the form of the mountain becomes even more clearly manifest—this is what is called "delusion."
When thought arises, nirvana manifests. As for the yakṣa king who invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma:
it means that when afflictions arise, the Buddha-way is perfected. This serves to suppress and reveal this precious, luminous, and wondrous nature.

Although one dwells within the great ocean of birth and death and amidst the mountains of the five aggregates, one is not robbed by afflictions, nor swept away by the waves of birth and death, nor captivated by external objects.
The winds of the realms stir; within the darkness of ignorance, that darkness cannot cause further gloom. Amidst the profound obscurity of the long night, the spiritual light alone is revealed.

Furthermore, it is said that when the ocean is tranquil and space is clear, the mountains do not appear; yet this only serves to show more clearly that the ocean of wisdom is perfectly serene, wherein the myriad phenomena of the universe are vividly and simultaneously reflected.
Body, mind, and the world are instantly dissolved; birth-and-death and nirvana [are no longer distinct].
It is timely and impartial; reaching this point, both Māra and Buddha are empty, and neither can be apprehended. Alas!

Truly, one must believe that this is the supreme crest-ornament dharma-gate of self-awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). Furthermore, the meaning of the title of this sutra is translated as "Incapable of Being Reached.
Only those with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can arrive there; this is intended to reveal that this dharma-gate is not within the sphere of mental activity, but only...
For those of the highest capacity, there is a single, sudden entry. One is not permitted to grope or settle upon [the object]; nor is one permitted to engage in conceptualization or mental grasping.
One simply contemplates it within the waves of the objective realm and the darkness of afflictions.
If one does not contemplate it, one will not know that such things exist within the ocean of birth and death. This sutra is for those whose faculties are matured.
This refers to the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, which declares that the seeds of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) are the Tathāgatagarbha. An ancient master said:
"The *Laṅkāvatāra* teaches that the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; it discards both the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness.
Therefore, Master Bodhidharma pointed to this as the Mind-Seal. Mazu Daoshi said: "The *Laṅkāvatāra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its core."

The School: Taking the gateless as the Dharma-gate. Therefore, when the masters of the School teach people, they insist that one must directly transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness to study, thereby exiting the paths of both ordinary beings and sages.
Yet those who explain this merely label names and establish doctrines, unaware that they are empty and futile.
How can this help later students, who likewise engage in mere intellectual speculation regarding the patriarchs’ mind-seal? It is just like this.
Alas! It is said in the first part of the "Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech":
"That this chapter is titled 'Heart' (citta) is because it takes the One Mind as its central tenet. That which is called 'quiescent extinction' (śānti) is the name..."
It is the single mind; that is, the ultimate mind of the self-nature of intrinsic nature.
All Buddhas have realized this mind and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings; they simply point directly to this mind. Therefore, it is said:
"All Buddhas awaken to the mind. (Old Commentary: This great sutra consists of one hundred thousand verses, four hundred thousand phrases, and three hundred and two [sections].)
It consists of one hundred thousand words and one hundred and fifty chapters; of these, only this single chapter has been transmitted here.
Although its text is extensive and its scrolls numerous, in reality, it all collectively and suddenly reveals this Dharma of the One Mind.

Within the twelve divisions of the canon, this sutra belongs to the "Unprecedented" division (*adbhutadharma*); within the five teachings, it belongs to the Sudden Teaching of the Mahayana, which further encompasses both the Sudden and the Perfect.
This refers to the immediate revelation of the perfect, single mind (*ekacitta*), for the five natures (*pañcagotra*) and the three vehicles (*triyāna*) all equally realize it.

If explained according to the five meanings of the Tiantai school, it is named after its singular metaphor; for the *Laṅkāvatāra* jewel is used as a metaphor for the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatā*).

Just as jewels on a mountain and jewels in a city are inhabited by both Buddhas and Māras, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the body-and-mind are the basis upon which all sages and ordinary beings rely.

Because it is quiescent, it takes the *tathāgatagarbha* as its essence; that is to say, because the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and because its intrinsically pure nature manifests as the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.

It takes the ultimate mind of the self-nature of nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva-paramārtha-citta*) as its thesis, for it is what is equally realized by all noble ones and ordinary beings. It destroys the heterodox, reveals the orthodox, and severs...

Its function is to give rise to faith where doubt existed. It serves to tear asunder the net of false views and doubts held by non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles, causing them to develop resolute, correct faith in the One Vehicle.
Its pedagogical characteristic is likened to "matured ghee" (*pakva-sarpis*);

this means that it teaches that the five natures and the three vehicles all possess the potential for attaining Buddhahood, though they have not yet received their prophecy. They can be transformed into the Way through a single change, just like that matured [ghee].

Just as clarified butter (*sarpis*) can be transformed into *ghṛta* (ghee) with a single change because the effort required is slight, this [text] briefly indicates the capacity for opening up provisional means (*upāya*) and revealing the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), serving as a precursor to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

If discussed in terms of its fundamental tenets (*abhiprāya*), it takes the mind of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-citta*) as its tenet and self-awakened noble wisdom (*svasaṃvedyāryajñāna*) as its goal;
furthermore, it takes the signless dharma (*animitta-dharma*) of self-awakened noble wisdom as its core.
Taking the gates as the primary principle and silent realization beyond words as the goal,
it is thus heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea, adorned with various precious flowers,
together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas, who had come from various different buddha-fields.
From all directions, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the power of their mastery over immeasurable samādhis and their playful exercise of supernatural powers—
with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader— had the crowns of their heads anointed by the hands of all the Buddhas.

They skillfully understand the meaning of the objective realms that are manifestations of their own minds. They universally manifest according to the various types of beings through diverse mental forms and immeasurable gates of liberation.
They have attained ultimate penetration into the five dharmas, the three self-natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.

The commentary states: This passage describes the circumstances of the teaching. Regarding "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), it means: "In this manner, I have heard this Dharma from the Buddha.
"At one time" refers to the occasion when the faculties [of the disciples] and the response [of the Buddha] met; it is not a fixed designation. "Buddha" is the teacher;
"mountain" is the location of the teaching; and "bodhisattvas" are the audience. These were established by the compiler because of the Buddha’s entrustment.
I command that this statement be placed at the beginning of all sutras; there is no need for further elaboration.
That which is adorned with various precious flowers upon the summit of the mountain refers to this unsurpassed Summit Dharma, the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, which is the causal ground of all Buddhas.
As for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have come from various Buddha-fields, it is because...
This is shown because herein neither the noble nor the ordinary are established. Regarding "Mahāmati as the leader": this Dharma cannot be reached by the mind or consciousness;
it is permitted that only great wisdom may enter it. From "one's own mind" onwards is the praise of its virtues.

As for the various sentient beings, their various minds and forms, the immeasurable gates of liberation, the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and so forth—such as non-self and so on.
All phenomena are merely objects manifested by one's own mind; yet only those of great wisdom can skillfully understand their meaning and ultimately penetrate them.

Both translations state that the Bhagavān was dwelling on Mount Malaya at the seashore, within the city of Laṅkā, which was occupied by the yakṣa king Puraṇa. This was because the Buddha, for the sake of the sea-dwelling nāgas...
Having taught the Dharma in the royal palace for seven days, he emerged from the great ocean. Raising his eyes, he beheld the city upon the mountain peak and spoke these words:

"In the past, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, taught here the Dharma realized through their own noble wisdom—a realm that is not within the scope of the speculative false views of non-Buddhists, nor the sphere of practice of the two vehicles."
“O Kāśyapa, I shall now likewise reveal this Dharma to King Brahmana.
At that time, the Yakṣa King, hearing the Buddha’s voice through the Buddha’s supernatural power, immediately requested the Buddha, together with his retinue, to return to his city. And so forth.
Both translations include the causal conditions for the Yakṣa King’s inquiry into the Dharma; this sutra omits them.
If the reader synthesizes those other translations with this one, they will immediately perceive the essential purport of this sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Māti, traveled through all the Buddha-fields.

Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse:
The commentary states: This is a separate account of the ritual for the principal disciple (dangji) to behold the Buddha.
Mahāmati is the one who serves as the principal disciple; this unsurpassed Dharma-gate cannot be sustained by anyone other than one of great wisdom.
As for his traveling together with Maitreyī—Maitreyī is also translated here as "Wisdom"—it is as the saying goes: "Those who have attained realization travel together on the path to Nirvāṇa."
The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness; since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is ever like a dream; since wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Knowing that there is no self in persons or phenomena, and that afflictions and their latent tendencies are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
There is no nirvāṇa in anything; there is no Buddha who has attained nirvāṇa, nor is there nirvāṇa within the Buddha.
Far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened, and having abandoned both existence and non-existence—this is the tranquil contemplation of the Muni, which is utterly free from birth.
This is called "non-grasping. It is pure in both this life and future lives. The commentary states:
"This correctly initiates the fundamental purport of the entire sutra. The term *jñeya* (爾燄) is a Sanskrit word;

here it means "the knowable," or alternatively, "the cognitive obscuration" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). "There is no nirvāṇa for all" [is rendered in the Wei translation as] "being free from both existence and non-existence. This is because...
"All" refers to the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). "Nirvāṇa" refers to the non-phenomenal. As for "non-existence," both of these are empty. Thus, the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra* says:
"Where there is contention, one speaks of birth and death; where there is no contention, one speaks of nirvāṇa.
Both birth and death and nirvāṇa are ultimately unobtainable. Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "There is no Buddha apart from nirvāṇa; there is no nirvāṇa apart from the Buddha."

[The term] *pan* [refers to] being far removed from both the perceiver and the perceived; it is the departure from both existence and non-existence. One should know that these two are merely false views of discrimination.

Thus, in the two translations by Paramārtha, it is said that after the Yakṣa King invited the Buddha into the city of Laṅkā and completed his offerings, he questioned the Buddha regarding two dharmas, saying: "The Tathāgata constantly teaches that even the Dharma itself should be abandoned."
How much more so regarding what is not the Dharma? How can one abandon these two kinds of dharmas?
What is the Dharma? What is not the Dharma? The World-Honored One replied: "The distinguishing characteristics of the Dharma and non-Dharma are conceptual constructions of ordinary beings;
they are not the vision of noble wisdom. ... Furthermore, what is the Dharma? It refers to the two vehicles and all outsiders..."

The Path consists of the abandonment of false conceptualization. To claim that things such as "existence" or "reality" are the causes of all phenomena—such dharmas as these should be relinquished and abandoned;
one should not engage in conceptualization or grasp at their signs therein. Upon seeing the dharma-nature of one's own mind, there is no further attachment.
For all practitioners of meditation who observe with the correct contemplation of *vipaśyanā*, this is called "abandoning all phenomena. What is it that is not a phenomenon?
It is that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, without characteristics, and eternally free from conceptual discrimination; such is the vision of reality as it is.
Whether existence or non-existence, such objective realms do not arise at all; this is called abandoning what is contrary to the Dharma. Liu Qi said:
"To see things as they truly are is called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). To see otherwise is called wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
To engage in conceptual discrimination is called dualistic grasping (*dvaya-grāha*); all these are false and deceptive, and one cannot attain quiescence (*śānti*). Quiescence is called..."
One mind. That which is called "one mind" is the Tathāgatagarbha. The Tathāgatagarbha is the realm of wisdom entered within one's own body;

therein one attains the samādhi of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, this verse praises the Buddha as being free from both existence and non-existence.
How profound! The dualistic views of existence and non-existence are thorns to the Dharmakāya. What is called "the noble wisdom of self-awakening" (svapratyātma-āryajñāna)...
There is nothing else. It is simply knowing this and being detached from this; there is no further real dharma to be attained.
This is the ultimate essence of this sutra. If a practitioner knows this, they may be said to practice non-practice and realize non-realization.

If even for a single thought-moment one has not forgotten practice or realization, one falls back into this [duality] once more; how much more so if one takes conceptual discrimination, speech, or written words as attainment?
If an observer contemplates in this manner, they may be said to recognize the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena.

This is precisely what Mahāmati asks below regarding the two dharmas of existence and non-existence; the World-Honored One merely causes him to distance himself from and relinquish these. Therefore, all things are "not.
If one truly distances oneself from and relinquishes these, what else could it be but the self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*)? Thus, the subsequent verses flow [from this point].
Zhi says: "If one contemplates the Buddha in this way, he is tranquil and free from arising and ceasing. Realśikṣa says:

"Such a person, in this and future lives, will be free from attachment and have nothing to grasp. Thus, the essential purport of the entire sūtra does not extend beyond the Yakṣa King’s single question and these verses of praise by Mahāmati.
The introductory section above is concluded. Below follows the main body of the teaching, which is divided into two parts.
First, directly pointing to the one mind as true suchness (tathatā) to reveal that the three realms are mind-only, which has two sub-sections. △ First, questioning by means of several phrases.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha with verses, spoke his own name:
"I am named Mahāmati; I have attained mastery in the Mahāyāna. Now, by means of one hundred and eight points, I respectfully inquire of the Most Honored One."
The Knower of the World, having heard those spoken verses, surveyed the entire assembly and addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying:
"O sons of the Buddha, you may now all ask whatever you desire; I shall explain for you the realm of self-awakening."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and questioned him with verses.

It is recorded that Mahāmati first questioned the Buddha regarding the one hundred and eight meanings; this was because he relied upon the single mind (ekacitta) to explain the transformations of the five [dharmas].
This question concerns the phenomena of the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two forms of selflessness, and the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment.
The traditional interpretation that the one hundred and eight phrases represent the antidotes to the one hundred and eight afflictions misses the fundamental intent.
Nevertheless, "one mind" is the Buddha’s teaching on the mind; what is called "quiescent extinction" is named the one mind. Originally, there were no ten realms, nor were there form or mind.

The characteristics of the primary and secondary [realms] are merely delusions that constitute birth and death; thus, the one mind transforms into the three realms. When awakened to, they constitute nirvana;
thus, the three realms are transmuted into the one mind. Yet, birth and death are phenomena (*dharma*), while nirvana is the absence of phenomena (*adharma*).
Both of these arise from the false views and conceptual discriminations of ignorant beings. And this quiescence...

Within the mind of cessation, these things do not originally exist. Thus, that which Great Wisdom (Mahāmati) inquires about consists of the various differentiated characteristics of the ten realms—the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, delusion and awakening, cause and effect, and mental activities.

In essence, these do not transcend the categories of ordinary beings and sages, or existence and non-existence; they are merely phenomena of dualistic opposition arising from discriminative false views. Little do they realize this quiescence...
The extinction of the single mind cuts off all dualistic oppositions. Thus, the verse says: "Whether 'existence' or 'non-existence,' both of these are entirely abandoned.
As the Buddha was about to point directly to the ultimate source of the mind, he addressed each [objection] in turn and refuted it, saying, "It is not so.

This is precisely the departure from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is the exit from the paths of ordinary beings and sages, and is solely the noble wisdom of self-awakening belonging to the Buddhas.
Regarding these realms: even those of great wisdom cannot avoid falling into numerical categories, let alone others.

I, the fool, maintain that these one hundred and eight phrases are all established based on the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms, arising as fourfold views regarding the phenomena of existence.
That is to say, ordinary people and non-Buddhists view the three realms as truly existent phenomena; this constitutes the "existence" phrase. Second...

Riding upon the [Buddha’s] vision, one sees that the three realms are non-existent; this constitutes the "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" phrase. The Bodhisattva sees that the three realms are both the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti);
this constitutes the "both-existence-and-non-existence" phrase. Yet, turning back to point toward the Buddha’s vision, one sees that the three realms are neither ultimate nor conventional;

this constitutes the "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" phrase. This is what is clarified by the True Teaching (saddharma). In contrast, the external paths (tīrthika) establish their own tenets based on existence and non-existence.
The four propositions—identity, difference, both, and neither, as well as permanence and impermanence—each involve the adherence to a single view.

None of these transcend the conceptual constructions and deliberations of ordinary worldly sentiment. Thus, there are eight views regarding what is false or correct, and a hundred objects of perception.
Therefore, Paramārtha said: "The one hundred and eight views are all, within the state of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), nothing but slander.
If one is already free from the four propositions, then the hundred negations are naturally dispelled. What afflictions, then, could there be to abandon? And what Buddha-way could there be to grasp?"
Therefore, a monk asked the Great Master Mazu: "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, I pray that you will directly point out the meaning of the West for me.
The Master said, "I have a headache today and cannot explain it for you. Go ask Zhizang."
How is mindfulness purified? How does mindfulness increase? How is delusion perceived? How does delusion increase?
(The Tang translation reads: "How do conceptual constructions arise? How is conceptual construction purified? How does confusion arise? How is confusion purified?")
The Record states: This question is based generally upon the two paths of delusion and enlightenment within the arising and ceasing of the one mind.
Yet, while Mahāmati requested a hundred and eight points of meaning, he opened his discourse by immediately asking about these four phrases.

This is because the true source of the one mind is equal for both sages and ordinary beings, being utterly devoid of any marks of distinction; it is only in terms of the division between delusion and enlightenment that the ten realms of existence arise.

[This explains] the various differences in the characteristics and natures of correct causes and effects. However, as we are now about to exhaustively investigate the source of the ten realms, we first present the perspectives of delusion and enlightenment.
That is to say, when one is deluded regarding the One Mind, correct wisdom is inverted into discursive thought (*vikalpa*), and suchness (*tathatā*) is inverted into names and forms;
this is the growth of delusive thoughts. When one awakens to the One Mind, discursive thought itself becomes perfected wisdom.

Wisdom. The names and marks are precisely suchness (*tathatā*). This pure mindfulness perceives delusion and confusion. Nevertheless, these are all matters pertaining to the extremes of delusion and awakening.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Those who follow the flow of transmigration falsely perceive birth and death; those who loathe the flow of transmigration falsely perceive nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Mahāmati asks based on the gate of arising and ceasing, wherein delusion and awakening stand in opposition. For this reason, he first [uses] purity...
Contemplating the mindfulness of impurity, one perceives the delusions of views and the non-perception of the origin of delusions.

Subsequently, all that is pointed out consists of the various distinctions between delusion and awakening within this context. The Buddha answers based solely upon the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the single mind;
therefore, at the beginning of the citation of the question below, he immediately declares: "Whether arising or not arising, nirvāṇa and the characteristic of emptiness, as well as saṃsāra..."
"Self-nature" refers to the two phrases "this very arising is non-arising" and "nirvāṇa is the mark of emptiness," which collectively summarize the entirety of Mahāmati’s questions.
The two characters "transmigration" (*pravṛtti*) utterly refute Mahāmati’s views; that is to say, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are merely the deluded, weary, inverted marks of flowers in the sky.
Therefore, these are all subsumed under transmigration, and by means of the three [marks of] lack of self-nature...
These words fully reveal the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and utterly destroy the doubts of Mahāmati.

Yet, although the World-Honored One answers in this way, it still remains within the realm of arising and ceasing and of dualistic opposition. Only in the source of the mind of quiescent extinction is there none of this at all.
Therefore, having completed the restatement of the question, he directly points it out, saying: "It is not so. This is precisely what is meant by: "Even dharmas should be relinquished..."
How much more so regarding what is not the Dharma? Whether it be existence or non-existence, one must be free from both.
The student who realizes this may be permitted to enter the Laṅkāvatāra.
Why are there lands, emanations, and marks, as well as various non-Buddhists? What is the sequence of being without sensation? Why is it called "without sensation"?
Why is one called a "Son of the Buddha"? To what place does liberation lead? Who is bound, and who is liberated?
The Record states: This is a general inquiry as to why the names and characteristics of the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—and the manifestations of the lands exist.
"Lands and transformative appearances" refers generally to two types of lands: the Land of Real Reward Adornment and the Land of Common Dwelling for Mundane and Holy Beings.

Because these are discussed in terms of names and characteristics, the Land of Tranquil Light is not mentioned. "Various non-Buddhists" refers generally to ordinary beings within the three realms. "Without receiving succession" means...
Next, "non-reception" (anupādāna) generally refers to those in training (śaikṣa) of the three vehicles; "no reception" generally refers to those beyond training (aśaikṣa) of the three vehicles;
"Son of the Buddha" specifically refers to Bodhisattvas. "Liberation" refers to nirvāṇa, while "bondage" refers to saṃsāra.
Who binds one to saṃsāra? Who liberates one into nirvāṇa? Indeed, nirvāṇa here refers to the realm of the Buddhas.
What are the realms of dhyāna? How do the three vehicles arise? I pray that you will explain these for me. From what do dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) arise?
What is the agent and what is the action? Why are there various differing explanations? How does growth occur? [The Tang translation says: "How do all existences arise?

What are the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)? What is the cessation of perception (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha)? By what cause does one awaken from meditative absorption? What...

What is it that performs the functions of arising, moving forward, and sustaining the body? How does manifestation arise through discrimination? How are the various stages (bhūmi) produced? The commentary states:

These fifteen phrases separately inquire into the distinct characteristics of the nine realms. The first three phrases inquire into the causal conditions by which the practices of the Three Vehicles exist.
The [next] phrase concerns dependent origination and inquires about the True Dharma. The final two phrases inquire about the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).
From what cause does wrong view arise? What are the two phrases regarding its increase? [These two questions concern] why the causes and effects of the three realms exist.
Regarding the two phrases on the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*): Why do those of the Hīnayāna delight in dwelling in tranquil concentration and not rejoice in preaching the Dharma?
For what reason do they awaken from that concentration and descend? [These four phrases concern] why Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas delight in preaching.

The Dharma brings forth beings. How does it give rise to the various stages (*bhūmi*) in a single phrase? Question: For what reason are the names and designations of the Bodhisattva stages established?
Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence (*tribhava*)? What is their body and where is it located? To what place do they go when reborn? And who is the most excellent son?

By what cause does one attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and mastery in samādhi? What is the nature of the mind in samādhi? O Most Victorious One, please explain this to me. The commentary states:
These eight lines specifically inquire about the characteristics of the practice of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*).

That is to say: for what purpose do those of the Three Vehicles depart from the triple world (*traidhātuka*)? Having departed from the triple world, where are they reborn? Having cast off this body, what kind of body do they receive?
Ultimately, where does he abide? Why is he called a bodhisattva and a disciple of the Buddha?
Furthermore, for what reason do you speak of the matters of supernatural powers and samādhi? I do not know what the characteristics of the mind in samādhi are like.
What is called the "storehouse" (ālaya)? What are the mind (manas) and consciousness (vijñāna)? What are birth and cessation? What is the returning after having seen? What is the lineage (gotra)?
What is the non-lineage and the measure of mind (cittamātra)? How are the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) established, as well as the meaning of non-self (anātman)?
How is it that there are no sentient beings? How is it that they are spoken of according to worldly convention? How is it that the views of annihilationism and eternalism do not arise?
How is it that the Buddhas and the non-Buddhists are not contradictory in their characteristics? And how will the various diverse schools appear in future ages?
The commentary states: These sixteen phrases constitute a general inquiry into how the nature of the mind is one, yet why the perceptions of sentient beings are so diverse.
The first four phrases ask: If the Tathāgatagarbha-mind is one, why is it also called the Ālayavijñāna?
Why is it also called the Manas and the Manovijñāna? Furthermore, why is it described as the deluded perception of arising and ceasing, and also described as non-arising?
"Extinction of mind. Having seen this, one returns. The Wei translation says "severing what is seen," and the Tang translation says "retreating from all views";

both convey the meaning of non-arising and non-extinction. Next are the two phrases concerning the spiritual lineage (*gotra*): they mean that both the noble ones and ordinary beings equally receive this mind.
How is it, then, that it is further said that those of the three vehicles possess the spiritual lineage, while non-Buddhists and *icchantikas* do not? Yet [the text] speaks of that mind...

Are they all limited? Next are the three phrases on establishing characteristics: since the mind is already without characteristics, by what cause are the characteristics of self, person, sentient being, and life established?
And for what reason is it further said that there are no such characteristics of self, person, sentient being, or life?
Next are the five phrases on conventional discourse: why do ordinary beings and non-Buddhists within the triple world give rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism?
This refers to what is called "worldly discourse," namely the two views of annihilationism and eternalism held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
How, then, can these two views be prevented from arising? How can sentient beings and Buddhas be equal and non-dual? Regarding the next two lines concerning the future world:
since the Buddha has already provided the teachings, how is it that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples again give rise to various differences?
It is seen. How is it empty? What is its cause? How does it perish moment by moment? How is it born from the womb? Why is the world immovable?
For what reason is it like a phantom, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, a mirage in the heat, and the moon reflected in water?
For what reason are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the limbs of awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) taught? What causes the disorder of the lands?

How does one come to hold views regarding existence? The commentary states: These twelve phrases collectively inquire about the world and sentient beings—all phenomena characterized by marks—and ask why there is the difference between arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing, permanence and impermanence, and the true and the false. First...
Two lines. The Wei translation states: "What is called emptiness? What is meant by mindfulness not abiding?

This is likely a question regarding how the dependent world-realm comes to have its formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness; it specifically mentions emptiness and destruction to encompass formation and duration.
"What is the phrase 'birth from the womb'? Question: Why do sentient beings, who are the primary retribution [of karma], undergo the flux of birth and death?
It is because by mentioning "birth," "death" is implicitly included. "What is the phrase 'the world is immovable'?
This meaning encompasses the aforementioned world and sentient beings, wherein one currently perceives change and impermanence; why then is it said to be eternally abiding and immovable?
The term "all worlds" (*sarvaloka*) refers to the two worlds of sentient beings and insentient things. For what reason are the following four lines said to be "like an illusion or a dream"?
The Chinese translation states: "How is it that all worlds are like illusions and also like dreams? The intended meaning is:
since the aforementioned sentient beings, worlds, and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) currently exist as real entities, for what purpose is it said that they are like illusions and so forth?

[The answer is: "Indeed. For what reason are the latter two lines of the *bodhyaṅga* [verse] spoken? That is to say: how does one awaken to the fact that all worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) above are unreal?
That which is eternally abiding in its own essence (*svabhāva*) constitutes right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Thus, the *bodhyaṅga* and *bodhi* collectively refer to right knowledge.
How are the two lines regarding the disorder of the land [to be understood]? That is to say: how does one perceive those aforementioned worldly phenomena as real?

That which possesses impermanence is called the view of existence; it is a delusion, for it is the incessant arising and ceasing of phenomena. This "view of existence" is precisely false conceptualization and discrimination.
[The above section] generally inquires into names, characteristics, false conceptualization, and correct wisdom. [The following section] inquires into suchness (*tathatā*).
How is it that there is neither arising nor ceasing? How is the world like a flower in the sky? How does one awaken to the world? How is it explained as being beyond words?
Who is it that is free from false conceptualization? Why is the analogy of space used?
The commentary states: These six phrases inquire about *tathatā* (suchness). The Tang translation says: "How is the world known? How is one free from words?

How is it like a flower in the sky—neither arising nor ceasing? The intended meaning is: how does one awaken to the fact that all phenomena of arising and ceasing within that world are, in their very essence, *tathatā*, free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of names and designations? Just as...
Flowers in the sky neither arise nor cease; they are far removed from deluded thought and discrimination, being just like empty space. This is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).

[This concludes] the preceding general inquiry into the characteristics of the arising of the five dharmas and their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). [The following] is the inquiry into their differentiated characteristics.

How many kinds are there of reality as it is? How many perfections and mental states? By what cause are the stages transcended? Who reaches the state of non-apprehension? What are the two kinds of selflessness?
How is the flame purified? How many kinds of knowledge are there? How many are the precepts and the natures of sentient beings?
The Record states: These eight phrases inquire solely about the distinct characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) and *samyagjñāna* (right wisdom).

The first four phrases concern the fact that true suchness (*bhūtatathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are one; yet, how can there be differences in cultivation and realization, such as sudden versus gradual?

Therefore, it asks: "How many kinds are there of suchness? and "How many *pāramitās* are there? This refers to the distinctions in causal practice. "The various stages" refers to the levels of attainment.

"Stages," "transcending," and "surpassing" refer to the cause by which one attains the sudden leap across all stages (*bhūmi*). "Reaching the state of non-apprehension" asks about the ultimate stage of Buddhahood.
What are the [following] four lines? They ask about the distinctions of correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*). The two types of self are the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
*jñeyāvaraṇa* (the obscuration of the knowable) is what is meant here. Yaśomitra says: "How is the knowable purified? It is because of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

Purifying that which is known is achieved through right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) alone, which destroys the two obstacles. Since right wisdom is singular, how can there be the bestowing of teachings according to the faculties [of beings]?
If so, how many kinds of wisdom are there? The root-natures of sentient beings are not uniform; how many kinds of instruction and precept are there?
From the initial question up to this point, the discussion has generally relied upon the true source of the one mind, categorized by way of delusion and awakening.

The distinctions among the five dharmas—namely, the conceptualization of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*), correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*)—are established through their mutual relation in order to reveal the characteristics of the causes and effects of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) regarding both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*). This intends to show that these do not depart from the one mind;

therefore, they are ultimately subsumed back into suchness and correct wisdom. From the passage beginning with "Who afterwards gives rise to the various natures of jewels" until the end of the inquiry:

It merely concerns the various distinctions— such as names, characteristics, deluded thoughts, dependent origination, the noble and the ordinary, the primary and the secondary, the great and the small,
and the defiled and the pure— of all phenomena, as well as the manifold differences in mental inclinations, desires, voices, and physical forms.
Who gives rise to the various natures of jewels, such as mani-gems and pearls? Who gives rise to all languages and the diverse natures of sentient beings?
By whom are the fields of knowledge and the arts revealed?
The commentary states: "The fields of knowledge and arts" refers to the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*). The academic traditions of the Western Regions take these as their standard;
thus, there is the *Pañcavidyā-śāstra*. The first is the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), which explains glosses and word definitions, and clarifies categories and distinctions.

The second is the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), which refers to technical skills, mechanical devices, and the calculation of yin-yang and calendrical cycles. The third is the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), which refers to...

The first is the science of mantras (vidyā-mantra), which restrains and wards off malevolent influences; the second is the science of medicine (cikitsā-vidyā), comprising pharmacology and the application of acupuncture and moxibustion; the fourth is the science of logic (hetu-vidyā), which refers to the investigation of what is correct and what is erroneous, and the critical examination of what is spurious;
the fifth is the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā), which refers to the thorough elucidation of the subtle principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles. The first three are external arts.

Regarding the latter two internal teachings: how many kinds of *gāthā* are there? How many kinds of long verses and short phrases constitute them? What is meant by "treatise" (*śāstra*)? (The Wei translation asks:

How many kinds of birth are there?

The commentary states: This question concerns the different configurations and forms in which Buddha-fields are established. These are explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World" (*Gandavyūha*), hence the concluding remark:
"Thus, there are immeasurable [arrays]," such as the *Indra-jāla*. *Indra* here means "Emperor" (*Ti*).

They interpenetrate one another, their radiating lights meshing together;
the worlds are likewise. What is the transformation Buddha? What is the retribution-born Buddha? What is the *tathatā* (suchness) Buddha? What is the wisdom Buddha?

The commentary states: This question asks how it is that the Buddha is the one true reality, yet there are differences in name and meaning. He who universally responds to sentient beings according to their capacities is the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha).
He who recompenses their past causes is the *saṃbhogakāya* (Reward Buddha). His essential nature, which is non-dual, is the *tathatā-buddha* (Tathatā Buddha).
The manifestation and illumination of original enlightenment constitutes the Wisdom Buddha. This wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Although there are four names and meanings, they belong exclusively to the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Why is it that one does not attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? For what reason is enlightenment attained by becoming free from desire at the Akaniṣṭha heaven?
The response states: This question asks why, since the Buddha has manifested his body and shared in the afflictions of common people, he did not achieve Buddhahood in the desire realm.
He attained enlightenment at the place of detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
After the Sugata entered parinirvāṇa, who shall uphold the True Dharma? For how long will the Teacher of Gods remain? And for how long will the True Dharma abide?
(In both translations, "Teacher of Gods" is rendered as "World-Honored One.")
The commentary states: This question concerns the duration for which the Dharma will abide, as well as who shall uphold the True Dharma after its extinction.
To "uphold the True Dharma" refers precisely to the transmission of the Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye.
Regarding the *siddhāntas* and views, how many kinds are there for each? As for the divisions of the *vinaya* for bhikṣus, what are they and by what causes and conditions?
The commentary states: "This question concerns the distinctions among dharmas. *Siddhānta* is a term where Chinese and Sanskrit are presented together.

*Sid* means "universal" (*paryanta*); *dānta* (here rendered as *tán*) means "bestowal" (*dāna*). It refers to the Buddha universally bestowing four dharmas upon sentient beings; therefore, it is called *siddhānta*. There are four [types].

The Dharma consists of: the worldly (loka), the person (pudgala), the remedial (pratipakṣa), and the ultimate meaning (paramārtha). These are explained in detail as they appear in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*;
that is, the various types of capacities for which [the teachings] are intended and the various ways in which they are perceived. Vinaya is here translated as "Discipline" (lǜ).
Regarding the section on Bhikṣus, this refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts of a Bhikṣu. Question: What is Vinaya? For what purpose, moreover, [is it established]?
Now, regarding the classification of bhikṣus:

for those sons of the Most Victorious Ones, as well as the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, by what cause do they undergo a hundred transformations, and how is it that they are free from a hundred perceptions?
"What is mundane supernormal power? What is supramundane? And what are the seven stages? I pray that you will explain these for us. The response states:
"This question concerns the causes by which the dharmas of the persons of the three vehicles differ. The Tang translation says:
"All sons of the Buddhas, as well as the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—how do they transform their basis? How do they attain mundane supernormal powers? What is...
One attains transcendence. Furthermore, for what reason does the mind abide within the seventh stage? According to this, one knows that the two phrases regarding the "hundred transformations" mean:
by what cause can a Bodhisattva of the first stage manifest bodies throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds and attain a hundred kinds of samādhi?
"Non-reception" (anupādāna) is precisely samādhi. Regarding "worldly penetration," it refers to the holy person of the fifth stage; by what cause [does this occur]?

Yet one is able to penetrate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to engage with the mundane world for the benefit of living beings. At the seventh stage, the "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṅgama*), it is called "transcending the world.
How many kinds of Saṃgha are there? What constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha? What is the science of medicine (*cikitsā-śāstra*)? And what are its causes and conditions?
The commentary states: This question concerns the distinctions among the Saṃgha and the fact that the teachings suited to various capacities are not uniform.
"Destruction of the Saṃgha" refers to those who do not possess the precepts. As for "medical treatises," this does not refer to worldly medical arts;

rather, it means that the Buddha, as the King of Physicians for the three realms, establishes his teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, just as one administers medicine according to the specific ailment. Therefore, they are called "medical treatises."

The Treatise states that the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* mentions both old and new physicians, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* contains the parable of the physician. The Tang translation describes this as "extensively explaining medical treatises.
Thus, it should be understood that this refers to the Buddha-dharma itself. From the passage beginning with "How is it that for the sake of transformation...
up to this point, there is a general inquiry as to why distinctions exist within the Three Jewels.
For what reason did the Great Muni proclaim these words: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I"?
This question arises because the preceding statement explained that the Buddha has four names with different meanings;
why then does he further state that multiple Buddhas such as Kāśyapa and others are himself? Furthermore, this [statement] is not distinct from the former.

Why do you speak of annihilation and permanence, as well as self and non-self? Why do you not at all times proclaim the true meaning, yet instead analyze and teach the "mind-only" (cittamātra) for the sake of sentient beings?

The commentary states: Because this concerns the distinctions among the aforementioned dharmas, it further inquires into the differences between the heterodox and the orthodox, and between the provisional and the real.
"Annihilationism, eternalism, and self" constitute the heterodox tenets of external paths; "non-self" constitutes the orthodox Dharma of the Buddha;
and "mind-only" refers to the dharmas of deluded conceptualization and mental enumeration. The intent is to ask: why are annihilationism, eternalism, and self described as heterodox?
Question: For what reason do you say that "non-self" (anātman) is the True Dharma?
Since non-self is indeed the reality, why do you not always speak of this true reality, yet instead speak to sentient beings of unreal phenomena such as the deluded mind and mental factors?
For what reason are there the *Naranārīvana* (Forest of Men and Women) and the *Harītakāmālaka*?
The record states that this question concerns the diversity of forest trees and their fruits. The *Naranārīvana* is also called the *Śītavana* (Cemetery Forest);
its fruits resemble the forms of men and women, and when ripe, they are beautiful and lustrous in color, yet before long they fall to the ground.
It resembles a corpse; its stench and filth are unbearable. Many disciples of the Buddha rely on this forest to practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Mahāmati asked: "For what reason does this forest exist? [The answer was: "It is named after two fruits: *harītakī* and *āmalaka*."
All of these may serve as medicine. *Harītakī*: formerly called *hálìlè*, now called *hálìdàjī*;
this means "brought from heaven. *Āmalaka*: its fruit is like a jujube; the intent is that both are fruits of trees.
For what reason do they appear in the forms of men and women?
Mount Kīla, the Cakravāḍa mountains, Vajra, and all the other mountains are adorned with immeasurable jewels and filled with sages and gandharvas.

The commentary states: This question asks why the assembly of the eight classes of beings does not dwell among humans or in the heavens, but instead resides within the Iron Ring Mountains and the seven golden mountains.
The Tang translation says: "Sages, gandharvas, and all others completely fill [the space]."
"What are the causes and conditions for all these? I pray that the Buddha will explain them to me. This concludes the questions posed by Mahāmati;
excluding the word "and" (*ca*), the terms used—such as "how," "for what cause," "for what reason," "what kind," and "who"—constitute the essential meaning.
There are more than one hundred and thirty such phrases, yet their significance does not exceed ten realms and four gates. However, regarding that which the World-Honored One...

Although the transmission of the sutra is not yet complete, the text of these four fascicles elucidates the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the eight [consciousnesses].
The principles regarding the names, meanings, and the opening and closing of the four gates of the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*) are hereby sufficient.

As for those who contemplate this, they should realize them for themselves by applying their understanding to the text. What follows is the World-Honored One’s response by restating the question; first he restates it, and then he answers it. △ First:
The Unsurpassed Knower of the World, having heard those verses spoken concerning the various gateways to the perfections of the Mahāyāna—the foremost essence of the Buddhas’ minds—exclaimed:

The record states: "This refers to the introductory arrangement and the words of the Buddha’s approval.

The preceding verse—translated into Chinese as 'At that time, the World-Honored One heard his request for the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna, the supreme Dharma-gate of the hearts of all Buddhas'—concerns the questions posed by Mahāmati regarding the characteristics of the distinctions between the ten realms of the environment and its inhabitants. This is precisely [the subject].
Ordinary beings of the three vehicles and those of external paths falsely perceive and discriminate realms of existence.
Indeed, Mahāmati, it is because they give rise to doubt regarding these matters that they do not understand from what cause such phenomena arise; thus they pose this question.
Why, then, did the compilers immediately designate this as the subtle Buddha-mind and the supreme Dharma-gate? It is because of the *Vajra*... [text truncated]
The *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "All worthies and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma; how much more so the world of sentient beings?
All conceptual discriminations are merely discriminations of one's own mind. If discrimination does not arise..."
The very essence of this is precisely what is called the "sacred wisdom of self-awakening" of all Buddhas.

Therefore, that which you have asked regarding the sacred and the mundane, the environment and its inhabitants, the false and the correct, cause and effect, and the eternally abiding self-nature—this is itself the subtle and wondrous Buddha-mind; it cannot be seen except by the clear vision of wisdom.
For what reason is this so? Therefore, it is set aside for discussion.
Birth and non-birth, nirvāṇa, emptiness, and the momentary—all these lead to the realization that there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

The commentary states: "This is the Blessed One’s summary response to the meaning of Mahāmati’s questions; that is to say, although the questions were of many kinds, they do not go beyond [this point]."

This means that both the mundane and supramundane realms are all phenomena of deluded vision characterized by the flux of arising and ceasing, each and every one of them.
"In the ultimate sense, they are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This concludes the summary restatement of the meaning, having provided a silent response.
The significance has already been seen in the preceding notes; hereafter, each point is merely a general restatement of Mahāmati’s questions.
However, some of the previous questions were either abbreviated or omitted, and the World-Honored One has supplemented them all. This is intended to mutually elucidate one another.
However, because his words were spoken spontaneously, they appear inconsistent and disparate; yet their underlying meaning is complete.

[This applies to] the Buddha’s various *pāramitās*, the Buddha’s sons (*jinaputra*), the *śrāvakas*, the *pratyekabuddhas*, the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and those who practice in the formless realms.
