Second is the perfuming of views and craving that arises from it, because it has the function of accomplishing the *discriminative consciousness of phenomena* (*pravṛttivijñāna*). The aforementioned inconceivable perfuming is the root.
This is fundamental perfuming; it is the perfuming of views and craving.
Mahāmati, if those various unreal and false states that veil the true consciousness are extinguished, then all sense-faculties and consciousnesses are extinguished;
this is called the extinction of marks (*nimitta-nirodha*).
The commentary states: This explains the "extinction of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*) among the two preceding types of extinction. "To cover" means "to turn back.

That is to say, when the flow [of consciousness] is turned back and becomes entirely unified, one suddenly accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Then, all defilements vanish instantly, and the sense organs, objects, consciousness, and mind fall away simultaneously;
this is called the extinction of characteristics. The Tang translation says: "The *ālayavijñāna* is false discrimination."
When various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished, all sense-faculties and consciousnesses are extinguished; this is called the extinction of characteristics (*nimitta-nirodha*).

However, while arising proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, extinction first involves the flow-continuum (*pravṛtti*); now, as it ceases, it proceeds from the coarse to the subtle, and thus the characteristics are extinguished first.
Mahāmati, as for the cessation of continuity: when the cause of continuity ceases, then continuity ceases. When that from which it proceeds and its objective referent cease, then continuity ceases.
Mahāmati, why is this? Because these are its supports. The support refers to the habitual perfuming of beginningless false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The objective referent refers to the false discrimination regarding the objects of consciousness, such as the manifestations of one's own mind.
The commentary states: This explains the cessation of the "flowing stream" among the two previously mentioned types of cessation. "Continuity" (*saṃtati*) is synonymous with "flowing stream.

This means that while the eight consciousnesses are like a profound, still abyss fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing, they nevertheless form seeds through the wind of the first seven consciousnesses stirring habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, it exists. However, since this arising and ceasing arises because of the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), when that which it depends upon ceases, then this continuous flow (*pravāha*) of succession ceases of its own accord.
Thus it is said: "When the cause of the succession ceases, the succession ceases. This explains the cessation of the flow within the context of the arising and ceasing of the flow.
It refers to the cessation of that from which [the flow] proceeds and the cessation of its objective referent (*ālambana*).
As for "the cessation of the continuity," this explains the cessation of the flow within the arising and ceasing of the characteristics.

That is to say, the seventh evolving consciousness (*vijñāna*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; yet, due to the internal perfuming of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of fundamental, beginningless ignorance, and because the external wind of the six sense-objects stirs the ocean of the mind, the internal and external factors fan each other, and thus the waves of the seven consciousnesses arise.
Waves! Now, when the ignorance from which the internal gate arises has ceased, the winds of external objects subside, and the essence of the mind becomes a deep, still pool;
the waves naturally subside, and the seven consciousnesses are immediately unborn.
That the continuity ceases as soon as that which it follows and that which it takes as its object have ceased is because all moving phenomena depend upon ignorance.
Because it arises, it is explained as "that upon which it depends. This "dependence" refers to the perfuming of beginningless deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

This beginningless deluded conceptualization is, in fact, fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*); it is what is currently termed the "seven consciousnesses" (*saptavijñāna*) in the continuity of rebirth (*pratisandhi*).

Therefore, because these [defilements] constantly bind the eight consciousnesses, they cannot be transformed into wisdom. "Object" (*ālambana*) refers to the objects of the consciousnesses, such as the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of one's own mind;
"delusive conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) refers to the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

These are originally the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-aspect) manifested by the eight consciousnesses, which in turn become the objects perceived by the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-aspect) of the eight consciousnesses. This is precisely what is elucidated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* regarding the cause.
This refers to the conditions upon which [consciousness] depends. Now, it is said that when the cause of continuity is extinguished, the deluded attachment to arising and ceasing vanishes;

when the objects of perception are extinguished, the sense organs and their sensory data naturally dissolve. In this way, the ignorance of the eight consciousnesses is precisely the equal, suchness-like, and non-arising/non-ceasing right gnosis.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "Only because delusion is extinguished do the mental characteristics follow in extinction. As for what arose previously:
They arise in mutual dependence; now, they also cease in mutual dependence. This concludes the section above, which establishes the true *vijñapti-mātra* through the analysis of dharmas.
Below follows the section that uses analogies to decisively refute the two views.
Mahāmati, it is like a lump of clay and its atoms; they are neither different nor non-different. The same applies to gold and its ornaments.
Mahāmati, if the lump of clay were different from its atoms, it would not be composed of them; yet in reality it is so composed, therefore they are not different.
If they were non-different, then there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its atoms.

The commentary states: This uses a metaphor to establish the preceding "True Consciousness-Only" argument (*tathatā-vijñaptimātra-pramāṇa*), intending to preemptively refute the heterodox attachments to the dual views of identity-and-difference and annihilation-and-permanence.

The phrase "for example, a lump of clay and its subtle atoms" precisely demonstrates that the unarisen and undying [nature] and the arisen and ceasing [phenomena] combine to form the eighth *ālayavijñāna*, thereby revealing that the true and the delusive are not identical.
It is not different. This is shown because the characteristics of the noble and the ordinary are likewise so. Therefore, it is further fashioned with gold ornaments.
Since those non-Buddhists postulate a distinct cause, this analogy is presented in order to refute their view.

In this way, Mahāmati, if the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) were different in their true nature, the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.

The commentary states: "This correctly explains that they are not different, thereby refuting the false attachment of non-Buddhists who hold that there is a separate dharma acting as the cause of production.
The meaning is that if the first seven [consciousnesses] were different from the eighth, then the eighth consciousness would not be the [cause] of the first seven.
It acts as the cause for the arising [of phenomena]. Since it now serves as the cause for those [phenomena], we know they are not different.

Because the true aspects of the first seven consciousnesses are originally the essence of the clarity and brightness of the eighth consciousness, and the true aspect of the eighth consciousness is originally True Suchness (Tathatā), the two translations by the Wei and Tang dynasties mention only "transforming consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), without the two characters for "true aspect. However, those [texts] merely refer to the eight...

Consciousness is not different [from its nature]. However, this translation adds the two characters "true appearance" (zhēnxiàng) to clarify that the true and the delusory are not different, thereby revealing that the delusory is itself the true.
This meaning is self-sufficient. "True appearance" refers to the very essence of the eight consciousnesses, which is original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*) or *tathatā*.
When it is now said that the *ālayavijñāna* is the cause, it means that the *tathāgatagarbha* is not merely the cause of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
It is also the cause for *nirvāṇa*. As the later text states: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it is able to universally produce all realms of rebirth.

If [the storehouse consciousness] were not distinct [from the evolving consciousnesses], then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease; yet its own true nature does not, in fact, cease. This is...

Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not that the consciousness of self-characteristics ceases; rather, it is only the consciousness of karmic activity that ceases. Mahāmati, if the consciousness of self-characteristics were to cease, then the ālayavijñāna would cease.
Mahāmati, if the ālayavijñāna were to cease, that would be no different from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists.
The Record states: This explanation is not uniform, as it is intended to refute the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

It means that if the eight consciousnesses were one, then when the first seven ceased, the eighth—the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—would also have to cease. If the storehouse consciousness were to cease, what would witness non-arising?
Thus, the eight consciousnesses merely extinguish the false and illusory habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of conceptual proliferation; this is what is meant by "extinction."
In reality, the self-nature of the eight consciousnesses is fundamentally the true suchness of original enlightenment and is truly not subject to extinction.

Therefore, it is said that "it is not the true characteristic of the self that the consciousnesses extinguish. The Treatise states: "That which is called 'extinction' refers only to the extinction of mental phenomena, not the extinction of the substance of the mind. It further states:

It is solely because ignorance ceases that the mental characteristics cease accordingly; it is not that the consciousness of mind ceases. This "characteristic of karma" refers precisely to the characteristic of karma among the aforementioned three characteristics;
it is a general designation for the delusions and karma of ignorance, termed simply the "characteristic of karma. The intended meaning is that which is to be extinguished.
However, these are merely the delusions of karma and the habitual tendencies of falsehood; how could the true nature (*tathatā*) ever be extinguished? Therefore, the Sūtra further states:
"If the true nature were to be extinguished, the ālayavijñāna would be extinguished. If the ālayavijñāna were to be extinguished, it would not differ from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists.
The Tang translation says: "The true nature of consciousness is not extinguished; only its karmic aspect is extinguished. If the true..."

Regarding the cessation of characteristics: the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) should cease. If the storehouse consciousness were to cease, it would not differ from the nihilistic doctrine of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The above section concludes the preliminary refutation of the two views. The following section correctly distinguishes and examines the heterodox schools.
Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists propound such a doctrine as this: they claim that when the grasping of objects ceases, the flow of consciousness also ceases;
and if all flows were to cease, the beginningless flow would have to be severed.

The commentary states: This is derived from the nihilistic doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and is thus intended to distinguish and refute their heterodox tenets. The Tang translation says:
"Those non-Buddhists speak thus: 'When the consciousness that takes up the continuity of objective realms ceases, then the beginningless, continuous consciousness ceases.
Now, the consciousness that takes up the continuity of objective realms refers precisely to the first six consciousnesses, along with the coarse aspects of the seventh consciousness."
The "streaming-forth" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the essential nature of the eight consciousnesses as well as the subtle characteristics of the seventh consciousness.
Those non-Buddhists, seeing only the cessation of the coarse characteristics of the preceding sixth and seventh consciousnesses, claim that all eight consciousnesses are extinguished.

This is why they are said to sever the Buddha-nature; therefore, the Buddha refutes them, saying: "If the streaming-forth of consciousness were to cease, then the beginningless streaming-forth would have to be severed."
This directly reverses the preceding text to clarify that while the *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal aspect) of karma ceases, its *tattva* (true nature) does not cease.

This non-ceasing is what the "Precious Mirror" refers to as the "eternally flowing true nature. As for why the non-Buddhists claim that all eight consciousnesses cease simultaneously, it is because they do not understand that the eighth *ālayavijñāna* is the cause of arising;
they mistakenly believe there is some other distinct dharma that serves as the cause of arising.
Because it is the cause of birth, the Buddha subsequently sets forth their calculation, saying:
"Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists speak of a causal flow of birth; they claim that visual consciousness does not arise from the conjunction of form and light, but rather from another cause.
Mahāmati, as for that cause, they speak of it as the Primal Matter (prakṛti), the Person (puruṣa), the Sovereign Lord (īśvara), or Time (kāla)."
If [it were] like a subtle atom (*paramāṇu*), the commentary states: "This arises from the false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists regarding the cause of birth. The Tang translation says:

"Those various non-Buddhists claim that the continuous consciousness arises from a creator; they do not say that visual consciousness arises from the conjunction of conditions such as form and light."
[They] arise [thus], because they assert only an agent (*kartṛ*) as the cause of arising. What is this agent?
That which they imagine—the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), the *puruṣa* (spirit), *īśvara* (the Lord), time, and atoms—is posited as the capable agent.

This is precisely because these non-Buddhists do not understand that consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is the cause for the arising of all phenomena; instead, apart from consciousness, they separately establish the *pradhāna* and so forth as the cause of arising.

The origin [of views] refers to what are called "divergent causes" (*hetu-vipratipatti*). Although there are many types of speculative theories held by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Regions, they generally do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are seven such positions refuted therein, yet among them, the Blessed One specifically addresses only five here.
The seven mentioned in the treatise are: first, the Sāṃkhya teachers, who postulate twenty-five principles (*tattva*), including the twenty-five *avyakta-tattvas*.

That is to say, starting from the Self (puruṣa), there is the primary principle of primordial darkness (tamas). From primordial darkness arises intellect (buddhi); from intellect arises the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
from the ego-sense arise the five objects of the senses; from the five objects arise the five great elements (mahābhūta); and from the five great elements arise the eleven faculties.
These constitute twenty-five principles, with the Self as the supreme nature (prakṛti). Within this, that which is supreme and subtle is precisely that Self.

I am also [refuting] the two Vaiśeṣika masters who reckon the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) as the causes for the arising of all things—namely, substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), activity (*karman*), greatness (*mahat*), inherence (*samavāya*), and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
They falsely claim that these six all possess a real nature (*svabhāva*), and that all phenomena arise from these six categories.
Furthermore, within the category of substance, they cling to the existence of nine dharmas: earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth.
Time, direction, and harmony; furthermore, they calculate that the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is composed of atoms (paramāṇu), and thus they maintain that atoms are eternal and indestructible.
Herein, "time" and "atoms" refer precisely to those postulated by the Vaiśeṣika school. These are the three types of externalists.

As for the calculation regarding Maheśvara: they reckon that his essence is truly pervasive and eternal, and is capable of producing all phenomena; herein, "sovereignty" refers precisely to what they conceive him to be.

Among the four types of existence, there are seven kinds of non-Buddhists who reckon that the seven dharmas—Mahābrahmā, Time, Space, Primordial Limit (*ādi*), Spontaneity (*svabhāva*), Space (*ākāśa*), and the Self (*ātman*)—are eternally abiding, substantially existent, and possess all functional capacities to produce all phenomena. And this...
The "Middle Person" is none other than that Great Brahmā; it refers to the Great Brahmā Heaven being able to give birth to all things.
Furthermore, this "time" is also the "time" among the nine dharmas of the *satya-vākya* (true statements).

Regarding the two schools of phonologists (*śabda-śāstrin*), one holds that sound is eternal, capable of serving as a definitive measure to express and signify all phenomena, while the other holds that it arises depending on conditions. These are: first, arising in dependence on conditions; second, manifesting in dependence on conditions. That is to say:
Sound is eternal; it is definitively capable of expressing and signifying all phenomena.

Seventh, there are the Lokāyatas (Materialists), who reckon that the four great elements are substantial and eternal, and are able to produce sentient beings; they claim that atoms are substantial and eternal, and are able to produce coarse matter.

Furthermore, regarding the atoms within this context, those who calculate them as *paramāṇus* (extreme subtles) follow these seven types. As for the five types indicated by the Blessed One, they lack only two;
these are supplemented by the two natures (*svabhāva*) of cause and condition from the Grammarians (*śabdavādin*).

Although the categories of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are numerous, the entities they grasp do not exceed four types: namely, the fixed [nature], such as the Sāṃkhya school’s *prakṛti*; the one [nature]; the many [natures]; and the unmanifest.

Regarding these [theories], such as the Vaiśeṣika school and others, they maintain that things are definitively distinct. Others, such as the Ahrīka heretics, hold that things are both one and different.
And others, such as the Ājīvika heretics, hold that things are neither one nor different.

All of these fail to comprehend the true principle of Consciousness-Only—that the true and the false are neither identical nor different—and thus falsely cling to them as being definitively one or definitively different, engaging in such deceptive sophistry.

This discussion addresses the horizontal arising of the two views of eternalism and nihilism. However, within this context, only two types of false views—namely, identity and difference—are singled out;
the Buddha has already refuted these by demonstrating that a lump of clay and its atoms are neither identical nor different.
Furthermore, both of these are forms of nihilistic views. Why? If one were to claim they are definitely identical, then when the seven consciousnesses cease, [the self would likewise cease].

If one holds that the eight consciousnesses also perish along with it, one falls into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). If one asserts that they are definitely distinct, then when the continuous consciousness perishes, there would be a separate, different cause;
having established this different cause, it would follow that [the result] is without a cause, which is likewise the view of nihilism.

However, regarding the five factors such as the "supreme essence" (*śreṣṭhatva*) and so forth mentioned by the World-Honored One, these constitute the view of nihilism in this context, whereas in the treatises they are all considered adherents of the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Why is this? It is because that which they grasp as "eternal" is precisely what constitutes "annihilation" within this [system].
Why so? Because non-Buddhists do not understand the true principle of the eternal nature of Consciousness-Only;

they claim that all eight consciousnesses are subject to annihilation, while simultaneously grasping at other phenomena as being truly eternal. Thus, since they already grasp those other phenomena as eternal, their original...
To perceive true permanence and instead treat it as annihilation—this is why they grasp at it as permanent and thus fall into this nihilism.
This is precisely taking the impermanent to be permanent and the permanent to be impermanent; it is a truly inverted view.
This meaning is profound and abstruse; those who understand it are rare.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). They are: the self-nature of accumulation, the self-nature of essence, the self-nature of characteristics, the self-nature of the great elements, the self-nature of cause, the self-nature of conditions, and the self-nature of accomplishment.
The Record states: "This is from the sectarian treatises of false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). The Wei translation says: 'Non-Buddhists have seven kinds of self-nature.

Observing these words 'non-Buddhist' (waidao), it follows from what was previously stated—that non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena do not arise from consciousness, but rather from other causes—and they falsely assert that the five [categories], such as 'supreme' and 'subtle,' are real and eternal."

They are able to give rise to all phenomena. Viewed from this perspective, the first five refer to the phenomena that are grasped as objects, whereas these seven types of self-nature (*svabhāva*) indicate that there are seven categories within the teachings established by them.

However, these seven are all merely false conceptualizations (*parikalpita*) of a self-nature existing separately from consciousness. Explaining the meaning according to consciousness, [the first] is the nature of collection (*saṃgraha-svabhāva*).
"Accumulation" (saṃghāta) means gathering together. This refers to the twenty-five principles established by the Sāṃkhya teachers. The treatise states:
"However, the principles such as 'Greatness' (mahat) are composed of three things. It further states:

"The various principles such as 'Greatness' are composed of many things, like an army or a forest," because they maintain that the five great elements and the eleven faculties arise from the triad of the initial intellect (*buddhi*), the mind (*manas*), and the five sense objects (*viṣaya*).

Because it arises from an accumulation, it is called the "cloud-like nature" (*megha-svabhāva*). As for "nature as intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-svabhāva*), this refers to that which establishes *pradhāna* (the Primal Nature) as its intrinsic nature.
Regarding "characteristic as intrinsic nature" (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*), "characteristic" refers to matter (*rūpa*) characterized by resistance;

this refers to the six categories (*padārtha*) established by the Vaiśeṣika masters: substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*). And...
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and all material phenomena characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*) serve as the causes for arising.

Regarding the "intrinsic nature of the great elements" (*mahābhūta-svabhāva*), this refers to the eternal great elements established by the Lokāyata school, which are capable of producing all phenomena; this is precisely what was stated previously regarding how subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) can produce coarse matter.
As for the "intrinsic nature of the cause" (*hetu-svabhāva*) and the "intrinsic nature of the condition" (*pratyaya-svabhāva*), these two refer to the [two types of] conditions.

According to the proponents of the *śabdavāda* (phonetic theorists), there are two [types of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): first, that which arises dependent on conditions, taking sound itself as the cause for the arising of phenomena;

because this takes sound alone as the cause, it is called "the intrinsic nature of the causal essence" (*hetu-svabhāva*). Second, that which is manifested dependent on conditions, taking the conditions that produce sound as the cause;
because of this, it is called "the intrinsic nature of the conditional essence" (*pratyaya-svabhāva*). As for "the intrinsic nature of the established essence" (*siddha-svabhāva*), this refers to...

This refers to the "synthetic" category among the six categories. Because they maintain that all phenomena are formed through the combination [of elements], it is said that their nature is established through self-nature (*svabhāva*).
These seven kinds of self-nature do not, in total, exceed four positions: namely, arising from self, arising from another, arising from both, and arising without cause.
Now, the self-nature of the cause is "arising from self," while the self-nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is the condition...

Arising from self-nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely arising from another. Arising from the nature of accumulation, the nature of characteristics, and the nature of completion is precisely arising from both.
Arising from mere nature is precisely causeless arising. In sum, these do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;
they are all false conceptualizations and perverse attachments, and are not my ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, the subsequent text states: "I have seven kinds [of arising]."

The Ultimate Truth. [Section marker] The preceding section has completed the refutation of heterodox schools. The following section demonstrates the seven kinds of noble meanings to distinguish them from false views.
This is divided into two parts. △ First, the demonstration of the correct meaning.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). They are: the realm of the mind (*citta-viṣaya*), the realm of discernment (*prajñā-viṣaya*), the realm of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*), the realm of vision (*darśana-viṣaya*), the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stages of the sons [of the Buddha], and the realm of the Tathāgata’s own self-attainment.
Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-citta*) regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
By means of this mind of the ultimate reality regarding intrinsic nature, the Tathāgata accomplishes the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending-superior dharmas.
Through the noble eye of wisdom, he enters into and establishes the system of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) according to how they are established.
He stood and did not engage in debate with the heterodox views of the non-Buddhists.

He declared: "This emerges from the authoritative measure of the Tathāgata’s true teaching; it takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as its thesis, and is thus not the same as the heterodox treatises of evil views.
The Wei translation states: "I have seven kinds of ultimate truths, etc."; that is to say, these seven of mine...
These various realms are the nature, self-nature, and ultimate reality-mind (*paramārtha-citta*) of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
By means of this nature, self-nature, and ultimate reality-mind, they accomplish the supreme mundane and supramundane dharmas of the Tathāgatas.
This is the noble eye of wisdom that enters into specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

The "Suchness" (*tathatā*) established is truly suchness; it is called "conformity," meaning that what I have established is an establishment in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), and does not share in the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

"Entry" (*praveśa*) means realization. "Specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*) refers to the True Suchness of the One Mind. "Common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) refers to the causal conditions of the eight consciousnesses.
This means that I have already realized and entered the state of Mind-Only and Consciousness-Only, and thereby establish the mundane and the supramundane.

This is the supreme dharma-gate in the world. It does not compare with the false establishment of external paths (tīrthikas), who posit a heterodox cause as the fundamental source of arising phenomena;
therefore, it is said that it does not share in the evil views of external paths. △ Next, its errors are refuted.
Mahāmati, how is it that [the teachings of] non-Buddhists share in evil views? It is because they perceive the false imaginings of their own domain;
they do not realize that what appears is the manifestation of their own minds, and thus they lack penetration.
The commentary states: This passage cites and explains the reason for the evil views of the non-Buddhists mentioned above.
The Buddha taught that his seven kinds of ultimate reality (paramārtha) are what is observed by the noble eye of wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*) through the power of true knowledge and vision.

In contrast, those evil views of the non-Buddhists are merely what is seen within the realms of their own deluded conceptualizations (*vikalpa*); this is because they do not realize that these are [their own] projections.

Because they do not understand the extent to which these are manifestations of the mind’s false conceptualization, they thus give rise to seven kinds of false attachments regarding annihilation and permanence,
regarding identity and difference, and fail to realize their lack of ultimate reality.
"Mahāmati, foolish ordinary persons formulate a dualistic theory regarding existence and non-existence, and regarding self-nature and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The commentary states: 'This summarizes the formation of the evil views of externalists, who formulate a dualistic theory within the context of the ultimate truth.
The Wei translation says: 'All foolish ordinary persons, [seeing that] there is no substantial entity, [erroneously] speak of it as the ultimate truth.'"
Second, the theory of dual views (*dvaitavāda*). This refers to the false establishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) due to failing to realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Because one follows the deluded and inverted false views of ignorance, one propounds the theory of dual views within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This concludes the preceding section on how various non-Buddhists have maintained such theories; it generally covers the two [extremes] of non-Buddhists: identity and difference, and annihilationism and eternalism.

Seeing is not true. Having established the valid cognition of True Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), [the author] subsequently harshly rebuked the two views of the non-Buddhists, asserting that both their cause and effect are unreal.
Because they do not realize that all is manifested by the mind alone, they falsely cling to existence and non-existence, thereby falling into the conceptual proliferation of nihilism.
Thereafter, he fully demonstrates the gate of the contemplation of Mind-Only, intending for practitioners to rely upon it.
With a mind that is neither born nor extinguished, one contemplates by thoroughly realizing that all phenomena are merely mind, like an illusory realm;

thus, one will certainly attain the two fruits of the eternally abiding transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). The above exposition on the seven kinds of noble meanings to distinguish them from false views is concluded.
Below follows the third section: the correct discernment of false causes to demonstrate the true cause. △ First, the discernment of false causes.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the cessation of the suffering of the three realms of existence arising from false discrimination, the cessation of the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma,
and how the illusory objects manifested by one's own mind are seen according to their appearance.
The commentary states: This follows upon the preceding point that non-Buddhists fail to realize that the realm of phenomena is merely mind-like and illusory;
they falsely construct dualistic views and thus cannot extinguish the suffering of the three realms of existence.
Now, in order to show practitioners the dharma-gate of "mind-only as illusion" as the path of correct cultivation, this is first revealed here. The Tang translation says: "If one understands..."

Objects are like illusions, manifested by one's own mind; thus, one extinguishes the suffering of the three realms of existence born of deluded thought, as well as the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma.
The "suffering of the three realms of existence" refers to the fruits of suffering within the triple world. All these fruits of suffering exist solely in dependence upon deluded thought.
Therefore, it is said that "deluded thoughts are the suffering of the three realms of existence. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which initiates karma.
Attachment (*tṛṣṇā*) is craving and lust, which moistens birth through ignorance. These two constitute the karmic causes for the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms;
they are what is termed "delusion" (*moha*). Karmic conditions are those formed from these two types of deluded afflictions: ignorance and attachment.
The karma of birth and death binds one so that one cannot attain liberation; therefore, it is called "karmic conditions.

Yet, the reason these karmic causes and their resulting suffering cannot be extinguished is entirely due to failing to realize that all objective realms are manifestations of the mind alone, and instead following the flow of deluded perceptions.
Furthermore, although those non-Buddhists possess the desire to escape suffering, [they remain bound].

Furthermore, they do not know the essential method for escaping suffering, nor do they understand what it is they cultivate; they practice specifically based on the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
This is precisely because they seek to abandon suffering while using suffering as their means, relying upon these various views and becoming deeply attached to illusory phenomena.
Because the causal ground is thus not true, the resulting fruit is circuitous; therefore, they waste their diligent efforts in vain, achieving no realization whatsoever. Such is the Buddha’s intent.

This means that if practitioners realize that objects are like illusions, appearing solely as manifestations of the mind, then the causes and effects of the triple world are extinguished right at that moment.
Therefore, from this point down to the passage "falsely claiming to be omniscient," there is a general refutation of the two views of the non-Buddhists as being untrue.
From the passage "Furthermore, as for other śramaṇas... down to "one's own *siddhānta* is excellent," [the text continues].
"You should train yourself thus. This universally demonstrates the gateway of the contemplation of Mind-only.

Mahāmati, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who wish to manifest a cause and effect that is either seedless or with seeds, or who maintain that things and time abide, or that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases arise and abide through conditions, or who say that once arisen they cease; [these are all to be understood as such].
The Record states: This refers to the heterodox schools (tīrthikas) who, based on the two views of existence and non-existence, falsely establish a distinct cause. The Tang translation says:
They falsely conceptualize that which is neither existent nor non-existent, manifesting various phenomena outside of cause and effect that abide according to time;

or they conceptualize that the aggregates, elements, and bases arise and abide dependent on conditions, and once having existed, they immediately perish. This specifically points to the heterodox schools' reliance on the view of annihilationism (*uccheda*).

They constantly hold two views: outside the true causal measure (*pramāṇa*) of *vijñapti-mātra*, they falsely establish alternative causes, asserting that "existence" is the cause of arising and "non-existence" is the cause of non-arising.
Taking this existence and non-existence as the cause of arising, they manifest all worldly activities as the fruit of arising.
Thus it is said: "They desire to manifest the causality of the seedless and the seeded," yet they do not realize that all worldly [phenomena]...
The realms (*dhātu*) are sustained by false conceptualization; furthermore, one falsely calculates that they abide in dependence upon time.
Or again, one calculates that the aggregates (*skandha*), realms, and bases (*āyatana*) abide in dependence on conditions such as the four great elements, time, and direction.

Or again, one falsely calculates that all phenomena of the aggregates, realms, and so forth, having once existed, then perish and are never born again. These are all views of nihilistic annihilation; none are true causes.
Therefore, the following section refutes them. Now, there are two kinds of non-Buddhists (tīrthika): the internal and the external.
The internal refers to those śramaṇas who give rise to false conceptualizations based upon the Buddha-dharma; the external refers to the brāhmaṇas.
Mahāmati, whether it be continuity, entities, birth, existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, or the truths—these are the doctrines of nihilism and annihilationism.
Why is this? Because they cannot be apprehended in the present, and because the beginning [of things] is not within one's scope of perception.
Mahāmati, it is like a broken jar that no longer performs the function of a jar, or like a scorched seed [that no longer sprouts].
It performs the function of producing a sprout.
The commentary states: "This is a general refutation of non-Buddhists whose causal ground is not true; therefore, their resulting fruit becomes one of destruction.

The term "they" refers to the two types of non-Buddhists mentioned above, internal and external. That is to say, those non-Buddhists, by relying on the two views of existence and non-existence, do not...
Because they realize that [all things] are mind-only, the causes and effects they establish all result in nihilism and continuity—meaning the continuity of birth and death.
This is because they do not understand the linking of rebirth (*pratisandhi*), and thus falsely point to the primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*) or the four great elements as the cause of birth.
This is just like the practice here in this land where people claim that human beings are produced by the two qi of yin and yang and the five elements. If such were the case...
"Whether arising or existing. The Tang translation says: "Whether activity, or arising and ceasing, or all existents (*bhava*). "Activity" refers to whatever is performed;
"arising and ceasing" refers to birth and death; "all existents" refers to the various phenomena of the three realms mentioned above.
Because their arising has distinct causes while their death results in annihilation, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) ultimately do not exist.
Regarding permanence: if it refers to nirvāṇa, they point to the five aggregates as being nirvāṇa;

if it refers to the path, they consider such acts as pulling out one's hair, fumigating the nose, lying on thorns, smearing oneself with ashes, or observing the precepts of cattle and dogs to be the means for escaping suffering. Regarding karma: this refers to the cause of karma;
they falsely conceive of things such as "perfection" and "eternity" to be the cause of karma. Regarding fruit: they falsely take such states as annihilation to be the true fruit. If...
[They] maintain that the primordial darkness (*ādikṣaya*) is the ultimate truth (*satya*).
Such as these, all fail to understand *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and thus completely fall into the doctrine of nihilism and annihilationism. Why is it considered nihilistic?
Because they hold that all that is presently manifest is not real, and because they do not perceive the beginning [of existence]. The Tang translation says: "Because they do not see the root."

Because they are severed from the fundamental reality of mind-only and consciousness-only, such various conceptual proliferations (prapañca) are ultimately of no benefit. They are like a broken jar, which cannot perform the function of a jar;

or like a scorched sprout or a rotten seed, which cannot perform the function of a sprout. The broken jar is a metaphor for the absence of fruit; the scorched sprout is a metaphor for the absence of cause.
The activities of the non-Buddhists are also like this.

Thus, Mahāmati, if the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases has been extinguished, is being extinguished, or will be extinguished, it is seen as the false conceptualization of one's own mind.
Because there is no cause, there is no successive arising for them.
The commentary states: This combines the two preceding metaphors to prove the non-Buddhist claim that there is neither cause nor effect.

That is to say, those non-Buddhists claim that these phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases do not arise from the karmic formations performed in previous lives, but rather from some other cause.

This implies that what was previously established has been utterly annihilated. Furthermore, they claim that if the suffering experienced in the present life is exhausted, one will no longer receive retribution in future lives. This implies that the present, too, has become annihilated. If [this were so] in the present...
Once extinguished, it would then be permanently severed and annihilated for all future time. Such views are all merely what is perceived through one's own deluded imaginings;
they falsely posit diverse causes when, in truth, there are no causes at all. If there is no cause, there can be no fruit;
therefore, there can be no sequential continuity of arising.

Mahāmati, if it were further claimed that consciousness—whether without seeds or with seeds—is produced by the conjunction of three conditions, then tortoises would produce hair and sand would yield oil;
your own tenet would be destroyed, contradicting the definitive meaning. Such faults exist in the doctrine of "with seeds" and "without seeds."
All activities performed would be entirely empty and devoid of meaning.

The commentary states: "This explains the shifting arguments of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). The Buddha’s intention was that he feared those non-Buddhists, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra), would immediately shift their arguments, claiming:
'I [the non-Buddhist] say that the aggregates, elements, and bases arise from both existing and non-existing seeds, together with consciousness.'"

It arises from the conjunction of three conditions; how could it be without cause? Nevertheless, although the non-Buddhists speak of consciousness, they ultimately falsely speculate on the two views of existence and non-existence, and take the *ātman* as the sovereign. Therefore, the Buddha cites their position to instruct them, saying:

"If you further claim that existence, non-existence, and consciousness arise through the conjunction of three conditions, then by such logic, hair should grow upon a tortoise, and [oil should be extracted from] sand."

It would follow that oil could be produced [from sand], yet such a principle does not exist. A tortoise originally has no hair; this is the absence of a cause (*ahetu*). Sand is not the source of oil;

this is the absence of an effect (*aphala*). If you speak in this manner, your own tenet is destroyed; it becomes nothing but causeless and effectless, resulting in total annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
This contradicts the definitive and true principles of our Mahāyāna. Thereupon, he rebuked him, saying: "Existence and non-existence..."

The second [view] entails the fault of such annihilationism. Since its basis does not exist, all performed activities are entirely empty and meaningless—*tāṅ* (唐) translates this as "entirely empty and useless.
However, "performed activities" refers to matters such as the ascetic practices (*duḥkha-caryā*) and teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
"Empty" (*kōng*) means "in vain" (*wang*). This refutes their reliance on false views for practice, which leads them to undergo suffering in vain.
It is laborious and ultimately yields no benefit. Mahāmati,
those non-Buddhists who claim that things arise from the conjunction of three conditions describe their methods of practice, the specific characteristics of cause and effect,
and the nature of seeds— whether manifest or unmanifest— existing in the past, future, and present, which have been handed down as established principles since time immemorial.
The stage of conceptualization (*vikalpa-bhūmi*) revolves; one perceives one's own past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and speaks thus.
The commentary states: "This explains the meaning that all activities performed above are entirely empty and of no benefit.

*Upāya* (translated as *āgama* in the Wei version and *jiaoli* [teaching and principle] in the Tang version) refers to the doctrines and methods of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*). That is to say, those non-Buddhists...

Those who falsely conceptualize three conditions and take non-causality as the cause of arising—regarding all undertakings, whether they be teachings, the specific characteristics of cause and effect, or the modes of arising of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases throughout the three times—all such undertakings result in the proliferation of nihilistic discourse;
they are entirely empty and useless. Furthermore, these wrong views, wrong teachings, wrong causes, and wrong effects lead one into a cycle of...
The succession of generations has been one of the blind leading the blind for a long time. Thus it is said: "From the very beginning, the established practice has been handed down.

"Established" (*cheng*) means created; "handed down" (*cheng*) means transmitted and inherited. This refers to the fact that the activities performed by those predecessors have been transmitted as their teaching;
it is not true knowledge and vision, but rather a turning based on the ground of one's own deluded perceptions. "Awakening" (*jue*) here refers to deluded seeing.
Furthermore, due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of their own false views and faults, they speak in this manner, asserting that all such activities are entirely empty and useless.
Now, as for the origins of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) in the Western Regions: the first was Kapila, which means "Yellow-Headed";
he maintained that the effect exists within the cause. Next was Ulūka, which means "Hooting Owl"; he maintained that the cause...

The second [position] holds that there is no fruit within the cause. The third is the *Lekhasava* (Sanskrit for "asceticism" or "austerity"). This school calculates that there is both fruit and no fruit within the cause.
This tradition was transmitted from these non-Buddhist outsiders until the time of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, when there were six great masters;
thus it is said that they have inherited and maintained their established doctrines from the very beginning.
Thus it is, Mahāmati: foolish ordinary people, bitten by evil views, crooked and deluded, lacking wisdom, falsely claim to speak as one who possesses all-knowledge.
It is recorded that these are the teachings of false teachers and false doctrines; they are not merely useless, but conversely become harmful. Yet they—
These false teachers are all deluded ordinary persons who lack correct knowledge and vision;

they are harmed by their own wrong views, being crooked, intoxicated by delusion, and obscured within this state, unable to awaken on their own. Among the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions, each teacher has obtained three kinds of teachings:
first, the teaching of omniscience; second, the teaching of attaining supernatural powers; and third, the teaching of the Vedas. First.
Regarding those who claim omniscience: each gives rise to a single type of view based on their own calculations. Their understanding is sharp and clear, and they apply this view to all phenomena;
thus they are called "non-Buddhist followers of omniscience. In reality, they possess no wisdom, yet they falsely claim to speak with omniscience.
Consequently, from the very beginning, they have maintained a tradition of established doctrines—what is known as "one blind man leading a multitude."
The blind lead one another into the fire pit; this is what must be earnestly cautioned against. Therefore, the subsequent text says:

"A practitioner of the correct path should not associate with the discussions of external paths and evil views. The preceding general heading stated: "The suffering of the three realms of existence is extinguished through deluded thought;
one perceives the illusory objects manifested by one's own mind according to how they appear. This shall now be explained. Prior to this, [the text] has successively refuted external [views].

The path is not caused by false views; both are equally deluded imaginings that serve as the causes of suffering within the three realms of existence. These are, in fact, the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma.

The Buddha’s intention in admonishing practitioners is this: by recognizing those false causes and not falling into false views, one realizes that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone, like illusory states.
Only then can one directly realize the noble wisdom of self-awakening. Therefore, [the text] proceeds below:

This section extensively demonstrates the methods for practicing the illusory-like dharma-gate, enabling practitioners to rely upon them for cultivation so as to extinguish the causes of suffering within the three realms of existence and attain the fruits of the two types of transformation (āśraya-parāvṛtti). From the passage beginning with "If again...

down to the end of the chapter at "one should personally study and practice according to one's own *siddhānta*," there are approximately three hundred and fifty-odd words that collectively clarify and reveal the realization of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*).

The gate of contemplation on the illusion-like nature is difficult to explain according to the literal text; by comparing it with the corresponding sections of the Tang translation, its meaning will become clear of itself.
The preceding eight sections, which correctly distinguish false causes, are now complete. The next chapter specifically demonstrates the true cause.
Mahāmati, as for those other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who provide such predictions:
this distinguishes them from the two aforementioned types of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and specifically points to two types of practitioners of correct cultivation.
Therefore, it is stated that all other things as well—
such as those seen apart from their own nature, including floating clouds, fire-wheels, gandharva-cities, the unborn, illusions, mirages, water-moons, and dreams— are likewise [unreal].
The internal and external mind manifests; these delusions are beginningless fabrications that do not depart from one’s own mind.
The Record states: "This is precisely the method for observing the mind according to the orthodox teaching. The Tang translation says:
"Observe that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, like clouds in the sky, like a whirling firebrand, like a *gandharva* city, like a magical illusion," and so forth.
Blazing flames are like the moon in water, like what is seen in a dream; they do not depart from one's own mind.
Due to beginningless false perceptions, they are grasped as being external. Now, in this context, the two characters "unborn" (wúshēng) appear frequently.
This refers to contemplating all phenomena as lacking intrinsic nature, like floating clouds; contemplating all phenomena as unborn, like illusions; and contemplating all...
Phenomena are manifested solely by the mind, like the events in a dream. Regarding "internal and external mind":

the internal mind refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which contains the seeds of false habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time. These seeds perfume and give rise to the six consciousnesses, which transform into what appears to be external objects;
yet these are not actually external objects. Therefore, it is said that they are manifested by the internal and external mind. This is the cause of beginningless, false conceptualization.

That which is transformed by conditions is like the events in a dream; it is not, in reality, separate from one's own mind. Furthermore, the word "and" (ji) serves to distinguish this from the preceding analogy:
those who practice desire-conduct should directly perceive all objective realms as being merely manifestations of the mind alone, just like a dream.

The causes and conditions of false conceptualization are extinguished; this is the teaching spoken apart from false conceptualization. (The Tang translation says: "Having performed this contemplation, one severs the conditions of discrimination and also leaves behind the names and meanings grasped by the deluded mind.
One contemplates the ālayavijñāna, which is the storehouse of the body that establishes the objects of experience.

The commentary states: "This directly indicates the object of contemplation. 'Discursive thought' refers to the mind of mental-verb-based discrimination (*manojalpa-vikalpa*). 'That which is spoken of' refers to the objects of discrimination.
'Appropriation and establishment' refers to the external vessel-world, namely the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). 'Body' refers to the faculty-body (*indriya-kāya*).
This means that this faculty-body and the vessel-world are based upon the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the eight consciousnesses; yet people do not realize this."
All is manifested by the mind alone, like events in a dream; yet one conversely clings to them as the objects of self, what belongs to the self, and personal enjoyment.

Now, directly observing that the intrinsic nature of the eight consciousnesses is fundamentally pure and originally non-existent, one realizes that the world, the body, and the mind are merely manifestations of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
When one contemplates in this way, all causes and conditions of deluded conceptualization are utterly swept away and extinguished. This is called...
Since the nature of characters is empty, the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind fall away at once; thus it is said they are all "detached.

This refers to investigating apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and seeking apart from the realm of deluded thoughts. However, "contemplation" (guan) is precisely the observing of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

It is that which is observed; therefore, it is said that one "observes the ālayavijñāna of the body as the object of observation. This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. The treatise states:

"When a bodhisattva first generates the mind [of enlightenment], they immediately observe the essence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as the nature of dependent origination consisting of cause and effect."
If one wishes to enter the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), since the nature of consciousness itself lacks substantiality, what is there to be contemplated?

Nevertheless, it takes the conceptual differentiation of mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*) as its object, because all objective spheres have nothing other than names and words as their essence. Since nothing exists prior to [the object] apart from the conceptual differentiation of mental discourse, the following passage directly reveals the fundamental essence:

[The text continues: "If one were to depart from the conceptual differentiation of mental discourse, there would be nothing before [the mind]. Thus, the text below directly demonstrates the essential nature.
Regarding the apprehension of the objects of consciousness: the apprehending mind (*grāhaka*) and the apprehended object (*grāhya*) are not in correspondence.

The commentary states: "This directly points to the essence of the mind; as long as there is subject and object, they are not in correspondence. This refers to the characteristics of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
This refers to "self" and "what belongs to self," which stand in opposition as two distinct characteristics; therefore, they are not in accord.

When one thoroughly realizes that within the objective sphere of consciousness both subject and object are in a state of non-correspondence, one then perceives one's own mind. Thus, the ancient masters said:
"Forget subject and object; extinguish images. This is a singular virtue of this dhyāna, for as soon as one applies the mind, there is immediately non-correspondence.

The realm of non-existence is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing (when the object is empty, the mind is tranquil). One enters into the conceptualization that arises from one's own mind (the Tang translation says:

"there is neither the grasped nor the grasper, nor arising, abiding, or ceasing"; contemplating thus, one dwells constantly without abandoning it; the Wei translation says: "contemplating thus, one observes that one's own mind is what constitutes arising").
The commentary states: "Now, since both mind and objects are empty, yet one again gives rise to sequential entry into discrimination and speaks of 'permanently abiding' or 'arising.
This is precisely what is meant by 'one should abide nowhere while giving rise to the mind. *Above, the accomplishment of the contemplation of the mind was shown.
Below, the attainment of the fruit through the completion of the contemplation is shown.*
Mahāmati, before long those bodhisattvas shall attain the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa through great compassion, skillful means, and the unconditioned means.
Mahāmati, they regard all realms of sentient beings as being entirely like illusions;
without exerting effort regarding causes and conditions, they remain detached from internal and external objects, seeing nothing apart from the mind, and gradually enter the state of signlessness.
The successive entry into the samādhi realms from stage to stage is recorded as follows:

"This reaches the attainment of the Tathāgata’s body," which generally demonstrates the characteristics of attaining the two types of *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) through the perfection of contemplation.

These two fruits refer to: transforming defilement into purity, whereby birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*; and transforming delusion into awakening, whereby afflictions... [are transformed].

Affliction is itself bodhi. This means that for a bodhisattva who practices correctly, if they achieve the contemplation of mind-only, they will before long attain the equality of defilement and purity;
they will then deliver all sentient beings through the effortless practice of great compassion and skillful means.

One observes sentient beings as being like illusions; there is neither the mark of one who crosses over nor the mark of those crossed over. Since they arise from conditions yet have no origination, it is said that one does not exert effort regarding causes and conditions.
Because the mind and its objects are of one suchness, it is said that one is far removed from internal and external realms.

There is only the single true mind; apart from this mind, not even a fragment of a thing can be found. Wisdom and True Suchness (Tathatā) are equal and equal, both free from the grasping subject and the grasped object.

Because one grasps at signs, it is said that "nothing is seen outside the mind. When this contemplation becomes purely refined, one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and first ascends to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
As it gradually increases in clarity, one proceeds from the Second and Third Grounds up to the Eighth Ground.
Therefore, it is said that one enters the state of signlessness in successive stages, gradually ascending through the various grounds and abiding in the realm of samādhi.
Understanding that the three realms are like an illusion, one investigates and discerns them; thus, one shall attain the illusory-like samādhi (māyopama-samādhi).
Having transcended the manifestations of one's own mind as being non-existent, one comes to abide in the Prajñāpāramitā.
The commentary states: This refers to the transition from the eighth stage to the tenth stage, wherein one emerges from the ultimate truth and enters into the conventional.

It means that at the eighth stage, having severed the innate grasping at a self through effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), one realizes the principle of the emptiness of the self; hence it is said that "what is manifested by one's own mind is non-existent.

Nevertheless, one still remains fallen into the emptiness of the self and remains deluded regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); being unable to realize the emptiness of emptiness itself, one is thus unable [to proceed further].
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* establishes three empowerments and seven exhortations to draw them forth and rescue them.
This involves using the contemplation of illusion to observe that the triple world is illusory and unreal, and employing illusory great compassion to deliver illusory sentient beings;

thus it is said that one attains the Illusory Samādhi. Consequently, only at the ninth stage is one able to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, while only at the tenth stage can one [fully accomplish this].

He emanates bodies throughout the ten directions to serve all Buddhas; thus it is said that he "transcends non-existence" and attains the unimpeded *prajñāpāramitā*, for he has severed the innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

If one cannot transcend non-existence, the Chan school calls this "the Dharma-body falling"—referring to those who sit atop a hundred-foot pole. Although they have gained entry, [they have not yet reached the end].
This is not yet the ultimate truth. One must advance further from the top of the hundred-foot pole; only then does one manifest the entire body throughout the great trichiliocosm. Thus it is said:
"Transcending what is manifested by one's own mind and realizing its non-existence, one attains abiding in the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Having abandoned those births and the skillful means previously practiced, through the vajra-like samādhi, one enters the body of the Tathāgata and enters the transformation-body of suchness.
Possessing mastery over supernormal powers, compassion, and skillful means, fully adorned and complete, one enters equally into all buddha-fields and the abodes of non-Buddhists.

The Record states: "These Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment, by means of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), suddenly sever the ignorance of the initial arising-characteristic (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) and suddenly enter Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). That 'arising' refers precisely to the ignorance of the initial arising-characteristic; therefore, the Treatise says:

'When the Bodhisattva stage is exhausted and skillful means are perfected, there is a single thought-moment of correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*). One awakens to the mind's initial arising, yet the mind has no initial characteristic, because it is remote [from such characteristics].'"
Because one is free from subtle conceptualization, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind; the mind is then eternally abiding, which is called ultimate awakening.
Therefore, it is said that one "enters accordingly" the body of the Tathāgata. "Accordingly" (sui) means "immediately" (ji). The Treatise states:

"By means of such great wisdom of skillful means, one eliminates ignorance and perceives the fundamental Dharma-body, which is equal to True Suchness (Tathatā) and pervades all places. Hence, it is said "accordingly."
Entering the body of the Tathāgata, one follows into the transformations of Suchness (*tathatā*). Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable karmic activities and various functions;

hence it is said that his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are sovereign. Endowed with the adornments of compassion, skillful means (*upāya*), and wisdom, the Great Being Avalokiteśvara—through the Vajra-samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, which is like an illusion—achieves realization in a single thought-moment. Suddenly...
Transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one immediately attains a single power of compassion with all Buddhas of the ten directions above,

and shares a common reliance on sorrowful longing with the sentient beings of the six realms below. Therefore, it is said that one enters equally into all Buddha-fields and the abodes of external paths.
"Detached from mind, thought, and consciousness, this bodhisattva gradually transforms his body and attains the body of a Tathāgata.
This record states that it concludes the practice of contemplation; that is to say, the bodhisattva who practices correctly performs the contemplation of "mind-only consciousness."
This is to depart from the spheres of mind, thought, and consciousness; it is precisely this that constitutes the Bodhisattva’s gradual transformation of the body of birth-and-death.
It is the expedient means for attaining the two fruits of the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is the Tathāgata’s own Dharma-body. Therefore it is said:
"The samādhi like an illusion—by a mere snap of the fingers, one transcends the stage of no-more-learning. The Bhagavāns of the ten directions all enter through this single path to Nirvāṇa."
However, regarding this dharma-gate of sudden realization, one directly contemplates *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) and suddenly awakens to one's own mind.

Yet, it is further said that this is "gradual," meaning: "In principle, there must be sudden awakening; through awakening, [delusions] are simultaneously eliminated. In practice, things must be gradually removed;

they are exhausted through successive stages. As Muzhou said: "If a person suddenly awakens to their own mind in a single thought-moment, there still remains the manifestation of what has accumulated from beginningless lifetimes."
The stream of consciousness (*vijñāna-srotas*) produced by karma is gradually purified and eliminated; therefore, it is called "gradual cultivation.

What is referred to as the "streaming consciousness" is the continuous flow of arising and ceasing, which is precisely the seeds of innate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) of both [the cognitive and afflictive] obstructions.

Thus, to be free from mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) and to suddenly awaken to one's own mind, thereby gradually attaining the body of a Tathāgata, refers precisely to the purification of the currently active stream of consciousness.

What was previously stated—that the speaker and the spoken, as well as arising and ceasing, are free from conceptual construction—refers precisely to being free from the sphere of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).
From stage to stage, until one reaches the abandonment of those [notions of] arising and so forth, this is gradual cultivation; there is no cultivation apart from this.

Therefore, when the Gate of the Patriarchs (the Chan school) instructs people, they need only investigate by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and departing from conceptual construction.
Seeking through objective spheres (*viṣaya*). This is why it is so called, Mahāmati.

Therefore, Mahāmati, one who wishes to attain the body that conforms to the Tathāgata should distance themselves from the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) (this refers to distancing oneself from the spheres of false conceptualization).

One should distance themselves from the causes and conditions of the mind, from the skillful means of mental activity, and from the false fabrications of the conceptualizations of arising, abiding, and ceasing (this refers to distancing oneself from mind, intellect, and consciousness). Only...

The mind proceeds directly. One observes the faults of beginningless falsehood (referring here to fundamental ignorance from the outset). The cause of the habitual tendencies of conceptual construction (the "cause" refers to the seeds of the two obstacles within the eight consciousnesses).
One contemplates that the three realms of existence are non-existent (observing that the triple world is fundamentally empty). The Buddha-ground is birthless;

one reaches the noble state of self-realization (by directly observing the birthless, one may reach the noble wisdom of self-realization). With mastery over one's own mind, one reaches the stage of unconditioned practice.

The commentary states: This summarizes the preceding text and directly points to the expedient means of "mind-only. When one is free from the grasping of the two apprehensions [subject and object], the mind becomes sovereign;

there is no need for further expedients of cultivation or development. The Tang translation renders this as "effortless practice" (anābhoga-caryā), which is precisely "unlearned wisdom" (asikṣita-jñāna).
This is spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). A sutra states: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;

yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it. If one is free from deluded thoughts and attachments, then teacherless wisdom and spontaneous wisdom will manifest immediately. Therefore, it is said that one has "arrived."
Like a mani jewel that reflects various colors, it enters the subtle minds of sentient beings and manifests transformation bodies according to their mental capacities.

(This analogy of the mani jewel reiterates the aforementioned entry into the Tathāgata’s body and so forth. The gradual progression through the stages (*bhūmi*) is established in continuous succession. (This teaches the ritual procedures for delivering sentient beings.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself well in the *siddhānta* [the established tenets].
The commentary states: This passage records the benefits of contemplation and earnestly exhorts one to practice and uphold it.

It means that a bodhisattva who is correctly practicing and wishes to swiftly attain the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and realize the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom (*svapratyātmāryajñānagati*) should directly contemplate that the single mind is originally pure and fundamentally unborn.
Apart from this single mind, not even a fragment of a thing can be found. One should contemplate in this manner.
At that time, as one gradually becomes fully matured, one suddenly realizes [the truth] in a single thought-moment;
it is not obtained from without. Thus, the merit of benefiting oneself and others is perfected herein. Therefore, the teaching first introduces the gate of contemplating "mind-only.

This is further summarized and earnestly admonished, exhorting one to practice and uphold it, saying: "This Dharma-gift of mine is most excellent; you should study and cultivate it. The sutra [continues]:
That "the Buddha’s words take the Mind as their essence" refers precisely to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure mind.

This is that which all sentient beings fundamentally possess. However, if one is now deluded and follows defiled conditions, then the characteristics of the three realms of affliction and birth-and-death arise from this. If, on the other hand, one awakens and follows pure conditions, then bodhi...
The two fruits of transformation—the attainment of nirvana—are established based upon this.

Thus, afflictions and bodhi, birth-and-death and nirvana, are all merely manifestations of the shifting states of delusion and awakening, defilement and purity. Therefore, they are all but the illusory, weary, inverted appearances of flowers;
within the Tathāgatagarbha, these things have never existed from the beginning. Hence it is said: "Seeking in the past and future, one is deluded."

One awakens to the fact that birth and death are ultimately unattainable. Yet, when a person can reach the realization that all is fundamentally non-existent, such that the realms manifest in daily life are seen as utterly unattainable, one may be said to have arrived at the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
This is the mind-seal (*citta-mudrā*) transmitted from the Buddhas and Patriarchs above; the subtle methods for attaining realization through one's own effort are fully recorded in this chapter.

As for the point of "consenting" (*kěn*)— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "至其肯" (zhì qí kěn). The term "肯" (kěn) in this context refers to the moment of decisive acceptance or realization, often associated with the "Great Doubt" (*dà yí*) being resolved.*
The essential point lies in the single phrase: "Furthermore, it is apart from the realm of the delusive conceptualization of mind, thought, and consciousness.

Thus, the World-Honored One repeatedly and earnestly exhorted and cautioned in this manner. If students understand this, they may be said not to have failed their own inherent nature, nor to have betrayed the Buddha’s grace.

This concludes the specific demonstration of the True Cause. [End of Section] Above, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only has been briefly clarified to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
The section on causes is concluded. Below, the eight consciousnesses are explained in detail to demonstrate the characteristics of consciousness and wisdom.

Next, the eight consciousnesses are explained in detail to demonstrate the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). This section is divided into two parts. **Part One:

Explaining the Characteristics of the Eight Consciousnesses.** At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, regarding what you have taught concerning the mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), mentation (*manovijñāna*), the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*), and the self-natures (*svabhāva*):

[the Tang translation says, ‘I pray that you will explain for me the five dharmas, the self-natures, the characteristics, and the various wondrous Dharma-gates’]. These are the practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.”
The objective realms perceived by one’s own mind are non-conjunct; this reveals all that is taught. (The Wei translation says:

"It is the place where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practice, for they remain far removed from the conjunction with the objective realms of false views of their own minds, and are thus able to shatter the substance and characteristics of all speech and metaphors. The Tang translation says: "This is the entry into the realm of one's own mind by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, being free from the characteristics of the objects of their practice.

It establishes the true characteristic, the heart of the teachings of all Buddhas. (The Tang translation says: "It accords with the meaning of reality; it is the heart of the Buddha-teachings. For this reason, it is [called] the Land of Laṅkā.
The great Bodhisattvas dwelling on Mount Malaya spoke of the realm of the *dharmakāya*, which is the ocean-like *ālayavijñāna* praised by the Tathāgata (the Wei translation says:
"They spoke of observing the realm of the great ocean waves of the *ālayavijñāna*, for it is the *dharmakāya* taught by the Tathāgata"; the Tang translation says:
"We pray that for the sake of this assembly of Bodhisattvas on the mountain, you will follow the past Buddhas and speak of the realm of the ocean waves of the *ālayavijñāna* and the *dharmakāya*").
The commentary states: This question clarifies the transformation of the single mind (*citta*) in order to explain the detailed teaching that consciousness has eight aspects.
The question asks: "Mahāmati, you previously asked how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses.

The World-Honored One fully answered this, directly demonstrating the contemplation of consciousness as mind-only (*cittamātra-vijñapti*). Thus, the task of transforming the ordinary person into a sage was completed. Mahāmati then...
Furthermore, why does this [text] take mind, consciousness, mentation, the five dharmas, and the three natures as its subject matter? The answer is:

This sutra points directly to the quiescent single mind (*ekacitta*). Yet, this single mind is fundamentally devoid of delusion or enlightenment and does not belong to the category of either sage or ordinary person.
Therefore it is said that the five dharmas and the three self-natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are both discarded.

Because they follow the distinction between delusion and awakening, there is the differentiation between the real and the false. As for the phenomena of transformation, they likewise do not transcend these four dharmas.
Thus, Mahāmati first posed his questions in one hundred and eight statements, to which the World-Honored One replied with the first.
That "all are entirely non-existent" is because, within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), there is no room for exhaustive inquiry.

When Mahāmati subsequently asked how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing there are for the various consciousnesses, this was because such verbal explanations can indeed exist within the gate of birth-and-death (saṃsāra).

Although the World-Honored One had previously shown the contemplation of mind-only and consciousness, briefly clarifying the gates of cultivation and realization, [the interlocutor] had not yet fully attained it.
