The wondrous transformation of the single mind remains unknown as to why the various consciousnesses arise. Therefore, I request that you explain the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the various wondrous dharma-gates.
This is intended to reveal that one may suddenly realize *tathatā* (suchness) within the very process of arising and ceasing. Thus, the Tang translation states:
"I only pray that you will explain the realm of the *dharmakāya*, which is like the ocean waves of the *ālayavijñāna*. Now, regarding the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*manovijñāna*)...
Consciousness. This refers to what was previously stated briefly as three kinds of consciousness; here it is explained extensively as having eight aspects. The five dharmas are:

name (*nāma*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*parikalpa*), correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*). The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are: conceptualization, dependent origination (*paratantra*), and perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
The two forms of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*) refer to the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. What is now called the "subtlety of transformation" is truly...
Based on the single mind of *tathatā*, which is free from names and free from marks, true wisdom shines alone; it is primordially perfected by nature.

When both person and phenomena are forgotten, and both the holy and the ordinary are severed—this is because one is deluded regarding the single mind and [thereby] creates the eight consciousnesses; thus, *tathatā* follows conditions.
Transformations become the realm of names and marks; correct wisdom, in its dependency, turns back into the mind of delusive thought.
Mind and objects stand in opposition, arising through mutual conditioning; person and phenomena are both manifested, while the holy and the ordinary remain far apart.

By awakening to the one mind as the *tathāgatagarbha*, the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms. Names and marks are themselves suchness (*tathatā*); conditioned arising has no inherent nature. Fundamentally...
Spontaneously perfected, both person and phenomena are empty; the holy and the ordinary are equally extinguished.

By realizing the eternal within the very midst of arising and ceasing, it is said that the ocean-waves of the *ālayavijñāna* are the realm of the *dharmakāya*. This is why they constitute the true mark of the heart-mind of all Buddhas.
This is the objective realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening, for it is free from the self-nature of the mind.
This is the realm of the Dharmakāya; therefore, the Wei translation states: "It is because it is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata of the Dharmakāya.

Nevertheless, the distinction between transformation lies solely in arising and non-arising. If one realizes that arising is fundamentally non-arising, then the primordially existing Dharmakāya manifests of itself.
Therefore, below this, the World-Honored One directly [addresses] the cause by which consciousness arises, in its entirety.
The essential purport of the sutras does not generally exceed this. As for the successive and alternating refutations and difficulties intended to shatter the views of externalists:
it is because they do not comprehend that objects are the manifestation of one's own mind that they give rise to false and arbitrary conceptualizations. Thus it is said:
"As long as one has not realized that objects are mind-only, various kinds of discrimination arise; once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises."

If, upon meeting, there is no inherent nature in that which arises through conditions, and that which arises through conditions lacks inherent nature, then the principle of non-arising will become vividly clear to the mind and eyes;
all verbal expressions will then be merely superfluous words. Let the wise contemplate this deeply.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "For four causes and conditions, visual consciousness arises. What are these four? They are:
(1) the failure to realize that what is grasped is a manifestation of one's own mind; (2) attachment to the habit-energy of false appearances from beginningless time;

(3) the intrinsic nature of consciousness itself; and (4) the desire to see various forms and marks. Mahāmati, these are called the four kinds of causes and conditions, like the place where a stream flows."
"The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) gives rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses.
The commentary states: "This explains the cause for the arising of the seven consciousnesses; it precisely reveals the meaning that what is dependently originated lacks intrinsic nature.

Regarding the four conditions, the Chinese translation says: 'Namely, because one is unaware that [objects] are manifestations of one's own mind and thus grasps at them,' and so forth, beginning from time without beginning..."
At that time, one comes to grasp at form due to false habitual tendencies; because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is thus;
and because one delights in seeing various forms and appearances—these are the four causes and conditions. Truly, the mind is fundamentally without arising, yet it arises by reason of objects.
It is through these four kinds of causes and conditions that what is fundamentally unarisen arises. Objects exist and draw forth the mind.
Regarding karmic activity: because one does not realize that all appearances are manifested by mind-only, one falsely gives rise to grasping and attachment;
thus, the mind arises without awakening. Since beginningless time in the past, each has possessed its own category of seeds;

now, as the mind and its objects meet, habitual tendencies internally permeate them, and false discrimination arises. Therefore, that which was originally unarisen arises, for the mind possesses the capacity to cognize objects.
Function: When the conditions of the objective sphere arrive, the mind arises as a matter of natural law (*dharmatā*).

Because it loves the *ālayavijñāna* and delights in the *ālayavijñāna*, taking it as its sovereign, it naturally finds pleasure in seeing the various sensory objects; thus, the mind arises spontaneously.

This is a general statement regarding the manner in which each of the seven consciousnesses arises due to its own respective object. It cites one case as an illustration for the rest; therefore, it speaks of them individually.
With the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; in reality, ignorance is its cause and the objective sphere is its condition.
The eight consciousnesses depend upon one another; thus it is concluded: "Where the water flows, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) gives rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses.

Therefore, the subsequent text says, "like visual consciousness and so forth. A question is raised: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that visual consciousness arises from nine conditions, while auditory consciousness [arises from] only...

"From eight; nose, tongue, and body, three and seven; the latter, three, five, three, and four. Why does this statement say that the first seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) all possess the four conditions?

The answer is: that [previous passage] merely speaks of the number of conditions possessed by the eight consciousnesses, whereas this [passage] describes the manner in which the seven consciousnesses arise.
Therefore, it says: "Where the water flows, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*)."

Mahāmati, just as the visual consciousness arises simultaneously with all the sense organs, atoms, and pores, yet arises sequentially according to its respective objects, so it is with all [consciousnesses].
It is like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and colors, or like a fierce wind blowing across the waters of the great ocean.
The Record states: "This speaks of the simultaneous and gradual arising of the various consciousnesses, demonstrating that their sequence and timing differ. The Tang translation says:

"As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with the others. Regarding the evolving consciousnesses in all sense organs, atoms, pores, eyes, and so forth, they may arise simultaneously, like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and colors; or they may arise gradually, like a [fierce]..."
The wind blows upon the waters of the great ocean; the sense organs (*indriya*) are the pores, and the objects (*viṣaya*) are the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).

When the organs and objects come together, consciousness arises therein. As for the terms "sudden" and "gradual," they refer to the five types of direct-perception consciousness (*pañca-pratyakṣa-vijñāna*) and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Each and every sense organ pervades the entire Dharma-realm; this is called "perfectly accomplished" (*pariniṣpanna*). Therefore, when the eye-organ first perceives a form, at that initial moment no discrimination has yet arisen;
it is simply like a reflection in a mirror, without separate analysis. Thus, a single atom of form manifests universally across all the sense organs.
If this is true for one atom, it is so for every organ. Hence, it is said that [perception] arises instantaneously, just as a mirror reflects images.
As for their characteristics: when one reaches the second moment and turns toward the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to give rise to discrimination, the five sense organs are separated;
the various objects differ according to their respective organs, and their sequence also varies. Therefore, it is said that they arise gradually, like the wind sucking up the seawater.
If the practitioner realizes sudden birth, they will penetrate the principle of non-arising—that all is the manifestation of one’s own mind—as clearly as observing fruit in the palm of one's hand.

External objective conditions act like winds that toss the ocean of the mind, causing the waves of consciousness to flow without interruption. This occurs because of the conjunction of the signs produced by causes, whether they appear different or not different.

Due to the deep-seated attachment to the characteristics of birth from karma, one is unable to comprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and the other [sense objects]; thus, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) arise.

Mahāmati, you should know that that which is simultaneous with those five groups of consciousness—the cognition of the distinctions and divisions of causes—is the cause of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
The commentary states: This describes the manner in which the eight consciousnesses act as mutual causes for one another in their arising.

It means that while the ocean of the mind is clear and deep, it is incessantly tossed by the winds of external objects; thus, the waves of the seven consciousnesses arise in continuous succession without interruption.
This generally clarifies that the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning; yet, because the mind is drawn by objects, the various consciousnesses arise.

This demonstrates that the eight consciousnesses originate due to the cause of ignorance and objective conditions. Regarding the "differences and non-differences" of the characteristics produced by these causes:
This refers to the identity of mind and object (*cittārtha-ekalaksana*), which establishes the meaning of original non-arising. This phrase clarifies the union of mind and object;

they both possess the characteristics of being both different and not different. That which is "different yet not different" is the cause, namely the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, which constitutes the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).

This refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect). Since the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are collectively subsumed under the *darśana-bhāga*, they differ [from the eighth consciousness] in that each of the eight consciousnesses now cognizes its own respective object.

Yet, because there is only one ultimate, pure reality (*ekam tattvam*), they do not differ. Regarding the difference and non-difference of objects: the cause is the *avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa* (the mark of ignorance and karma);

the "produced mark" (*kṛta-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the transformed *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). This is because the six sense-objects and the four great elements are collectively subsumed under the *nimitta-bhāga*. Now...

They are different because they correspond individually to the various sense faculties; they are not different because their source is originally a single essence. Regarding the unity and difference of the mind and its objects:

the cause is the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, while the resulting characteristics are the deluded mind and deluded objects. They are different because the mind and objects stand in opposition to one another;
they are not different because they are manifested solely by the mind, being originally the one true mind. This is the combined characteristic of karma and birth.
The term "and so forth" (etc. is translated in the Tang version as "the characteristics of karma and birth. This means that those external objects originally manifest only from the mind;

however, due to the non-awakening of ignorance, one fails to realize that they are only mind. Consequently, one gives rise to deep attachment, grasping at and seizing them as a real self and real dharmas.
Thus, the seven consciousnesses exist because of ignorance. From this firm attachment arises the love of self (*ātma-sneha*).
Failing to understand that form and the other sense objects are like illusions and lack substantial reality, one falsely gives rise to craving and attachment.

Thus, the eye encounters them and they become "form," and the ear encounters them and they become "sound," and so forth. Therefore, it is said that because one cannot understand the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and the others, the fivefold body of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) evolves.
This means that the five consciousnesses exist by virtue of the seventh consciousness. Furthermore, as for the five consciousnesses...
At the moment of perceiving an object, the very first thought-moment apprehends the intrinsic nature of that object without being accompanied by names or words and without any deliberative mind;

therefore, it belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). At the same time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises together with the five sensory consciousnesses, either because it discriminates the segmented and differentiated objects of the five sense-fields or because the sixth mental consciousness is produced; thus it is said: "That very [consciousness] is the five consciousnesses."
Co-existent with the body, one should know that the cognition of distinct segments [of objects] due to causal differentiation is the cause of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This, then, is how the six consciousnesses arise based on the five [sensory] consciousnesses; this is what is meant by "the various consciousnesses arising through mutual causality.

Generally speaking, the first seven evolving consciousnesses belong to the discerning function of the eighth consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part). However, the first five [consciousnesses] engage with the five sense-objects.

At that time, in reality, the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously. However, the very first moment, when no discrimination has yet arisen, is designated as the "first five" and also called the "clearly manifest mental consciousness.

But from the second moment onward, when there is discrimination regarding characteristics such as the distinctions between good and evil, it is designated as the "sixth discriminating mental consciousness.
Thus, these five, the eighth, the sixth, and the seventh are distinguished by their degree of intimacy or distance [from the fundamental nature].
This is their dialectical analysis.

That body undergoes transformation; yet it does not form the thought, "I am undergoing a successive causal transformation. Rather, it is the transformation of the attachment to false imaginings manifested by one's own mind.
These various mutually exclusive characteristics arise together, as one discriminates between objects and their segmented distinctions; this is what they call "transformation."
The Record states: "This passage speaks generally of the eight consciousnesses as being produced through conditions and lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

It secretly reveals the meaning that birth is fundamentally non-birth, thereby establishing the aforementioned [point that they are] neither different nor non-different. The intent is that all consciousnesses are originally unborn and fundamentally lack any characteristic of difference;

it is only in relation to their respective apprehension of their own objects that they are said to arise, and thus appear different. The Tang translation says: "However, those various consciousnesses do not..."
This is the thought: "We arise simultaneously, acting as mutual causes for one another.
Regarding the objects manifested within our own minds, we engage in conceptualization and attachment, arising together without distinction. Each perceives its own object;

because they arise dependently without intrinsic nature, they do not form thoughts yet act as mutual causes for one another. Because they arise dependently and lack intrinsic nature, each perceives its own [object]."
Objects are fundamentally without differentiation. If one knows that objects are without differentiation, then the principle of non-arising naturally accords with reality.
As the Great Sūtra says: "For example, like the waters in a river, rushing and flowing together in a torrent; yet the dharmas do not know one another, and each is likewise so.

To "each clearly cognize its own object" refers to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), which are the objects of the first six consciousnesses, as perceived by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
These are the objects of the seven consciousnesses. The root-body, seeds, and the vessel-world are the objects of the eighth consciousness.

For example, when a practitioner enters the meditative absorption of *dhyāna-samādhi*, subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) transform without being perceived, leading them to think, "Consciousness has ceased," and subsequently enter the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In reality, it is not that consciousness ceases before entering the attainment; it is due to these habitual tendencies.
The seeds do not cease; therefore, they are not extinguished. They are extinguished because the conditions for their transformation and appropriation are incomplete.
The commentary states: "The following two sections describe the subtle arising and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses, which cannot be known by those in inferior samādhis.
When practitioners of the Two Vehicles enter dhyāna, they claim to have extinguished consciousness; however, what they extinguish is merely the six consciousnesses, which no longer grasp [objects]."

They take the cessation of objects to be the cessation of consciousness; yet the seeds of habitual tendencies within their storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) have not actually been extinguished.
The Chinese translation states: "When practitioners enter into samādhi, because the power of habit arises subtly, they do not perceive it.
They merely think, 'I have extinguished all consciousnesses and entered samādhi,' yet in reality, they have not extinguished consciousness in entering samādhi."
Because the seeds of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been extinguished, they merely do not grasp at objects; this is what is called the "extinction of consciousness.
Mahāmati, such is the ultimate limit of the subtle storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Except for the Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas who dwell on the stages, no one—including Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of external paths—can reach it by the power of the wisdom obtained through their meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). All [others] are unable to do so.
One cannot fathom or resolve this. The Record states:
"The practitioners of the Two Vehicles and the external paths, because they do not know that the eight consciousnesses are the root of birth and death, practice in a confused and erroneous manner.
The followers of the Two Vehicles take what is meager as sufficient; the externalists arbitrarily give rise to false views. This is because of birth..."
The cessation of the mind is the fundamental cause for cultivation. Because the ground is not true, the resulting fruit is circuitous.

Now, wishing to turn back from delusion to return to truth and transform consciousness into wisdom, one must suddenly awaken to the self-manifesting nature of the mind and, as it truly is, understand that objective realms are illusory.
Only by clearly seeing the subtle, continuous flow of one’s own mind can one transcend birth and death and realize the eternal and true.
Therefore, the following section clarifies this:
the characteristics of the remaining stages, wisdom, skillful means, the analytical determination of phrases and meanings, the maturation of supreme and boundless roots of goodness,
and the departure from the false fabrications of the deluded imaginings manifested by one's own mind.
The commentary states: "From here below, it specifically refers to those who practice according to reality; only such practitioners are able to enter this Dharma-gate.
The Tang translation says: "Only those who practice according to reality, through the power of wisdom, comprehend the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*)."
They have thoroughly mastered the meaning of words and phrases; they have extensively gathered roots of goodness under boundless Buddhas;
and they are able to know that what they perceive is but their own mind, without engaging in false conceptualization. Therefore, a sutra says:

"Those who can believe this Dharma have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas."
Therefore, it is said that only those whose boundless roots of goodness have reached maturity can enter this Dharma-gate;
it is truly not something that can be trusted by those of shallow faculties and inferior understanding.
Seated in meditative repose within mountain forests, practicing the lower, middle, and superior stages, one is able to perceive the continuous flow of the delusive thoughts of one's own mind.

One receives the empowerment of all Buddhas across immeasurable lands, attains the power of mastery, supernatural faculties, and samādhis, and is surrounded by spiritual friends and the assembly of Buddha-sons.

He has completely transcended the false conceptualizations of the mind, intellect, and consciousness—which are the self-nature and objective realms manifested by one's own mind—as well as the ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance; he has thus entirely crossed over all such causes.
The commentary states: This clarifies the swift efficacy of practicing according to reality.
A practitioner of true cultivation who dwells in seclusion within mountain forests and practices the gate of the contemplation of Mind-Only is able to perceive the subtle flow of their own mind.

When they suddenly realize non-arising in a single thought-moment, they attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis and supernormal powers, and receive simultaneous empowerment from the Buddhas of the ten directions. The Buddha...
His retinue will naturally surround him, and he shall instantly and completely liberate himself from the mind, consciousness, the realm of conceptual construction, karma, craving, and ignorance.
Therefore, it is said that such causes have all been transcended; this is what is called the most supreme spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, all practitioners should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
It is recorded that the Buddha-dharma possesses both causes and conditions: internally, the true suchness (*tathatā*) inherently present within one is taken as the cause for its awakening;

externally, the assistance provided by teachers, friends, and spiritual friends is taken as the condition for its manifestation. Among the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity, there has never been one who did not rely upon spiritual friends.
And because one is thus able to attain enlightenment, the World-Honored One concludes by exhorting those who practice according to reality:
"One should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friend.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
It is like the vast ocean waves, which arise from the forceful winds; the great billows surge through the dark abyss without ceasing for a moment.

The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is eternally abiding, yet when stirred by the winds of objective realms, the various waves of consciousness leap forth and arise in succession.

The commentary states: This verse in summary describes how external objects act as winds that toss the ocean of the mind, causing the waves of consciousness to flow without interruption—appearing as various colors such as blue and red, as conch shells, milk, and rock sugar, as diverse flavors of fruits and flowers, and as the sun, the moon, and their radiance.
Neither different nor not different, like waves arising from the water of the sea, so too are the seven consciousnesses; they arise in conjunction with the mind. The commentary states:

This verse uses the relationship between cause and effect—whether they are different or not different—to clarify the process of gradual arising. Blue and red refer to the object-field of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*); the conch shell refers to the object-field of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*);

milk refers to the object-field of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*); rock honey’s bland taste refers to the object-field of flavor (*rasa-viṣaya*); and flowers and fruits [refer to the object-field of touch]. The old commentary states:

Regarding the *dharmāyatana* (mental objects): the *Zongjing lu* states that present flowers and future fruits—various *dharmāyatanas*—serve as the objective spheres (*ālambana-viṣaya*) for their respective consciousnesses.
This is what is meant by the wind of external spheres tossing the ocean of the mind, such that the waves of the seven consciousnesses continue in succession without interruption.
The light of the sun and moon serves as a metaphor for the relationship between the mind and its objects, whether they are different or not different.
Because they do not realize that objects are merely mind, they give rise to false discrimination and are thus moved by it.
Just as the waters of the ocean transform into various shifting waves, so too are the seven consciousnesses; they arise in conjunction with the mind.
This refers to the locus of the *ālayavijñāna*, where various consciousnesses arise.

The commentary states: "This verse explains that just as waves arise upon the flowing water, so too do the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise from the *ālayavijñāna*," thereby clarifying their simultaneous arising.
That is to say, these seven consciousnesses are entirely waves transformed by the eighth consciousness; they originally possess no substantial reality, but are but the single mind.
There is no longer any sequence of before or after; therefore, the text below states that they are not different characteristics.

This means that by means of that mental consciousness, one contemplates the meaning of various characteristics. There are eight non-disintegrating characteristics: even the characteristic of signlessness is itself signless.
The commentary states: Because these verses are without distinction, each cognizes its own object. Since each cognizes its own object, it says:

"That is to say, by means of that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one contemplates the meanings of various signs (*nimitta*). Because they are fundamentally without distinction, it says: "The characteristics are not destroyed;
there are eight signs, yet even signlessness is signless. The Tang translation reads: "Mind, thought, and mental consciousness constitute consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

It is taught by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The eight consciousnesses have no distinct characteristics; there is neither a characteristicizer (*lakṣaka*) nor a characterized (*lakṣya*). As for the statement that "the eight are not destroyed," the long discourse says:

"Each has its own distinct characteristic, yet they evolve together. This refers to the fact that the eight are not destroyed as characteristics. This is because it was stated in the preceding chapter on arising and ceasing:

"The manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness of discriminating objects (*vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna*)—these two are both destructible and indestructible characteristics, serving as mutual causes for one another."

That which is destructible refers to the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses, the mind of arising and ceasing. That which is indestructible refers to the self-substance of the eighth consciousness, the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because it is indestructible yet appears destructible, it is dependently originated without intrinsic nature; fundamentally non-arising yet appearing to arise.
Because it is destructible yet remains indestructible, dependent origination is without intrinsic nature; though arising, it does not arise. (Prose and Verse)
Verse: They mutually illuminate one another to reveal the meaning of true non-arising. The *Zongjing* says:

"These eight consciousnesses, from time immemorial, are unmoving throughout the three periods of time and unchanging through the four phases; they are truly and eternally abiding, and their self-nature is pure."
The indestructible marks are fully perfected and complete, lacking nothing.

Since all such merits are identical to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are likewise without marks (*animitta*). Because they are all without marks, it is said that there are eight indestructible marks, and even these "without marks" are themselves without marks.
Just as the waves of the ocean are without distinction, so it is with the various consciousnesses and the mind; their difference cannot be apprehended.
The commentary states: "This uses a metaphor to clarify the meaning of non-distinction."

"Mind (*citta*) is called the accumulation of karma; the intellect (*manas*) is called the extensive accumulation. The various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) cognize their respective objects; the five are taught as those that manifest before the senses. The commentary states:
This verse explains the reasons for the names assigned to the eight consciousnesses. The eighth is named "mind" (*citta*), because it receives perfuming (*vāsanā*) and maintains the seeds (*bīja*);
as the master of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is said to "accumulate karma. The seventh is named "intellect" (*manas*), because it is characterized by its biased attachment to a self (*ātman*).
The dharmas are constantly and critically examined. Associated with the four afflictions, the six preceding consciousnesses perform karma, taking this as their root;

hence it is said they "extensively gather and collect. These six are collectively termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), yet because they confront the five present sense-objects, they are called the "five consciousnesses.

Because they discriminate the five past sense-objects, they are named the "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*); thus it is said that "the various consciousnesses cognize what is cognized," in contrast to the present objects.
Thus he spoke of the five.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked in verse:

"Blue, red, and all other forms and characteristics cause sentient beings to give rise to various consciousnesses. Like waves, there are manifold phenomena; how is this so? We pray that you will explain it."

The commentary states: When Mahāmati heard the World-Honored One previously teach that there are eight non-disintegrating marks and that even the markless is itself markless—such that both mind and objects are empty—he now hears the term "mind" used in the sense of "gathering-in" (saṃgraha) and so forth, and consequently suspects that the World-Honored One’s own words are contradictory.
Therefore, the objection is raised that both mind and objects are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The intention [of this objection] is as follows:

since it is said that the winds of the six objective spheres (*viṣaya*), such as blue and red colors, give rise to the waves of the seven consciousnesses, these objects must be substantially real. Furthermore, it is said that "mind" is named for its activity of collecting (*saṃgraha*) [objects].

"Mind" (*manas*) is defined as the extensive gathering [of objects]; the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) cognize their respective objects of cognition. The five [sensory consciousnesses] are taught in relation to present objects and so forth;

thus, the mind truly exists. Now, since both the mind and its objects exist substantially and yet differ from one another, why did the Blessed One say that there are no signs (*animitta*), nor any difference between signs, and that these are unapprehendable?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"The various colors, such as blue and red, do not exist at all within the waves; it is the mind that accumulates karma, which is taught to awaken all ordinary beings."

The Record states: This is a general response to the meaning of the question. The ocean is originally still and clear, yet waves arise because of the wind; thus, the objective realm is originally non-existent.
The mind is originally a profound and tranquil abyss, yet consciousness is triggered by conditions striking it; thus, the mind is originally empty.

Since both the objective realm and the mind are originally empty, the statement that "the realm arises from the mind" and that "gathering [objects] is called the mind" and so forth is merely for the purpose of awakening ordinary people.
This merely follows the words of others; therefore, the Tang translation says: "Blue, red, and all other forms and images cannot be found within the waves.
To speak of the mind giving rise to various appearances is to awaken the various ordinary beings."
Those karmas are entirely non-existent; they are detached from what is grasped by one’s own mind. That which is grasped is itself without anything to grasp, being identical to those waves.
The commentary states: "This explains that both the mind and its objects are empty. Since those karmas are entirely non-existent, the mind is fundamentally unarisen.
It is separated from what is grasped by one’s own mind; it is the object that is grasped. Since it is separated [from such grasping], the object fundamentally does not exist.

Thus, both subject and object are quiescent, and both mind and its objects are empty. It is like those waves on the sea: their turbulent nature is fundamentally unmoving. Therefore, the Tang translation says: "But they are fundamentally unarisen;
separated from what is grasped by one's own mind, the grasper and the grasped are identical to those waves."
The body established through enjoyment is the manifest consciousness of sentient beings; therein all karmas appear, just like waves upon water. The commentary states:
"This explains that the mind and its objects are not distinct. The "body established through enjoyment" (in the Tang translation, *kāya-vastu-pratiṣṭhā*) refers to the six sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
These are the means by which sentient beings sustain their lives and enjoy existence; one grasps these [objects] and...
Regarding those who abide in the world: all of these are manifestations of mind alone; therefore, it is said that they are the manifest consciousness of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings do not realize that objects are mere manifestations of mind, they grasp at them and cling to them as a real self and real dharmas.
Based on this, they create karma and give rise to the suffering of birth and death; thus it is said that "all karmas are manifested therein. This is truly due to [the self-]...

The mind grasps at its own mind; thus, that which is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon. Therefore, the mind and its objects appear to exist. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not illusory.
Since even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established? Thus, the mind and its objects are fundamentally empty, like waves upon water:
though they exist, they do not truly exist. Because they exist yet do not exist, they are said to be without marks and without differentiation.
They are distinct; yet their difference cannot be apprehended.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva spoke again in verse:
"The nature of the ocean waves can be distinguished by their surging and leaping; The storehouse consciousness and its karma are likewise so—why is it not realized?"
The commentary states: This uses an analogy to challenge the doctrine. The intent is to ask:
if the characteristics of karma are like waves, why can waves be seen while the characteristics of karma cannot?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Ordinary beings lack wisdom; the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is like a vast ocean. Karmic manifestations are like waves; by means of this analogy, the principle is understood."
The Record states: Because the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is subtle and difficult to know, ordinary people lack the wisdom to perceive it;
therefore, the analogy of ocean waves was employed merely to bring about their understanding. It does not mean that the karma-consciousness possesses visible characteristics.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again spoke in verse:
Just as the rising sun shines equally upon beings of inferior, middling, and superior capacity, so does the Tathāgata illuminate the world, proclaiming the truth for the sake of the ignorant.
Having already categorized all phenomena, why does [the Buddha] not speak of reality?

The response states: This is because the nature of phenomena is difficult to illustrate through analogies. When the World-Honored One previously addressed sentient beings of inferior understanding, he spoke only of the six consciousnesses and the three poisons as the foundations for establishing defilement and purity, without yet mentioning the eight consciousnesses; therefore, Mahāmati harbors doubt.
It is said: "The Tathāgata illuminates the world like the sun rising in the sky; he responds universally to all heights and depths and ought to preach the Dharma with impartiality.
For what reason has he previously divided the various dharmas and not taught this reality? Does this not fall into the fault of partiality? A verse says:
"The ādāna-vijñāna is extremely profound and subtle; its habitual tendencies and seeds form a torrential stream."
"I do not reveal this to the foolish and ignorant, fearing that they would conceptually grasp it as a self. Therefore, the following response states:
'It is not that I do not speak the truth; rather, it is their own minds that are not true.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"If one speaks of reality, that mind has no reality. It is like waves upon the ocean, or images in a mirror, or a dream."
All appear simultaneously; the same is true for the objects of the mind. Because objects are not present [simultaneously], karmic activity arises sequentially.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which cognizes the object of cognition; the mental faculty (*manas*) is likewise so called. As for the five [sensory consciousnesses], they manifest [according to conditions] and possess no fixed order.
It is like a skilled painter and his apprentices who lay on colors to depict various forms; my teaching is also like this. The colors themselves possess no patterns;
they are neither the brush nor the canvas. Yet, for the sake of delighting sentient beings, they are interwoven in a variegated manner to produce myriad images.

The commentary states: This clarifies that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, the teachings include the establishment of secret and indeterminate methods.
If one’s preaching does not accord with the listener's capacity, it will ultimately be nothing more than idle talk.

If one were to preach the ultimate truth to those whose minds lack sincerity, it would instead lead them to doubt and disbelief, turning the finest nectar (amṛta) into a poisonous drug. Thus, the following verse says:
What has been taught is not what was intended; for those [beings], it was not taught because they were incapable of receiving such teaching, not because of any secret withholding or parsimony.
However, the Dharma that is taught originally possesses no division between a prior stage of conventionality and a subsequent stage of reality.

Even when the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) are spoken of, they are never discussed without implicitly including the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*). It is simply that the words do not manifest all at once, and thus there is a distinction of sequence.
Why is this? It is because the mind and its objects manifest simultaneously and instantaneously, like waves on the ocean, reflections in a mirror, or events in a dream;

they do not arise sequentially. Fundamentally, there is no distinction between the eight consciousnesses; it is only because the conditions of the objective realm are incomplete that sequential karmic productions arise.
Therefore, it is said that the discernment of the objects of the dharma-realm constitutes the six consciousnesses; the grasping of an internal self constitutes the seventh consciousness;
and the confronting of the five present sense-objects constitutes the five consciousnesses. Thus it is said: "Consciousness is that which cognizes what is cognized;
the mind (manas) is so called because it intends; the five [consciousnesses] manifest through appearance. In reality, there is no fixed order, as they function according to conditions.

This is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), like a master painter who creates an image and his disciples fill it with colors. Although the colors come later and the image precedes them, they ultimately do not exist outside of the form.
The Dharma I teach is exactly like this. Yet, the Dharma is fundamentally ineffable; thus, it is like the fact that colors originally have no patterns.
Being free from both words and letters, it is neither brush nor canvas. It merely employs speech and symbols to benefit beings according to their capacities.
Thus it arises. Therefore, like one who delights sentient beings, one paints an image with variegated colors;
while speech and distinct practices are employed, reality transcends names and words. Discriminative analysis is for those at the initial stage of practice; cultivation reveals the ultimate truth.
The state of true self-awakening is free from all conceptual perceptions; this is taught for the sons of the Buddha, while the foolish engage in extensive discrimination.
All various things are like illusions; though they appear, they lack reality. Such various explanations are established according to specific circumstances.
What has been spoken is not what should have been spoken; for them, it was an improper teaching. The record states: "The Dharma is fundamentally beyond words;
when expressed through speech, its true principle is lost. Thus, the Wei [translation] says: "Speech is removed from the reality; reality is removed from words.
To demonstrate through speech that which is unspeakable is merely to differentiate provisional responses for those of initial capacity. If it were as...
It is only for those who truly practice that one may speak of the reality; for reality is the realm of self-realization, wherein all dualistic distinctions between subject and object are abandoned.
It cannot be entered by those who lack superior faculties and sharp wisdom; therefore, it is taught for the sake of the Buddha’s sons.
As for the foolish, they cannot understand unless there is extensive conceptual analysis. Thus, what is spoken of is provisional.
If it is true that all various dharma-gates are entirely like illusions, and from the beginning there is no real dharma given to people, then it is said:
"Although they appear, they have no reality. Such various explanations are established according to individual faculties; they are all provisional manifestations.
The reason why the teaching of the Dharma must employ skillful means (*upāya*) is that what is taught would not be appropriate for some, and thus for them it would constitute a failure to teach.
Therefore, he exercised provisional skill out of necessity; this was not the Buddha’s original intention. Thus, during his three-week contemplation, his purpose lay herein:
just as a skilled physician prescribes different remedies according to each patient's condition, so the Tathāgata teaches sentient beings according to their inclinations and capacities.
"It is not the realm of false conceptualization; it is also not the portion of the śrāvakas. This is the realm of self-realization taught by the Compassionate One. The commentary states:
"Sentient beings possess various desires and various recollections, thoughts, and discriminations. Only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are;
therefore, he teaches the Dharma according to each individual's capacity, enabling them to emerge from suffering and attain happiness. This is the Tathāgata."
The realm of self-awakening is not something that can be known by ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, or those of the two vehicles. Therefore it is said:
"It is not the realm of deluded conceptualization; it is also not within the scope of the śrāvakas."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know the realm of false discrimination consisting of the grasped and the grasper as manifestations of one’s own mind, he should leave behind crowds, worldly habits, and sleep;
throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he should constantly awaken himself and practice skillful means.
He should also distance himself from the doctrines, discourses, and verbal expressions of those with evil views, as well as from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the characteristics of the vehicle (*yānalakṣaṇa*): one should thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of the delusive imaginings that appear as one’s own mind.
The commentary states: "This teaching commands one to practice according to the Dharma. The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra says:

"Just as a person may count another's jewels while possessing not even half a coin of their own; so too is it with much learning when one does not practice the Dharma. Therefore, hearing the Dharma is most precious.

Contemplation and Cultivation. The World-Honored One’s intention was that he had already explained how all objects of false conceptualization—both the grasper and the grasped—are manifestations of one's own mind.

If one wishes to thoroughly understand the realm of Mind-only, one should distance oneself from the various evil discursive thoughts of agitation and depression, practice according to reality, and employ skillful means for observation; after a long time, one will naturally attain thorough penetration and understanding.

This is the awakening. This section exhorts practice; the following shows the method of cultivation. [The preceding section on] clarifying the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses is now complete.
Next, the characteristics of the three wisdoms are clarified.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established the characteristics of wisdom and abides therein,
they should diligently practice and study the three aspects of the higher noble gnosis.

The commentary states: Previously, eight aspects of consciousness were clarified; here, three aspects of wisdom are clarified. This is a provisional teaching intended to provide the means for practicing according to reality as it is.
One thoroughly realizes that this is the manifestation of one's own mind, and not the realm of the deluded ignorance of non-Buddhists or the Two Vehicles, as described above.
Therefore, it is called "establishing the aspect of wisdom. Once one abides in this, [the following occurs].
If one wishes to realize this through direct experience, one should diligently cultivate and study the three characteristics of the aforementioned noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

These three characteristics constitute the sphere of the noble wisdom of self-awakening; therefore, it is called "noble wisdom" to distinguish it from the inferior samādhis of non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles.
What are the three characteristics of noble wisdom that one should diligently cultivate? They are: the characteristic of non-existence;
the characteristic of the sphere of the self-vow of all Buddhas; and the characteristic of the ultimate realization of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.

Having attained these through practice, one is able to abandon the mental state of the "crippled donkey" regarding the characteristics of wisdom and attain the eighth stage of the Supreme Son (Bodhisattva). Thereupon, with respect to those aforementioned three characteristics—
Cultivation and birth.
The commentary states: "This indicates the names of the three marks. The old sub-commentary says:

"The contemplation of the impermanence of birth and death within the triple world during the seventh stage is called 'the wisdom of the lame donkey,' because it cannot proceed further due to not yet having attained the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*)."
Using this as an analogy, the following explains the characteristics.
Mahāmati, that which is characterized by non-existence refers to the characteristics of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and outsiders; these arise from their cultivation.

(The Wei translation says: "It means observing the characteristics of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists. The Tang translation says: "It means that by habituating oneself to all the characteristics of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists, one is able to give rise [to them].

Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of the sphere of one's own vows (*svapraṇidhāna-viṣaya*), it refers to that which is produced through cultivation within the sphere of the vows made by previous Buddhas.

Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of the ultimate self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-niṣṭhā-lakṣaṇa*), it is the absence of any conceptual attachment to the characteristics of all phenomena, attaining the body of the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi-kāya*), and proceeding toward the stage of the Buddhas.

Regarding the passage on "the arising of the course of conduct," the commentary states: "This explains the characteristics of the three marks; it corresponds precisely to the meaning of the three contemplations.

The Buddha contemplates the triple world as being neither real nor unreal, neither identical nor different. Because he contemplates all phenomena as not being real, it is called the 'mark of non-existence'."
Furthermore, regarding the statement that those who practice the Two Vehicles or external paths are born [into this state], Master Sengzhao says:
"The Three Vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā*) and thereby attain the Way; the only difference lies in the magnitude of their mental capacity.

Because externalists and followers of the Two Vehicles do not penetrate the emptiness of nature, they falsely give rise to views of annihilationism and nihilism. Since Bodhisattvas have realized that all is but the manifestation of one's own mind, there is fundamentally nothing [external].
Although their awakening is the same, that which they realize differs. This is intended to make them know that it is not ultimate and thus not to take it as realization;
furthermore, it is to suppress and transform those wrong views. Therefore, it says: "Contemplating the characteristics of the Two Vehicles and external paths.

This corresponds to the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Regarding "the characteristics of the sphere of one's own vows": this refers to those who have been born through cultivation within the sphere of the self-vows of the former Buddhas. Because...
When one contemplates that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are not empty, then every phenomenon is true and eternal, and the characteristics of the world are permanently abiding.
Since the characteristics of the world are permanently abiding, there is not a single phenomenon that is not true and eternal, nor is there a single category that is not the locus of one’s own vows.

Therefore, so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time and the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhagotra*) may not be severed, the Buddhas do not abandon their activities of delivering sentient beings. As the Sūtra says: "I..."
He originally established this vow, desiring that all sentient beings be no different from himself. Therefore, the Wei translation says:
"The Buddhas themselves originally made the vow to abide in and sustain all dharmas. This refers to the meaning of provisional contemplation (*parikalpita*).

Regarding the phrase "the ultimate characteristic of self-realized noble wisdom, wherein one has no conceptual attachment to the characteristics of any dharma, and attains the illusion-like samādhi, etc.": this means...
One contemplates the three realms as being neither identical nor different, and does not grasp at the marks of either dharmas or non-dharmas.
Thus one attains the illusion-like samādhi and proceeds toward the wisdom of the Buddha-ground; this is the meaning of the Middle Way contemplation.

Since it was stated above that "one constantly awakens oneself through the skillful means of cultivating the mind," he thus informs them that the three aspects of noble wisdom are such, desiring that they practice by employing these and abandon anything contrary.
This is false wisdom.

Mahāmati, these are called the three characteristics of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). If one accomplishes these three characteristics of noble wisdom, one will be able to reach the ultimate realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should diligently cultivate and study these three characteristics of noble wisdom.
The commentary states: "The realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening cannot be entered by means of these three kinds of expedients; therefore, they are exhorted to practice and study.

Thus, having first clarified the basis for the causes of both the real and the delusory, and having extensively demonstrated the eight consciousnesses to reveal the characteristics of the causal conditions of arising and ceasing, [the text proceeds].

[The preceding section] concludes. The following clarifies the return from delusion to truth by distinguishing the characteristics of false and correct causes and effects through the five dharmas and selflessness.
This is divided into two parts. First, the differentiation of the false and the correct, providing an immediate demonstration of the principle and practice of the One Vehicle’s causes and effects.

This further has two sections. First, the elucidation of the mind of the causal ground. This also has two sections. First, the refutation of the false to reveal the correct, thereby demonstrating the eternally abiding reality.
The Principle. Furthermore, there are two parts. The first concerns the refutation of false causes through three gates to reveal the true cause, which is divided into five sections.

The first clarifies the five dharmas, which is further divided into six subsections. △ First, the refutation of names, marks, and delusive thoughts. This section on the mind of the stage of practice extends from here until the end of the chapter on the Five Uninterrupted Practices in the third fascicle.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of great bodhisattvas, [recited] the *Sūtra on the Differentiation of the Self-Nature of Noble Wisdom-Objects*.
Empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of all Buddhas, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we pray that you will expound for us the *Sūtra on the Differentiation of the Self-Nature of Noble Wisdom-Objects*, which is the basis for the differentiation of the one hundred and eight phrases."

(The Tang translation says: "I only pray that you will explain for me the Dharma-gate of the intrinsic nature of the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) as the basis for the distinctions of the one hundred and eight phrases.
The commentary states: The previous one hundred and eight phrases were a general inquiry into the Dharma-gate of the five dharmas, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth;

because these were treated from the perspective of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it was said that "all are non-existent. Now, [the request is] to distinguish each one individually; therefore, it is said, "based on the one hundred and eight phrases."
This is the characteristic of differentiation.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, based on this differentiation, teaches that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter into the imagined nature of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
Because he differentiates and teaches the imagined nature, they are then able to thoroughly know the pervasive [nature].
Universally observing the selflessness of persons and phenomena, one purifies delusive conceptualization and illuminates the various stages (*bhūmi*). (The Tang translation states:

"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, for the sake of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have fallen into [the grasp of] specific and general characteristics, explain these gateways of the distinctions of the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Having known this, one is then able to purify the contemplation of the two kinds of selflessness and illuminate the various stages.
One transcends all the pleasures of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all non-Buddhist paths, and contemplates the Tathāgata’s...
The sphere of activity of the inconceivable definitively abandons the five dharmas and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The Dharma-body wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is well-adorned (the Tang translation says: "adorned by the Dharma-body wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas"). They give rise to illusory spheres (the Tang translation says:
"entering that which is like an illusion") and ascend to the Tuṣita palaces of all Buddha-fields, up to the Akaniṣṭha palaces. Having attained...

One attains the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body (the Tang translation states: dwelling in the Tuṣita palaces of all lands and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, one accomplishes the body of a Tathāgata).

The commentary states: This question arises from the following intent. Previously, Mahāmati posed comprehensive inquiries regarding the mind (citta), thought (manas), consciousness (vijñāna), the five dharmas, the three natures, and various wondrous dharma-gates;
yet the World-Honored One had only answered concerning the characteristics of the arising of the eight consciousnesses.

As for the remaining points, he has not yet received detailed instruction on each one. It is simply that [Mahāmati] does not know what constitutes names, marks, and conceptualization (nāma-nimitta-vikalpa), nor how...
This is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*). This is the dharma-gate of the noble wisdom that discriminates the self-nature of phenomena.

Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly, specifically requested again: "I pray that you will explain the dharma-gate of the self-nature of the reality of noble wisdom, which is the basis for the distinctions of the one hundred and eight phrases.
For the multitude of Bodhisattvas did not understand this dharma-gate of the self-nature of noble wisdom.
Therefore, one falls into the false discrimination of self-characteristics and common characteristics. Once this is understood, one can practice according to the Dharma,
purifying the contemplation of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), realizing that all is but mind (*cittamātra*), illuminating the various stages (*bhūmi*),

thereby transcending the paths of non-Buddhists and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), attaining the realization of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable realm, and ultimately abandoning the five dharmas.

Regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): one attains ultimate, self-awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and achieves the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, the World-Honored One proceeds to reveal this point step by step:
first he clarifies the five dharmas, next he clarifies the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and finally he clarifies the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
As for "specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): it means that all phenomena possess both specific and general characteristics. True Suchness (*tathatā*)...
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); arising in accordance with conditions to form phenomena is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Each of the five aggregates and all phenomena possesses its own essence, which is the particular characteristic; their combination to form a person is the universal characteristic.

Because non-Buddhists and followers of the Two Vehicles do not realize that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, they falsely conceptualize and cling to them, asserting that such particular and universal characteristics truly exist.

Therefore, it is said that they fall into the [clinging to] self-characteristics and common characteristics. For this reason, they adhere to the notion that all phenomena arise from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause;
all of these rely upon the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and do not pertain to the reality of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Although the World-Honored One refuted the two views of existence and non-existence, his intention was to reveal that all phenomena are unarisen (*anutpanna*). To clearly perceive that all phenomena are unarisen—
This is what is called the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There is a class of non-Buddhists who, through false conceptualization and attachment, imagine that there is nothing at all.

They perceive that causes have been exhausted and conceive the notion that 'a rabbit has no horns. Just as a rabbit has no horns, they claim that all phenomena are likewise so. Mahāmati, furthermore, there are...
Other non-Buddhists, having perceived the distinctions between seeds, qualities (*guṇa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), substances (*dravya*), spatial locations, and horizontal phenomena (*tiryag-dharma*),
become attached to them and conceive the notion that while horizontal phenomena such as rabbit horns do not exist, oxen possess horns.

The commentary states: This passage describes how non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), based on their attachment to the notions that rabbits have no horns while oxen do, give rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding all phenomena.
This serves to refute [the claim that] among the five dharmas, names and appearances arise from false imagination (*vikalpa*).

This is because all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind; they are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), and thus there is no room for views to arise. Nevertheless, those non-Buddhists do not understand this.
It is mind-only. Through the horizontal arising of false conceptualization, one perceives all phenomena according to their causes and they are exhausted accordingly.

Consequently, one conceives of a rabbit having no horns and gives rise to the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*). Because one perceives the great elements (*mahābhūta*), qualities (*guṇa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and other such entities as possessing shape, dimension, and distinct spatial divisions, by clinging to the notion that the rabbit has no horns, one subsequently gives rise to the perception that the ox has horns.
There is a view [to this effect]. However, the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) does not belong to existence or non-existence;

rather, names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) such as "existence" and "non-existence" all arise from false conceptualization and discrimination. "Elements" (*mahābhūta*) refers to the four great elements. *Guṇa*, *paramāṇu*, and *dravya* are all [types of] atoms (*rajas*).
To arise where there is nothing is called "transverse" (*tiryak*). The above summarizes the speculative views; the following refutes them.

Mahāmati, those who fall into these two views do not understand that all is the measure of mind (*cittamātra*); rather, they cause the proliferation of delusions regarding the objective spheres of their own minds (the Chinese translation states:
"They fall into the two views and fail to realize that it is only mind; they merely increase their conceptual discrimination within their own minds").

Mahāmati, the body, objects of enjoyment, and the established world—all such things are merely manifestations of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Mahāmati, the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise thus: it is free from existence and non-existence.

One should not form such a conception. (The Tang translation says: "One should know that the horns of a rabbit transcend both existence and non-existence; all phenomena are likewise. Do not give rise to discrimination.

Mahāmati, if one again forms the conception that a rabbit has no horns while remaining within the duality of existence and non-existence, this is called a false conception. Because that [non-existence] is observed in dependence upon [existence], one should not form the conception that a rabbit has no horns.
The commentary states: "This mutually refutes the view of non-existence. The Tang translation says: "How can a rabbit's horn be apart from existence and non-existence?
Because they are mutually dependent. The intended meaning is that since all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, one should not further form the conceptualization of 'non-existence.

To take a rabbit's horn—which is fundamentally non-existent—and yet further form the conceptualization of its non-existence is called false view and deluded imagination. Furthermore, a rabbit has no horns.
It is seen that because the horn arises dependent upon the ox, they are said to be mutually dependent.
Since it is not realized that the ox's horn is likewise unattainable, the subsequent passage states:
"Even down to the analysis of the intrinsic nature of a minute particle (*paramāṇu*), nothing at all can be apprehended.
The commentary states: "This mutually refutes the view of existence (*bhāvadarśana*). The Tang translation says: "Analyze the horns of an ox until they reach the level of minute particles."
If one seeks its essential nature and characteristics, it can ultimately never be found. This is because those who maintain that rabbits have no horns do so on the premise that cow horns truly exist;
thus, they maintain that rabbit horns truly do not exist. Yet they fail to realize that cow horns are likewise non-existent.

If one analyzes cow horns down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) and subtle particles (*aṇu*), they ultimately resolve into emptiness. Thus, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is entirely unattainable.
All phenomena are likewise so, Mahāmati.
They are beyond the realm of the noble ones; one should not form the notion that "a cow has horns" (the Tang translation says: "The sphere of noble wisdom is far removed from such views;
therefore, regarding this, one should not engage in conceptual discrimination").
The commentary states: This says that because the noble wisdom clearly perceives that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, one should therefore remain far removed from the two views.
The intent is that only by not forming the two views of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena can one draw near to and accord with the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
However, existence and non-existence are merely names and marks, while the two views are but false conceptualizations.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding those who have attained freedom from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), having already perceived the non-arising of conceptualization, do they, through subsequent inference, deliberation, and investigation, conclude that conceptualization does not arise and thus declare it to be 'non-existent'?"
The commentary states: This sets forth a further argument intended to demonstrate that both mind and objects are devoid [of intrinsic nature].

Upon hearing it said that one who clings to the non-existence of a rabbit’s horn does so because of the existence of a cow’s horn, Mahāmati reasoned that if one analyzes the cow’s horn until it can no longer be apprehended, then the cow’s horn is likewise non-existent;
therefore, one should not form such conceptualizations. Based on this, he advanced a further argument, meaning that for this reason, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise.
Is it not because one observes that the horns of an ox do not exist that one knows the horns of a rabbit are fundamentally non-existent?

Is this not why one speaks of "non-existence" based on the non-arising of deluded conceptualization? Therefore, the Tang translation says: "Is it not by means of false perception that one gives rise to comparative inference?"

If one considers whether [the object] is non-existent through false conceptualization, then although one knows that the horns of an ox do not exist, one ultimately clings to the horns of a rabbit as being non-existent;

thus, one has not yet abandoned the view of non-existence. To reject existence and cling to non-existence is the common malady of these outsiders (*tīrthika*). Previously, the clinging to non-existence based on the existence of a cause was refuted;
here, the clinging to non-existence based on the non-existence of a cause is refuted. As it is said: "It is better to give rise to the view of existence like Mount Sumeru..."

One must eliminate even a mustard-seed-sized fragment of the view of non-existence on the mountain of ignorance; only by directly seeking the departure of both mind and objects can the dualistic views of existence and non-existence be dispelled.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not because of non-perception that one says the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise, nor that one says 'there is no [horn]'.

Why is this? Because conceptual construction arises dependent upon that [object]. One gives rise to the conceptual construction of a horn by depending upon that [basis]; thus, it is said to depend on and be caused by that.

Since it is neither different nor non-different [from its basis], it is not the case that one says 'there is no horn' simply because the conceptual construction does not arise through non-perception."

The commentary states: This directly demonstrates the meaning of non-arising. It means that when mind and objects are free from mutual dependence, they are fundamentally non-arising and do not admit the arising of thought;
therefore, it says that "non-observation does not give rise to delusive thoughts. Why is this so?
That which is called "delusive thought" arises because of those objective realms. Because mind and objects are treated as opposites, discrimination arises. As for what is said...
That is to say, if a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself is established as dependent.

Previously, it was stated that to maintain the existence of a cow's horn while asserting the non-existence of a rabbit's horn is certainly a false imagination; thus it was said that "false imagination arises based on that horn.
Now, if one maintains that a rabbit's horn is non-existent because the cow's horn is fundamentally non-existent, this too is a false imagination, for it is established by depending upon the horn.

They are distinct. Therefore, it is said that delusive thoughts arise based on horns; because these delusive thoughts ultimately arise from the existence or non-existence of horns, they do not transcend the horns and are thus mutually illusory.
Hence, it is said they are neither different nor non-different. Furthermore, a rabbit's horn is naturally and fundamentally non-existent and need not be conceptually distinguished;
how could one come to know of the rabbit's horn only after observing that the cow's horn is non-existent?
Is it that the horn does not exist? Therefore, it is said that because one does not perceive it through investigation, one speaks of the non-existence of the horn.
Mahāmati, if the conceptualization were different from the horn, then it would not arise dependent upon the horn. If it were not different, then it would be identical with it.

The commentary states: This explains the aforementioned departure from difference and non-difference in order to reveal that false conceptualization (vikalpa) lacks intrinsic nature, thereby clarifying that the mind is fundamentally non-existent.

If one were to say that the object and the mind are definitively different, this would mean that false conceptualization possesses a separate intrinsic nature and does not arise dependent upon the horn.
Since it now arises dependent upon the horn, they are not different. If one were to say that the object and the mind are definitively one, this is... [the passage ends].
If the mind has no object, what is there to differentiate? If one raises up an object, there is no mind; who then performs the differentiation?
These two are not one. That they are neither one nor different sufficiently demonstrates that deluded thoughts have no intrinsic nature.
Even when analyzed and sought down to the level of subtle atoms, they are entirely unfindable. Since they are not different from horns, they likewise lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
When both are devoid of intrinsic nature, what phenomenon exists, and for what reason, could one say that it is non-existent?

The commentary states: The previous passage spoke of the mind having no intrinsic nature; this passage speaks of objects having no intrinsic nature, thereby clarifying that objects are fundamentally non-existent.

Therefore, the word "also" (亦) is used to distinguish this. While a rabbit’s horn is fundamentally non-existent and thus lacks intrinsic nature by its very absence, even though an ox’s horn exists, if one analyzes it into infinitesimal atoms and seeks it through such investigation, it likewise cannot be found. It is also [without intrinsic nature].
It would be no different from a rabbit’s horn; thus, existence itself lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is said that "that also is not a nature.

Since both existence and non-existence lack intrinsic nature, the object is fundamentally non-existent. When both mind and object are absent, what phenomenon could possibly present itself to the intellect?
Why then do you insist on the existence of difference and yet speak of non-existence? Thus, the Tang translation says: "different from..."
To claim that there are horns when one says there are no horns—such conceptual discrimination and determination is irrational. Since neither [of the two] exists, what could depend on what?

Mahāmati, if horns do not exist because they are non-existent (as the Tang translation says: "if they are mutually dependent, they are not established"), then to observe their existence and say that the rabbit has no horns is incorrect.

One should form this conception. The commentary states: These words reveal the true mind by means of transcending all dependencies. The Tang translation says: Because one depends on existence, one speaks of the non-existence of a rabbit’s horn;
one should not engage in such discrimination. That is to say, when both existence and non-existence are abandoned, there is nothing left to discriminate; hence it is so stated.
If there is no [substance], then there are no horns. If there are no horns, then there is no relative opposition.

Since relative opposition does not exist, to claim that one speaks of the non-existence of a rabbit's horn based on observing the existence of a cow's horn is entirely a false view. One should not make such distinctions.
"Mahāmati, because they rely on incorrect causes, their assertions of both existence and non-existence are unestablished.

The commentary states: "The non-Buddhists do not realize that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn from the beginning; instead, they falsely conceptualize existence and non-existence as the causes of birth. These are not true causes.
Because the ground [of their practice] is not true, the resulting fruit is circuitous and distorted; therefore, it is called an 'incorrect cause.'"
Therefore, it is said that both existence and non-existence are unestablished. The preceding section dispels the two views of existence and non-existence;

its intent is to overturn deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and realize correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). The subsequent section reveals that emptiness and form are of one suchness (*tathatā*); its intent is to overturn names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), which are themselves suchness.
Furthermore, the former refutes the view of non-existence, while the latter refutes the view of existence.
Mahāmati, furthermore, there are other views held by non-Buddhists who are attached to the substantiality of form, emptiness, matter, shape, and spatial dimensions.
Being unable to properly understand the limits of space, they claim that form is separate from space, giving rise to the false discrimination of views regarding such limits.

The commentary states: This describes a speculative view. The Tang translation says: "Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who perceive the boundaries of space within the forms and shapes of matter, and thereby give rise to attachment, asserting that matter is distinct from space, thus initiating conceptual discrimination."
Mahāmati, space is form; it enters into the categories of form. Mahāmati, form is space; it is established by way of the nature of the container and the contained.
One should understand that the phenomena of form and emptiness are to be distinguished through conceptual differentiation.
