The commentary states: "This clarifies that emptiness and form are of one suchness. The Wei translation says: "Because one distinguishes space by depending on form, and distinguishes form by depending on space.
The Tang translation says: "One should understand the demarcation between form and space in this way. The Sūtra says:
"For example, just as space pervades all places, whether they be material or immaterial, so does this space follow [them]."
It enters into the midst of the elements of form (*rūpa-dhātu*). This emptiness is itself form; it is not emptiness external to form.

Because form is itself emptiness, they are established as the nature of that which sustains and that which is sustained. This nature of form is intrinsically empty; it is not an emptiness resulting from the cessation of form.
"Mahāmati, when the four great elements arise, their own characteristics are each distinct; they do not abide in space, yet it is not that space does not exist in them.

The commentary states: This clarifies that the nature of form (*rūpa*) is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*), in order to refute the non-Buddhists' attachment to the four great elements as being the source of birth.

This is the cause. It refers to the conceptual attachment to the horizontal phenomena of form and location. When it says, "Because of the non-existence of a rabbit's horn, there arises the view of the existence of an ox's horn," the phrasing implies both affirmation and negation.

This is because those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to the notion that each of the four great elements possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) capable of producing all phenomena, and thus they hold these to have nothing to do with emptiness. Therefore, it is said: "When the four great elements arise, their specific characteristics are each distinct."
Even if it is argued that [space] does not abide in emptiness, we further refute this by stating that it is not because of that [matter] that space exists.

Because they do not know that the nature of matter (*rūpa*) is itself emptiness, they falsely calculate it to be the cause of production. Now, since the nature of matter is empty, this matter is fundamentally non-existent.

That the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are fundamentally non-existent, yet are grasped as the cause of production, is to have no cause. Because there is no cause...

To claim that [external objects] are the cause of birth—is this not a false conceptualization? There are many kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders in the Western Regions, yet their conceptualizations do not go beyond the two views of nihilism and eternalism, existence and non-existence.
This is truly because they do not comprehend that all is the manifestation of one's own mind; thus, they fail to understand the true cause.

Although they maintain the view that things exist, it ultimately reduces to the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuka*). The World-Honored One refutes this through various means, revealing only the correct cause in order to dismantle their notion of causelessness.
In this way, Mahāmati, one observes that because a cow has horns, a rabbit has no horns. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one were to analyze the horn of a cow...

[They analyze] atoms; furthermore, they analyze atoms as not abiding for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). (The Tang translation says: "Furthermore, when those atoms are analyzed, they do not appear for even a moment.
Upon what basis do they observe them and say they do not exist? If you say it is by observing other things, then those phenomena are likewise [non-existent].

The commentary states: This general assembly [of conditions] is neither existent nor non-existent. By observing all phenomena through this analogy, one gives rise to correct wisdom and accords with suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, those who calculate "non-existence" do so because they perceive the existence of the cow's horn; thus, they cling to the non-existence of the rabbit's horn.
Now, if one were to analyze the cow's horn down to its subtlest atoms (*paramāṇu*), it too cannot be apprehended. Nevertheless, the cow that serves as the cause—

The horn itself does not exist. Furthermore, what could possibly be compared or observed such that one speaks of the non-existence of a rabbit's horn? Indeed, all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent;
they appear to exist due to deluded perception. If for a single moment not a single thought arises, dualistic views will be severed, and true wisdom will shine alone.
When the mind and its objects are in suchness (*tathatā*), one who contemplates in this manner is said to possess right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

Any other mode of contemplation is erroneous contemplation (*mithyā-darśana*). Therefore, it is said that when contemplating other things, those phenomena are likewise so. Thus, the conclusion exhorts:
"One should abandon divergent views and delusive thoughts, and contemplate the delusive thoughts manifested by one's own mind."

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "You should abandon the false conceptualizations of differences regarding the horns of a rabbit, the horns of an ox, space, form, and color.

You, all you Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas, should contemplate the false conceptualizations manifested by your own minds and enter accordingly as the most excellent sons of all Buddha-lands, employing the skillful means of what is manifested by your own minds."

The Teacher [instructed them]—[the Tang translation says: "For the sake of all sons of the Buddha, he spoke the method of practice for observing one's own mind"]—at which time the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Form and so forth, as well as the mind, do not exist; form and so forth nourish the mind.
The commentary states: This clarifies that the false objects of the six sense-fields and the deluded discriminating mind have never existed from the beginning.
It is only because one does not realize that objects are mind-only that deluded discrimination arises; therefore, it is said that "form and so forth nourish the mind."

The commentary states: "The body and its enjoyments" refers to all objects such as the necessities of life and dwelling places; these are the reflected images manifested by the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness).
Therefore, it is said that "the storehouse consciousness manifests sentient beings. Because they do not understand this, they falsely give rise to grasping and attachment.
"Mind, mentation, and consciousness; the five self-natures of phenomena; the two kinds of selflessness and purity—these are what the Teacher of Extensive Exposition has taught.
The commentary states: "This clarifies the intent of the Tathāgata’s teaching, wherein both the provisional and the ultimate are simultaneously revealed.
However, these various dharma-gates—mind, mentation, consciousness, the five self-natures, the two selflessnesses, and so forth—are for those who do not yet understand that all is but mind-only."
It was established out of necessity merely to shatter their false conceptualizations. In reality, the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty;
the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded. Only the One Mind is shown, with no other dharma whatsoever.
This is the manner in which the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma; therefore, it is said that this is what is taught by those who provide extensive explanations.

Length, shortness, existence, non-existence, and so forth, arise from one another in mutual succession. Because of non-existence, existence is established; because of existence, non-existence is established.

When the analysis of phenomena down to the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*)—as the Chinese translation says, "the analysis of phenomena down to the subtle atom"—no longer gives rise to the false imagination of form (*rūpa-vikalpa*), this is the locus established by the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).

This is not what those with evil views delight in; it is not the sphere of the awakened conceptualizations of outsiders (as the Chinese translation says, "not the domain of the practices of non-Buddhists"). It is likewise so for the Śrāvakas. O Savior of the World!
This is what has been taught: the realm of self-awakening. The record states:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world do not transcend the mutual definition of long and short, nor the reciprocal arising of existence and non-existence;
they all exist through successive opposition and discrimination. Even when analyzed down to the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), their essence is empty. Regarding this:
To realize that objects such as form are merely mind and thus not give rise to discrimination—such a subtle and profound Dharma-gate is something those with evil views do not delight in hearing.
It is by no means the realm of non-Buddhists or the Two Vehicles; rather, it is the realm of self-awakening taught by the Tathāgata.
*Above, [the argument] was refuted by means of categories such as existence and non-existence, form and emptiness, identity and difference, and so forth.*

The section on names, marks, and conceptualization among the five dharmas is concluded. △ Below, the correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are revealed. First, to reveal the correct wisdom:
thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, in order to purify the stream of manifestations within his own mind, again requested the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha as follows:
He asked: "World-Honored One, how does one purify the stream of manifestations within the own-minds of all sentient beings? Is it sudden or gradual? The Buddha replied:

"This refers to clarifying the meaning of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) among the five dharmas, specifically regarding the purification of the habitual tendencies of the stream of manifestations within the minds of sentient beings.
This is because the stream of manifestations arising from the daily mental habits of all sentient beings is, in its original nature, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata."

Wisdom. Because of non-awakening, one follows the current of ignorance and turns along with the mind, intellect, and consciousness; thus, the noble wisdom of self-awakening remains hidden and does not manifest.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he guides beings by means of that which is inherently present, merely causing them to realize their own inherent nature;
therefore, it is said to be "purified and removed. It is not that there is some real dharma added to sentient beings. Thus, the Great...
The Sūtra says: "How marvelous, how marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata;
yet, because of delusive thoughts, inverted views, and attachments, they do not realize it. If they were free from delusive thoughts, inverted views, and attachments..."
Then all-knowledge and teacherless knowledge will manifest before one. This is what is meant by "purifying the stream of manifestation through clear, correct knowledge.
(Tang Commentary): It is said that that which purifies is the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), and that which is purified is the stream of manifestations of one's own mind.

The intention [of this commentary] is to attribute noble wisdom to the Buddha and to apply the stream of manifestation solely to sentient beings. However, it is feared that this does not accord with the original intent.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Purification is gradual, not instantaneous. It is like the mango fruit, which ripens gradually and not all at once.
In the same way, the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings is likewise gradual, not instantaneous.

It is like a potter fashioning various vessels, which are completed gradually and not all at once; so too is the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings."

It is likewise gradual purification and not sudden. Just as the great earth gradually produces all things rather than producing them all at once, so too does the Tathāgata purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings; it is likewise gradual purification and not sudden.
For example, when a person learns music, writing, painting, or various other arts and crafts, they are accomplished gradually and not instantaneously.
In the same way, the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings is likewise accomplished gradually and not instantaneously.
The commentary states: The preceding section clarifies the four gradual [teachings], while the following clarifies the four sudden [teachings].

It is like a bright mirror that suddenly manifests all forms and images without characteristics (the Tang translation says: "It is like a bright mirror that suddenly manifests various marks, yet remains free of discrimination").
In the same way, when the Tathāgata purifies the stream of manifestations from the minds of all sentient beings, he likewise suddenly manifests the formless.
There is no objective realm of purity whatsoever; rather, like the orbs of the sun and moon, it instantaneously illuminates and reveals all forms and images.

In the same way, for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the habitual tendencies arising from their own minds, the Tathāgata likewise instantaneously reveals the most supreme realm of inconceivable wisdom.
Just as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) instantaneously discerns and knows that which is manifested by its own mind, so too does the Tathāgata.
As well as the establishment of the body and the enjoyment of objective spheres, so it is with those various *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas.
They simultaneously ripen the objective spheres where sentient beings dwell, because the practitioner is established therein in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Chinese translation states:

"For example, the *ālayavijñāna* discerns and manifests the objective spheres, the self-body, resources, and the vessel-world all at once, not sequentially. Mahāmati, the *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata is also like this; he simultaneously matures the realms of all sentient beings and establishes them in the ultimate.")

Just as the Dharma-Buddha acts as the support for the Nirmāṇa-Buddha (the *Tang* translation says: "just as the Dharma-Buddha suddenly manifests the Reward-Buddha"), so too is the self-realized state of the noble ones.
It illuminates and causes the extinction of the false conceptualizations and evil views regarding the existence or non-existence of the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: This is based on the sudden and gradual methods of transformation to clarify the principle that while realization must be sudden, the elimination of phenomena must be gradual.
Previously, both the sudden and the gradual were understood as referring solely to the Buddha; however, upon careful examination of the analogy, "gradual" carries the meaning of maturation.

The meaning of "sudden apprehension," "manifestation," "illumination," and "function" refers exclusively to the Buddha in the case of the sudden [teaching], and exclusively to the capacity of the practitioner in the case of the gradual [teaching].

This is because the Tathāgata, possessing the perfected noble wisdom of self-awakening, abides in the *Sāgarāmudrā-samādhi* (Ocean-Seal Samādhi) and illuminates the *dharmadhātu*, manifesting it with universal equality.

It is like a bright mirror reflecting images, leaving nothing out in its minute detail; he discerns the capacities of beings and preaches the Dharma for them, just as the sun and moon [shine upon all].
Ascending to heaven, clouds and rain moisten all universally. Yet, because mountains have heights and depths, those who receive the light do so at different times;

because roots have magnitude and smallness, their maturation occurs with varying speed. What is meant is that the Dharma is fundamentally not different; the difference lies only in the capacities of the recipients.
Thus, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, it is like a lion training its cubs: though he looks around and lets out frequent roars, he exerts his full strength in every instance. This...

Therefore, the methods of transformation contain secret and indeterminate meanings. Nevertheless, these are all explained in terms of the Buddha’s sudden and gradual teachings because he preaches the Dharma by relying on the three bodies (*trikāya*).
There are four meanings regarding the sudden and gradual: namely, the sudden-sudden, the sudden-gradual, the gradual-sudden, and the gradual-gradual.
This is truly because the minds of sentient beings are, in their original nature, the noble wisdom of self-awakening; it is only due to...

The perfuming of ignorance transforms [the mind] into the evolving consciousnesses of manifest karma. Now, as these evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom, because ignorance has varying degrees of thickness, there are differences between sudden and gradual approaches to the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who, in a single thought-moment, suddenly awaken to the originally existing Dharmakāya-wisdom, they will illuminate their own minds and realize that the phenomena of body, mind, and the world have never existed therein, forever departing from all clinging and grasping.
Conditioned by this, all faculties, measures, and characteristics cease. In a single thought-moment, one suddenly realizes the noble wisdom of self-awakening.

This is what is called the Dharma-Buddha preaching the sudden teaching; it suddenly purifies the stream of manifestations of the self-mind of sentient beings. This is the sudden within the sudden. If there are sentient beings...

By the power of the habitual perfuming of the teacher’s instruction, although one is able to realize one's own mind, due to the force of the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), one cannot suddenly abandon the conceptualized realms of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna-vikalpa*). Rather, one contemplates that all phenomena arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
that the entire body, mind, and world are like an illusion and unreal, being merely manifestations of one's own mind; and thus gradually severs [delusion].
Ignorance. To realize the noble wisdom of self-awakening, one first understands, then practices, and finally realizes.

This is the teaching of sudden and gradual methods spoken by the Reward Buddha (Sambhogakāya) to purify the flowing stream of sentient beings. This "sudden and gradual" is actually "gradual and sudden.

If sentient beings, despite encountering external conditions, cannot suddenly awaken to their own minds, they should merely rely on the giving taught in the Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata’s provisional teachings.
Through morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, one gradually observes and gradually detaches from the mind and its objects, thereby attaining right knowledge and vision.
This is the gradual teaching spoken by the transformation Buddha, which gradually purifies the stream of manifestations within the minds of sentient beings; this is "gradualness."
Viewed from this perspective, although [the teaching] is gradual for the Buddha, it is also sudden, because it manifests through equality; therefore, "sudden" applies solely to the Buddha.

For sentient beings (the *kṣetra*), it is both sudden and gradual: because the roots of goodness have been accumulated over many lifetimes and have now matured, they suddenly awaken in a single thought-moment.
Although sudden, it is also due to the gradual; therefore, "gradual" applies solely to sentient beings. Thus, the following passage cites them accordingly.
The third section concerns the manner in which the Buddhas preach the Dharma, explaining the meaning of sudden and gradual teachings.

Although the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation Buddha) preaches the gradual Dharma, because the three bodies (*trikāya*) are one essence, even that which is gradual is also sudden. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful expedients (*upāya*), he assists in manifesting the primary truth.
The above concludes the manifestation of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). Below follows the manifestation of suchness (*tathatā*).
Mahāmati, the Dharma taught by the Buddha states that all phenomena arise from the seeds of habitual tendencies manifested by one's own mind, characterized by their individual and common marks.

They are caused by the attachment to the nature of conceptual construction and its continuity; they are manifold, unreal, like illusions, and cannot be apprehended through any such manifold attachments.

The commentary states: This clarifies that the Reward Buddha (Bhogabuddha) preaches the dharma of dependent origination without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), thereby establishing the meanings of the sudden, the gradual, and the sudden-within-the-gradual, in order to manifest suchness (*tathatā*).
Because the reward body descends from the Dharma-body, it is said that "the Dharma relies upon the Buddha.

Since true suchness does not abide in its own nature but follows conditions to form all phenomena, it is said to "enter into specific and general characteristics. Ignorance acts as the cause for their arising.

Regarding the three subtleties, it is said: "The cause is the habitual tendencies manifested by one's own mind. Regarding the growth of the six gross states with objective realms as conditions, it is said:
"The cause is the attachment to the self-nature of continuous delusive thought. This means that the single mind of True Suchness (tathatā), following conditions, forms all phenomena.
Since all phenomena are dependently originated and lack intrinsic nature, their various manifestations are unreal, like illusions; such is the root of delusive thought.

There is none. It arises from conditions; yet that which arises also lacks intrinsic nature, and is therefore ungraspable. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* takes the dependent origination of the dharma-realm as its central tenet.
For this reason, it is said here that the Reward Buddha teaches the dharma of dependent arising. Below, this is illustrated through a metaphor.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by clinging to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises.
Mahāmati, it is like a master illusionist who, relying on grass, wood, tiles, or stones, creates various illusions and manifests the diverse forms and colors of all sentient beings.
Various kinds of false conceptualizations arise; yet those conceptualizations themselves lack any true reality.
The commentary states: "This uses a metaphor to explain and establish the meaning that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises based upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is said that by clinging to the dependent nature, one gives rise to the imagined nature."
The conjurer represents the mind; the grass, trees, tiles, and stones represent the conditions of ignorance; the various forms and images represent all phenomena;
and the observer’s manifold discriminations represent sentient beings’ failure to realize that everything is but mind, giving rise to various false conceptualizations.
All of these are entirely like illusions and lack reality. Thus, it is not only that false objects fundamentally do not exist, but the deluded mind as well.
Fundamentally, they do not exist. Because they arise through conditions, they are like illusions.
Thus, Mahāmati, based upon the dependent origination-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises.

This consists of various minds of imagination, various characteristics and activities of the imagined state, and the imagined state of the habitual tendencies of attachment; this is the characteristic of the imagined nature.
"Mahāmati, this is called the teaching of the Dharma by the *dharmatā-niṣyanda-buddha* (the Buddha of the outflow of the nature of reality).
The commentary states: "This uses the Dharma to correspond with the metaphor. The Tang translation says: "It is also like this:

due to the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of grasping at objects, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) appears in various forms within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature)."
Mahāmati, this is called the arising of the nature of false conceptualization; it is the teaching on the characteristics of dharmas expounded by the Buddha as they flow from the nature of dharmas.

Mahāmati, the Dharma-Buddha is free from the characteristics of the self-nature of the mind; it is established and enacted as the objective realm perceived by the noble ones through their own self-realization.
The commentary states: This clarifies that the Dharma-Buddha preaches the Dharma, thereby fulfilling the meaning of "sudden within the sudden.

Generally speaking, all that transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness to manifest the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom constitutes the dharma-characteristics taught by the Dharma-Buddha. Since this sutra is purely sudden, its significance is seen herein;
thus, at the beginning of the fifth chapter on dharmas, Mahāmati requests: "I only pray that you will preach for me the Dharma-body... and so forth.
This is the Dharma that has been taught.
Mahāmati, as for the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation Buddha), he teaches generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, as well as mind and wisdom.

He teaches the transcendence of the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), and sense bases (*āyatanas*), the liberation from the characteristics of consciousness, and the analytical observation and establishment [of the path] that transcends the views of non-Buddhists and the views of formlessness.
The commentary states: This clarifies the characteristics of the transformation Buddha preaching the Dharma, thereby fulfilling the meaning of the preceding "gradual" progression.
Because non-Buddhists falsely perceive formlessness as the ultimate, it is called "the perception of the perception of formlessness."

Mahāmati, furthermore, the Dharma-Buddha is free from objective referents (*ālambana*). Being free from objective referents, all activities, sense-faculties, means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and characteristics are extinguished.
It is not a realm clung to by the self-characteristic attachments of ordinary people, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.

Rather, it is established as the ultimate, distinctive characteristic of the noble ones' personal realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). Therefore, Mahāmati, this is the ultimate, distinctive characteristic of the noble ones' personal realization.
One should diligently practice and study; that which appears as the manifestation of one's own mind should be eliminated.
The commentary states: "This conclusion returns to the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*), directly pointing to the sudden within the sudden, thereby demonstrating the ultimate essence of this sutra.

Having previously discussed at length the characteristics of the three Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma, the reason for concluding with an exhortation regarding the Dharma-Buddha is intended to mean that there is still something to be grasped.
Because the mind takes objects as its conditions, it falsely perceives realms and engages in conceptual discrimination and attachment; this is termed "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*).
To be free from such objective conditions is precisely the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Furthermore, while the previous three characteristics were described as the "characteristic of the ultimate noble wisdom of self-realization," the present description as the "characteristic of the ultimate differentiation" intends to reveal that the three bodies of the Buddha are one essence, and what is taught therein—
The Dharma is the provisional means that realizes the real, the gradual path that realizes the sudden, and the differentiation that realizes the ultimate;
it simply intends for practitioners to rely exclusively upon the most sudden of the sudden in their cultivation. The above concludes the manifestation of correct wisdom as suchness.
Below follows the refutation of the two kinds of false causes. First, by means of the false causes of the Two Vehicles, the correct cause is revealed.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of characteristics of the Śrāvaka-vehicle’s pervasive discrimination:
namely, the characteristic of attaining the distinction of the noble self-realization, and the characteristic of attachment to the nature of the imagined self-nature.

The commentary states: This arises because the Dharma-Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is the self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), which is not the domain of ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or non-Buddhists.
Therefore, it follows the terminology of the Śrāvakas and non-Buddhists to demonstrate the reason why [this teaching] is not their noble wisdom.
Nevertheless, while the followers of the two vehicles practice based on the Buddha’s teachings, they fail to realize that provisional means are themselves the reality. Thus...
One merely attains the distinctions within noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), but does not attain the distinctions within the ultimate state of noble wisdom.

For this reason, one remains long stalled at the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇapurī*) without ascending to the "jeweled site" (*ratnasthāna*). Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) falsely posit a divine self (*ātman*), thereby turning their backs on the true and eternal;

thus they are deeply attached to false views. To cause practitioners to depart from these provisional and erroneous [views], one must then attain the ultimate distinctions of self-awakened noble wisdom.
This is the characteristic of establishing a distinction.
What is the characteristic of the noble self-realization of the Śrāvakas? It refers to the spheres of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;

the truths, detachment, and cessation; and the knowledge of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as they truly are—namely, the cessation of their individual and common characteristics, and the non-subversion of external characteristics.

The mind attains tranquility. Once the mind is tranquil, one attains the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, the fruits of the path, and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti-vimokṣa*).
Yet, they are not free from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*). Such a śrāvaka dwells in the noble bliss of self-realization;
this is called the śrāvaka who has attained the distinctive characteristics of the noble state of self-realization.
The commentary states: "This distinguishes [the practitioner] from the heterodox causes of the two vehicles. There are two types of śrāvakas:
first, those of sharp faculties, who practice by relying on the Four Noble Truths and enter through the contemplation of emptiness;

second, those of dull faculties, who practice by relying on the contemplations of the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) according to the provisional teachings, and who analyze form to grasp at partial emptiness. This passage clarifies the śrāvaka of sharp faculties. Therefore...
The Tang translation says: What is the distinctive characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-realization?

It refers to clearly perceiving the realms of the truths of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, which are free from desire and characterized by quiescent extinction; thus, regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, whether individual or collective—
Because one understands the external non-disintegrating marks as they truly are, the mind abides in a single object.

Having so abided, one further attains liberation through the dhyānas, samādhis, and the fruits of the path, and emerges [from saṃsāra] to abide in the bliss of the realm of personally realized noble wisdom.

Not yet having abandoned habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*), this is called the characteristic of the stage of the Śrāvaka’s dwelling in the realm of personally realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Nevertheless, they clearly perceive the realms of impermanence and non-self; this is what is meant by attaining the Way through the equal contemplation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
However, because they crave the bliss of samādhi and do not give rise to the mind to deliver sentient beings, it is said that they "dwell."

The bliss of the realm of self-realized noble wisdom cannot transcend the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) because one has not yet abandoned the seeds of the habitual tendencies of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of death and rebirth; as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "One is the death and rebirth of limited segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*)."

This refers to the coarse ripened fruits of the three realms, whether wholesome or unwholesome, produced by all contaminated (*sāsrava*) karmas through the power of the conditions of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The length of one's body and life has fixed limits determined by the force of causes and conditions; therefore, it is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*).
Second is the inconceivable death and rebirth of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*), which is produced through the power assisted by the conditions of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This extraordinary, subtle, and distinct fruit of maturation transforms the physical body and life-span through the power of compassion and vows; because it is not restricted by fixed limits, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
Since it is primarily induced by the support of untainted meditative concentration and vows, its wondrous function is difficult to fathom, and thus it is named "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has attained the blissful dwelling of the distinguished characteristics of self-realized noble wisdom does not [abide] in the bliss of the gate of cessation or the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Out of compassion for sentient beings and in accordance with his original vows, he does not realize [that state as a final end].

Mahāmati, this is called the bliss of the distinguished characteristics of self-realized noble wisdom attained by the Śrāvaka; yet the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding that same attainment of the distinguished characteristics of self-realized noble wisdom...
"Joy. One should not practice or study this.
The commentary states: This universally addresses potential objections to clarify that although the objects of observation for Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas are the same, what they realize differs;
this demonstrates that the distinction between them lies in the magnitude of their mental capacity. A question is asked: "Does the Bodhisattva also attain this self-awakening?"
This is the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). Why is it not the same as that of the śrāvakas? Therefore, the Tang translation states:

"Although bodhisattvas also attain this realm of noble wisdom, because they have compassion for sentient beings and are sustained by their original vows, they do not realize the gate of quiescence or the bliss of samādhi.
By contemplating emptiness, they do not take realization as their goal; this is how they differ from the śrāvakas."
Therefore, he exhorted him, saying: "O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should not practice or study within this state of bliss of self-realized noble wisdom.
Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the attachment to the imagined nature of things as held by Śrāvakas? It refers to the primary elements (mahābhūta), blue, yellow, and so forth.

Having seen that the red, white, solid, moist, warm, and moving [elements] are not produced by an agent, and having previously heard the excellent teaching on their specific and general characteristics,
one gives rise to the conceptualization of intrinsic nature regarding them.
The commentary states: This clarifies the śrāvakas of dull faculties. It means that these śrāvakas do not know how to contemplate emptiness;
rather, they practice based on the contemplative gates such as the eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ) taught in the provisional vehicle according to the sacred teachings.

They contemplate the four great elements and other phenomena as having real intrinsic and common characteristics. Although this is not the same as the non-Buddhists' reckoning of a creator or a producer, they nevertheless cling to them.

Those various phenomena are regarded as having a truly existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet they are not apart from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the Chinese translation asks:

"What is the characteristic of the attachment to the intrinsic nature through discrimination? It refers to knowing such phenomena as solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth;

these are not produced by a creator, yet based on scripture and reasoning, one perceives their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and discriminates with attachment."

[This refers to] "clinging. The Wei translation says: "To differentiate as having real entities and to grasp at false appearances" means to falsely cling to those phenomena, regarding them as truly existent.

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know these and abandon them, entering accordingly into the mark of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and extinguishing [the notion of] the person (*pudgala*).
"I see the marks. This refers to the gradual establishment of the successive stages (*bhūmi*) in a continuous succession.

The commentary states: "This is a summary exhortation to abandon faults. Śrāvakas have already attained the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), but have not yet attained the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Since the selflessness of persons is itself an attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), the cessation of the mark of the selflessness of persons is precisely the entry [into the path].
The Dharma has no characteristic of self;
this is called the nature of the śrāvakas. It is the characteristic of attachment to the imagined nature.
The commentary states: This is the name of the [preceding] section. That is to say, when one is free from those two kinds of śrāvaka views, it is then termed "correct wisdom. Therefore...
He exhorts them to abandon [their views]. This concludes the section above, which used the false causes of the two vehicles to demonstrate the true cause.
Below follows the section that uses the true cause of noble wisdom to refute the false causes of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
regarding the realm of the self-realized noble path and the realm of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) spoken of by the World-Honored One as 'eternal' and 'inconceivable'— World-Honored One,
is this not the same as the 'eternal' and 'inconceivable' causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya) taught by the non-Buddhists?"
The commentary states: The preceding section clarified the departure from the views of the two vehicles; this section clarifies the departure from the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is because non-Buddhists reckon the *ātman* (self) to be the cause of birth, which is not a true cause; they take the impermanent to be permanent, which is not true permanence.

All such views are collectively false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). To depart from these is what is called right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); therefore, he poses this question with the intention that the Buddha speaks of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*).
Noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) are truly eternal and inconceivable; yet non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also speak of the eternal and the inconceivable.
Is what the World-Honored One has taught not the same as what those non-Buddhists have spoken?
Below, the Buddha answers that it is not comparable to what the non-Buddhists have spoken because their causal characteristics (*hetulakṣaṇa*) are different.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The eternal and inconceivable is not attained through the causal conditions of the various non-Buddhists.

The commentary states: That which the Tathāgata describes as eternal and inconceivable takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as its cause and the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) as its characteristic;
it is what is called the true cause, the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is not that false conception of a *puruṣa* or *ātman* held by those non-Buddhists.
Consequently, they take the impermanent to be permanent; therefore, this is not the same as those treatises.
Why is this so? The eternal and inconceivable [reality] of the various non-Buddhists is not established by means of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: This explains the reason for the difference between the inquiry and the exposition.

That which is "eternal" and "inconceivable" refers to the falsely established *puruṣa* (spiritual self), which is not accomplished through the characteristics of noble wisdom of self-awakening or through the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*). Therefore, it is said that it is "not accomplished by means of its own characteristics."
If that which is eternal and inconceivable were not established by means of its own true nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), for what reason would it manifest as eternal and inconceivable?
The commentary states: This precisely demonstrates that it is not truly eternal. That is to say, that which is eternal and inconceivable must necessarily rely upon a true cause.
If it were not a true cause, how could it manifest the meaning of the eternal and inconceivable?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the inconceivable were established through its own characteristic as a cause, it would necessarily be eternal;
however, because it possesses the characteristics of a causal agent, the eternal and inconceivable cannot be established.
The commentary states: This is a concession and refutation intended to counter a shifting argument.

Fearing that the opponent, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching that the true and eternal is established by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), might shift their position and say, "My teaching of the eternal and inconceivable is also established by its own characteristic;
why then is it not the same as the Buddha's teaching? Therefore, [the text] concedes: "If that non-Buddhist's inconceivable were indeed established by its own characteristic..."
If it were established [as such], then that too would have to be truly eternal. However, this is merely due to the postulated agent being taken as the cause.
Yet the agent is not a true cause; since the cause is not true, how could one obtain an eternal fruit? Therefore, an eternal and inconceivable [nature] is not established.
Below, the true cause is revealed.
Mahāmati, my ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is eternal and inconceivable. It is established through the characteristics of the cause of ultimate reality;

it is free from existence and non-existence, and it possesses the characteristics of self-realization. Therefore, it has characteristics. Because it is the cause for the wisdom of ultimate reality, it has causes. Because it is free from existence and non-existence, it is so.
For example, it is like non-action, space, nirvana, and cessation; therefore, it is eternal. Thus, Mahamati, this is not the same as the heterodox theories of an eternal and inconceivable [self].
The commentary states: This clarifies that the Buddha taught that both causes and characteristics are simultaneously true, thereby manifesting the true, eternal, and inconceivable. The Buddha said:
"When I speak of the eternal and the inconceivable, it is established based upon the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth) through causes and characteristics.

By departing from the two views of existence and non-existence, one attains the characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-realization; therefore, there is the *dharmatā* (true reality), and one attains the wisdom of the ultimate truth."
Because it is the cause, it is the true cause. It is free from all conceptual proliferations of existence and non-existence; its very substance is quiescent extinction.
Like the three unconditioned dharmas, it is eternally free from all faults and is therefore truly eternal.
This is why it differs from the heterodox views of the non-Buddhists who propound an eternal and inconceivable [self].
In this way, Mahāmati, this permanence and inconceivability are that which is attained by the noble wisdom of self-realization of all Tathāgatas.
Because it is thus, one should practice and study that which is attained by the noble wisdom of self-realization—this permanence and inconceivability.
The commentary states: This [passage] refers to the true permanence; therefore, it exhorts one to practice and study it.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the permanence and inconceivability of the non-Buddhists is due to the nature of impermanence and the characteristics of diverse causes.
It is not permanent by virtue of the power of its own causal characteristics.
The commentary states: This clarifies why the doctrines of the non-Buddhists regarding permanence and the inconceivable differ from those taught by the Buddha.
The reason they differ is that what they establish posits a creator outside of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as the cause of production;
thus, it is a divergent cause. The Buddha takes the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) as the cause; thus, it is the true cause. This...
This is why they differ. Thus, the Tang translation states: "The heterodox [schools] claim that the eternal is inconceivable;

it is eternal because of the cause of the characteristic of impermanence and change, not because of the power of its own intrinsic characteristic as a cause. That is to say, because they rely on a changing cause, it is not truly eternal."
I take the power of the causal characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization as my basis; it is not the power of the causal characteristics of the agent of self-characteristics.
Therefore, it is truly eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the "eternal" and "inconceivable" of the various non-Buddhists refers to their view of impermanence regarding the existence and non-existence of created things.

Having done so, they conceptualize and reckon it as permanent. Mahāmati, I too, having seen that the nature of what is produced by such causes and conditions—whether existent or non-existent—is impermanent, speak of that permanence as being without cause, based on the realm of the self-realized noble ones.
The *Shuji* (Commentary) states: "This is established based on what the non-Buddhists themselves have asserted, in order to reveal the true refutation [of their position].

For while the various non-Buddhists, seeing that all phenomena exist and then cease to exist, falsely imagine that there exists a separate, permanent creator, the Tathāgata likewise sees that all phenomena exist and then cease to exist, and thus declares them to be impermanent.
Therefore, the Tang translation says: 'The permanence of the non-Buddhists is inconceivable.'"
Consideration: Having observed that produced phenomena exist and then cease to be, and having established their impermanence, one infers that this [Self] is permanent.

Furthermore, I observe that produced phenomena exist and then cease to be, and having established their impermanence, I do not on that basis assert that [the Self] is permanent. If one were to combine this with the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-linga*), it would be as follows:
"The permanent and inconceivable" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is certainly permanent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because it is produced" is the reason (*hetu*).
Because of its nature as a product, it is like a jar or similar objects. A jar or such things that are produced are impermanent phenomena.
Since the reason does not deviate from the example, the thesis of permanence is not established. Impermanence is a property of the subject; it certainly cannot be the thesis of permanence.

The reason given is "because of being a product," with the example being "like a jar or similar objects. Since jars and the like, being products, are impermanent phenomena, that which was proposed [as permanent] is overturned.
This establishes what was to be refuted. However, they rely on false conceptualization and inference, whereas I rely on the direct perception of the noble wisdom of self-realization;
therefore, what I have taught is not within the scope of their discourse.

Mahāmati, if furthermore those non-Buddhists establish the eternal and inconceivable based on causal characteristics, yet their own causal characteristics—whether as existence or non-existence—are like the horns of a rabbit, then this "eternal and inconceivable" is merely a conceptualization of speech.
Such is the fault of the non-Buddhists. Why is this? Because it is merely a conceptualization of speech, like the horns of a rabbit; its own causal characteristics are not [real].
The commentary states: This refers to what non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceive of as a creator;

thus, taking that which has no cause to be a cause, they ultimately fall into nihilism, being like a rabbit’s horn. Therefore, what they establish—claiming the impermanent to be permanent—is merely empty words and nothing more.
It lacks substantial reality. Therefore, the Tang translation says: "The non-Buddhists establish the eternal and inconceivable through such causal characteristics.
These causal characteristics do not exist; they are like the horns of a rabbit. Thus, the eternal and inconceivable are merely conceptual constructions and nothing more than verbal expressions.
Why are those causes like the horns of a rabbit? Because they lack the characteristics of their own causes, as they are not... [the first...]
The single meaning has the noble wisdom of self-realization as its causal characteristic; therefore, it is said that the causal characteristic is not within the realm of others.

Mahāmati, my permanence and inconceivability arise because they have the characteristic of being realized through self-awareness. They are permanent because they are free from the nature of being produced, whether as existence or non-existence;

they are not the impermanence of external things being either existent or non-existent. Mahāmati, those who speculate and calculate based on external existence or non-existence [do not understand this]. If there were again external existence or non-existence...
It is impermanent. They conceptualize it as permanent and do not contemplate or recognize its permanence; yet they do not know the mark of the inconceivable self-cause.
Thus, they remain far removed from the state of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*). Such persons should not speak [of this].

The commentary states: This clarifies that the Tathāgata takes self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) as the cause, thereby establishing a distinction from the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
For the non-Buddhists give rise to the dualistic views of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena; thus, they falsely conceptualize the impermanent as permanent.
Because they do not know the characteristics of their own causal nature, they depart from the sphere of self-realized noble wisdom.
The realms are remote from one another. The Tathāgata’s teaching is free from all such faults; therefore, it cannot be compared to those [other systems].
The preceding section clarifies that the biased attachments of the two vehicles and the false views of the non-Buddhists are all not correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*).

This is intended to reveal that by abandoning these, one realizes the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). The following two chapters clarify correct gnosis by means of the principles of neither extinction nor arising.
This is precisely suchness. (Circle) The above section on refuting the two kinds of false causes is completed. Below, there are two parts regarding using the fruit to verify the cause.
△ First, refuting the extinction-view of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, various śrāvakas, fearing the suffering of the conceptualization of birth and death, seek nirvāṇa; they do not understand birth...

The distinction between death and nirvāṇa: all natures are conceptual constructions and lack intrinsic nature. (The Wei translation says: "Because they do not know that there is no distinction between the world and nirvāṇa. The Tang translation says:)

Not knowing the distinction between the characteristics of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa, they consider everything that exists to be merely a product of false discrimination, for it has no inherent existence.

They imagine that when the future sense-faculties and their objects cease, that is nirvāṇa; yet this is not the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) through the noble wisdom of self-realization. (The Tang translation states:

"They falsely calculate that the cessation of the future sense-faculties and their objects is nirvāṇa, not knowing that they must realize the realm of self-cognizing wisdom and transform the supported storehouse consciousness into Great Nirvāṇa. Therefore, the ignorant speak of three vehicles and speak of proceeding toward the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
There is nothing that exists. Therefore, Mahāmati, those ignorant people do not understand that the realms of the past, future, and present Tathāgatas are manifestations of their own minds;
instead, they cling to external realms manifested by the mind. Thus, the wheel of birth and death constantly turns (the Tang translation says:

"Those deluded people speak of three vehicles and do not say that there is only mind and no external objects. Mahāmati, those people do not know the realms of their own minds as taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; they grasp at objects external to the mind and thus perpetually revolve in the wheel of birth and death without ceasing).
The commentary states: These words declare that all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning and cannot be further extinguished;
this is shown to reveal the true, eternal, and inconceivable cause, and to clarify that by means of delusive thoughts one realizes right wisdom, and by means of right wisdom one manifests suchness.
This is to destroy the views of extinction held by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). However, the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) does not exist from the very beginning;
it is merely manifested by the mind alone. Through the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it exists based on deluded conceptualization and discrimination.

If one realizes that conceptualization has no intrinsic nature, then consciousness is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*). If one illuminates all things with correct wisdom, then all phenomena are thusness (*tathatā*) in their very essence.
It is quiescent and extinguished; how could it admit of further extinction? The two vehicles are deluded and unable to comprehend this;
they falsely grasp the non-acceptance of future existence as *nirvāṇa*. Is this not a great error—to claim that merely exhausting birth and death constitutes liberation?
In truth, they have not attained universal liberation; therefore, they constantly revolve within the cycle of birth and death without ceasing.
This is because they fail to realize that all is a manifestation of the mind-only (*cittamātra*) and thus give rise to various false discriminations. ○ Above it was said that there is no extinction;
below it is said that there is no arising. △ Next, the view of arising held by non-Buddhists is refuted.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are unarisen; this is what has been taught by the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present. Why is this?
Because they are manifestations of one's own mind, and because their nature—whether as existence or non-existence—is free from arising through either being or non-being. Mahāmati!

All natures are unarisen; all phenomena are like the horns of rabbits, horses, and the like. These foolish worldlings do not realize that the nature of their own conceptual construction is merely conceptualization.

Because of this conceptualization, Mahāmati, all phenomena are unarisen. For those who enter the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, the characteristics of the self-nature of all natures are unarisen;
this is not the dualistic realm of the conceptual constructions of those foolish worldlings.
The commentary states: These words declare that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, thereby demonstrating the true, eternal, and inconceivable cause;
they reveal that suchness itself is the luminous, correct wisdom, and they serve to refute the externalists' view of arising.

This is because the non-arising of all phenomena is the heart-seal transmitted by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; it is to be realized through personal correspondence, as it is manifested solely by the mind.
Dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature. It transcends the two views of existence and non-existence, like the horns of a rabbit or a horse;
it is not that something exists and then ceases to be, for its arising is fundamentally non-existent. Because ordinary, deluded beings do not realize this, they falsely cling to it as being existent.
However, this principle of the non-arising of phenomena is the domain traversed by the self-realized noble wisdom, not the sphere of the dualistic views discriminated by the foolish.

The self-nature body establishes the characteristics of the nature of the destination. Mahāmati, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) evolves through the appearance of the grasped and the grasper;
fools fall into the two views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and long for the birth of all natures. Thus, the false discrimination of existence and non-existence arises;
this is not the way of the noble ones. Mahāmati, you should practice and study therein.
The commentary states: This concludes the preceding two chapters to clarify that both arising and ceasing are merely false perceptions. Therefore, the Tang translation says:
"The body, the objects of livelihood, the vessel-world, and so forth—all these are reflections of the ālayavijñāna.
The two aspects of the grasped and the grasper appear; those deluded beings fall into the two false views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Thus, regarding...
Within this, delusions give rise to the discrimination of existence and non-existence. Thus, the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world are fundamentally unborn from the beginning;

they are merely the reflected manifestations of the eight consciousnesses. The seventh consciousness delusively gives rise to grasping and discrimination, taking them to be a real self and real phenomena.
This is simply the ignorant person seeing birth within that which is unborn; it is not the way of the sages and worthies. The intent is to bring about the cessation of this very arising and ceasing.

Because one realizes the true and eternal, one should cultivate and study those dharmas. If one truly understands that arising and ceasing are themselves the eternal, then deluded thoughts immediately become perfected wisdom;
names and marks are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, even those of the two vehicles and external paths can give rise to the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the text below clarifies the five types of unconditioned lineage (*anantarya-gotra*). [Section] Five: Examining the Fruit.
Knowing the cause means that by examining the presently active fruit, one is fully able to know the past cause of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five types of immediate lineage (*gotra*). What are the five? They are:
the immediate lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the immediate lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the immediate lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle, and the indeterminate lineage.
Regarding "distinct lineages" (translated in the Tang version as "without lineage"), the commentary states:

This refers to the five different natures, which clarify that while the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) inherent in sentient beings is one, they differ solely due to external conditions, thereby establishing the ultimate distinctions in the self-realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*). However, as for the mind...
The Buddha and sentient beings—these three are without distinction; from the beginning, there has not been the slightest interval between them.
Fundamentally, there is no differentiation between the three vehicles or the five natures. It is only because external conditions and habitual perfuming are not uniform that the five natures differ.
Thus, while the fundamental capacity (*indriya*) is not distinct, the difference lies with the teacher. Therefore, those who previously strove to practice according to reality should...
One should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Therefore, the following passage states:

"When those evil views are overturned, then those of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists shall attain the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; even the icchantikas will also create the conditions for their deliverance.

This is where the meaning of "inducing the provisional to enter the real" is revealed. Regarding the term "lineage" (*gotra*): it is called a "seed" (*gotra*) because of its similarity [to its fruit], and it is called a "nature" (*prakṛti*) because its essence is identical. Furthermore, [it is so called because...]
"Seed" (*gotra*) means "cause" and "category. This refers to the fact that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is fundamentally one;
however, due to the熏習 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) from having heard the teachings in the past, seeds belonging to their respective categories have been formed. Therefore, it is called "lineage" (*gotra*).

Regarding this meaning of lineage, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that there are two types: first, the "innate" (*prakṛtistha*), which refers to that which has been perfumed since antiquity; second, the... [text fragment ends].

"Arising at the beginning" refers to newly perfumed [seeds]. "Originally existing" refers to that which has existed naturally within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) since beginningless time;
it consists of the seeds of defilement and purity perfumed over long eons. This is precisely what is called the "seed abiding in its original nature."

Just as when the Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, those who heard it did not attain full maturity until their present lives, when they finally received the Buddha’s transformation.
This is the perfuming of the pure dharma that constitutes the seeds abiding in the fundamental nature (*prakṛtistha-bīja*).
It is like Ānanda and Mātanga: though they shared affection through successive kalpas, even until this life—still...
These serve as the causes and conditions for obstructing the Path. These defiled dharmas are perfumed to form what is called the "innate seeds" (*prakṛtistha-bīja*).
Because they have continued uninterrupted throughout long kalpas, they are named "innate seeds. Second, regarding those that are "initially arisen":

this refers to seeds formed through repeated perfuming by manifest activity since beginningless time, continuing until the present life, through the perfuming of seeing and hearing the defiled and pure dharmas.
Furthermore, they serve as the seeds for future defilement and purification; these are what are called "seeds produced through cultivation.
With these two types of seeds acting as causes, when one encounters external conditions—such as the instruction of a teacher—they are immediately activated and brought to maturity.
It is from this that the distinctions among the five natures (pañca-gotra) arise. Therefore, one must not fail to be careful in attending upon teachers and choosing friends. For this reason...
Contemplating these five types of spiritual lineage, those three lineages of the Three Vehicles are truly matured by hearing the Dharma spoken by the three preceding Buddhas.
Specifically, by adhering to the provisional teachings spoken by the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha), one forms the Śrāvaka lineage;
by adhering to the teachings on dependent origination spoken by the *saṃbhogakāya* (Reward Buddha), one forms the Pratyekabuddha lineage; and by awakening to...
The Dharma taught by the Dharmakāya Buddha, which is free from objective referents (*ālambana*), constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata.
If one hears these three dharmas and possesses both faith and doubt, one constitutes the indeterminate lineage.
If, upon hearing these three dharmas of the Buddhas, one fails to give rise to faith and instead gives rise to heterodox views and slanders them, one constitutes the absence of lineage. Therefore:
The subsequent scripture states: "To abandon all roots of goodness means to slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. This is because the three Buddhas are of one essence;
every dharma is entirely true, and all serve to reveal the path of self-realized noble wisdom. Yet, those who hear this do not penetrate it; they follow what they grasp and cling to it as a seed.
Furthermore, the Dharma-nature itself does not differ; the difference lies only in the capacity of the individual. Therefore, it is called a "seed."
This is the distinct characteristic of the ultimate stage of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

How is one to know the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle that is uninterrupted? If, upon hearing it explained that the attainment of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) constitutes their abandonment and knowledge, the pores of his entire body bristle with joy and delight, and he takes pleasure in cultivating the knowledge of signs (*lakṣaṇajñāna*) rather than cultivating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The signs of awakening are called the *śrāvakayāna* lineage of immediate succession (*anantara-gotra*).
The commentary states: "This refers to the *śrāvakayāna* lineage of immediate succession. As for the phrase 'if they hear the teaching,' etc."

This is sufficient evidence that [the seeds] are awakened through the熏習 (vāsanā) of the teacher’s instruction; that is to say, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) become seeds. Regarding the "time of knowing and abandoning":

the old commentary states this refers to the time of knowing suffering (*duḥkha*) and abandoning its origin (*samudaya*), as well as the time of realizing cessation (*nirodha*) and cultivating the path (*mārga*). As for "delighting in the cultivation of the knowledge of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇajñāna*):

"characteristics" refers to the characteristic of universal emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and "knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the emptiness of self (*pudgalanairātmya*); these are what the Śrāvakas delight in cultivating. As for the object...
To give rise to the realization of the principle of the true mark of non-arising is not what they delight in; therefore, it is said that they do not cultivate it.
Due to the lingering, narrow, and inferior habitual tendencies of the former Śrāvaka vehicle, as soon as they hear what is taught, these tendencies are stimulated and manifest;
thus, the pores of their entire bodies bristle with joy and gladness.
The Śrāvaka perceives the eighth stage without interval; he abandons the afflictions of arising (*utpāda-kleśa*) but does not abandon the afflictions of habituation (*vāsanā-kleśa*).

He does not transcend the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*), but he transcends the death of分段 (*bheda-cyuti*). He utters the lion’s roar of the Teacher of Gods: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there is no further existence.
Thus, through the practice of knowing reality as it is, he realizes the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and eventually attains the awakening of parinirvāṇa.

The commentary states: This clarifies that the śrāvakas have not yet reached the ultimate in either severance or realization, yet they conceive for themselves the notion of having attained parinirvāṇa through satisfaction.
For while śrāvakas practice according to the Four Noble Truths, they only sever the afflictions of view and thought within the three realms;

they still have not exhausted the subtle delusions of ignorance as numerous as motes of dust, and thus they remain submerged in the saṃsāra of transformation. They have only attained the emptiness of persons, but have not [yet attained the emptiness of phenomena].
While the dharmas are empty, they nevertheless give rise to the notion of ultimate attainment; thus, amidst gods, humans, Māras, and outsiders, they let out a lion’s roar, proclaiming:
"Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished."
They do not undergo further existence and subsequently attain the realization of nirvāṇa; this is what is meant by "being content with little.

Those who see the eighth stage refer to the bodhisattvas of the eighth bhūmi in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Having realized the true suchness (*tathatā*) of self-emptiness, they delight in dwelling in samādhi and do not arise from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Consequently, the Buddhas exhort them, saying: "Arise, son of good family! Do not remain in this delight!"
Abiding in samādhi: this samādhi of yours is also attained by the two vehicles; therefore, it is said here that one sees the eighth stage.
Present activity constitutes active afflictions (*kleśa*), while seeds and habitual tendencies constitute latent afflictions (*vāsanā-kleśa*).
This is because the two vehicles only sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and have not yet severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Mahāmati, as for the various distinct and uninterrupted [views], there are those who perceive a self (ātman), a person (pudgala), a sentient being (sattva), a life-span (jīva), a nourisher (poṣa), or a spirit (puruṣa).
Those beings form such conceptions and seek parinirvāṇa.
The commentary states: This clarifies the lineage of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The Tang translation says:

"Furthermore, there are sentient beings who seek to realize *nirvāṇa*, claiming that they can perceive and know the self (*ātman*), the person (*pudgala*), the sentient being (*sattva*), the nourisher (*poṣaka*), and the grasper (*upādātṛ*); this, they say, is *nirvāṇa*.
These non-Buddhists falsely view all sentient beings as flowing forth from the self, and that the self is able to nurture and sustain all sentient beings."
They consequently established a "divine self" (puruṣa) as nirvāṇa; those who heard this took them as their teachers, and thus they became a heterodox lineage.
Alternatively, there are those within the Buddhist community who, upon hearing the teaching of nirvāṇa, cling to a mistaken interpretation and give rise to false views.
Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who assert that everything arises solely from a creator.
Having perceived all natures, they declare, "This is parinirvāṇa" (the Tang translation says: "Furthermore, some say: having seen that all phenomena exist because of a creator").
The commentary states: This [view] reckons substantiality, qualities, activities, the four great elements, time, direction, and the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*) as the causes of birth;
therefore, they are called "agents" (*kartṛ*). It falsely reckons these very things as *nirvāṇa*.
They form such a realization: "The view of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) is not their lot;
they have no liberation. The commentary states: "This refers to the false views of externalists (tīrthika), which are not liberation.

To say that 'the view of the selflessness of phenomena is not their lot' means that various externalists do not give rise to faith or joy toward the teaching of selflessness spoken by the Buddha; or..."
They give rise to slander. Because they have not yet attained the perfuming that forms seeds [of realization], it is called "inappropriate.
Alternatively, regarding the Dharma of Nirvana taught by the Buddha, they immediately give rise to hope and the notion that there is something to be realized;

or, through practicing according to the teachings, they experience some awakening and cling to what they have awakened to as a self, thereby falling into false views. As clarified in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, these are the four...
Their conceptual signs have not yet been forgotten; all of them lack the portion of the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Thus, while these outsiders are bound by afflictions (*kleśa*), those within [the Buddhist fold] are bound by phenomena (*dharma*); therefore, it is said that they possess no liberation.

Mahāmati, these śrāvaka-vehicle practitioners who belong to the lineage of the uninterrupted non-Buddhists lack the realization that they have not yet emerged [from saṃsāra] despite their sense of having emerged.
To overturn those evil views, you should practice and study accordingly.
The commentary states: This is a summary of the two types of dispositions—those of the śrāvakas and those of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
However, the śrāvakas falsely grasp at nirvāṇa, while the non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize a self (ātman); both, while not yet having attained liberation, give rise to the notion that they have.
These are all due to being erroneously conditioned by false teachers and false teachings. To cause them to turn away from such evil views, he exhorts them to practice.

Regarding "study": among the three characteristics of the aforementioned supreme noble wisdom, it refers to the characteristic of non-existence. This means that one becomes habituated to the characteristics of the two vehicles and external paths;
the meaning is seen here. The intention is to cause them to abandon their biased, deviant, and evil views, which is precisely what is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
One may enter the lineage of the Tathāgatas. Therefore, although such a person may be biased or heterodox, their nature is in fact free from the obstacles of the afflictions (*anantarya*).
Mahāmati, as for those of the Pratyekabuddhayāna lineage who are free from the obstacles of the afflictions:

if they hear it said that there are distinct conditions for their own realization, their body hairs stand on end and they weep with flowing tears; they do not cling to proximate conditions (the Chinese translation says: "they leave behind clamorous conditions and are without any defiled attachment").

When various forms of their own bodies and various supernormal powers—manifesting as diverse transformations of separation and union—are described, their minds enter into accord with these teachings (the Tang translation states:
"Sometimes, hearing it said that they manifest various bodies, whether gathering or dispersing, through supernormal powers and transformations, their minds accept them in faith").
If it is known that they possess the lineage of the uninterrupted *pratyekabuddha-yāna*, one teaches the *pratyekabuddha-yāna* accordingly; this is called the *pratyekabuddha-yāna*.
Regarding the characteristics of the *anantara-gotra* (the lineage of immediate succession): the commentary states, "This clarifies the *anantara-gotra* of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

'Individual causes and conditions' refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), which are the causes and effects of the three periods of time; hence it is called 'individual. Because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*)."

Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). This consists of two types. Those who appear during the era of a Buddha, who practice according to the teachings and realize the Way by contemplating conditions, are called *pratyekabuddhas* (solitary realizers through conditions).
Those who appear in an era without a Buddha, who realize non-existence by contemplating transformation, are called *pratyekajinas* (solitary realizers alone).
Here, as we clarify that seeds are formed through external perfuming, we speak only of *pratyekabuddhas*.
Mahāmati, there are four types of the lineage of uninterrupted succession for that Tathāgata-yāna: namely, the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the dharmas of intrinsic nature;

the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the dharmas devoid of intrinsic nature; the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the noble self-realization; and the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the excellence of external realms.

The commentary states: "This clarifies that the Tathāgata belongs to the lineage of immediate succession (*anantarya-gotra*). However, these four types [of dharmas] are stated as three types in the Tang translation:
namely, the dharma of self-nature and non-self-nature; the dharma of the noble wisdom realized within one's own body; and the dharma of the vastness of all external Buddha-fields.
This is explained by means of the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) to demonstrate that the Dharma-body and the Reward-body are of the same essence."
Indeed, self-nature (*svabhāva*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); being free from self-nature is liberation (*vimukti*); and noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is Prajñā.
This is because the non-attachment of the Dharma-body is liberation, the non-delusion of liberation is Prajñā, and the signlessness of Prajñā is the Dharma-body.
These three virtues constitute the secret treasury, collectively termed the Dharma-body. The excellence of external lands is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The Dharma...
The retribution for past deeds is one; therefore, it is inconceivable.

Mahāmati, if, upon hearing each of these four matters explained individually, as well as when the inconceivable realm established by the manifestation of one’s own mind, body, and wealth is explained, the mind is not startled or terrified, this is called the lineage of the Tathāgata-yāna without interruption.
The commentary states: "This constitutes the formation of the lineage (*gotra*) of the Tathāgata-yāna.
