At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the *Sūtra on the Mind of the Characteristics of Verbal Conceptualization*. World-Honored One, if I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas thoroughly understand verbal [expression]..."
The Sūtra on Explaining the Characteristics of the Mind of Delusive Thought (both translations are titled "The Dharma-Gate of the Mind").

By means of this, one can penetrate the two kinds of meanings—namely, speech and that which is expressed by speech—and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Through these two modes of speech and that which is expressed by speech, one purifies all sentient beings.

The commentary states: This also follows in the footsteps [of the preceding text] to extend a doubt and pose a question, thereby clarifying that false conceptualization (vikalpa) lacks intrinsic nature and refuting pervasive attachment (parikalpita-svabhāva).
This is because the end of the first fascicle states: "One should rely on the meaning; do not cling to words.
The intent is that words are the marks of false conceptualization, yet what is expressed can manifest the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Since it can manifest the ultimate truth...

Why is it called "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*)? Therefore, he asks about the characteristics of the conceptual construction of verbal expression and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that is expressed.
If one can thoroughly penetrate these two meanings, one will be far removed from pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*).
Furthermore, by means of this dharma-gate, one may also purify sentient beings.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are four kinds of conceptualization of verbal expression:

namely, verbal expression of signs (*nimitta*), verbal expression of dreams, verbal expression of attachment to past false conceptualizations, and verbal expression of beginningless false conceptualization."
Regarding "discursive speech": it arises from attachment to the marks of one's own false imaginings. Regarding "dream speech": it arises from recollecting previously experienced objects;
once awakened, those objects are found to be without intrinsic nature. (The Tang translation states: "That is to say, dream [speech] arises from recollecting objects previously experienced.")

Having awakened, one recollects. That which arises based on unreal objects as a conceptual attachment to erroneous speech is produced by following the recollection of the actions previously committed by an enemy (the Chinese translation says:

"it means that it arises from recollecting the actions previously committed by an enemy"; "error" refers to faults). That which is speech arising from beginningless conceptualization is produced from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of one's own seeds—the fault of beginningless false attachment to delusive proliferation (the Chinese translation says:
"it arises from the habitual tendencies of beginningless frivolous discourse and false grasping"). These are called the four.
Regarding the various characteristics of the conceptualization of verbal expression, the commentary states: "This demonstrates the characteristics of the conceptualization of verbal expression.

It refers to the false perception of the bodies, limbs, and facial features—whether beautiful or ugly—of men and women, as well as all characteristics of the vessels and objects of livelihood, whether beautiful or ugly; these arise through the false activation of discrimination."

Discourse refers to discourse based on names and signs. Discourse regarding dreams refers to the false conceptualization and discrimination of auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, beauty or ugliness, and so forth, by recollecting objects previously experienced during a dream after one has awakened.

Discourse arising from the attachment to past false conceptualizations refers to the false production of discrimination and the resulting discourse concerning the actions previously performed by oneself or others—such as enemies or kin, love or hatred—and the like. This is called discourse based on the attachment to past false conceptualizations.
It is said that, since beginningless time, the eight consciousnesses contain the seeds and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of their own class of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
When these suddenly surge forth, discrimination arises; this is called "discursive speech of beginningless delusion.
All forms of speech do not transcend these four [categories], because delusion serves as the cause of speech. Apart from these four, there is no speech. There is none.
The locus of verbal expression is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), yet the ultimate truth cannot be manifested by verbal expression.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested the World-Honored One regarding this meaning:

"I pray that you will further explain the realm manifested by the conceptualization of verbal expression. World-Honored One, where does it arise? For what reason? How does it occur? By what cause do the multitudes [of beings]..."

Conceptualization gives rise to verbal expression (the Wei translation says: "I pray that you will again explain for me the characteristics of the four kinds of false attachments to speech; from where do the speech of sentient beings arise?
How do they arise? By what cause do they arise? The Tang translation says: "I pray that you will further explain the characteristics of the sphere of activity of linguistic discrimination").
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Sound is produced through the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, palate, and teeth" (the Tang translation says:
"It arises depending on the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, uvula, teeth, and tongue").
The commentary states: This demonstrates the characteristics of the causes and conditions of speech.
That is to say, the speech produced by sentient beings takes the four preceding types of false discrimination as their cause, and these eight [parts], such as the head and chest, as their conditions;
thus, verbal expression arises. As Laozi said: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows—it is empty yet inexhaustible; it moves and produces all the more."
This is what is called the "wind of delusive thought" (*vikalpa-vāyu*) arising without cause, fanned by the winds of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, it is said to be non-existent.
By observing the characteristics of speech in this way, one sees that the substance of sound is empty and fundamentally does not exist.

The linguistic expressions of sentient beings are like this; however, as for the spoken words of the Buddha, they are like the sound of a celestial drum. Therefore, his preaching of the Dharma possesses six qualities.
The fourteen kinds of Brahma-voice are particularly not to be compared with discursive thought (*vikalpa*).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, are speech and discursive thought different, or are they not different? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
Verbal expression and conceptual construction are neither different nor not different. Why is this? It is because they arise from the same cause.
Mahāmati, if verbal expression were different from conceptual construction, then conceptual construction would not be its cause.
If they were not different, then speech would not manifest meaning; yet it does manifest it. Therefore, they are neither different nor not different.
The commentary states: This demonstrates that both speech and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, if conceptual construction and verbal expression each possessed their own intrinsic nature, they would necessarily be distinct entities.

If they were not produced dependent upon causes and lacked anything to be indicated, they would necessarily be identical. Now, since speech arises from conceptual construction, it is not a distinct entity; speech is merely...
This is the characteristic of sound. Because the substance of sound is straightforward and lacks ornamentation, it is like wind blowing through a hollow; it reveals nothing in itself.

Through the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it emerges in various winding and complex forms, thereby revealing [objects]. Thus, the subject and object are clearly distinct, yet they are not fixed as one.
Since they are neither identical nor different, both are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, they possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is speech itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), or is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Neither is speech the ultimate truth, nor is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because the ultimate truth is the noble bliss; it is that which is entered through speech."
"Meaning. It is not that verbal expression is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The commentary states: "This demonstrates that the ultimate truth is free from the characteristics of verbal expression.

Mahāmati’s intention is that while ordinary beings can manifest conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through the verbal expressions of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the sages likewise employ verbal expression.

This demonstrates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Now, since conceptual verbalization is neither identical to nor different from it, one must understand whether the authoritative word of the Sage (*āptavacana*) and the ultimate truth are different or not. Therefore, he asks:
"Is speech itself the ultimate truth—thus they are not different—or is that which is expressed the ultimate truth—thus they are not non-different? The Buddha answers:
That is to say, it is neither different nor non-different; both [positions] are incorrect. The Tang translation says: "For what reason?
Because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the state of bliss experienced by the noble ones (*ārya*). One enters it by means of words, yet it is not identical to the words themselves.

This 'state of bliss experienced by the noble ones' is the realm of the Buddhas' own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), which transcends mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), and cannot be reached through verbal expression. Yet, the ultimate truth is expressed through words."
Meaning is like a finger pointing at the moon. Just as a finger can only point toward the moon but cannot reach it, one observes the moon by means of the finger, yet the moon is not the finger.
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is that which is entered through verbal expression; the verbal expression itself is not the ultimate truth.
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is that which is attained through the self-realization of noble wisdom; it is not the sphere of cognition characterized by verbal conceptualization.
Therefore, verbal conceptualization does not reveal the ultimate truth.
The commentary states: This clarifies that verbal expression not only is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), but it also cannot manifest the ultimate truth.
This is to demonstrate that the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is free from the characteristics of verbal expression.

Since the ultimate truth is the realm attained through the self-awakening of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), it is not a realm of awakening accessible through the conceptualization of verbal expression; yet, [ordinary beings] rely upon verbal conceptualization.
How could it be displayed? For there are merely words, and no actual meaning at all. The purport of the "separate transmission outside the teachings" is that to raise the mind is already an error;
to stir a thought is already a deviation. It is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.

Subject and object are both forgotten; mind and phenomena are both severed. It can only be realized through direct correspondence. How could it be reached through deluded thoughts, speech, or conceptual discrimination?

Discursive speech arises and ceases, fluctuates, and originates through a succession of causes and conditions. If it originates through a succession of causes and conditions, it does not manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Mahāmati, because the characteristics of self and other lack intrinsic nature, the characteristics of discursive speech do not manifest the ultimate truth.

(The Tang translation states: "The ultimate truth is devoid of the characteristics of self and other; language possesses characteristics and cannot manifest [it]. Furthermore, Mahāmati, [discursive speech] follows and enters into the self-...
Because the mind is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), the various marks of external natures—whether existent or non-existent—are not revealed by the conceptual proliferation of verbal expression.

(The Tang translation states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is merely one's own mind; all various external marks are entirely non-existent; they cannot be revealed by linguistic discrimination. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon the marks of conceptual proliferation regarding verbal expressions.
The commentary states: This further clarifies why verbal expression cannot reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
There are three reasons why, in the final analysis, verbal expression cannot reveal the ultimate truth: because the ultimate truth is neither arising nor ceasing;
it is profoundly still and eternally quiescent; it is unmoving and unshakable; and it does not belong to causes and conditions.
Arising from a combination [of causes], how could the characteristics of speech—which arise from the conditions of birth, cessation, and fluctuation—ever manifest it?
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is transcendent and free from dependence; it possesses no characteristics of self or other.
How could the characteristics of speech, which involve the duality of self and other, ever manifest it? The ultimate truth is merely... itself.
The realm of mental direct perception is eternally free from all various external marks.
How could it be manifested through the conceptualization of external objects or the language of discursive thought by that deluded mind?
For these three reasons, verbal expression can ultimately never manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, as a concluding exhortation: if one contemplates the ultimate truth...
One must depart from the conceptual characteristics of verbal expression before one may enter;
that is to say, only by departing from the deliberations of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and ceasing the pursuit of the realm of delusive thought, can there be a slight degree of resonance.

Therefore, it was said previously: "One should rely on the meaning and not cling to verbal expression. Thus, one day when the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Listen attentively!"
Contemplating the Dharma of the Dharma-King, the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All natures lack intrinsic nature, And likewise lack verbal expression. The profound meaning of emptiness within emptiness— Fools are unable to comprehend it."
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like a reflection in speech; it is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) taught by me to the sons of the noble ones who possess self-realized wisdom.
The commentary states: This verse directly reveals that only that which is beyond words constitutes the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

It is only by washing away the practitioners' habitual tendencies toward names and language that one can truly realize it. However, this verse is somewhat abbreviated; the Tang translation says: "All phenomena lack intrinsic nature."
Nor is there any verbal expression; the meaning of emptiness within emptiness is not perceived. For this reason, the foolish wander in saṃsāra.
All phenomena are without intrinsic nature, transcending verbal expression and conceptual discrimination. All existences are like dreams and magical illusions; they are neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
Just as a king or a householder, in order to please his children, first gives them things that resemble the real, and later gives them the actual ones—so do I now.
It is likewise so. First, similar teachings were spoken; only later was the Dharma of the personally realized *bhūtakoṭi* expounded for them.

By examining this parable of the king and the elder, it is sufficient evidence that all the dharmas taught during the forty years prior to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* were merely words of similarity and did not reveal the ultimate reality.
Now that they have passed through various refinements and their faculties are matured...

[Having reached] maturity, he then explains the path of self-realization that transcends words—the very teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which first uses the three vehicles to guide the children, and subsequently bestows upon them all equally the great white ox-cart, adorned with precious objects, so that they may gallop about, play, and experience joy.
This is the ritual procedure for the Dharma-teaching of the Sage. [The interlocutor] asks: Regarding these various judgments...

As for the teaching, it merely states that the *Lotus Sūtra* "opens up the provisional and reveals the real," yet we have not heard it said that this sūtra was intended from the outset to perform such opening and revealing.

How, then, can these two be reconciled? The answer is: It is because all Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition—that is, they desire to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As for this "Buddha’s knowledge and vision":
This is precisely what is called "the direct perception of mind-only" and "the noble wisdom of self-realization.
It is the meaning of the true Buddha-nature, the Tathāgatagarbha heart, which is inherently possessed by all sentient beings. There is only this one matter; there is nothing else.
Because the Buddhas and holy ones appear in the world by relying upon and taking this as their cause, the Dharma they teach from beginning to end is direct.

This is merely to reveal and clarify this single matter. Previously, because sentient beings possessed meager virtue and heavy defilements, I did not dare to show it all at once, fearing that they might be startled, doubtful, or disbelieving, which would instead lead them to commit the transgression of slandering the Dharma. Therefore, out of great compassion, I remained patient and concealed it;
only when the collective wills of the assembly became steadfast and pure was it fit to speak the truth. Hence, this sutra reveals it all at once.

The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is the noble wisdom of self-awakening. If there is one who awakens to this mind, they will instantaneously ascend to the stage of Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, without the need for laborious cultivation over many kalpas; this is what is called the Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching (*tunjiao*).

It is termed the "Sudden Mahāyāna" because it seeks to reform the gradual defects of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Nevertheless, as it precedes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is provisionally established [as such].
To reveal and clarify: when the Sages preach the Dharma, the beginning and end are unified, and the preceding and following parts are mutually dependent;

thus, there are teachings that are secret and indeterminate. Furthermore, although the dharmas they teach are of many kinds, they generally do not exceed the four principles of principle, practice, cause, and effect.
Each of these possesses both provisional and ultimate aspects. When each of these four returns to its ultimate limit and enters into the One Reality, then—

The holy man’s task is now complete. Yet, throughout the forty years of his teaching, the dharmas he expounded did not transcend the oppositions of mind and object, subject and object, reality and falsehood, or birth-and-death and nirvana; thus, those who heard him took them to be real dharmas.
As long as one has not yet abandoned the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of conventional designations, one will ultimately remain outside the gate, dwelling in a grass hut.

Upon reaching this sutra, however, everything is overturned from its very depths; the nesting place is shattered, and all attachments are completely transcended. It suddenly reveals the self-awakened noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) of the single mind.
This represents the ultimate limit of manifesting the principle. Nevertheless, that which is revealed here is the opening and clearing away of the three vehicles.
Provisional principles are established to manifest the true principle of the One Vehicle. This true principle, which is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), shall serve as the true cause;
this is precisely what is meant by "taking the mind that is neither born nor extinguished as the fundamental cause for cultivation. Upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, [this point is fully realized].

Thus, by taking this true wisdom as the cause, one supports sublime practice; consequently, even a single flower or a single incense offering, a raising of the head or a bowing of the head, or joining the palms and invoking the name—all lead to the attainment of the Buddha-way. Therefore, true practice accords with the true fruit.
What is here revealed and manifested is the opening up and removal of the provisional practices of the Three Vehicles in order to manifest the actual practice of the One Vehicle. For...
These practitioners of true cultivation hope to attain the fruits of reality; therefore, each person of the Three Vehicles is granted a prediction of enlightenment.

Only after serving many Buddhas will they finally achieve the Way of Buddhahood. Were it not for relying on this true cause, even if they were to pass through further kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they would likely remain forever stranded at the "Transformation City.
Although the essential tenets of these two sutras differ, their underlying principles are in fact in profound accord. As for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, however—
The principle, practice, cause, and effect are each and all true; this is the thorough convergence of previous provisional teachings, all returning to the single reality.

The three vehicles are comprehensively gathered, and the five natures equally enter. The principles, practices, causes, and effects of the human and dharmas throughout the entire dispensation are harmonized and unified, all entering the Tathāgata’s wondrous sea of adornment.
This clearly demonstrates that the Buddha’s teaching from beginning to end is a single, consistent thread. Contemplate this.
If one does not understand these general protocols for expounding the Dharma, even if they have realized their own mind, they will be unable to instruct the ignorant.
This is what is meant by "the penetration of the essence [of the school] but not the penetration of the teaching," which is like the sun being shrouded by clouds;
nor will they reach the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because they have not attained the original intent of the Tathāgata. May those who observe this take note accordingly.
Tired of its prolixity. △ The above section, clarifying that false conceptualization has no intrinsic nature, concludes the refutation of the parikalpita (imagined) nature.
The following section clarifies that both mind and objects are extinguished, thereby revealing the pariniṣpanna (perfected) nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us that which is free from oneness, difference, bothness, and neitherness; existence, non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence;

and permanence and impermanence—that which is not traversed by any externalists, but is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is free from the imagined nature of specific and general characteristics, and enters into the foremost reality."

Regarding this meaning, the *Record* states: "This also follows in the footsteps [of the previous discussion] to pose a question, intending to clarify that both mind and objects are extinguished, thereby manifesting the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

This is because, in the first fascicle, the Buddha rebuked the non-Buddhists for failing to realize that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), and thus falsely [clinging] to the primary..."

The meaning [of this] is that the two views of existence and non-existence, or permanence and annihilation, as well as the adherence to the fourfold logical positions (*catuṣkoṭi*)—such as identity, difference, both, or neither—are the domain of ignorant conceptualization; they are not the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
Therefore, while the dependent and the imagined natures arise, the perfected nature remains unmanifest. Now, Mahāmati has heard the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
It is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects; thus, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.

Having transcended the four propositions, the hundred negations are all dispelled. This is not the realm of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), but rather the realm traversed by the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
Yet, one does not know what the ultimate nature of this realm of noble wisdom is beyond the four propositions.
If the mind comprehends this, then the two natures are suddenly dispelled and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is revealed;
one may thus enter the meaning of the foremost reality. Therefore, this question is specifically raised to clarify the perfected nature.
The continuity of the various stages (*bhūmi*) gradually advances through progressively higher degrees of purification, entering the state of the Tathāgata stage.

This occurs through the power of the fundamental vow that is effortless (*anābhoga*). (The Tang translation reads: "By the power of the effortless fundamental vow. It is like a mani-jewel of manifold colors;

its objective spheres, characteristics, and practices are boundless. (The Wei translation reads: "Like a wish-fulfilling jewel, the characteristics of cultivation within immeasurable spheres proceed spontaneously. This pertains to the divisions of the manifestations of one's own mind.
Characteristics. [I pray that] I and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may, regarding all dharmas— which the Tang translation describes as "all dharmas are the various manifestations of one's own mind"—
be free from such views of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and its specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
so that we may swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and cause all sentient beings to be fully endowed with every form of peace and happiness.
The commentary states: This passage describes the benefits obtained through the causal dharma; it is for this reason that the question is posed.

It means that if one attains thorough penetration of the meaning of being free from the four extremes and enters the reality of the Dharma, one may gradually advance through the various stages (*bhūmi*) until reaching the stage of the Tathāgata.
Therein, by means of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), one brings sentient beings to maturity, just as a *maṇi* jewel manifests transformations according to the mind.

Universally responding to all, one awakens to the fact that there is only mind and its objects. This not only distances one from the views of externalists, but also removes the dualistic vehicle’s (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) deluded views of self-characteristics and common characteristics regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Thus, with little exertion, one swiftly attains bodhi; benefiting both oneself and others, the benefits of the Dharma become abundant. Because of these great advantages, I ask this question.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! That you are able to ask me about such a meaning brings great peace and happiness, and provides great benefit, out of compassion for all devas and people of the world. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!

We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Ignorant ordinary people, not knowing the measure of the mind, grasp at internal and external natures based on identity, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence, and impermanence, as being intrinsic nature. They practice [these views]...
Due to attachment to false conceptualization,
it was recorded that Mahāmati asked about seeking the sphere of activity of noble wisdom apart from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*),
as if there were actually four extremes to be abandoned and actual noble wisdom to be attained. The meaning of the Buddha’s response was that, fundamentally...

There are no four propositions to be abandoned, nor is there any noble wisdom to be attained. Why? Because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), both the false and the true are simultaneously transcended.
As for the four propositions, they arise because ignorant ordinary beings fail to realize that all manifested realms are merely the mind, like a dream;
they falsely grasp at all internal and external phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus give rise to delusion.
The views that differentiate between identity and difference arise from the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) as their cause;
they are merely false attachments and do not constitute the reality of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). This is because the mind and its objects are like space, having nothing upon which to rely.
Since the objects of discrimination do not exist, how could the deluded mind that discriminates them exist? If the single mind does not arise, then—

All phenomena are inherently quiescent; how could there truly be four propositions to be abandoned? It is merely the exhaustion of ordinary sentiments, with no separate "sage-understanding" (ārya-jñāna) to be found.
If one gives rise to sage-understanding, one immediately falls back into ordinary sentiment; therefore, even sage-wisdom is unattainable. Thus, the Tang translation concludes:
"Within the dharmas realized by sage-wisdom, one should remain free from all conceptual divisions such as arising, abiding, ceasing, unity, and difference."
It is distinct. Upon reaching this realm, where words and thoughts are cut off, one finally arrives at the ultimate limit.

Thus, when a monk asked Master Mazu, "Leaving behind the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, I pray that you will directly point out the meaning of the First Patriarch’s coming from the West," the Master replied, "Today my head aches;
I cannot speak for you. Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī questioned the layman Vimalakīrti regarding the gate of non-duality, the layman—
[The assembly] remained silent. Therefore, the World-Honored One, in his response below, used twelve parables to elucidate the point.

The first seven parables illustrate that objects of perception are fundamentally non-existent; they show how the ignorant falsely give rise to conceptual discrimination, thereby demonstrating that such deluded thoughts have no reality.

This clarifies that, fundamentally, there are no four propositions to be abandoned. The subsequent five metaphors illustrate how the Buddha’s teaching is established according to the capacities of his audience;
it is intended primarily to destroy attachment, much like using a wedge to extract a wedge. Originally, there is no substantial dharma given to anyone.
Thus, the verse says: "Verbal teachings are merely provisional names; they likewise possess no characteristics. This clarifies that even noble wisdom is ultimately unattainable. However, this...
The metaphors used in this chapter may appear manifest and easy to perceive, yet in reality they are profound and difficult to clarify.

Those who contemplate them must skillfully realize their meaning and strive to accord with the Buddha’s mind. As it is said: "In receiving the words, one must grasp the essence; do not establish your own rules.
Let the wise contemplate this deeply.
It is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, who see a springtime mirage and perceive it as water; they run toward it in delusion, unaware that it is not water.
In this same way, foolish people, conditioned by false conceptualizations from beginningless time, have their minds scorched by the three poisons.
Delighting in the realm of forms, they perceive arising, abiding, and ceasing, and grasp at internal and external natures, thereby falling into the views of identity, difference, both, or neither.
The notions of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, as well as permanence and impermanence, are all subsumed under false views.
The commentary states: "This metaphor universally reveals that the objective realm is fundamentally unarisen, yet it is grasped through the mind's conceptual discrimination.
Indeed, a mirage is not originally water; however, because a herd of deer is driven by thirst, they perceive it as water and falsely pursue it."
Yet they do not know that it is fundamentally not water. This serves as an analogy for how all objective realms are fundamentally unborn and likewise devoid of anything desirable.
Due to the seeds and habitual tendencies of beginningless craving in foolish beings, the three poisons are internally perfumed and externally manifest as active afflictions.
Driven by thirst and craving, they falsely give rise to greedy seeking and desire toward all forms and objects; this is [the case].

Within the state of non-arising, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing. One grasps at the faculties, the body, and the internal and external phenomena of the vessel-world, giving rise to false views of the four extremes—such as permanence, impermanence, unity, and difference—without realizing that these are fundamentally non-arisen from the beginning.
This is merely the grasping of delusive thought; it is not right view.

It is like a city of the gandharvas: ordinary, ignorant people lacking wisdom give rise to the notion of a city; due to the manifestation of signs from the attachment of beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), [the city appears].

(The Tang translation says: "Because ignorant people, from time immemorial, have clung to the seeds of the city through false perfuming, they conceive the notion of a city. That city neither exists nor does not exist.

In this way, these non-Buddhists, due to their beginningless clinging to the habitual tendencies of falsehood, rely on views of oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence; they are unable to understand that which is the manifestation of their own minds.

The commentary states: This metaphor further explains the meaning above. It means that the reason those deluded people falsely give rise to greedy attachment toward what is not desirable and engage in fourfold conceptual discrimination is that they do not know all objective realms are merely manifestations of the mind.
As it is said: "One's own mind grasps one's own mind; through what is not illusory, illusory phenomena are formed."

Suppose, for example, there were a person who, in a dream, saw men and women, elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, cities, gardens, mountains, rivers, and bathing pools, all variously adorned, and entered into them. Upon waking, he would still recollect them. Mahāmati, what do you think?
Would such a person be considered wise for continuing to recollect and not let go of what was previously seen in the dream? Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "No."

"Indeed, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "In this way, ordinary people are bitten by evil views; the wisdom of the outsiders does not know that the nature of what appears to one's own mind is like a dream.
They rely on views of identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence, as well as the views of permanence and impermanence."

The commentary states: This analogy provides a general explanation of the preceding meaning. It means that non-Buddhists do not understand that what is manifested by their own minds is like the realm of a dream;
they falsely give rise to grasping and attachment, and through craving and pursuit, they arbitrarily conceive views of identity and difference regarding this [reality].
Therefore, these are deluded and evil views, rather than wise insight.
For example, it is like a painted image that is neither high nor low, yet foolish commoners conceive the notion of it being high or low.

In the same way, future non-Buddhists will be filled with the habitual tendencies of evil views; relying on views of oneness, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence, they will destroy themselves and others.
This also applies to those who hold the discourse of transcendence from existence and non-existence and the absence of arising.

[The text] says: "It is non-existent. (The Wei translation states: "Those heterodox teachers destroy themselves and others by speaking thus: 'All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; existence and non-existence are quiescent. Such people are called those with incorrect views. The Tang translation states:

'Regarding the discourse on the absence of birth and the transcendence of existence and non-existence, they also declare it to be non-existent. This is the view that slanders cause and effect. It uproots the foundation of virtue and destroys the causes of purity.

Those who seek excellence (both translations render this as "those who desire the sublime Dharma") should keep far away from such [views]. Thus it is said: They fall into the view that both self and other exist.
Once false conceptualizations have ceased, one falls into the extremes of superimposition and denial. Due to such evil views, one shall fall into hell.
The commentary states: This is a metaphor for the heterodox, arrogant, and stubbornly held evil views of non-Buddhists who, conversely, slander the True Dharma and repudiate cause and effect.
It serves as a stern warning that practitioners must resolutely and utterly sever these tendencies. "The mind is like a master painter, painting forth all forms."
Thus, all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind; in their very essence, they are quiescent and unborn, without high or low.
Yet those non-Buddhists, relying on their own views of arising and ceasing, pride themselves on being superior.

They turn away from the Buddha-dharma’s discourse on the absence of existence and non-existence and the state of non-arising, slandering it as nihilistic. This slander negates cause and effect and uproots the foundation of all goodness. It destroys...

Regarding the cause of purity: one should know that such a person falls into the false conceptualizations of self and other, existence and non-existence, and lapses into the two views of nihilism and eternalism.
Because of these evil views, they shall fall into hell; therefore, I admonish practitioners who seek the supreme Dharma to swiftly distance themselves from them.
For example, it is like a person with cataracts who sees floating hairs and says to others, "Look at this!
Yet those floating hairs ultimately possess neither intrinsic nature nor lack of intrinsic nature, because they are seen by some and not seen by others. (The Wei translation states:

"For example, it is like a person with cataracts who sees a mass of hair in empty space and tells others, 'It is thus, thus—blue, yellow, red, and white. Why do you not look? Mahāmati, that mass of hair is fundamentally without substance. Why? Because it is seen by some and not seen by others. Such is the case with the non-Buddhists.
With false views and expectations, they rely on the views of oneness, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; and permanence or impermanence.
Thus they slander the true Dharma, bringing ruin upon themselves and others.

The commentary states: This analogy explains the aforementioned meaning of destroying oneself and destroying others. That is to say, those non-Buddhists rely on their own false views to teach others to conform to their own;
it is just like one with cataracts seeing hair-tufts in the sky, yet turning around to reproach others for not sharing their vision.
However, these hair-tufts in the sky are seen only by those with diseased eyes; those with healthy eyes do not see them.

It is not seen. This serves as an analogy for the four propositions of identity, difference, existence, and non-existence; these are merely what false views grasp, whereas right view is free from them.
Yet those externalists remain stubbornly attached, asserting their own views while disparaging others, slandering the True Dharma, and teaching it to others in turn.
It is said that from the very beginning, this has been passed down through successive generations, forming a habitual conditioning that leads both themselves and others into ruin.
This is a great harm to the Dharma; therefore, one must earnestly admonish practitioners to distance themselves from it quickly.

The intent is that one should not only avoid associating with such people, but furthermore, one must not harbor the view that these four propositions are truly existent. Thus, they are compared to hanging hair.
It is like a fire-wheel: it is not a wheel, yet the foolish perceive it as a wheel, while the wise do not.

In this same way, the evil views and aspirations of the outsiders give rise to the notion that all natures arise from oneness, otherness, both, or neither; from existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; and from permanence or impermanence.

The commentary states: This metaphor explains the meaning of the fourfold negation of intrinsic existence (*svabhāva*). A whirling firebrand is not actually a wheel; it is merely that deluded people falsely conceive of it as a wheel.

This serves as an analogy for how phenomena lack the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); it is simply that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), through their perverse attachments, falsely give rise to these four conceptualizations.
Therefore, it is said that "all natures arise. Yongjia said: "All numerical phrases are not numerical phrases; what connection do they have with my numinous awareness?
They are like bubbles on water resembling mani-jewels; the ignorant and small-minded, lacking wisdom, conceive the notion that they are mani-jewels and pursue them with attachment."
Yet those water bubbles are neither *maṇi* jewels nor non-*maṇi* jewels, because they are subject to being grasped or not grasped.

In this same way, the false imaginings of the evil views of the outsiders, perfumed by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), speak of birth where there is nothing at all, and speak of cessation regarding that which exists through conditions.
The commentary states: This metaphor illustrates that the non-Buddhists' false attachment to the fourfold propositions regarding cause and effect is not true.

A water bubble merely resembles a *maṇi* jewel; it is not actually a *maṇi*. Yet, those who are foolish, small-minded, and lacking wisdom take it to be real. When a person of wisdom sees clearly, they do not accept it as such.
This serves as an analogy for the fourfold propositions of the non-Buddhists: they merely resemble oneness and permanence, but are not truly so.

This is the Way of Permanence. Because of that lack of wisdom, they grasp at the false as being real. If one realizes that all is a manifestation of mind-only through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then one does not grasp it.
Therefore, it is said: "Because of grasping and non-grasping. However, because they are merely perfumed by deluded habits, they falsely perceive arising within the unborn;
thus it is said: "To speak of arising where there is nothing, and [arising] from dependent origination."

Furthermore, they cling to the annihilation of all phenomena and destroy the principle of dependent origination; thus it is said that those who speak of existence through conditions are speaking of cessation.
Consequently, they falsely construct four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) to argue at random. Moreover, their causes are not true causes and their effects are not true effects;
they falsely grasp what is unreal as being real, just like a child who mistakes a bubble for a mani-jewel. Yet, regarding those four propositions:

It is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If one realizes that conceptual construction lacks intrinsic nature, then the essence of the four positions (*catuskoṭi*) is empty, and there is nothing to be abandoned.
Therefore, the seven preceding metaphors collectively clarify that there are no four positions to be abandoned.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*). Having established these respectively, one attains the self-realization of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svasaṃvedana*), which is free from the two natures (*svabhāva*).
Yet, one still engages in the conceptual attachment to the existence of intrinsic nature (*bhāva-svabhāva-vikalpa-abhiniveśa*).
The commentary states: "From here below, it clarifies that even noble wisdom (āryajñāna) cannot be apprehended. The Tang translation says:

"Having established the three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa), regarding the dharmas that are internally realized by noble wisdom and are free from the two natures (svabhāva), one gives rise to the conceptualization of their having existence. The Wei translation says: [same as above].
And he spoke these words: "There truly exists a Dharma realized within by the Noble Ones, which is free from the two natures because of false conceptualization.

The World-Honored One intended to reprimand Mahāmati, saying: "I have already established for you the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*) to determine right and wrong and cause you to abandon erroneous attachments. Why have you come to this point again regarding self-realization?"
Within the dharmas that transcend the two natures through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), does there again arise the view that a real, existent noble wisdom can be apprehended?
If noble wisdom were to have a real, existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that could be apprehended, this too would be a false view. Therefore, the treatise says:

"To posit a slight entity before oneself, claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), because there is something apprehended, is not truly abiding in consciousness-only. This means that if...
To not forget even the slightest glimpse of insight is still a matter of the shore of birth and death; only when there is neither wisdom nor attainment can one be said to have reached the ultimate.
As for the three measures (*pramāṇa*), they are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), and authoritative testimony (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*).

Regarding direct perception: "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifesting clearly; it refers to the vivid realization of an object that is free from verbal designations and devoid of conceptual deliberation, being immediate and personal.
It is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it attains the essence of phenomena, is free from false conceptualization, and is not erroneous.
As for inference (*anumāna*), "inference" means to infer by analogy; that is, because one comes to know through inference and measurement by means of reasons and examples.
Inference consists of three members. Valid testimony (*āptāgama*) refers to taking the holy teachings of the Tathāgata as the standard. [The five-membered syllogism...]

The "treatise" (*śāstra*) consists of the five members: the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). These are fully set forth in the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*.
When it is said that there is the establishment of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five members, this refers to what was briefly explained earlier in the first fascicle.

In total, these do not go beyond the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five members of a syllogism (*pañcāvayava*). For instance, what is called "the manifestation of one's own mind" and "the noble wisdom of self-realization" are all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

What is called "being like an illusion, water, moonlight, a reflection, a flower in the sky," as well as the use of metaphors such as atoms, lumps of clay, and jars, to elucidate the meaning, are all inference (*anumāna*). As for what is said regarding all Buddhas and Tathāgatas...

The sequence of "provisional first, then real," as well as the various teachings on the Dharma-body Buddha, the Reward-body Buddha, and the Transformation-body Buddha, are all authoritative sacred word (*āptavacana*).
These are all established by means of the three measures of knowledge (*trividha-pramāṇa*).

What is meant by "I take the Tathāgatagarbha, the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as my thesis" and "the non-Buddhists take the self (*ātman*) or the supreme nature (*prakṛti*) as their thesis"—both are indeed theses. As for "I take the ultimate... [the text continues].

The single meaning has the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and so forth as its cause; it takes the seeds of beginningless false habitual tendencies (*anādikāla-vikalpa-vāsanā-bīja*) as its cause.
Furthermore, such things as the conditioned and the unconditioned, the produced and the unproduced, the permanent and the impermanent, and so on, are all causes.
Analogies include space, the Buddha’s relics, the sprout of a plantain tree, and a broken jar; these are all metaphors. Within these three branches, there is naturally an internal synthesis.

The phrasing of these compositions all follows the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*); thus it says, "having established [the position]. This is because the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma does not transcend the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism as its standard model.

Mahāmati, when the mind, intellect, and consciousness undergo transformation, and the manifestations of one’s own mind—the grasping subject and the grasped object—along with all false imaginings are severed, the practitioner abides in the stage of the Tathāgata, which is the noble wisdom of self-realization. Regarding that state, they do not form conceptions of existence or non-existence. (The Tang translation states:

"All practitioners transform the mind, intellect, and consciousness; free from the grasped and the grasper, they abide in the stage of the Tathāgata and the noble dharma of self-realization, giving rise to no conceptions regarding existence or non-existence. Furthermore, if a practitioner...

Regarding those who give rise to the perception of grasping at the nature or non-nature of objects: they grasp at nourishment and grasp at a self, a person, [a being, and a life-span] (the Tang translation states:
"If practitioners give rise to attachments to existence or non-existence regarding objects, they then cling to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span").

Mahāmati, if one speaks of their intrinsic nature, self-nature, or specific and general characteristics, all such things are spoken by the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, not the *dharmakāya* Buddha. Furthermore, all such verbal expressions...

Because it arises from the expectations of the foolish, it is not established as a distinct realm (*gati*) or as a self-natured phenomenon (*dharmasvabhāva*) for those who have attained the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi through the self-realization of noble wisdom; thus, it is not conceptually displayed.

The commentary states: This rebuke addresses Mahāmati’s improper arising of views regarding existence and non-existence within the dharma of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), thereby clarifying that fundamentally no such noble wisdom is to be found.

It means that once practitioners have transformed the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) and departed from the grasping of subject and object, they abide in the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realization; how could they then again [seek] that self-awareness?

Does one form conceptions of existence or non-existence within noble wisdom? If one gives rise to grasping at existence or non-existence therein, then one is attached to the views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
What is called "preserving the self" and "awakening to the self" are both termed obstacles.

Just as the subtle four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are clarified in the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, because one still retains realization and has not yet forgotten the subject-object duality, if one were to speak of "the nature of that very nature" (*tasya svabhāvasya svabhāvaḥ*) and below, it would obstruct the turning of the difficult objection. That is to say, the difficult objection states: "True Suchness (*tathatā*), self-nature (*svabhāva*)."
"Nirvāṇa, realization, the Buddha-lineage, dependent origination," and so forth—all these are the words of the Buddha. Why, then, do you now say that no wisdom can be attained?

The World-Honored One replied: "If one were to say that within the dharma of the noble self-realized wisdom there truly exists an intrinsic nature that arises in dependence upon conditions, this would be what is spoken by a *nirmāṇa-buddha* (an emanation Buddha), not what is spoken by a *dharma-buddha*. However, the *nirmāṇa-buddha*..."

To speak in this manner is also not my original intention. It is merely because sentient beings, out of ignorance and desire, seek something to be realized and grasp at it as a fruit, only then being willing to advance toward the path.
If one were to say that there is no self, no wisdom, and no attainment, they would give rise to terror.
Therefore, having no other choice, I have provisionally established these teachings in accordance with their capacities; they are not, in fact, ultimate dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that [these views] all arise from the expectations and perceptions of foolish people;

they are not intended as a detailed exposition for those of superior faculties who have generated the aspiration to advance toward the self-nature of phenomena, who practice according to reality, and who have attained the dwelling in the bliss of the samādhi of self-realized noble wisdom.
The meaning is that this sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna is specifically for those of the highest faculties.
This demonstrates the realm of noble self-realized wisdom, which is free from mind, thought, and consciousness; it is the true Dharma taught by the Dharma-Buddha.
How could one possibly cling to those provisional teachings in the hope of attaining realization? Question:

Regarding the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), why is it also said that they possess both specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)? Answer: The intrinsic essence of all phenomena is realized only through wisdom; it cannot be expressed in words.
It is beyond reach. One should realize the suchness (*tathatā*) of its essence; this is called the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If the nature of a phenomenon (*dharmasvabhāva*) is within the reach of verbal expression and is an object of conceptual cognition (*prajñaptijñāna*), its specific characteristic cannot be attained; this is called the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Now, within this school of the Sudden Teaching Mahāyāna:

This is suddenly revealed as the ultimate mind (paramārtha-citta), which is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and possesses only the essence of its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), entirely lacking the essence of common-characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).

Since the own-characteristic is attained solely through direct perception (pratyakṣa), it is said to be "revealed for the sake of those who, having entered the dharma of self-nature, attain the blissful dwelling of the samādhi of noble wisdom’s self-realization. Question: Regarding the own-characteristic spoken of by the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇabuddha)—
"What is the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*)? The answer is: The transformation Buddha explains that the self-nature of *tathatā* is quiescent and unchanging;
this is called the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*). That it manifests as all mundane and supramundane phenomena according to defiled or pure conditions is called the common characteristic.

Now, Mahāmati, one who thinks that there is a real, attainable noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is precisely clinging to the Buddha-nature as a causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*), [waiting] for conditions."
This is because there is something realized.
It is like the reflection of a tree appearing in water; it is neither a reflection nor not a reflection, neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree.

In the same way, the views of the non-Buddhists, perfumed by habitual tendencies and characterized by false conceptualization and attachment, rely upon the notions of identity, difference, both, or neither.
There are notions of existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, and impermanence; yet one is unable to know that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
The commentary states: "The following five metaphors are used to demonstrate that, fundamentally, there is no holy wisdom (āryajñāna) to be attained.

This metaphor illustrates the Buddha manifesting his body like a reflection in water: the water represents the minds of sentient beings, and the tree represents the Buddha’s Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and Bodhi-body (bodhikāya), as well as his vows.

The body. This is because the Dharma-body is not a body; it manifests through the power of vows. Therefore, when the water of sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears within it.
As for what is manifested, it is originally the manifestation of the self-mind of the Dharma-body that has always been inherent in sentient beings.
Because the interaction between stimulus and response is inconceivable and consists solely of the single mind, both the shadow and the tree are non-existent.
Externalists do not realize that all things are manifestations of the mind alone; therefore, they falsely cling to views such as identity and difference.

For example, just as a bright mirror manifests all forms and images according to conditions, yet remains free from conceptual construction—being neither an image nor not an image, yet appearing as both image and non-image—the deluded fool, through conceptual construction, forms the notion that it is an image. In this same way, the evil views of the outsiders manifest as images within their own minds;
they conceptually construct and cling to them based on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence.
This is not a view of impermanence as non-existent.

The commentary states: "This metaphor illustrates that the Buddha responds to things without a [discursive] mind, accomplishing matters according to conditions and manifesting distinctions according to the capacities of beings, like a mirror reflecting images.
The Wei translation says: "Because one sees when there is a condition, and does not see when there is no condition."
For example, when wind and a hollow vessel come together, sound is produced; yet that sound is neither an intrinsic nature nor a non-nature.

In the same way, the false imaginings of the evil views of the non-Buddhists rely upon the notions of oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.

The commentary states: This metaphor illustrates the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, which arises through the conjunction of conditions, just as sound exists only after the meeting of wind and water.
Therefore, all vocal teachings are fundamentally devoid of substantial reality; the ignorant falsely take them to be real.
Thus, the Tang translation says: "It is like an echo in a valley."

For example, on the great earth where there is no grass or wood, there are mirages of flowing rivers with surging waves like clouds. (The Tang translation says: "When touched by the rays of the sun, the flames and waters ripple and move.
These are neither of the nature [of water] nor of a non-nature, because they are characterized by both greed and non-greed.

In this same way, foolish people, perfumed by the habitual tendencies of beginningless falsehood, engage in false conceptualizations and attachments based on arising, abiding, and ceasing; on identity and difference; on conjunction and non-conjunction; and on existence and non-existence.
There is that which is neither non-constant nor constant. This refers to the gate of abiding in its own phenomena, which is likewise like a mirage, waves, and surging currents.
The commentary states: "This metaphor illustrates how all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding.

Thus, where there is no grass or trees upon the great earth, mirages flow like rivers and surging waves rise like clouds. Yet, the nature of dharmas (dharmatā) is unborn; regarding these unborn dharmas, one falsely..."
One perceives arising and ceasing. Thus, the Tang translation says: "Within the gateway of the dharma-nature realized by noble wisdom, one perceives arising, abiding, and ceasing;
unity and difference; existence and non-existence; both and neither, and so forth."

For example, it is like a person who, through incantations and mechanical devices, creates something that does not belong to the category of sentient beings (the Chinese translation says: "a wooden puppet; it has no essence of a sentient being").
It is a piśāca ghost (piśāca means "one who devours vital energy"; the Chinese term is "dian-ghost") that, through skillful means, brings about movement and activity.

Just as the deluded thoughts of the ignorant falsely cling to coming and going, so too do the evil views and aspirations of the non-Buddhists rely upon the notions of identity, difference, both, or neither.

To hold views of existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, or permanence and impermanence is to be attached to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and to establish what is unreal.

It is recorded that this metaphor illustrates that the Buddha’s body is neither a body nor not a body; it merely brings sentient beings to fulfillment through the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Fundamentally, it possesses no marks of coming or going, appearing or disappearing. Yet ordinary fools, failing to understand this, falsely take it to be real.

Mahāmati, therefore, those who wish to attain the reality of the noble wisdom of self-realization should abandon the evil views and false imaginings of arising, abiding, and ceasing; oneness and difference; bothness and neitherness;
existence and non-existence; being and non-being; permanence and impermanence, and so forth.

The commentary states: This refers to the practitioner of contemplation who, having abandoned the deluded views and conceptualizations of the four extremes—such as identity, difference, and so forth—will naturally enter the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). This is because the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the Buddha are a single suchness without duality.
If one contemplates that the three realms and five aggregates are empty, illusory, and unreal, their very substance is suchness itself. This is precisely it.

Regarding the noble wisdom of self-realization: if, within the gateway of the dharma-nature of the noble wisdom of self-realization, one gives rise to views of a Buddha or views of dharmas, and discriminates between identity and difference and so forth, one immediately falls into the false views of the non-Buddhists.

This is because, regarding the realm manifested from the single mind of quiescence, to give rise to views based on the four propositions is merely conceptual construction; it is not a real dharma. Therefore, fundamentally there are no four propositions.
It can be transcended. If, for even a single thought-moment, no thought arises, and emotions are forgotten and attachments fall away, one is inherently as they are (*tathatā*).

As it is said: "Simply exhaust all ordinary sentiments; there is no separate 'sage's understanding. Therefore, there is likewise no sage-wisdom to be attained. Upon reaching this state, both ordinary sentiment and sage-understanding—
Only when all [notions] are simultaneously and completely swept away does one achieve the ultimate state of self-awakened noble wisdom (*svayambhū-āryajñāna*).
If even a hair’s breadth of a view remains unextinguished, one immediately falls into the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Now, there are three different types of non-Buddhists:
first, those outside of the Buddha-dharma; second, those who are attached to the Buddha-dharma; and third, those who study the Buddha-dharma and become non-Buddhists. First, those outside...
Regarding the Way (Mārga), there are three fundamental sources: first, Kāpila, here translated as "Yellow-Headed," who maintains that the effect exists within the cause;
second, Ulūka-Sāṃkhya, here translated as "Huhu," who maintains that the effect does not exist within the cause; and third, Ṛṣabha.
This is called "asceticism" (*duṣkara*). They calculate that within the cause, the fruit both exists and does not exist. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra* states:
"The Kāpila school holds to the error of 'oneness' (*ekatva*), meaning that the action and the agent are one, and the characteristic and the characterized are one;
such as these are termed 'calculating oneness. The Ulūka-sāṃkhya school calculates 'difference' (*anyatva*), while the Kāru-bodha school calculates 'both oneness and difference.'"

It is also different. If the son of Vatsa calculates that things are neither identical nor different, all the divergent calculations of the various non-Buddhists do not depart from these four positions.
Branching out from these, down to the time of the Buddha's appearance, there were six great masters:
first, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who calculated that there is neither birth nor death; this is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Second, Maskarī Gośālīputra...
1. Ajita Keśakambalin reckoned that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings have no causes or conditions and occur spontaneously; this is the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). 2.
Pakudha Kaccāyana reckoned that sentient beings attain the Path through the ripening of time, like the exhaustion of the number of threads on a ball of yarn.
3. Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta reckoned that the suffering of karmic retribution is atoned for by throwing oneself from cliffs and plucking out one's hair.
Fifth is Kālāma Kauṇḍinya, who calculates that things both exist and do not exist. Sixth is Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, who calculates that the results of karma performed are fixed and cannot be altered.
In sum, these do not transcend the two views of existence and non-existence, or of annihilation and permanence;
they are non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). Second, as for those non-Buddhists who are attached to the Buddha-dharma, they originated with the Vātsīputrīya school.
The Vaipulyavādin was a man who, relying on his own cleverness, read the Buddhist scriptures and developed a distinct view that arose based upon the Buddha-dharma;

thus he received this name. The Vātsīputrīya read Śāriputra’s Abhidharma and formulated his own interpretation, asserting that the "Self" exists outside the four propositions within the "Ineffable Store.
What are the four propositions? The non-Buddhists calculate that [the Self] is identical to form (*rūpa*).
"I am," "form is the self," "the self is within form," and "form is within the self. The same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandhas*).

These constitute twenty types of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This is precisely the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states that by destroying these twenty views of a self-identity, one becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Now, the doctrine of the Vatsīputrīyas regarding the self is different from that of the six heretical teachers, yet it is not the Buddha-dharma; all treatises reject it.

Thus, it is the dharma of heterodox persons who have attached themselves to the Buddha-dharma. Those who study the Buddha-dharma through the three trainings yet become followers of external paths are said to give rise to afflictions by clinging to the gates of the Buddhist teachings and failing to enter into the principle. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one does not attain Prajñā..."

Through skillful means, one enters Abhidharma and thus falls into the view of existence; one enters emptiness and thus falls into the view of non-existence; one enters *vibhajya-vāda* (analytical discourse) and falls into the view of both existence and non-existence.
The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "To cling to that which is neither existent nor non-existent is called the doctrine of the deluded;

by perversely grasping the True Dharma, one instead becomes a heterodox person. Therefore, if one studies the four gates of the Mahāyāna without grasping the intent of Prajñā, [one will not attain liberation].
One immediately falls into the four types of denial and is consumed by the fires of perversion, thereby becoming a person of perverted dharmas.

Thus, the Hīnayāna clings to the two extremes of the provisional and the real; the Mahāyāna clings to the two extremes of emptiness and existence. The Hīnayāna’s clinging to the existence of phenomena external to the mind is attachment to existence (*bhava*).

The Mahāyāna’s repudiation that both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are entirely non-existent is attachment to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, one becomes a student of the Buddha-dharma [only by avoiding these].

This is the view of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Because they all fail to penetrate the realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as the manifestation of Mind-only, they falsely give rise to these calculations.
Now, this sutra subdues the heterodox and reveals the orthodox, refuting them all at once; therefore, the seven metaphors in the preceding section refute the external non-Buddhists.

This includes an appended discussion on the four propositions of the non-Buddhists regarding the Buddha-dharma, intended to demonstrate that the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) is fundamentally free from the four logical extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Furthermore, five subsequent metaphors refute those who study the Buddha-dharma yet become non-Buddhists, thereby proving the quiescent single mind (*ekacitta*).
Thus, there is no noble wisdom to be attained; if all views are extinguished, the single mind manifests of itself. The observer should know this and not—
Tired of such tediousness, at that time the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Like an illusion, a dream, the reflection of trees in water, A mass of hair, or a mirage in the heat— Thus one should contemplate the three realms of existence; Ultimately, one attains liberation."

Just as the mirage of a thirsty deer causes its agitated and deluded mind to perceive water where there is no actual substance of water, so too do the seeds of consciousness move and perceive objects;
thus do the delusions of the ignorant arise, like that which is obscured by a cataract.
In beginningless saṃsāra, one clings to and grasps at a self-nature; like using a wedge to extract a wedge, one abandons the grasping of desire.
Viewing things as being like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, or flashes of lightning, one attains liberation and forever severs the continuity of the three marks.
In that state there is no agent, like a mirage in the sky (the Tang translation says "like a mirage in the air"). To know all phenomena in this way is to have nothing known.
The commentary states: This universally employs various metaphors; originally, the verse did not contain four lines that could be omitted.
Both the Wei and Tang translations first present the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and subsequently present the three realms as being unreal, like shadows and like illusions.
This is because sentient beings, regarding this single body and mind of the five aggregates, are unable to realize it as being like a shadow or an illusion, and thus falsely conceptualize it as such.
Because of this reality, they are unable to attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death within the three realms. However, the dharmas of the five aggregates are fundamentally unarisen;

it is only within this state of non-arising that one falsely perceives arising and ceasing. Thus, it is like a thirsty deer who, in a place where there is no water, falsely conceives the notion of water.
In this same way, all sentient beings are driven by the seeds of the karmic consciousness and the perfuming of habitual tendencies. Therefore...
Ordinary beings falsely perceive birth and death; those of the external paths and the two vehicles falsely perceive nirvana. Thus it is said that movement and stillness are seen as objective realms.
These all arise from the deluded conceptualizations of ignorant people, like one with cataracts falsely seeing flowers in the sky.
Therefore, within beginningless birth and death, they engage in false calculations and grasping, claiming there is a real intrinsic nature, and thus give rise to notions of identity and difference.
There are four types of wrong views, such as existence, non-existence, annihilationism, and eternalism.

Out of compassion for those who are deluded, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma that transcends these four extremes to shatter their hearts of greedy attachment, just as one drives out a wedge with another wedge; thus, he causes them to abandon grasping and clinging.
It is not that there are four propositions to be abandoned as real entities. Rather, those dharmas are fundamentally without action and are not substantial realities;
they are merely like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, lightning, or mirages. As it is said:
"Birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday. If one can contemplate in this way, then all dharmas are quiescent in their very essence.
It is extinguished. There is, in reality, no characteristic of either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Therefore it is said: "To know all phenomena in this way is to have nothing to know.
Because there is nothing to know, all views naturally vanish; the four propositions are instantaneously dispelled, which is precisely what is called the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
The verbal teachings are merely provisional names; they likewise possess no inherent characteristics. Yet, regarding them, one gives rise to false imaginings.

The aggregates and formations are like falling hair, like a painting of falling hair, a magical illusion, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, a whirling firebrand, or a mirage in the heat—though non-existent, they appear to sentient beings.

The same applies to permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, as well as their conjunction and non-conjunction. This beginningless succession of faults is the deluded false imagination of the foolish.
Just as various colors appear within a bright mirror, water, clear eyes, or a wondrous mani jewel, they exist though they are in reality non-existent.
All natures appear like a painting or a mirage in the heat; various colors manifest, yet they are non-existent, like a dream. The commentary states:
"This verse also indicates that no noble wisdom (āryajñāna) can be apprehended. The Tang translation says: "The aggregates are like [the appearance of] hair-tufts [in the eyes]."
Within this, false discrimination arises; it is merely a conventional designation. When one seeks its characteristics, they cannot be found.
That is to say, the phenomena of the five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent, being false and unreal, like illusions, dreams, and the like.

Because ordinary fools do not realize that these are but manifestations of mind-only, they falsely give rise to discrimination and thus produce the four types of clinging. If one understands that all those phenomena are merely what is manifested by the mind, [the four clingings will cease].
Like a bright mirror, still water, or a pure *maṇi* gem, although they manifest various forms, they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning.
Their very substance is perfectly luminous; this is precisely the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*). Beyond this, no other noble wisdom can be found.

The preceding section, which universally refutes the two views to reveal the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), is hereby concluded. The following section concludes by demonstrating that [this state] is free from faults and transcends all negations.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these four positions: namely, identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence;
as well as permanence and impermanence. It is free from the conceptualizations of affirmation and denial regarding existence and non-existence.

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma takes as its primary focus the compilation of the True Truths, dependent origination, the Path, cessation, and liberation. (The Wei translation states: "The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma relies upon...")

Because the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the liberation of the cessation of causes and conditions, he teaches the Dharma [showing that it] is not a substantial nature (*svabhāva*), not a sovereign creator (*īśvara*), not without cause, not atoms (*paramāṇu*), not time (*kāla*),
and not a continuity of self-nature (*svabhāva-saṃtati*).
