[Only when these are exhausted] can one finally emerge from the three realms. Why, then, do you speak here specifically of severing only the three fetters? Answer:
Regarding the five dull [afflictions], we speak specifically of "doubt" because once the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, greed and delusion will naturally not arise.

Since the Buddha’s teaching has tamed the mind, hatred does not manifest. As for the conceit of pride (*māna*), it is not mentioned because it is not severed until the four fruits [of the path]. This is because one has not yet entered the Buddha’s...

Regarding the time of the Dharma: initially, the honored one—the celestial Māra—was suspicious of the Buddha; now that he has been led to enter right faith, he no longer doubts the Buddha, but rather doubts the Dharma.
Having already perceived the principle of the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya), he also does not doubt himself; therefore, it is specifically said that he has "severed his doubts.

As for why only the five benefits are mentioned and not the other three, those [other three] were all the false views of non-Buddhists (tīrthika); since he has now relied upon the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, this [is the case].

It is not mentioned. Furthermore, "delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Because one is attached to *nirvāṇa*, although craving for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) has been severed, craving for *nirvāṇa* has not yet been severed;
therefore, both are not objects to be abandoned. Hence, it is not mentioned.
He ascends and advances further, attaining arhatship.
The commentary states: "This collectively demonstrates the characteristics of severing the fetters and attaining the fruit.
"Ascending and advancing further" means that he is able to suddenly sever the highest-grade of the highest-grade afflictions (*kleśa*), thereby realizing the highest-grade fruit of arhatship.

Mahāmati, there are two kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (the view of a self-identity): namely, that which is innate and that which is conceptualized (the latter being translated in the Tang version as "discriminated"). This is like the conceptualization of dependent origination and the conceptualization of the imagined nature.
The Record states: "This demonstrates the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in order to explain the characteristics of the practice for the first fruit [of the path].

'Entity' (*satkāya*) refers to the five aggregates of body and mind; that is to say, it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). 'Co-arising' refers to 'name,' meaning the four aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth.

These have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the beginning, but take conventional designations as their essence. Because of this, a uniform false attachment has persisted since time without beginning; therefore, it is called [the view of a self-entity]."

The innate view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is that which discriminates through false conceptualization; this refers to form (*rūpa*). It means that these illusory forms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not exist from the beginning.
They are merely produced through false conjunction by the power of causes and conditions. For example, it is like a magician who uses a false name for a person.

Fools, failing to understand this, falsely calculate that there is a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and they discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly, giving rise to perverse greed and desire.

Therefore, it is said that the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises from the attachment to the various imagined natures (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) based upon the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*).

This is because those [imagined natures] are neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; they are unreal, being merely the marks of false imagination (*vikalpa*). Thus, through the false imagination of fools, there arise these various imagined natures.

Attachment to the characteristics of intrinsic nature is like a mirage, where a thirsty deer perceives it as water; this is the false discrimination of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) of a srotāpanna.
By means of the non-self of persons (pudgalanairātmya), they grasp at the absence of intrinsic nature and thereby sever their long-standing attachment to ignorance.
The commentary states: This explains the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

However, the illusory and false physical bodies of oneself and others have never existed from the very beginning; they are merely forms produced by the provisional combination of the four great elements through the illusion of karma based on deluded thought (*vikalpa).

They are like illusory persons arising in dependence upon conditions—just as, for example, a skilled worldly magician conjures various men and women, while the foolish person [perceives them as real].”
They do not understand; they give rise to false discrimination and cling to beauty and ugliness. Therefore it is said: "Based on dependent origination, there is the nature of clinging.
Furthermore, those dependently arisen provisional aggregates suddenly exist where they were previously non-existent; in reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Since they are neither existent nor non-existent, they lack substantial reality. Yet, out of ignorance, ordinary beings falsely give rise to clinging and grasp them as being real.

Just as a mirage in the heat is fundamentally not water, yet thirsty deer falsely conceive the notion that it is water—this is what is called the mark of the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) of a *srotāpanna*.
The Wei translation states: "Because of ignorance, from beginningless time they have falsely grasped at marks;
this defilement of the view of a self-identity can only be abandoned by seeing the non-self of persons. Therefore, it is said: "This is..."

The *srotāpanna* possesses the deluded view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This is eliminated by apprehending the absence of intrinsic nature through the realization of the non-existence of a person (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
One severs this long-standing ignorance and attachment at the stage of the initial path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), having realized the emptiness of the self (*ātma-śūnyatā*);
thus, by singularly destroying the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one cuts off the discriminative view of a self.

Mahāmati, as for that which is co-emergent: it is the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) of the srotāpanna. This is because the four aggregates (skandhas) of one’s own body and those of others are devoid of the characteristics of form;

because form arises from the primary elements and their derivatives; because they are mutually dependent causes and conditions; and because the great elements and form do not aggregate [as a single entity].
The Record states: This explains the mode of activity (*ākāra*) for abandoning the innate view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). The Tang translation says:

"By universally observing that the four aggregates, such as sensation (*vedanā*), lack the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); because form arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); and because these primary elements are mutually causal.
That is to say, one should analogously observe the four aggregates, such as sensation, in both oneself and others; however—

Names exist, yet they originally lack substantial reality. Furthermore, although the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) possesses provisional characteristics, it is merely produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
these elements arise through mutual conditioning to form this shape. Once this shape has arisen and birth is received, the other four aggregates coexist simultaneously;
thus, they are said to be "co-arisen" (*sahaja*). However, within the four great elements, there is no sovereign ruler; who then could...

Is it that they aggregate to form "form" (*rūpa*)? Therefore, it is said that "form does not aggregate. If even the *rūpaskandha*, which possesses substantiality, is empty, how much more so the other four aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*), which originally lack the characteristics of form and exist only as names; are these not empty?

Nevertheless, this [notion of] "co-nascent" (*sahaja*) merely refers to the four aggregates depending upon form, spoken in terms of the false attachment to the self-characteristics of body and mind; it is hardly [the same as] co-nascent [ignorance].
This is ignorance. A student should know this:

for a *srotāpanna*, when observing the categories of existence and non-existence, they do not manifest; thus, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed. When the view of a self is severed in this way, craving does not arise.
This is called the characteristic of the view of a self.

The Record states: This refers to the accomplishment of the practice of contemplating the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "With categories" refers to form (*rūpa*); "without categories" refers to the four aggregates (*catvāraḥ skandhāḥ*).
It means that a *srotāpanna* is able to contemplate their own and others' five aggregates as entirely empty and without a master; thus, the view of a self-identity is severed.
If the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, then craving does not arise. When craving does not arise, the cause of birth is forever cut off, and one no longer undergoes rebirth.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The cause of all sufferings is rooted in craving; if craving is extinguished..."

Because there is no basis for dependence, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, and one realizes the first fruit [of the path]. This is called the characteristic of severing the view of a self-body.

Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of doubt: it means that because one has attained the characteristic of right vision regarding the Dharma, and because the two previous kinds of false conceptualizations of the view of a self-body have been severed, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise.
One does not give rise to the view of another teacher as being pure or impure. This is called [the characteristic of severing doubt].
"Doubt is severed by the stage of Srotāpanna. The commentary states:
"This explains the mode of activity (*ākāra*) for severing doubt. The treatise says: 'Doubt has the nature of hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths (*satya*).
It functions as an obstacle to non-doubting, certain faith (*niścaya-śraddhā*). There are three kinds of doubt: namely, doubt regarding the principles, doubt regarding..."

Regarding "not doubting the Dharma": one who has attained the characteristics of having clearly seen the Dharma means that, regarding the true Dharma (satyadharma) thus attained, they are well able to investigate and perceive that ultimate truth;
therefore, they have no doubt concerning the principle. Furthermore, because the two previous types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have been abandoned, doubt cannot arise regarding any phenomena.
This constitutes not doubting the Dharma, for it is only when one is directed toward the principles of the Dharma that doubt occurs.

Furthermore, they doubted that person; knowing only those whom they revered—such as celestial māras and non-Buddhist teachers—to be their great masters, they instead harbored doubts toward the Buddha, wondering whether he was pure or impure.
Now that the principle has been seen as true, one no longer doubts the Dharma, and thus no longer doubts that person.
Therefore it is said that one does not give rise to the notion of a "Great Teacher" regarding anyone else; this is called the characteristic of doubt abandoned by a *srotāpanna*.

Mahāmati, as for the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): why does a *srotāpanna* not cling to precepts? It is because they clearly perceive the painful nature of the places where rebirth occurs;
therefore, they do not cling to them. Mahāmati, "clinging" refers to the foolish who resolutely undertake and practice ascetic austerities for the sake of...
Because they delight in various requisites and enjoyments, they seek rebirth; however, such a person does not grasp at them, except for the dedication toward their own supreme self-awakening.

Through the skillful means of practicing the characteristics of the outflow-free Dharma that is free from false discrimination, they uphold the branches of the precepts. This is called the Stream-enterer’s severing of the grasping at the characteristics of the precepts.
The commentary states: This explains the aspect of abandoning the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Now, while tainted precepts and virtues are indeed the causes for rebirth as humans or devas, the reason a *srotāpanna* does not cling to them is that they clearly perceive the characteristics of suffering inherent in the places of birth.
As for those who do cling, it is because ordinary fools are greedily attached to worldly pleasures within the various realms of existence; thus, they maintain ascetic practices.
Precepts. They vow to be reborn there; therefore, ordinary people vow to be born among humans and devas, and thus observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action.

Furthermore, foolish outsiders, fearing the appearance of suffering in the future, observe the precepts of oxen, dogs, and so forth—such as plucking out their hair, fumigating their noses, lying on thorns, or throwing themselves upon needles—performing various ascetic practices, thinking that if they exhaust the suffering of this present life, [they will be free].
To come here and experience uniform pleasure is the wrong precept of grasping at signs; however, a *srotāpanna* does not grasp such signs.
Nevertheless, they do possess the category of upheld precepts, which seek only the most supreme, untainted, and non-conceptual Dharma.

Therefore, what they cultivate is the "precept conjoined with meditative concentration" (*samādhi-saṃvara*), which is by no means the wrong precept of grasping at signs held by the foolish and deluded. This is so.
This is called the severance of the characteristics of grasping at precepts. The *srotāpanna* severs the three fetters; thus, greed and delusion do not arise.
If a *srotāpanna* were to think, "I am not possessed of these fetters," there would be two faults: falling into the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the failure to sever the various fetters.

The commentary states: This fetter is named "severing faults. Now, craving arises from the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi); delusion arises from doubt and the grasping at precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Since these three fetters are now severed, the causes are eliminated and the conditions do not arise. Thus, the three fetters have been abandoned.
If one harbors a mind that seeks to sever [defilements], one likewise falls into the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and is consequently unable to sever the various fetters (saṃyojana).
These constitute two faults. Therefore, the Wei translation states: "If one acts in such a manner, one does not depart from the three fetters."

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of many kinds of desire. Which of these desires is to be abandoned? (The Tang translation says: "There are many kinds of greed;

which greed is to be relinquished? The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is that which delights in women, being entangled in and greedily attached to them, employing various means to commit evil deeds of body and speech, experiencing pleasure in the present while planting the seeds of suffering for the future—that [desire] shall not arise. For this reason..."
Why? Because they have attained the bliss of samādhi and right reception (*samāpatti*). Therefore, that [craving] is severed;
it is not the craving for nirvāṇa that is severed. The commentary states: "This indicates the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) that is to be severed.
The Sūtra says: "All sentient beings sustain their lives through sexual desire. That which causes the birth and death of all sentient beings to never cease is craving and..."
This refers to sensual desire (*kāma*). The stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), knowing that present sensual pleasure is the cause of future suffering, forever severs the mind of lust;

therefore, it is said that "it does not arise. Why is this? Because the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*) cannot be compared to the pleasure of the five worldly desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*);
by attaining the bliss of meditative concentration, one is thus able to sever that sensual pleasure.
However, they have only severed desire and greed, but have not yet severed the craving for nirvana. Why is this?

It is because those of the Two Vehicles are attached to the bliss of samādhi and cessation, and thus do not give rise to even a single thought of delivering sentient beings; therefore, the Buddha rebuked them, saying:
They drink the wine of nirvana and recline upon the bed of non-action. Yet they are also called "scorched sprouts and ruined seeds.

For this reason, it is specifically stated here that they do not seek nirvana through the severance of craving. Observing that they do not sever the craving for nirvana, one sees that these individuals of the first fruit—whether of sharp or dull faculties—simply sever the three fetters and directly realize the fourth fruit.
Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of a sakṛdāgāmin? It means that one suddenly illuminates the characteristics of form and the characteristics of the arising of false discrimination;

because one sees that the characteristics [of grasping] do not arise and has clearly perceived the characteristics of the progression toward dhyāna, one returns to this world only once more to exhaust the limits of suffering and attain nirvāṇa. For this reason, he is called a sakṛdāgāmin.
The commentary states: This explains the characteristics of the two fruits. *Sakṛdāgāmin* means "one who returns once. "Suddenly" (*don*) refers to the single return.
"Form-characteristics" (*se-siang*) refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). "Discursive thought" (*wang-miang*) refers to the four aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*).

This means that by means of the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one suddenly illuminates the arising-characteristic of the five aggregates and does not give rise to mental discrimination; thus, the Wei translation says "not" (*fei*).
Because false conceptualization and views do not arise, it is said that "the marks of vision do not arise. This is because one skillfully perceives the characteristics of the stages of dhyāna.
Such individuals are ordinary beings of sharp faculties who, without passing through three, five, or seven births, sever their fetters and do not enter the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

Having resolved upon the path at once, they immediately ascend to the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*). They require only one more return to realize *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that they "come here suddenly."
"O World-Honored One, one reaches the end of suffering and attains *nirvāṇa*. Viewed from this perspective, the aforementioned *srotāpanna* possesses three faculties (*indriya*).
Because these faculties vary in sharpness or dullness and afflictions (*kleśa*) vary in thickness or thinness, there are differences in the distance required to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Now, these two fruits [the *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*], along with the subsequent *anāgāmin*, all pertain to those ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) whose faculties are sharp and whose afflictions are thin, who have..."
The mind then ascends directly to the fruit. Regarding those who attain realization in a single lifetime, it is likely not a gradual progression from the former to the latter.

Why? Because it was previously stated that those very delusions give rise to the śrāvaka lineage; therefore, this refers merely to the stages as defined by the shallow and deep observation of the five aggregates.

Mahāmati, what is meant by an Anāgāmin? It refers to one who, having perceived the faults of arising regarding the characteristics and the nature—or the lack of nature—of form in the past, future, and present, causes false conceptualization not to arise; and because of the severance of the fetters, such a person is called an Anāgāmin.
The commentary states: This explains the characteristics of the three fruits. *Anāgāmin* means "one who does not return.

However, whereas the previous *sakṛdāgāmin* was only able to contemplate the non-arising of the five aggregates in the present without generating discrimination, but had not yet contemplated the future, they must therefore return once more before attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Now, this *anāgāmin*, possessing roots and faculties of great sharpness, is able to...

One contemplates that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) throughout the three periods of time is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, one perceives that all places of future rebirth are characterized by the afflictions and calamities of suffering.

Thus, through wearying of suffering and severing its accumulation (*samudaya*), one prevents the deluded thoughts of the latter four aggregates from arising. This enables the immediate and sudden severance of the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*).
One attains realization in this very life and shall not return again; hence it is called "non-return" (*anāgāmin*). This, moreover, proceeds from...
"O Mahāmati, as for ordinary persons who enter directly into the third fruit and suddenly realize non-arising:

an arhat, Mahāmati, is so called because they possess the powers and insights of the various dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations; and because their afflictions, suffering, and false imaginings have no inherent nature.
For these reasons, they are named arhats."
The commentary states: This explains the characteristics of the four fruits of spiritual practice.

That is to say, this stage of Arhatship is the ultimate destination reached by those of both the sudden and gradual faculties across the three preceding stages. Upon reaching this stage, one spontaneously masters all dhyānas and samādhis, as well as the eight liberations;
furthermore, one is able to partially realize the ten powers, the three knowledges, and the six supernormal powers.
All have been fully accomplished. As for the various sufferings summoned by the arising of afflictions and the production of karma, these have all been eternally severed.
All delusive thoughts have been extinguished without remainder; therefore, they are named Arhats. Now, regarding these four fruits:
All of these are based on the direct observation of the false dharmas of the five aggregates to clarify that the śrāvaka lineage arises from that very same delusion;
it is merely because of the sharpness or dullness of their faculties that there are the three aforementioned distinctions.

In reality, they are all collectively termed "śrāvakas" to manifest the common characteristics underlying these differences, and this is not like what is taught in other sutras regarding the existence of fixed, distinct stages.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of three kinds of arhats. Which of these is being referred to here?

World-Honored One, is it the one who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility (the Wei translation says ‘attained definitive cessation’; the Tang translation says ‘exclusively tending toward tranquility’)?
Or is it a bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifesting as an arhat through skillful means? Or is it a transformation created by a Buddha (the Tang translation says ‘that which is transformed by a Buddha’)?”

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Only those śrāvakas who have attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility [are so described], and not others. (The Tang translation states: "This refers to those who have entered tranquility, and not to others.

As for the others, they practice the bodhisattva conduct and are emanations manifested by the Buddha; because of their skillful means and original vows, they manifest birth within the great assembly to adorn the Buddha's retinue.
The commentary states: "This [passage] clarifies that these are not the true fruit. Mahāmati’s intention lies in distinguishing between the genuine and the spurious;
therefore, he asks which of the three types of Arhats this belongs to. The Buddha replied: "That which I have described refers to those Śrāvakas of fixed nature who seek quiescence;
having severed the fetters of the four abodes (*catur-vāsana-bandhana*) and emerged from the suffering of birth and death, they attain Nirvāṇa—these alone are so named."
Those called "Arhats" are not true Arhats. In the *Avataṃsaka*, Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) are the true Arhats;
they are those who practice the bodhisattva path within this [teaching] through skillful means and vows.
This refers to those who secretly maintain the conduct of a Bodhisattva while outwardly appearing as Śrāvakas. Those who are emanations created by the Buddha serve to adorn the buddha-fields and—
Because they belong to a retinue of followers, those two śrāvakas are not what is being discussed here by me.
However, since the fruit of these śrāvakas is not genuine, their cause is likewise not genuine; therefore, the following passage concludes with a refutation of this error.
Mahāmati, within the realm of conceptual construction, various teachings are expounded, such as "attaining the fruit" and "attaining dhyāna.

This is because both the practitioner of dhyāna and dhyāna itself are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (as the Tang translation states: "because both the practitioner of dhyāna and dhyāna are by nature detached"). What is manifested as the attainment of the fruit is actually the realization of the manifestation of one's own mind;
this is designated as "attaining the fruit."
The Record states: "These bonds of the Two Vehicles are not true causes; therefore, their fruits are not ultimate.

However, those śrāvakas who have entered quiescence merely realize partial emptiness and have not yet attained the true principle of the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), because ignorance remains entirely intact."
Based on the locus of deluded conceptualization, they preach various doctrines; therefore, these dharmas are not the true Dharma.
Because they merely exhaust birth and death and claim it to be liberation, they have in fact not attained all-encompassing liberation, yet they falsely claim to have attained the fruit.

They merely give rise to the extinction-concentration (nirodha-samāpatti) but have not attained the Śūraṅgama Great Samādhi, yet they falsely claim to have attained dhyāna. Amidst that which is unattainable, they are deluded...
There is an attainment; because those who do not penetrate dhyāna and those who have completely abandoned dhyāna falsely grasp nirvāṇa as the true fruit.
However, that extinction they attain is not true extinction; it is merely a manifestation of attaining a fruit spoken of from the false perceptions of their own minds.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "As one progresses and advances through successive stages, the characteristics [of delusion] are not eliminated. Thus.

This is the dhyāna practiced by foolish persons. The Treatise states: "To manifest before oneself a slight object and claim it to be the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, this is not truly abiding in consciousness-only. If even Bodhisattvas are thus, how much more so those of fixed nature?"
Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who wish to transcend the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless realms should abandon the appearances of what is manifested by their own minds.

(The Tang translation states: "If one wishes to transcend all the dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless realms, one should abandon all appearances manifested by one's own mind. Mahāmati, it is not the case that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) transcends what is manifested by one's own mind.
Why? Because there is still the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
The commentary states: This summarizes the aforementioned dhyānas practiced by non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and foolish worldlings;
as none are true causes, it serves as a warning to abandon such faults and sever these deviations. "Dhyāna" refers generally to the meditations of both the two vehicles and non-Buddhists.

"Immeasurable" specifically refers to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) cultivated by those in the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*). These include the tainted (*sāsrava*) dhyānas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the formless [attainments].

The "realms" (*dhātu*) specifically refer to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Although the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) mentioned above are distinguished as mundane or supramundane, in reality, they all collectively fail to transcend the characteristics of mental construction (*citta-mātra*).

Therefore, those who practice according to reality as instructed here should, if they wish to transcend the meditative absorptions of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists, remain far removed from what is manifested by their own minds (*svacitta-dṛśya-mātra*).
This refers to the characteristic (*nimitta*). The *Tattvasaṃgraha* states: "Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is of two kinds: the real and the apparent.

This [state] is apparent direct perception because the mental measure (*cittamātra*) has not yet been forgotten and there is still the grasping of characteristics (*nimittagraha*). Therefore, one must strive to transcend it. The word "however" (*ran*) here signifies permission.

This means that not only is the heterodox meditation (*vitatha-dhyāna*) of non-Buddhists forbidden for personal practice, but even the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) of the two vehicles—should it transcend the manifestation of one's own mind within my Dharma—is strictly not permitted. Why?
Because they still possess the measure of mind (*citta-mātra*); therefore, they must certainly be kept at a distance. As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Those practitioners who are unable to attain..."

Whether one attains unsurpassed *bodhi*, or even separately becomes a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, or becomes an outsider, a celestial being, a *māra-king*, or a member of the *māra*-retinue—it is all due to not knowing the two kinds of roots and practicing in a confused manner.
It is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal; even if it passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed, for sand is not rice.

Because this is the fundamental principle, those who wish to realize non-arising should take the distancing from mental characteristics as the primary meaning. Therefore, I specifically urge you on this point.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the cessation of all sensation and perception—none of these exist within the Mind-Only (*citta-mātra*).

The commentary states: This verse summarizes the meditations of the deluded worldlings. The "four immeasurables" refer to the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
they are practiced by the gods of the Great Fruit (*bṛhatphala*) heaven in order to eliminate the anger, distress, dissatisfaction, hatred, and attachment of sentient beings.
To cultivate these four minds constitutes the contaminated dhyāna of ordinary beings; it is hardly the Buddha’s four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*).
This is because the characteristics of the various dhyānas of those non-Buddhists and followers of the Two Vehicles are all merely individual false views;
they grasp at the appearances of their own minds, yet in reality, those [appearances] fundamentally do not exist.
The fruit of srotāpanna, the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (anāgāmin), and the arhat—all these have deluded minds.
For the meditator, there is meditation and its object; by severing [delusion] and knowing the true reality (satya), this is merely the measure of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
If one awakens to this, there is liberation.

The commentary states: This verse distinguishes the two vehicles as not being ultimate. It means that although the noble ones of the four fruits have attained realization, their minds have not yet departed from delusion and confusion.

Thus, even when they enter the contemplation of self-emptiness through the meditative concentrations they practice, the signs they observe—such as the skeleton, impermanence, suffering, and impurity—are all not free from conceptual attachment.
Furthermore, the true reality perceived upon the severance of afflictions likewise does not depart [from this state].
This is false seeing. Because one grasps at the characteristics of nirvana, it is said: "The practitioner of dhyāna [clings to] the object of dhyāna;

they sever and know the true reality (satya) through their views. This is merely the measure of deluded thought (*vikalpa*). If one awakens to the fact that these are not real, one immediately attains ultimate liberation.
"Knowing" refers to discrimination (*vibhāga*). The above concludes the general explanation of the dhyāna of foolish people. Next, the observation [of the dhyāna of the wise] is explained.
The Meaning of Dhyāna.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening: namely, the awakening of investigation and the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the marks of false discrimination.
The Record states: This demonstrates the two types of awakening—true and false—to explain the characteristics of the "contemplative meditation" among the four preceding types of dhyāna.
The Tang translation says: "There are two kinds of awakened wisdom: namely, the wisdom of contemplation, and the wisdom that grasps signs, discriminates, clings, and establishes [concepts].
However, dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent; they merely follow the movement of wisdom. If one relies on the correct...
If one observes with wisdom, then all phenomena are not existent. If one observes with false wisdom, then all phenomena are not non-existent.

If they were not non-existent, the four propositions would arise perversely; if they are not existent, then the single reality stands alone. When the single reality is established, the four propositions are transcended;
when the four propositions are transcended, the mind and its objects are severed. Since the mind and its objects are severed, both person and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished.
This is the dhyāna of investigating meaning (*arthapravicaya-dhyāna*). Because it is intended to destroy the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), the preceding text states:

"Having [realized] that the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) lack intrinsic nature—whether from one's own perspective, another's, or both—one then contemplates the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

The meanings of the signs of those stages progressively advance; this is called the dhyāna of investigating meaning. This will be clarified later in the text. However, here both the real and the false are presented together.
This is intended to cause one to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox.

Mahāmati, as for "discerning awakening," it refers to the discernment of the self-nature and characteristics of the nature of awakening; when these are analyzed and found to be unattainable apart from the four extremes, this is called discerning awakening.
The commentary states: This explains the observation of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).

It means that non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles falsely cling to all phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus arbitrarily generate the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Now, by observing all phenomena with correct wisdom, one sees that they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature.
Since phenomena lack intrinsic nature, the four alternatives have no basis. Through discernment and investigation, one remains outside the four alternatives.

Ultimately they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, the seeing that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature is called the dhyāna of examining the meaning (*arthacintya-dhyāna*).
Mahāmati, those four positions refer to being free from identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, as well as permanence.
Impermanence. These are called the four propositions. Mahāmati, that which is free from these four propositions is called all dharmas (the Chinese translation says:
"Therefore it is said that all dharmas are free"). Mahāmati, one should study and practice the examination of all dharmas through these four propositions.
The Record states: "Practitioners of this teaching should contemplate all phenomena by departing from the four propositions; this is called right contemplation.
If one contemplates otherwise, it is erroneous contemplation. Therefore, one should diligently cultivate and study."

Mahāmati, what is the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false discrimination? It refers to the grasping of the characteristics of false discrimination;

namely, the attachment to the unreal characteristics of the four great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—and the establishment of doctrines, reasons, characteristics, and analogies based on unreal attachments.
This is called the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false discrimination.
These are called the two kinds of characteristics of awakening.
The commentary states: This clarifies the false wisdom of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). However, those non-Buddhists do not understand that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.

They falsely conceptualize all phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Consequently, regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and air—they grasp at their characteristics, become attached to them, and engage in false discrimination. By means of propositions, reasons, and examples, they falsely establish these [notions].
This is called the false wisdom of attachment to the establishment of grasping at characteristics. Relying upon this false wisdom, they thus falsely conceptualize all phenomena.

The fourfold views of existence, non-existence, identity, and difference are false views. The intention is to cause the practitioner to abandon these false views; this itself is called right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Therefore, to be free from the four extremes is what is called the meditation on the meaning of investigation. Regarding the thesis, reason, and example: it refers to how non-Buddhists establish their own conclusions through these three members.
Because they are based on erroneous understanding, neither [the reason nor the example] is universally established (*aprasiddha*). Thus, [it is said] "therefore, the reason..."
The *Vidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Knowledge) points out those thirty-three errors; therefore, it is said that they are established through unreal construction.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes these two aspects of awakening, he reaches the ultimate realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*).

Being well-versed in skillful means (*upāya*), he observes the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) through the awakening to non-existence and attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*). (The Tang translation states: "By knowing this characteristic of wisdom, one is able to penetrate human affairs.")

There is no self in phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). By means of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*), one skillfully observes during the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Therein, one enters a hundred samādhis, attains distinguished samādhis, beholds a hundred Buddhas and a hundred Bodhisattvas, knows the events of a hundred kalpas of both the past and future limits, and illuminates a hundred buddha-fields.

The commentary states: This clarifies the characteristics of attaining the fruit through the perfection of contemplation. It means that when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first resolves their intent, they skillfully observe all phenomena with non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) as being fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

They thereby suddenly sever the dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-ubhaya-grāha*), and thus enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) from the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), proceeding through each subsequent stage up to the stage of the Tathāgata.

"Understanding" refers to the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), and "practice" refers to the ten practices (*daśacaryā*). Although these are called "understanding and practice," the intent is to show that one does not pass through the three stages of worthiness (*trayaḥ pṛthagjanabhūmayaḥ*), but rather ascends directly to the stage of Buddhahood at the very moment of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*). As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"At the moment of the initial resolve, one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one knows that all phenomena are the self-nature of the mind, and [thus] achieves [enlightenment]."

Regarding the phrase "entering the hundred samādhis" and so forth: the old commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that when a bodhisattva enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), they realize one hundred gates of illumination (*vidyāmukha*). These are: first, realizing one hundred samādhis within a single kṣaṇa;
second, seeing one hundred buddha-fields with the purified divine eye; third, by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) being able to... [the text continues].
1. He can shake a hundred Buddha-worlds. 2. He can travel to a hundred Buddha-fields to teach and transform sentient beings. 3.
He can manifest a hundred types of physical forms from a single body so that sentient beings may see them. 4. He can bring to maturity a hundred types of sentient beings who are to be transformed. 5.
If he wishes to benefit others, he can maintain his physical presence in the world for a hundred kalpas. 6. He can know the limits of the past and the future.

Regarding the events of a hundred kalpas: ninth, one is able to enter the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas through wisdom; tenth, one is able to contemplate the hundred classes of kinsmen with the body.
In the remaining stages, these qualities increase twofold at each level, as fully elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

One knows the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*), the excellence of great vows, mastery over spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*), and the consecration by the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha-abhiṣeka*).

One shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization (*tathāgata-svayaṃbhū-bhūmi*). Skillfully binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣaya-pada*), one brings sentient beings to maturity.
Adorned with various transformations and radiant light, one attains the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-realization (*svayaṃbhū-ārya-sukha-samādhi-samāpatti*).
The commentary states: These words describe the modes of practice from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the ultimate stage of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "skillfully binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases to mature sentient beings," this refers to skillful preaching of the Dharma—being able to expound inexhaustible phrases from a single phrase, and being able to expound inexhaustible dharmas from a single dharma, and so forth. Such are the modes of practice in the ninth stage of the *Avataṃsaka*. Question:

Question: This sutra is a teaching of the sudden dharma-gate; that which it expounds directly reveals that through sudden awakening to the one mind, one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood.
Why, then, does it repeatedly enumerate the characteristics of the ten stages at every point where correct wisdom manifests or where contemplative practice is perfected?
Is this not falling into a system of gradual progression? Answer: In this sutra, even the Noble Truths are not established.

What hierarchy could there be? This is merely citing the fruit to verify the cause. Furthermore, the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) are also called the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), for it is the ground of True Suchness (*tathatā*)—equal and signless—upon which the Buddha traverses.
If we can suddenly transcend all signs and our minds accord with the One Reality, we shall roam together with the Dharma-body; at every step and in every instance, we are naturally [enlightened].
Regarding its vast activity, it is not a gradual progression from stage to stage. By citing this supreme fruit, one seeks to reveal the true cause.
As for false causes or the absence of a cause, how could they possibly lead to such a state?
Furthermore, let the practitioner know that even this should not be considered sufficient; rather, one should aspire to ever-higher advancement so as to surely abide in purity.
One awakens to the supreme bliss of the noble samādhi and then comes to rest. The above concludes the explanation of the dhyāna of observing [the nature of] phenomena.
Below follows the explanation of the dhyāna of clinging to suchness (yathābhūta). First, one contemplates the suchness of the four great elements.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in the four great elements and derived form (*bhautika-rūpa*).
How is a bodhisattva skilled in the four great elements and derived form? Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this realization: "In ultimate truth, those four great elements are unarisen.
Regarding the non-arising of those four great elements, he performs such an investigation. Having investigated them, he realizes that names and signs are false.
One should contemplate the limits of conceptualization as being the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind; external natures have no inherent existence.

This is called the limit of conceptualization manifested by the mind, namely, the triple world (*tridhātu*). [The Tang translation states: "Contemplate that those great elements (*mahābhūta*) are truly unarisen, for the triple world is merely discrimination, seen only by the mind, and there are no external objects.

One contemplates that the nature of the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements is detached from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*), is thoroughly pure, and is free from "I" and "mine. It is the limit of divisions according to the true characteristic and its own characteristic.
"Abiding. The self-characteristic of non-arising is established. The commentary states:
"These words mean that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are fundamentally non-arising; this explains the *tathatā* (suchness) of objective conditions (*ālambana*) in dhyāna.

'Objective conditions' refers to deluded thought (*vikalpa*). 'The four great elements' refers to names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). However, deluded thought is originally right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and names and characteristics..."

It is inherently suchness (*tathatā*). Because those deluded beings do not realize that the three realms are manifested solely by the mind, they falsely perceive the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four derivative objects (*bhautika*) as truly existent. Thus, they falsely cling to the primary elements as the cause of birth.
This is to mistake correct wisdom for discursive thought (*vikalpa*), transforming suchness into names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*). Therefore, they merely give rise to grasping.
Due to their erroneous interpretations based on causal conditions and their various false attachments, they hold views regarding what is as it is and what is not as it is.
Now, the Bodhisattva observes those great elements with right wisdom and sees that they are quiescent in their very essence and truly unarisen.

He penetrates the insight that all names and marks within the triple world are merely products of deluded conceptualization and appear solely from the mind; fundamentally, there are no external objects.

When one contemplates in this manner, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*) are all found to be devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If the primary elements are devoid of intrinsic nature, then the four types of clinging are suddenly severed;

both object and self are empty. In this way, deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) becomes correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and one realizes that names and signs are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).
With the single mind abiding in the state of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*), all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely non-arising. Thus, the Tang translation [states]:

It says: "Abiding in the state of suchness, one accomplishes the mark of non-arising. This is why contemplating the non-arising of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is termed the "dhyāna of攀緣如" (*pán yuán rú*, *ālambana-tathatā*).
Since that which is the object of apprehension (*ālambana*) is itself suchness, it is not a case of "suchness as an object of apprehension.

Therefore, it says: "Skilled in the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), etc. Because one has realized that the four great elements do not arise, it is called "skillful. Non-Buddhists do not realize this, and therefore they are "unskillful."

Mahāmati, how do those four great elements give rise to derived matter (*bhautika*)? It is said that the great element of the delusion of moisture gives rise to the internal and external water element;
the great element of the delusion of capability (the Tang translation says "intense heat") gives rise to the internal and external fire element;

the great element of the delusion of movement gives rise to the internal and external wind element; and the great element of the delusion of the severing of form gives rise to the internal and external earth element.

The commentary states: This statement—that the four great elements arise from false imagination—is intended to refute the heterodox views that falsely reckon the four great elements to be the cause of birth.

It clarifies that the four great elements and derived matter are unwholesome, thereby establishing the meaning of awakening through the realization that the preceding characteristics of false imagination are grasped and clung to.
This is because those heterodox practitioners do not understand that the five aggregates and all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind alone.
They thus falsely calculate that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause of birth and are able to create all phenomena. Therefore, this critique asks:
"How can those four great elements they calculate produce derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)? The word "how" (*yathā*) is used here as a term of inquiry to pose a challenge.
However, I merely state that the four great elements arise from false conceptualization; they do not [arise] from the four great elements themselves.

Birth. This means that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) constitutes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); it is not the case that the four great elements themselves constitute the four great elements.
Furthermore, since conceptual construction lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the four great elements are fundamentally non-arising from the start.

Now, those deluded people, through their perverse attachments and erroneous understandings, not only perceive the arising of the four great elements, but moreover falsely cling to the notion that the four great elements can produce further production. This is why they are not skillful.

The four great elements produce derivative matter, from which four false reckonings arise. Thus, regarding what is "as it is" (*tathatā*) and what is "not as it is," these are merely the discursive expressions of fools;

they do not belong to the noble ones (*ārya*). Therefore, the conclusion below states: "This is not what I have taught. However, the text of this sūtra is concise and archaic, and the Buddha’s intent is profound and subtle;
it is most difficult to penetrate its underlying logic. The old commentary cites the passage on the continuity of worlds from the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
To explain this section: although there is textual authority for the literal interpretation, its actual meaning is difficult to reconcile.
Why is this? Because that passage explains the causes for the arising of the world and describes the manner in which things arise sequentially;

whereas here, it merely states that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), in order to refute the heterodox views that falsely reckon the four great elements as the cause of birth.

[The term] "ear" [is used]. While the two locations [of the terms] are identical, their meanings differ. If one clings to those explicit words [from other texts], one will instead obscure the intent of this sūtra.
May those who contemplate it refrain from making arbitrary judgments; the subsequent text shall naturally provide proof. The text says:

"That is to say, the four great elements such as earth and the derived matter possess conditions that are the four great elements, yet they are not those very four great elements themselves; rather, it is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that constitutes the four great elements."
As for causes: it is not that the four great elements act as causes for one another.
Both form and empty space are equally attached to false truths; thus the five aggregates accumulate, and the derived matter of the four great elements arises.

The commentary states: This follows the preceding text to cite the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), thereby clarifying that the four great elements cannot create or produce form, and thus refuting the four propositions of the non-Buddhists' false calculations, such as "form is the self" and so forth. "False Truth" (xiadi) refers to the "Obscure Truth" (mingdi).

This refers to the twenty-five *tattvas* (principles) established by the Sāṃkhya teachers. Specifically, it holds that the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is the primary principle, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter).

From *pradhāna* arises *buddhi* (intellect); from *buddhi* arises *ahaṃkāra* (ego-consciousness); from *ahaṃkāra* arise the five objects of the senses (*pañca-viṣaya*); from the five objects arise the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*);
and from the five great elements arise the eleven faculties (*ekādaśendriya*). Now, among these, form and space constitute four of the five great elements.

Furthermore, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves the eleven faculties (*indriya*). Yet those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) falsely reckon that the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) give rise to the five aggregates;

because they hold that space (*ākāśa*), being formless, can only harmonize with matter, they claim merely that the collection of the five aggregates arises from the "derived matter" (*upādāya-rūpa*) created by the four great elements.
"Together" (*saha*) means harmony and conjunction. Moreover, the Vaiśeṣika masters reckon the six categories (*padārtha*) to be the causes of production, namely: one...

There are nine categories: first, substance (*dravya*); second, quality (*guṇa*); third, activity (*karman*); fourth, the great elements (*mahābhūta*); fifth, commonality and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*); sixth, inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, within the category of substance, they maintain that there are nine dharmas, namely: the five great elements, time (*kāla*), space (*dik*), and inherence (*yoga*). These nine are able to produce all phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Therefore, the four types of false views—such as the deluded attachment that "form itself is the self," "the self exists within form," and so forth—are now about to be refuted by the World-Honored One.
First, he sets forth their calculation, saying: "Form and space coexist;

this is an attachment to false truths, falsely claiming that the five aggregates are an accumulation and that the four great elements produce derived matter. In the following text, he first refutes the notion of form.
This refers to the statement, "The self does not exist within form, etc. Subsequently, it refutes that the four great elements and derived matter can produce the five aggregates.

First, however, it refutes that form is identical to the self. Since non-Buddhists falsely reckon the eight consciousnesses to be the divine self (*ātman*), [the text] refutes this by means of the consciousnesses.
"Mahāmati, as for consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it takes pleasure in various traces and objective spheres (*viṣaya*), it continues into other realms of existence (*gati*).
The commentary states: 'This refutes the four views regarding form (*rūpa*)—namely, that it is not identical to the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

However, those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) falsely reckon that the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) can give rise to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); therefore, they falsely reckon that the self exists within form, and that form is itself the self."
The Buddha said that the so-called "self" (ātman) they postulate is, within my teaching, simply consciousness (vijñāna).
If one were to say that form (rūpa) is the self, then at the time of death, the four great elements of form would perish, yet consciousness would not perish.

Because this consciousness, due to its craving for and attachment to the objects of the six sense-fields, creates wholesome and unwholesome karma, it further brings about future retribution. Furthermore, in...

When one takes birth in other realms of existence, the continuity remains uninterrupted. If form were identical to consciousness, then when that form perishes, consciousness would perish along with it;
would this not be annihilation? Since birth in other realms continues in an uninterrupted succession, it is evident that consciousness does not perish.
Since consciousness does not perish, it is clear that form is not the self. It is not so.
However, form is not identical to the self; moreover, the four great elements and derived form cannot produce the five aggregates. Therefore, the following passage refutes this:

"Mahāmati, the four great elements such as earth, and the derived forms, have conditions consisting of the four great elements, yet they are not those very four great elements that serve as their conditions."
The Record states: This says that the four great elements cannot create derived matter.

For the non-Buddhists reckon that the four great elements are the creators and the five aggregates and all phenomena are the created; thus, these four great elements serve as the generative conditions for other four great elements. Condition.
This refers precisely to the [erroneous] cause. Therefore, the Buddha cites that calculation and refutes it, saying:

"The idea that the four great elements and the form-phenomena (rūpa-dharma) derived from them—the five aggregates (skandhas) and so forth—possess their own inherent nature as causes for those [aggregates], is merely a false imagination.
It is simply not the case that those four great elements serve as the cause for the five aggregates. Why? Because those four great elements cannot produce form to give rise to the five aggregates."
Therefore, the following section investigates and refutes this.

Why is that? It is because in the case of the characteristics of nature, form, and place, the skillful means employed lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise.

Mahāmati, it is through the combination of the characteristics of nature, form, and place, and the skillful means employed, that things arise; they do not arise from the formless. Therefore, the four great elements are created.
"Color-form (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) is the false imagination of the non-Buddhists; it is not mine.
The commentary states: This inquiry refutes the reason why the four great elements cannot create the five aggregates. "Nature" refers to the intrinsic substance of the four great elements.
"The locus of shape and characteristics" refers to the various forms—such as long and short, high and low, large and small—upon those dharmas.
"Method" (*upāya*) refers to the manner of construction. Since the Buddha stated that the four great elements cannot construct form, this [text] interrogates and refutes it, asking:

"Why can they not construct it? This is because when one investigates the self-nature, characteristics, and the method of construction of the four great elements as the constructors, none of these can be found; for they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Since they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are fundamentally unarisen;
being fundamentally unarisen, how could they possibly give rise to other phenomena? Thus, the notion that the four great elements are creators is false.
If it is claimed that the five aggregates and all other derived phenomena arise from the four great elements, this too is untenable. Why? Because the primary elements, as creators, must exist.
Regarding objects that possess substance, characteristics, and shape: since the creator is now possessed of form, the five aggregates created by it must likewise possess form;

they cannot be formless. The intention [of this argument] is that even if one grants that the four great elements can act as creators, they can only create the single aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) among the five aggregates. As for those other four aggregates which are formless, how could they possibly [be produced by them]?
To claim that [the self] is created by them is a false calculation. Furthermore, they calculate that form (*rūpa*) is the self;

yet even when form ceases, consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not cease. From this, it is sufficient to know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not created by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Now, observing that the four great elements themselves are fundamentally incapable of creating form, we see that those who calculate that form is created by the four great elements are merely following the deluded thoughts of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is merely a perverted view; it is not what I have taught. Therefore, it is said, "Not mine.

Based on the Buddha’s preceding statement that the four great elements, having form, cannot create that which is formless, the subsequent passage provides an explanation to establish this, clarifying the contemplation of the five aggregates as suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*). What are the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates? They are the five aggregates. What are the five?

They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Among these, four aggregates are non-material; that is to say, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness.

The commentary states: The Buddha said that that which has form cannot create that which is formless; therefore, he spoke of the self-nature and characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to clarify that four of these aggregates are not created by matter (*rūpa*).
This was intended to reveal that the five aggregates are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).
Mahāmati, as for form (*rūpa*), it consists of the four great elements and the derivative forms, each having distinct characteristics.

Mahāmati, it is not that non-form (*arūpa*) possesses the number four, like space. For example, space transcends numerical characteristics and is free from numbers, yet through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one speaks of "one space."

The commentary states: This explains that the four aggregates (skandhas) are formless and are not produced by matter (rūpa). "The four great elements" (mahābhūta) refer to the external four great elements;
"the matter produced [by them]" (upādāya-rūpa) refers to the internal four great elements—that is, the single aggregate of matter among the five aggregates.

It can be said that this one aggregate of matter is produced by the four great elements because it possesses the four dharmas of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, each with its own distinct characteristic; therefore, it possesses form. It is not [the case for the other four aggregates].
Because the four aggregates of the formless realm are like space. As for the four aggregates such as sensation and so forth, they have no physical form or characteristics;
they are just like space. They are merely designated as "four aggregates" through the conventional expressions of false conceptualization.
For example, space transcends all numerical characteristics, yet one merely speaks of it conceptually as "one space. How could there be a space that is formless and yet belongs to those [aggregates]?
"Are they created by the four great elements? To thus falsely reckon that the four great elements can create the five aggregates is entirely wrong view.

Mahāmati, such aggregates transcend numerical characteristics; they are free from number, free from existence and non-existence, and free from the four extremes. [They are] beyond numerical characteristics."
This refers to the speech of ignorant commoners, not that of the sages and worthies.
The Record states: "This is a general explanation that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are all empty. "Such aggregates" generally refers to the five aggregates. "Nature" (*svabhāva*).

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is not an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As for the other four aggregates, it means that not only are the four aggregates like space, but when one investigates the aggregate of form, each is found to lack self-nature; the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise, and form is fundamentally empty.

Thus, all five aggregates are empty, transcending numerical characteristics. Furthermore, how could they be designated by the number "five"? Therefore, it is said: "In this way, the aggregates transcend number."
Characteristics are apart from number. Since they transcend names and numbers, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally non-existent.

Since the five aggregates are non-existent, they are apart from both existence and non-existence. Being apart from existence, form (*rūpa*) cannot be said to exist; being apart from non-existence, the other four aggregates need not be said to be non-existent.
Thus, since both existence and non-existence are transcended, where could the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) find a foothold? Therefore, it is said: "apart from."
Nature and non-nature transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). Yet, once the four propositions are transcended, the hundred negations are simultaneously dispelled.
When the path of names and words is cut off, the aggregates (*skandha*) are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). How, then, could they be sought through numerical characteristics?
Therefore, those who calculate numerical characteristics merely speak like fools; this is surely not the power of the true knowledge and vision of the sages and worthies. Forever...
Jia said: "All numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases—what connection do they have with my numinous awakening? One must deeply realize this.
Mahāmati, the various forms and images of the sages are like illusions, free from the conceptualization of difference or non-difference; they are also like dreams and reflections.
The body of a person is neither different nor non-different [from its constituents]. Mahāmati, the realm of noble wisdom appears as the false conceptualization of the aggregates (*skandha*).
The commentary states: This explains away potential objections to clarify that the five aggregates are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).

Since the Buddha has previously taught that the five aggregates are all empty, the foolish may harbor doubts, wondering: "We clearly perceive the five aggregates in both the noble and the ordinary; why do you say they do not exist?"

Therefore, this commentary states: "When I say that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, it does not mean they are utterly non-existent. Rather, when observed by noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), they are seen to be like illusions and unreal.
That is to say, one thoroughly realizes that what arises through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and their essence is entirely empty.

It is merely that one does not establish them through false views such as identity or difference; how could it mean they are absolutely annihilated into nothingness? Nevertheless, these five aggregates..."
This is the radiance of the Dharma-body, like a body in a dream or a reflection in a mirror; it has no separate existence.

Therefore, it is said to be neither different nor not different. Thus I say that the five aggregates are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), yet foolish people do not realize this, but instead falsely give rise to dualistic views of identity and difference. Yongjia said: "The illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma."

The body—these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are, in their very essence, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). When the delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) of the five aggregates manifest, the Dharma-body manifests simultaneously;

it is merely that what is perceived differs according to whether one is a sage or an ordinary person. If one views through the discrimination of delusive thoughts, the Dharma-body is concealed and the five aggregates appear.
If one observes with sagely wisdom (*āryajñāna*), the Dharma-body appears and the [five aggregates... are [transcended].
The aggregates (*skandhas*) dissolve. Therefore, the preceding text states: "Yet that delusion also appears to the various sages, yet it is not a perversion.

Thus it is said that the movement of sage-wisdom is identical to the manifestation of the false imaginings of the aggregates. This is truly the suchness (*tathatā*) of false imagining; one who can contemplate this [realizes it].
This is what is called "dhyāna that takes suchness as its object. The subsequent text concludes by saying:

"This is called the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates; you should eliminate it. Having eliminated it, teach the Dharma of tranquility, severing all heterodox views regarding all Buddha-fields."

The commentary states: This knot is named "Transcending Faults. However, because one has not yet realized that the five aggregates are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), one gives rise to the deluded views of oneness, difference, arising, and ceasing.
All that is spoken of therein consists of dharmas of arising and ceasing; therefore, this knot says: "The five aggregates are thus empty and quiescent.
You should eliminate the views of self-nature and characteristics. By extinguishing these views of birth, you will immediately realize non-arising."
That which is taught is entirely the dharma of quiescence. Furthermore, one should use this realization to sever all the false views of the externalists.
Mahāmati, when quiescence is taught, the vision of the selflessness of phenomena becomes purified, and one enters the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). Upon entering the Immovable Stage—
Having attained mastery over immeasurable samādhis and the body of mental birth (*manomaya-kāya*), and having attained the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusory-like samādhi) to reach ultimate penetration,
they exercise power, clarity, and sovereignty to rescue, gather, and benefit all sentient beings. Just as the great earth supports and nurtures all living beings,
so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally save all sentient beings.
The Record states: "This marks the attainment of the fruit through the completion of the meditative practice of 'clinging to conditions' (*ālambana*).

When the meditative practice of 'contemplating meaning' was previously completed, one entered from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and immediately ascended to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).

By gradually observing and penetrating deeper until reaching the highest grounds, one suddenly perceives true reality (*tattva*) and gradually severs ignorance (*avidyā*); this is what is meant by 'sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation.'"

It is so. Now, when the practice of *ālambana-yathābhūta-dhyāna* (contemplation of objects as they truly are) is perfected, one suddenly ascends to the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), suddenly realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*), suddenly severs ignorance (*avidyā*), and suddenly abandons the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This is what is meant by "sudden awakening and sudden cultivation.

The three types of dhyāna mentioned above constitute the practices of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). While the dhyāna of the Two Vehicles is certainly subject to censure, although the latter two—though [superior]—...
It is superior. Yet, it still pertains to the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment. Thus, that verse says: "All vehicles are not ultimate. Why is this?

Because in the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), even if one personally realizes *tathatā* (suchness), it remains a matter within the realm of the *dharmakāya*, rather than a matter transcending the *dharmakāya*.
As for the Tathāgata’s pure *dhyāna*, however, it does not belong to the realm of cause and effect; therefore, it is the most supreme.

The "Vehicles" (yāna) constitute the essential purport of this sutra. This is why, having merely explained the first three types of dhyāna, it immediately speaks of the two fruits—erroneous and correct—whereas the Tathāgata-dhyāna cannot be spoken of;
its intent is to lead us to intuitively realize that which lies beyond words. Later, when Mahāmati specifically requested [an explanation], the World-Honored One merely said: "The former sages..."
The objects of knowledge are transmitted from one to another; they are merely a single phrase: "delusive thoughts have no inherent nature.
This is the direct pointing to the mind-seal (citta-mudrā) transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity, serving as the secret instruction (upadeśa) of the Chan school.

It is intended to reveal the essential purport of this sutra. Let the observer examine this deeply. The above concludes the explanation of the differences between the causes and practices of the heterodox and the correct. Below—
The text explains that the fruits and virtues of the heterodox and the orthodox are different. △ First, it demonstrates the fruits of the heterodox.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa among the various non-Buddhists. What are these four? They are: (1) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of things being non-existent;
(2) the nirvāṇa of the non-existence of the nature of various characteristics; (3) the nirvāṇa of awakening to the non-existence of the self-nature of specific characteristics...
“Pāṇa. The cessation of the continuous flow of the mutual characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called nirvāṇa by the various non-Buddhists;
these are the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists, not the Dharma taught by me.”
The commentary states: This section distinguishes the differences in the qualities of the fruits [of practice]. First, it demonstrates the false fruits.
Since the Buddha has previously taught that the causal practices possess both the true and the false, the fruits they evoke likewise possess the false and the correct.

Therefore, this first mentions the four kinds of *nirvāṇa* in order to reveal the unreality of the causal practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). [It continues with] "the nature, self-nature, and non-nature of *nirvāṇa*..."
"Bana" refers to the Sāṃkhya teachers, who falsely establish the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) as the primary truth, asserting it to have a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because this is not ultimate *nirvāṇa*, the Buddha, according to the circumstances, refuted them by saying: "That which they conceive of as 'self-nature' (*prakṛti*) is in fact no nature at all;
it is merely a false attachment. Therefore, it is said that "the self-nature of nature is the non-nature of *nirvāṇa*," regarding its various characteristics.

Regarding "nirvana as nature and non-nature": this refers to the false calculations of external paths (tīrthikas) who take the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*) to be nirvana, claiming that all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the entirety of empty space flow forth from a single category within their own bodies.
Furthermore, they calculate the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) to be nirvana, asserting that their own body and mind, as well as the empty space of the ten directions, are all...

Emerging from that [previous discussion], there are furthermore the Lokāyata materialists who reckon that the four great elements are substantial and eternal, and are capable of producing all phenomena.
Therefore, they seek the light of fire, delight in the purity of water, cherish the circulation of wind, and observe the formation of atoms;
each pursues their respective element as being eternally abiding. Because they reckon those various characteristics to possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the Buddha refuted them.
It is said: That which they calculate is in fact not a true nature (dharma), but merely a false attachment. Therefore, it is called "nirvāṇa as the non-nature of various characteristics and natures.
Regarding "nirvāṇa through the awakening to the non-nature of self-characteristics and self-nature," this refers to the Vaiśeṣika masters.

They reckon that all insentient things possess cognition. They establish six categories of meaning (*ṣaṭpadārtha*): namely, substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), universal existence (*mahāsattā*), particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).
Because they regard the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) as eternal, they claim that all vegetation throughout the ten directions possesses cognition.
They are no different from others. Grasses and trees become humans, and when humans die, they return to becoming grasses and trees throughout the ten directions.
