Furthermore, while karma and delusion are still raging, how can you falsely compare yourself to the sages of the Three Vehicles and take them as a fan for fanning away your own suffering, using them merely as a raft for self-deception? This is the height of folly. It is for this reason that I say:
To designate this as "destruction" is the characteristic of one who has fallen into the view of non-existence; it is thus. Alas for the Dharma of the Final Age!
You should recognize this with deep pain.
Mahāmati, for this reason I say: it would be better to hold a view of a person as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view that nothing exists.

Regarding the "emptiness-view of overweening pride," the commentary states: "This is an extreme statement regarding the faults of the emptiness-view; its intent is to urge one to strenuously abandon it. "The view of persons" refers to the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*). The Chinese translation says:
"I have spoken with this meaning and intentional purpose (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): rather than giving rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as large as Mount Sumeru..."

One should not give rise to the view of emptiness while harboring overweening pride, even if that pride were as high as Mount Sumeru. However, this was spoken with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-vacana*);
it does not mean that the arising of the view of a self is permitted. Rather, it is an extreme expression intended to show that the view of emptiness must not arise under any circumstances.
Although the view of a self is stubborn and difficult to transform, among the non-Buddhists there are those of sharp faculties who may still be converted through a single [instruction].

As it is said, [the mind] shifts with words. When it comes to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), it is most incurable. Even bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings do not yet recognize true emptiness;
they are called "those whose minds are confused by emptiness. How much more so for those who harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and give rise to the denial of existence? Yongjia said:
To be reckless and nihilistic regarding emptiness, to deny cause and effect, and to wander aimlessly into calamity and disaster—this is what is meant by that.
Mahāmati, those who possess the pride of non-existence are called destroyers; they fall into the views and expectations of self-characteristics and common characteristics.

Not realizing that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind—(the Tang translation says: "If one gives rise to such a view, one is called a destroyer; one falls into the desire for self- and common-characteristics, failing to understand that all dharmas are manifested solely by the mind")—one perceives external natures as impermanent, decaying moment by moment, and the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as a continuous flow that undergoes transformation and extinction.
To be free from the conceptualization of verbal signs is what is meant by a "destroyer."

The commentary states: This passage records the reason for rebuking the great error of the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, I say that those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are called "destroyers.

This is because they fall into the midst of attachment to the views of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), failing to realize that all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind.
"Self-characteristics and common characteristics" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth—their longing [for these].

Those who delight in desire are those whose internal faculties and bodies experience sensations, while externally they become defiled by the six sense objects, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, and becoming firmly attached to the five desires.
In reality, they do not understand that these are merely manifestations of their own minds. They pursue the external world, which is impermanent, undergoing moment-to-moment change and passing away;
internally, they rely on the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, which do not cease for even a single thought-moment, flowing into birth and death like the flame of a lamp.

Like a stream of water flowing gently, it never ceases for even a single moment. Yet you claim to have realized the unborn and undying, falsely asserting that birth and death are equal and that the nature of afflictions is empty.

Furthermore, you falsely discriminate regarding the nirvana realized by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas as being free from the marks of words, taking this to be your own understanding; in truth, you have not yet attained it.

This refers to those who claim to have attained what they have not yet realized, and those who claim to have realized what they have not yet realized—namely, persons of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Therefore, I declare them to be destroyers of the Buddha-dharma and those who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*). As stated in other sūtras: "It would be better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of non-existence even as small as a mustard seed, for the latter falls into a great abyss and cannot be transformed by any of the Buddhas."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Existence and non-existence are two extremes; even the realm of the mind (the sphere of mental activity, according to the Tang translation). By purifying that realm, the mind of equanimity is stilled.
There is no grasping at the nature of the realm, yet its cessation is not a state of nothingness. All phenomena are entirely suchness, like the wise."
The "Noble Realm. The commentary states:
This verse refutes the view that denies [existence], which is not true quiescence, nor is it the realm of the noble ones (ārya).
It means that both extremes of existence and non-existence are realms traversed by deluded conceptualization (vikalpa). However, [true] quiescence is equanimity.
It is not a sphere where the mind operates; one must first purify those realms of deluded conceptualization before attaining silent realization.

Furthermore, those people of overweening pride who falsely claim that not grasping the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion constitutes "extinction" (nirvāṇa) are merely negating existence through a nihilistic extinction;
it is not true non-existence. Therefore, it is said: "Extinction is not non-existence. If...

If, in the midst of daily activities and present circumstances, one remains unmoved in every instance and toward every object, such that mind and境 (objects) are in a state of *tathatā* (suchness), only then does one share the realm of the sages and worthies.

How much less could those whose daily conduct is driven by ignorance, whose karmic consciousness is vast and murky, and who create karma according to their passions, be recklessly compared to the sages and worthies? This single verse summarizes [the preceding discussion].
The verse refutes the errors of those who hold such views:

"To claim that there is arising without a seed, and that what has arisen subsequently perishes; to maintain that causes and conditions both exist and do not exist—such people do not abide within my teaching."

It is neither a non-Buddhist nor a Buddha; it is neither the self nor anything else (the Tang translation says "nor any other group"). Since it arises through the gathering of causes and conditions, how could it be non-existent?
Who gathers the causes and conditions for its existence, yet then says it is non-existent?
The commentary states: This verse borrows the terminology of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) to refute the great error of those who deny [causality].

The first verse all refers to the heterodox arguments of non-Buddhists; it means that those non-Buddhists, failing to understand that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning, falsely speculate that there is arising without seeds—“seeds” meaning causes—or they speculate that once arisen, things then perish, or they speculate...
The causal conditions of the aggregation of the four great elements and their subtle atoms can give rise to all phenomena.
Some reckon that all phenomena both exist and do not exist. Although these are called wrong views, they have not yet utterly negated all phenomena;
I have already sternly rebuked them, saying: "These are all heterodox doctrines and do not abide within my teaching. As for those who negate [existence], they falsely claim:
Not grasping the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is itself nirvāṇa; thus, both cause and effect are non-existent.
Yet this evil view is neither the doctrine of the non-Buddhists, nor is it the Buddha-dharma, nor is it what I have taught, nor is it the discourse of my other disciples.
How much less could it possibly be the present afflictions and conditions that give rise to the karmic fruits of birth and death?
Within this, every arising thought and every movement of the mind is none other than karma; it is none other than transgression. How, then, could there be no cause and no effect?

Furthermore, through the causal conditions of the accumulation of afflictions, there arise the karmic fruits of birth and death within the three realms and the retributions for good and evil, which follow one like a shadow follows a form. Who would dare, amidst these present, accumulated causes and conditions, to claim otherwise?
Yet you further say that it is utterly non-existent. Thus it is said: "Who assembles the causes and conditions for existence? and yet you say it is non-existent.
How profound is this pain! How deep is this reproach! Can those who contemplate this not stand in awe?
Those with false views debate the arising of phenomena, falsely imagining existence and non-existence. If one knows that nothing arises, there is likewise nothing that ceases.
Contemplating this as entirely empty and quiescent, one is free from both existence and non-existence.

The commentary states: This verse summarizes the ultimate aim as the contemplation of the mind. It means that those outside the Buddha-dharma are non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who produce dharmas through false views;
while those who study the Buddha-dharma yet remain like non-Buddhists are those who delusively reckon in terms of existence and non-existence.

All of these fail to realize that all dharmas are fundamentally unborn from the beginning, and thus are now likewise unextinguished. If they were to truly know that there is fundamentally nothing produced, [they would realize this truth].
Thus, even now there is no cessation. If one can contemplate that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, then they are, in their very substance, empty and quiescent.
When both mind and object are forgotten, the dualistic views of existence and non-existence will naturally be abandoned together.
Once these two views are abandoned, one will spontaneously realize the Dharma of one's own original abiding; it is attained without being sought. The above has revealed *nirvāṇa*.
The refutation of errors is now complete. △ Below, two types of penetration are shown to clarify that the ocean of fruition is beyond words.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle (*mūla-prativedha-lakṣaṇa*).
If the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle are skillfully distinguished, I and the other bodhisattvas shall thoroughly understand them."

Having thoroughly penetrated these marks, one swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and does not follow discursive perceptions or the various demons and non-Buddhists (the Tang translation says:
"Skillfully understanding this meaning, one does not follow any of the various false and deluded interpretations").
The commentary states: The following clarifies the realization that transcends words. Since it is intended to reveal that the ocean of fruition is beyond verbal expression, this question is posed.
Because those who study the Buddha-dharma above failed to grasp the Buddha’s intent, they gave rise to the view of nihilistic denial.
Failing to attain the "pervasive penetration" (*zongtong*) of self-nature, they misinterpreted the Buddha’s words and thus fell into such errors. This is because—
Because they have not yet abandoned the habitual tendencies of names and words (*nāma-vāsanā*), they are unable to forget language and attain silent resonance (*muk-yi*).

Therefore, Mahāmati, following the preceding [teaching], asks about the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*zong-tong-xiang*). The Buddha’s intention was that such persons are not only unskilled in the penetration of the ultimate principle, but also unskilled in the penetration of the teaching (*shuo-tong*);
thus, they misunderstand the Buddha’s meaning. Consequently, for one question, two answers are given.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, we shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics:
namely, the penetration of the principle (*tattvārtha*) and the penetration of the teaching (*deśanā*)."

The Record states: Because the characteristic of the penetration of the principle (*zongtong*) was asked about, the characteristic of the penetration of the teaching (*shetong*) was shown concurrently;

therefore, he instructed him to observe the mind beyond words. The *Zongjing* says: "Internally abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of one's own mind, dwelling on the stage of self-awakening, and entering the gate of noble wisdom—corresponding with this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the principle. This is the time of practice, not [the time of]..."

At the time of understanding, one acts because of understanding; when action is perfected, understanding ceases. Thus, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Therefore, the Wei translation says: "For my sake and for that of all bodhisattvas, establish the characteristics of the practice of the True Dharma.
The Buddha replied: "There are two kinds of dharmas: first, establishing the characteristics of the True Dharma; second, explaining the establishment [of those characteristics]."
*Dharmalakṣaṇa*. The Tang translation renders this as *zongqù fǎxiàng* (the doctrinal essence of dharmic characteristics) and *shuōfǎ fǎxiàng* (dharmic characteristics of the spoken teaching).

It should be understood that these two categories together constitute the essential gateways through which the Buddha reveals the entry into principle for practitioners of the three vehicles. That is to say, for all practitioners:

first, it is essential to realize one's own mind and thoroughly penetrate the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only; second, it is essential to skillfully master what the Tathāgata has taught.
All the teachings of the Buddha are spoken in accordance with the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, just as yellow leaves were used to stop a child’s crying;

fundamentally, no real dharma was given to anyone. Whenever one contemplates the Buddha's teachings, one must not rely on the literal words to form an understanding, lest one be driven by deluded conceptualization.
When one realizes this within one's own mind and can skillfully understand the ineffable intent of the Buddha-dharma, it is natural...
One shall not fall into the heterodox views of external paths, nor shall one cling to the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna and misinterpret it as one's own personal view,

thereby erring by falling into the state of an icchantika and destroying the Buddha-dharma. When viewed through these verses, the Sage’s intent emerges with absolute clarity from the preceding context.

Mahāmati, as for the penetration of the principle (*siddhānta-naya*), it refers to the characteristics of superior progress attained through one's own realization. It is far removed from the delusions of speech, words, and letters;
it proceeds toward the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and the specific characteristics of the stage of self-realization.

It is far removed from all false and delusive perceptions, subdues all externalists and hordes of Māras, and takes the path of self-realization as its object. Its radiance shines forth brilliantly; this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the principle.
The Record states: "This demonstrates the characteristics of the *zongtong* (the penetration of the essence). The Wei translation says:

"One is able to take up untainted, correct precepts, realize the characteristics of the dharmas practiced across the various stages (*bhūmi*), and remain detached from the false conceptualizations and the realms of demons belonging to all non-Buddhists;
one subdues all non-Buddhists and demons, and manifests the dharma of internal realization within oneself. The Tang translation says: "Transcending..."
All improper thoughts and reflections subdue demons and non-Buddhists, giving rise to the light of wisdom.

Viewing it from this perspective, when a practitioner first enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have not yet been shattered, all perceived realms are not actual realizations.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* meticulously distinguishes fifty grades of demonic realms; this refers to the period when the first three aggregates have not yet been shattered.

The manifested realms are precisely what this sutra calls "false conceptualizations. The various views arising before the latter three aggregates are destroyed are precisely what this sutra refers to as "all external paths and hordes of Māras.
Only when one now seeks to distance oneself from and subdue these can it be called the "right practice of the path of self-awakening.
Furthermore, the wisdom-light that is inherently present by its own nature spontaneously radiates.

It is thus. However, to transcend and subdue these [afflictions], nothing but the adamantine mind can do so; by upholding the self-nature’s adamantine, untainted (anāsrava) jewel-precepts, one cannot possibly sever them otherwise.
Therefore, the Wei translation says: "One is able to take up the untainted right precepts and realize the characteristics of the various stages (bhūmi).
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "If the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is exhausted, then your present sense-faculties will function interchangeably. From...

Within the mutual application [of these faculties], one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *śuṣka-vipaśyanā* (dry wisdom). From within this, the perfectly luminous and refined essence of mind issues forth its transformations.
In this way, one transcends the ten stages of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and even up to the ten grounds and the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
They enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments. This is what is called taking up untainted right precepts and realizing the characteristics of the practice of the various stages;
only then can it be termed the characteristic of supreme progress attained through self-realization.

As for those who deny [reality], since they cannot comprehend their own minds, even if they have the aspiration to practice, they are further unable to skillfully understand the truth taught by the Tathāgata.
Because they have not yet entered the gate of cultivation, they cannot distance themselves from discursive thought (*vikalpa*) and mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Consequently, they fall into the realms of various demons while believing themselves to have attained realization. This occurs because they have not yet grasped the untainted, correct precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) and are thus driven by evil habits;
it is therefore no wonder that their every action and deed takes demonic activity for their true practice.

What is the characteristic of the penetration of teaching? It refers to the teaching of the various doctrines of the nine divisions of scripture, which are free from characteristics such as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth.

By means of skillful expedients, one preaches the Dharma in accordance with the needs of sentient beings, enabling them to attain liberation. This is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching.

The commentary states: This demonstrates the characteristics of the "teaching that penetrates universally" (shōtsū). Regarding the Buddha’s preaching of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the mention here of "nine divisions" is because it encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
However, this "teaching that penetrates universally" does not merely consist in being able to thoroughly understand and skillfully expound the nine divisions of the teachings of both vehicles;
rather, it requires the realization that, from the very beginning, there is neither teaching nor demonstration.

Free from such characteristics as difference, non-difference, existence, and non-existence, he relies upon the state of non-conceptualization and ineffability realized by the Tathāgata through his own attainment.

Yet, through skillful means, he accords with the aspirations of sentient beings, teaching each according to what is appropriate and in accordance with their capacities, so that they may attain liberation—just like a raft used for crossing a river. Having already attained [this realization]...
[The opponent] then abandons it, for it is not a true dharma. If an observer can thoroughly comprehend this teaching of "non-teaching," they will naturally transcend words to contemplate the meaning;
they will neither grasp at the characteristics of dharmas nor grasp at the characteristics of non-dharmas.
Those who negate [the teachings] fail to understand their own minds and are thus unskilled in the meaning; they merely cling to verbal expressions as being real.

The Dharma. Those who take the Tathāgata’s definitive Mahāyāna and turn it into their own personal views, indulging freely in greed and anger—this is what is meant by turning the finest *amṛta* (clarified butter) into poison.
The Buddha said: "The Dharma I have taught is like a finger pointing at the moon. Therefore, all students, upon hearing the teaching, should naturally observe their own minds;
only by letting go of the finger can one perceive the moon. This is what is meant by "understanding the Dharma does not reside [in the words]."

He said: "To skillfully enter the limit of the wordless while being able to manifest verbal expression, like an echo pervading the world—this is precisely what is called the characteristic of the penetration of speech.
Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"The characteristics of the fundamental doctrine and the teaching of the common vehicle, The conditions of self-nature and the teachings of the Dharma— Those who see them well and distinguish them well Do not follow after various conceptualizations."
The commentary states: This verse summarizes the meaning of the two types of penetration (*pratisaṃvid*). "Skillful vision" refers to attaining the penetration of the essence (*zongtong*);
"skillful discernment" refers to attaining the penetration of verbal expression (*shuotong*). When both of these are skillful, one will no longer be driven by deluded conceptualization.
There is no true reality, yet it is imagined by the deluded as they do. How does such imagination arise? Liberation consists in the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*). The commentary states:
"This verse rebukes the ignorant for their lack of skill in the two types of penetration; thus, they give rise to inverted views. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent; there is neither grasping nor seeing. This very emptiness of nature is the Buddha; it cannot be apprehended."
Reflecting thus: "How could there be any real phenomena such as those discriminated by the foolish?
Since nothing exists to be discriminated, how can the foolish, within these non-discriminative phenomena, falsely imagine greed, hatred, and delusion to be liberation?
Therefore, it is said that "there is no reality," and so forth.
Observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as a continuity of arising, ceasing, and so forth, one increases two views; thus, being inverted, there is no true knowledge.
The commentary states: This verse concludes and rebukes the preceding chapter, clarifying the reason for such inverted views.
It means that the reason those deluded persons hold such inverted views is that they do not skillfully master the two types of penetration (*pratisaṃvid*); therefore, they do not know the Dharma.

The nature of things is empty and quiescent; yet, following deluded conceptualization and discrimination, one observes the internal faculties, external objects, and the realms of consciousness—all conditioned phenomena—as being truly existent.
Consequently, one falsely gives rise to grasping and attachment, clinging to objects moment by moment, with the mind never abiding.
Birth and cessation continue in succession, day and night without interval; they only serve to increase two views, allowing perversion and self-indulgence to create all manner of evil karma.
Regarding the Buddha’s teaching on practicing the True Dharma—which is beyond the characteristics of verbal expression—they are blind and possess no knowledge.
Therefore, I say that such people are called destroyers. There is only one true reality:
nirvāṇa is without fault (the Wei translation says, "Nirvāṇa is free from consciousness; this one dharma alone is real"; the Tang translation says, "Nirvāṇa is free from mind and consciousness;

this one dharma alone is real"). One should contemplate the delusions of the world as being like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees; although greed, anger, and ignorance exist, they are in reality...
There is no person; from craving arise the aggregates (*skandhas*). All that exists is like an illusion or a dream.
The commentary states: "This verse directly points to the one mind, teaching that one should practice the characteristics of the True Dharma."—Paramārtha.

"Reality" (*tattva*). "Nirvāṇa"—here translated as "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*)—refers to that which is the locus of reality; this is what it means. Regarding "sin": the old commentary states it refers to "deluded conceptualization.

The Buddha’s intention is that all things subject to discrimination are not real; there is only one dharma that is the locus of reality, namely the essence of the mind of quiescent extinction, free from deluded conceptualization.
This is because it transcends the path of language and is beyond the reach of mental activity.
Cessation is the most true state. Only this one reality is real; the other two are not true.

If one understands this and abides in the state of suchness, then one can observe that all worldly realms of body and mind, which are places of deluded conceptualization and discrimination, are like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees—all utterly unreal. "Illusions and dreams" serve as metaphors for the mind and consciousness.

The four aggregates are like a plantain tree; this serves as a metaphor for the aggregate of form. Once one realizes that this body and mind are not substantial, the grasping at a self is suddenly emptied.
When the grasping at a self is empty, even if the natures of greed, anger, and delusion still exist, there is no agent and no experiencer.
Therefore it is said that in reality there is no person. Since there is neither an agent nor a recipient, both mind and object are simultaneously extinguished.
Thus, this illusory body composed of the five aggregates born of craving, though it exists, is treated as being like a dream or a phantom.
As it is said: "When one returns to observe the world, it is like events within a dream; Māraṅgaka is but a dream—whom can anyone detain?"
Regarding your form, if you can contemplate it in this way, how could you then consider the non-appropriation of the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion as an attainment?
Contemplating in this manner is called right contemplation; contemplating otherwise is called wrong contemplation.
This is what is meant by establishing the characteristics of practicing the True Dharma; by means of this, one can transform afflictions into bodhi.

To transform birth-and-death into nirvana means that, within these very five aggregates, afflictions, body, and mind, one immediately attains the two fruits of the eternal transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Let the wise contemplate this deeply.

From the initial question in the first fascicle concerning the five dharmas and self-nature, up to this point, we have comprehensively examined the principle, practice, cause, and fruit of the One Vehicle.

The analysis of the modes of practice (*ākāra*) is concluded. Below, based on the preceding principles, the characteristics of the cause and effect of sudden realization and abandonment are demonstrated.

This section is divided into two parts. First, the manifestation of causal practice, which is further divided into two: first, self-benefit; second, benefit for others. Within the first, there are four sections.
△ First, it is explained that deluded thoughts are unreal in order to destroy the attachment to a self and sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain the characteristics of unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
(Question: What are the characteristics of conceptualization? How does unreal conceptualization arise? (Question: How does conceptualization arise?

Of what kind of phenomena is the name 'unreal conceptualization' used? (Question: What is its essence? The Tang translation asks: From what does it arise? By what cause does it arise? Within what phenomena does unreal conceptualization occur?"
(Question: Regarding the locus of deluded thought. The Tang translation asks: "By whom is it produced? The commentary states:

Having already completed the comprehensive discussion above on the principles, practices, causes, effects, and characteristics of the One Vehicle, the following clarifies the sequence of relying on practice to cultivate, sever delusions, and realize the Truth. This follows from what was stated in the preceding Chapter on the Virtues of the Fruit: "Awakening..."

The non-selfhood of persons and phenomena, the thorough knowledge of the two obstacles, the departure from the two kinds of death, and the severance of the two afflictions—this is called the awakening of a Buddha.
To clarify the practice of cultivation based on this, it is essential first to destroy the two attachments and sever the two obstacles.

This inquiry regarding "delusive thought" and so forth refers first to the severing of the obstacle of affliction and the destruction of the attachment to a self. As for the question concerning delusive thought:
This refers to how all sentient beings, as well as the heterodox views of the icchantikas, exist solely because of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, it is said that deluded conceptualization has no intrinsic nature; it is also said that the absence of deluded conceptualization is the state of true quiescence.

Mahāmati’s intention is to say that while it is stated that deluded conceptualization is unreal, one does not yet know what constitutes deluded conceptualization. Moreover, regarding the phrase "the absence of deluded conceptualization":
The locus of reality is quiescent and non-arising; not knowing this, how can delusion arise? What is it that arises? By what cause does it arise?
From where does it arise? For false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the very root of affliction (*kleśa*);
therefore, this section is titled "Destroying the Obstruction of Afflictions."
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning;
it will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness, out of compassion for all devas and humans in the world. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
"I shall explain this for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Various meanings and various unreal false imaginings arise from attachment to false imaginings."
The commentary states: This answers the nature of deluded thought (*vikalpa*) and the arising of deluded thought.

"Various" refers to all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, true or false—that constitute the mental objects of both the sages and ordinary beings. "Meaning" refers to names and characteristics.

That is to say, when one does not realize that these various phenomena are nothing but mind, and consequently gives rise to false discrimination within them, this is precisely what is called deluded thought. However...
A single moment of conceptual attachment gives rise to false discrimination (*vikalpa*). This is the general answer to the question; the following text explains the reason why.

Mahāmati, through attachment to the grasped and the grasper, one fails to understand that all is a manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), falls into the views of existence and non-existence, and increases the views of the outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Through the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination, one becomes attached to various external objects, and thus the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) become attached to false discriminations.
The arising of "self" and "what belongs to self.
The commentary states: This explains the reason for the existence of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). The Tang translation says:

All sentient beings, regarding various objects, are unable to comprehend that these are manifestations of their own minds; they calculate in terms of grasper and grasped, and thus falsely cling to them.
They give rise to various conceptual constructions and fall into the views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the habitual tendencies of the false views of externalists.
When the mind and mental factors arise in conjunction, they grasp at the existence of various external objects that can be apprehended, and they become attached to a self and what belongs to a self.
For this reason, it is called "false conceptual construction. This means that ignorance is the cause of deluded imagination. Because...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the failure to realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind; thus, one perceives what resembles external objects and clings to them as real.
This false conceptual attachment to the grasper and the grasped, which discriminates between existence and non-existence, is called "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the term "conceptual construction," it is interpreted according to the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. That "self" and "what belongs to the self" are the source from which conceptual construction arises; this refers to the falsity of names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*).

"Perception" (saṃjñā) is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, because mind and objects arise as mutual conditions. The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are all the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Calculating "self" and "what belongs to the self" constitutes the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Regarding "mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitasika*):

"mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign minds (*citta-rāja*), while "factors" refers to the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*), meaning those phenomena that belong to the mind. [The text] divides...
There are six categories: first, the five universal [mental factors]; second, the five object-specific [mental factors]; third, the eleven wholesome [mental factors];

fourth, the six root afflictions; fifth, the twenty secondary afflictions; and sixth, the four indeterminate [mental factors]. These are each possessed by the eight consciousnesses in varying degrees, as is fully explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if various kinds of unreal conceptualizations regarding various objects arise from the attachment to conceptualization,

and if there is attachment to the grasped and the grasper due to ignorance of the manifestation of one's own mind, falling into the views of existence and non-existence, increasing the views of externalists,

and through the habitual tendencies of conceptualization, becoming attached to various external objects, and [clinging to] the self and what belongs to the self within the mind and its mental factors— "
[This arises] from what is conceptualized and clung to.
The commentary states: "This, Mahāmati, cites the Buddha’s previous words in order to raise the following objection. This passage does not appear in the Tang translation. [Mahāmati asks:
"World-Honored One, if such various external objects and characteristics fall into the characteristics of existence and non-existence, yet are free from being and non-being, and free from views..."

"World-Honored One, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise. It is free from the characteristics of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), sense organs (*indriya*), parts (*avayava*), examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), and reasons (*hetu*) [the Tang translation says: 'free from all sense organs, means of knowledge, propositions, reasons, and examples'].

World-Honored One, why is it that in one place, false discrimination arises through attachment to the nature of manifold unreal objects, whereas in the case of the ultimate truth, discrimination does not arise through attachment to its characteristics? Will you not, World-Honored One, be teaching a doctrine of false causes?"
"Yes. (The Wei translation says: *Luo shijian lun*; the Tang translation says: "What is said deviates from principle. He speaks of one arising and one non-arising. The commentary states:

This is intended to clarify that taking the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation; therefore, he asks about the arising and non-arising of deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
This follows the World-Honored One’s previous statement that unreal deluded thought arises from attachment to various [phenomena].

"Because they arise from real objects (*bhūtārtha*), Mahāmati, you immediately raise an objection based on what has been said: 'The Blessed One also falls into the two views of existence and non-existence.
This is intended merely to clarify the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing. The meaning is this:

if false discrimination (*vikalpa*) arises from those various unreal objects of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then since that conventional truth itself falls into the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) of existence and non-existence..."

Regarding the view of characteristics: the World-Honored One repeatedly stated that the essence of those dharmas is free from both existence and non-existence, and free from the views of the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*).
Now, being free from the four extremes means that within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). As the Sūtra says:
"When one seeks faults in the various causes and measures of the world, they cannot be found; therefore, it is said that the ultimate truth is likewise free from measures and sense faculties."

This division is an analogy for the characteristics of causes. Since the two truths are equal and non-dual, why does the World-Honored One speak of the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) specifically in the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet not speak of the arising of conceptual construction in the context of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
Is it not the case that the World-Honored One is propounding a theory of false causes? For both truths are equally free from existence and non-existence; why then is this stated in only one place?

"Birth occurs in one place, while non-birth is taught in another. Thus, the Blessed One also appears to be like a fool, giving rise to two kinds of conceptualizations and falling into the theory of false causes.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "It is not that there is birth through deluded imagination in one case and non-birth in another. Why is this? Because [the notion of] existence and non-existence is a delusion."

Because thought does not arise, the external manifestation of existence and non-existence ceases; one awakens to the fact that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, and thus false discrimination does not arise.
The commentary states: This explains why one does not fall into the two views. The Buddha said:

"I do not give rise to false discrimination by calculating the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), nor do I give rise to false discrimination by calculating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Why is this so?"
Because I do not give rise to the dualistic mind that discriminates between existence and non-existence, and because I do not perceive the characteristics of conventional truth, it is said:
"Externally, the nature of things appears as both existent and non-existent. Because I realize that all phenomena are merely manifestations of my own mind, discrimination does not arise;
thus it is said: "Awakening to the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, false conceptualization does not arise."
Mahāmati, I say that because of the various marks of the false imaginings of their own minds, other foolish people have activities appearing before them;
thus, attachment to the nature and characteristics of these various false imaginings arises.
The commentary states: This explanation clarifies the reason for the deluded conceptualizations of foolish people.

What I have taught is not that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) gives rise to conceptualization; rather, I am speaking only of the various conceptualizations produced by the foolish people's own minds.
Because those foolish people perceive various activities appearing before them through false views, they do not understand that these are merely mind-only (*cittamātra*). Therefore...
One grasps at these as real and gives rise to various kinds of conceptual discrimination and attachment. For this reason, I say that they arise from false imagination (*vikalpa*).
That is to say, objective conditions have neither beauty nor ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly assign names, [these distinctions do not exist].
By what means are objective spheres established? Therefore, all that is conceptually discriminated is the discrimination of one's own mind. As a sutra says:
"If one does not understand one's own mind, how can one know the right path? Hence, this is explained in successive order.

How does a fool come to be free from the attachment to views of "self" and "what belongs to self," free from the errors regarding agent, action, and causal conditions, and awaken to the measure of the mind of its own conceptual construction (*svavikalpa-cittamātra*)?

Through the transformation of body and mind, they ultimately and clearly understand all stages (*bhūmi*), the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, and become free from the conceptual constructions of the views regarding the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the categories of phenomena. For these reasons, I speak of conceptual construction.
It arises from attachment to various unreal objects. By knowing the reality as it is, one attains liberation from the various false imaginings of one's own mind.
The commentary states: This is the World-Honored One’s own account of the fundamental intent of his teaching; that is to say, because I perceive sentient beings...
Regarding the various phenomena, they give rise to diverse attachments and conceptual discriminations, clinging to them tenaciously and refusing to let go.
How can such foolish people ever manage to abandon the false views of attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self"?

How can they ever distance themselves from the faults and afflictions of birth and death, which arise from the causal conditions of good and evil actions and their results? And how can they awaken to the fact that these are merely the manifestations of their own deluded minds?
How can one transform the body of the five aggregates to attain the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), transform the consciousness of ignorance into ultimate wisdom,
clearly understand all stages (*bhūmi*), and reach the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization? Free from the five dharmas, the three natures,
and the perceptions of objects and characteristics— out of compassion for those deluded sentient beings, it is for these reasons that I speak.

Discrimination arises from clinging to various unreal objects. It is intended to enable sentient beings to know things as they truly are, so that they may attain liberation from the various unreal discriminations within their own minds.
It is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to each realize their own minds that I speak; it is not that worldly conventions can give rise to discrimination. [This is] apart from...

Regarding the delusive discrimination of the five dharmas, the self-nature, and phenomena: since the five dharmas and the self-natures are all matters pertaining to the extremes of delusion and awakening, they are entirely transcended by ultimate, self-realized noble wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From various causes and conditions, this world arises; Through false conceptualization, one clings to the four extremes. They do not understand the penetration I have attained."
The commentary states: This verse generally rebukes the foolish who fail to comprehend the Buddha’s intent and instead give rise to interpretations based merely on the literal words.
When I say that all worlds arise through causes and conditions, my intention is to reveal that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;

yet the foolish do not understand this, and further, relying upon causes and conditions, they again give rise to the fourfold false views and conceptual discriminations. They do not know my [true] meaning.
This is the meaning of what is thoroughly understood.

In the world, there is no such thing as arising from existence, nor is there arising from non-existence. It does not arise from both existence and non-existence, nor is it from neither existence nor non-existence.
How can the ignorant harbor false imaginings regarding causes and conditions? It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor yet both existent and non-existent.
Observing the world in this manner, the mind turns toward the realization of non-self.
The commentary states: "This verse [indicates] that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning.

It means that the various phenomena of the world do not arise through the four propositions of existence or non-existence; therefore, I speak of dependent origination merely to reveal their state of being unarisen. How so?
Within the dharma of causes and conditions, do fools further give rise to deluded thoughts, forming views of the four extremes of existence and non-existence?
If one can observe all dharmas while remaining free from these four extremes, then in this very moment the mind will turn and one will attain non-self.
All natures are non-arising, because they arise from conditions. All that is produced by conditions is not self-existent. The commentary states:
This verse explains the reason why all phenomena are without arising. That is to say, all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising because they arise from conditions.
Since they arise from conditions, their arising is merely the arising of conditions; it is not self-arising.
It arises. Its arising is merely conditioned by activity; it is not self-originated. Therefore, it is said that "that which is produced does not exist of itself.
Because its own essence does not exist, it simply does not arise.

A phenomenon does not produce itself as a phenomenon, because there would be the fault of two phenomena, and because there is no fault of two phenomena; thus, no intrinsic nature can be found. The commentary states:
"This verse reveals non-arising by means of causes and conditions. The Tang translation says:

"An effect does not produce itself as an effect, because there would be the error of two effects, and because there are not two effects; thus, no intrinsic nature can be found. However, [the terms] "phenomenon" (*dharma*) and "effect" (*phala*)...
All are called conditions (*pratyaya*). This means that a condition does not condition itself; it must depend upon a cause (*hetu*).

It is like how a fruit does not produce itself as a fruit, but must depend upon a flower. If a fruit were to exist without depending on a flower, there would be the fallacy of two fruits, which would mean it is without a cause.

Therefore, if a condition were to produce [an effect] directly without depending on a cause, then this would be what the world reckons as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) being able [to produce things].
[Arising] would fall into the error of being causeless. If, however, it arises from causes and conditions, then these two errors do not occur.
Yet, since a condition must depend upon a cause, that condition does not arise [independently]. Since a cause must depend upon a condition, that cause does not arise [independently].
Since both cause and condition are thus non-arising, the dharma produced by them likewise has no self-nature (svabhāva) that can be apprehended. Because there is no nature...
Because it is attained, its arising is fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is said to be "unborn.

Contemplating all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which are free from the grasper and the grasped, and which are the measure of mind devoid of mind—I call this the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*).

"Measurement (*pramāṇa*) is the locus of intrinsic nature; it is free from both conditions and nature. Its nature is ultimately wondrously pure; I call this the 'measure of mind' (*cittamātra*). The commentary states:

This verse demonstrates the contemplation of the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind. It follows from the previous statement that because fools do not understand that all phenomena are merely manifestations of their own minds, they give rise to various unreal conceptualizations and discriminations regarding the unreal objects of various phenomena. Thus, [it is said]: "Because they do not understand..."

This is because it is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind. However, fearing that the listener may not understand what this "direct perception of one's own mind" (*svacittadṛśya-pratyakṣa*) entails, he specifically indicates it as follows:

When one correctly contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), if no mental discrimination arises regarding the perceived object, such that there is no second thought, then it is simply the one mind. This very mind, free from conceptualization, is it.

This is precisely the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of one’s own mind; therefore, it is called "the measure of mind that is without mind. What I refer to as the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*) is as follows:

regarding direct perception, it refers to the initial stage of the five consciousnesses, which, like the clearly discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), reflects the actual objects of the five sensory realms.
It appears with perfect clarity and without the slightest error; one does not give rise to a second moment of conceptual discrimination—this is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If, however, it flows into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) for a single moment and gives rise to mental discrimination regarding provisional phenomena such as long and short, square and round, blue and yellow, and so forth, this is then the mind of inference (*anumāna*).
What is now referred to as "all conditioned phenomena" refers to the objects of the five sense-fields (*pañca-viṣaya*), which are grasped by...
The "condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) is the sixth consciousness, the mind capable of discrimination. The "object-condition" (ālambana) is the realm of objects discriminated by those [consciousnesses].
"Detached" (viveka) means to be utterly severed. "Without mind" (acitta) means being without a second moment of discriminative mind. Therefore, the Wei translation says:
"Detached from both thought and the object of thought" means that when contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one simply does not give rise to mental discrimination;
naturally, subject and object are both severed, and there is a silent, numinous awareness. As the Sūtra says: "It is like the light of the eye clearly perceiving objects before it;
that light is perfect and complete, such that no aversion or attachment arises. Because there is no thought of aversion or attachment, it is called "no-mind. The Śāstra says: "The mind..."
The essence is free from thought. That which is free from the characteristics of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; this is what is called the "measure of mind that is no-mind.
However, as for the self-essence of this measure, both subject and object are utterly transcended, and both mind and境 (objects) are equally detached. It is ultimately wondrously pure;
therefore, it is merely said that there is the "manifestation-measure of one's own mind."
The "self" is a conventional designation for the worldly truth; it has no substantial reality. The aggregates are likewise designated as "aggregates," yet they too lack any substantial entity.

There are four kinds of equality: equality of characteristics, equality of causal nature, equality of arising, and thirdly, equality of selflessness; fourthly, equality of the cultivation and the cultivator.
The commentary states: These words describe the benefits gained through the perfection of contemplation.

That "self" of conventional truth refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of all sentient beings, each of whom clings to them as a self. These "aggregates" refer specifically to the internal five aggregates;

they are collectively termed "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and these constitute the objects of perception. This means that when one contemplates the physical bodies of oneself and others:
If one simply does not give rise to the mind that discriminates between the beautiful and the ugly, or the good and the bad, then the essence of the mind will be tranquil and empty.
Naturally, thoughts of love and hatred will not arise. It is as the saying goes: "It is just like a wooden man seeing flowers and birds.

This is what is meant by the non-arising of the single mind and the simultaneous stillness of all phenomena. As for that which is observed, it is merely like a reflection in a mirror, without further analysis. Therefore—
Both that and this—the faculties and the body—are entirely unreal. Being unreal, they are naturally equal and suchness. "Phenomenon" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the faculties and bodies of self and others.
"Cause" (hetu) refers to the cause of arising. "Nature" (svabhāva) refers to the nature of non-arising. "Cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to the person who is able to cultivate;
"cultivation" also refers to the dharma that is cultivated. What is called "equality" refers to the equality between phenomenon and non-phenomenon, and between arising and...
Birthlessness and non-birth, self and non-self—whether persons or phenomena, all are equal. Therefore, it is said that there are four kinds of equality.
This is accomplished through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Mind-Only; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*).
The transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization gives rise to various states of mind, and objects appear externally;

this is the conventional measure of the mind (*citta-mātra*). The commentary states: This refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transforming and appearing as external objects, which constitutes the conventional measure of the mind.

"False conceptualization" refers to the six consciousnesses; "habitual tendencies" refers to the defiled ignorance of the seventh consciousness. That is to say, the sixth consciousness relies upon the defiled [seventh consciousness].
The manas gives rise to the eight consciousnesses, which contain the seeds and habitual tendencies;

through perfuming and transformation, various conceptual minds arise and manifest as if they were external objects. One clings to these as a real self and real dharmas, yet they do not depart from "mind-only."
It is merely a false vision; therefore, it is called the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of the mundane world.
External appearances are not real, yet the mind perceives their various forms and establishes them as the body and possessions; this I call the mental measure.
The commentary states: These words refer to the "mental measure" (*citta-mātra*) of the first five consciousnesses. This means that although external objects appear, they do not actually exist.

They are, in fact, the direct objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; yet, through deluded perception, one grasps them and engages in various activities of all phenomena, taking them as resources for livelihood and as one's own dwelling place.
Based upon these, one establishes the bodies and possessions of the five consciousnesses. However, none of these...
Being free from "mind-only," I likewise speak of it as the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
Free from all views, and free from both the perceiver and the perceived, where there is neither attainment nor arising—I declare this to be the measure of mind.
The commentary states: These words refer to the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), thereby clarifying that [reality] is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of true mind-only.
That which is capable of discernment is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses; that which is discerned is the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses.

However, the self-nature of *tathatā* transcends both mind and objects, being free from everything; therefore, it is said to be "free from all views, as well as from conceptualization and its objects."
When thought reaches this point, it is utterly extinguished and finds no resting place; even the self cannot be apprehended. It stands independently in its very essence, quiescent and unborn.
Therefore, I say that this is the true manifestation of the mind-only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Neither existence nor non-existence; it is entirely free from both existence and non-existence. This is what is called the liberation of the mind;
I describe this as the Mind-only (cittamātra). Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm—these various bodies born of the will—I describe as the Mind-only.
The commentary states: These words refer to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of True Suchness as the One Mind, wherein both the true and the false are simultaneously transcended.

This clarifies the ultimate meaning of the absence of self (*anātman*). Because both mind and objects are transcended, it is not "nature" (*dharmatā*); because even "true" is not established, it is not "non-nature.
Only by being free from both the true and the false does one attain the quiescent, single-minded, ultimate liberation; therefore, I say:

This is called the direct realization of what is manifested by one's own mind. Thus, all that is spoken of—such as *tathatā* (thusness), emptiness, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nirvāṇa, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the various types of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*)—are merely different designations for this single direct realization of the one mind.
For within the *tathāgatagarbha*, when one seeks for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, they are utterly unfindable.
Because it is ungraspable, this is the state where the five dharmas and the three natures are all transcended, and the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded;
only then is it called the ultimate realm of the Tathāgata’s noble self-realized wisdom.
A practitioner must observe in this way to be able to know the meaning as it truly is, and only then can they attain liberation from the various afflictions and delusive thoughts of their own mind.

Therefore, I say that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind. [The preceding section], clarifying that deluded thoughts are unreal, has finished refuting the attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*) and severing the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
[The following section] clarifies that the nature of verbal expression is empty in order to refute the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and sever the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This consists of four parts. △ First, it clarifies that verbal expression is the root of the attachment to phenomena.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva should be skilled in speech and meaning (*artha*).
What is meant by a Bodhisattva being 'skilled in speech and meaning'? What is speech? What is meaning?"
The commentary states: This follows the preceding inquiry, intended to shatter attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and sever the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
First, it clarifies that verbal expression is the root of attachment to phenomena; for indeed, both mundane and supramundane phenomena are all dependent upon linguistic conceptualization.

To grasp [phenomena] as being substantially existent is, therefore, the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) regarding the meaning of words; this is termed the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

This is because the Blessed One previously cautioned: "One should rely on the meaning, not cling to the words. Subsequently, by following the meaning of words that are poorly expressed and generating understanding according to those words, one falls into error and the two views, giving rise to the fault of repudiating [existence]. All of these are the cognitive obscuration, which is the attachment to phenomena.

Therefore, the teaching is followed by the two general characteristics. It is said that by relying on the meaning of reality (*yathābhūta-artha*), one is able to liberate oneself from the various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of one's own mind. This is because improper linguistic meanings give rise to manifold faults.

When Mahāmati reaches this point, he asks how to understand "proper linguistic meaning" (*suvākya-artha*). This question concerns the skillful means (*upāya*) for understanding proper linguistic meaning.

This is intended to shatter the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). Furthermore, [the bodhisattva] does not know what constitutes "speech" (*vāk*) and what constitutes "meaning" (*artha*). This question concerns their characteristics.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha:

He said, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: “What is speech? It is the conjunction of words and letters through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Depending upon the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, palate, and cheeks, it arises from the attachment to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceptual constructions of self and other in verbal discourse. This is called speech.”
The commentary states: "This indicates the characteristics of speech. The Tang translation says: 'Speech' refers to that which takes the habitual tendencies of conceptual discrimination as its cause;
depending upon the throat, tongue, lips, palate, teeth, and cheeks, it produces various sounds and syllables for the purpose of mutual conversation.
This is called speech. [In this context], "cheeks" (fǔ) refers to the sides of the mouth; "gums" (yín) refers to the roots of the teeth.
"Mahāmati, what is meant by 'meaning' (artha)? It refers to that which is free from all characteristics of conceptual construction (vikalpa) and characteristics of verbal expression;

this is called 'meaning. The commentary states: This demonstrates the characteristic of meaning. That is to say, it is the severance of the path of language and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity;
this is the characteristic of meaning. Therefore, it is said to be 'free from' (vivarjita). 'Free from' means not being accompanied by [such characteristics]."

Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding such meanings as these, dwells alone in a quiet place and, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, takes self-realization as their object and heads toward the city of Nirvāṇa;
having transformed the body of habitual tendencies, they realize the realm of self-awareness (the *Tang* translation says:

"By means of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they contemplate and observe, heading toward the path of Nirvāṇa, the realm of their own gnosis, and transform all habitual tendencies"). They observe the characteristics of the progressive advancement between each stage (*bhūmi*). This is called...
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is skilled in the meaning (*artha*).
The commentary states: "This demonstrates the skillful means (*upāya*) for being skilled in the meaning. 'Hearing, reflection, and cultivation' refers to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

That is to say, one reflects upon and cultivates what has been heard; by relying on the light of the teachings of great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) expounded by a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), it passes from the ear and reaches the mind."
When the voice enters the mind, one penetrates through direct realization; when the final words are received, their meaning is attained.

By settling the mind in contemplative observation and investigating with careful reflection, one reaches the realm of self-knowledge within true suchness (*tathatā*) and quiescent extinction. Entering ever deeper moment by moment, one uses this to cultivate and transform habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Extinguishing the darkness of ignorance and giving rise to the light of wisdom, until the path of the mind is severed and there is a single moment of resonance—this is called attaining entry into the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
This is the skillful means of the true meaning. The wise should contemplate in this manner.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skilled in words and meaning contemplates that words and meaning are neither different nor not different;
he contemplates meaning and words in the same way. If words and meaning were different, then meaning could not be articulated by means of words.
One enters into the meaning by means of words, just as a lamp illuminates forms.
The commentary states: "This demonstrates that meaning is revealed through words, thereby clarifying that the function of words is both excellent.

Since it was stated above that meaning is fundamentally beyond words, there is a fear that deluded persons might cling to it as being a state of total annihilation; therefore, this is shown so that one may enter [the meaning] by means of words.
The meaning is as follows: although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to wordlessness.
The dharani is without characters, yet characters manifest the dharani. This is the true essence of the teaching; its purity lies in hearing the sounds.
However, regarding the meaning of these words, one must not hold the view that they are either identical or different. Thus, it is like a lamp illuminating forms:
although one sees forms by means of the lamp, one cannot say they are different; yet since the forms are not the lamp itself, one cannot say they are identical.
This, moreover, teaches the skillful means for correctly interpreting the meaning of words.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding such matters as non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nature, nirvāṇa, the three vehicles and the one vehicle, and the self-nature of the mind—

when one becomes attached to the meanings of these verbal expressions, one falls into the views of superimposition and denial, which are distinct from the actual establishment and distinct from false conceptualization.
Various delusive imaginings appear like illusions; just as with various illusions, ordinary, ignorant sentient beings form divergent delusive imaginings, which do not belong to the noble ones.

The commentary states: "This rebukes non-Buddhists for their false attachment to names and phrases, which constitutes the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa); therefore, it teaches [the distinction between] words and meanings."
One should contemplate this according to reality; one must not give rise to understanding based merely on the words. The Chinese translation says:

"If there are those who, regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nirvāṇa, the three vehicles and the single vehicle, the five dharmas and the various natures of mind, and so forth, grasp at the meaning according to the literal expression, they fall into the views of superimposition and denial, because they give rise to conceptual discrimination that differs from the true nature."
It is like seeing a magical illusion and reckoning it to be real; this is the vision of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.

That is to say, regarding all phenomena—whether defiled or pure, such as those that are neither arising nor ceasing—to grasp at their meaning according to the words and to be attached to the idea that the expression and its referent are one is called "establishment" (*samāropa*).
To reckon that the expression and its referent are different is called "denial" (*apavāda*). This is because, with respect to various...
Because various conceptual constructions arise from the locus of verbal expression, it is called "differentiated establishment" (*anyathā-vyavasthāna*).

Because these differentiated deluded imaginings (*vikalpa*) are all taken to be real, it is said that "various deluded imaginings appear like illusions. To reckon various illusory phenomena as being real is the vision of a truly foolish person.
As the ancients said: "The object of knowledge is not the obstacle; rather, one is obstructed by the obstacle, which in turn obstructs the object of knowledge."

However, that which is known is the true reality of quiescent cessation; how could it be an obstruction? It is merely because one clings to names and words that they become an obstacle, preventing one from entering realization.
This is what is meant by the four marks secretly influencing the spirit, such that one fails to perceive them and instead rejects them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who engage in the false conceptualization of speech establish various dharmas; because of those establishments, they fall into hell after death."
The Commentary states: This verse calculates that those who regard all dharmas as real through verbal expression have committed the fault of false views.
When the Buddha spoke of all the various defiled and pure dharmas, it was for the purpose of counteracting the mental illness of the deluded thoughts of all sentient beings;

thus, he established them based on conventional phenomena. Fundamentally, they are not real dharmas. Although meaning is revealed by means of words, the meaning does not reside in the words themselves.
He said: "If one reckons that each and every phenomenon—whether true or false—is substantially existent, this is a pernicious view;
therefore, upon death, one falls into hell.

Within the aggregates (skandhas) there is no self, nor are the aggregates themselves the self; yet it is not as those who hold such deluded imaginings claim, nor is it the case that there is no self at all."
The commentary states: This uses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a metaphor for the meaning of the verbal expressions of all phenomena (*dharma*).

Because there are only verbal expressions and no real meaning whatsoever, it is like how there is no self (*ātman*) within the aggregates. Since the true meaning is fundamentally beyond words and words are not themselves the meaning, it is like how the aggregates are not identical to the self.
Verbal expressions of all phenomena are fundamentally not truly existent; therefore, they are not like that [false] delusion.
Regarding the perception that the aggregates (*skandhas*) constitute a self: although this is not substantially existent, it does not fall into the extreme of annihilationism.

Therefore, just as those aggregates are not non-self either, when one contemplates the words and their meaning in this way, one does not fall into the views of existence and non-existence, or identity and difference.
All things possess a nature, just as ordinary, deluded people falsely imagine; yet if they were as they appear to them, everyone would perceive the Truth.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature, for both purity and impurity do not exist at all. They are unreal just as they are seen, yet it is not that they are non-existent.

The commentary states: This applies the Dharma to the preceding metaphor. The previous verse used a reductio ad absurdum to demonstrate that all phenomena are fundamentally not substantially existent.
That is to say, if all phenomena were indeed to possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) as those foolish people falsely conceptualize, [it would lead to logical fallacies].
Thus, one should see the locus of reality in each and every instance. At present, there is only language; the actual meaning has not yet been seen.
It is like saying that fire does not burn the mouth or that ice does not chill the teeth.

Observing this, it is sufficient evidence that all dharmas expressed through speech are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they all lack intrinsic nature, the purity or impurity of speech is not truly existent.
Nevertheless, what the Sages perceive regarding all phenomena is no different from that of ordinary, deluded beings;

it is only that the deluded conceive of them as real, whereas the Sages view them as mere illusions and transformations. Thus it is said: "They are not real, yet they appear as such. Nor are they non-existent.
The above explanation clarifying that verbal expression is the root of attachment to phenomena is now complete. △ Below, the wisdom and consciousness are demonstrated.
It is the source of bondage and liberation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If you and the other Bodhisattvas skillfully discern the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, you will be able to penetrate those characteristics and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Bodhi recorded:

Because this teaching above concerns the bodhisattva’s skillful engagement with the meaning of words, it specifically explains the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), intending that one should rely on wisdom and not on consciousness.
Now, that which possesses discrimination is consciousness; that which is without discrimination is wisdom. One should rely [on the latter].

To rely on consciousness results in injury to both; to rely on wisdom results in the goodness of both. This is because of the distinction between the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
If one observes through wisdom, then those conventional names and phrases will naturally cease of themselves.
"Mahāmati, that wisdom is of three kinds: namely, worldly, supramundane, and supramundane-superior. The commentary states:
'This enumerates the characteristics of wisdom as being of three kinds. As for consciousness, it is as previously mentioned:
briefly stated there are three kinds, and extensively stated there are eight; therefore, they are not fully detailed here."
What is mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*)? It refers to all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to the notions of existence and non-existence.
The commentary states: "This mundane wisdom is precisely the characteristic of wisdom among the six coarse [delusions].

When non-Buddhists claim to possess "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajña*), the "benevolent wisdom" spoken of here in this land, and the "discarding of wisdom" taught by Laozi—all are this very same wisdom.

The Buddha said: "Worldly wisdom and eloquence are difficult [to transcend], for by relying on this wisdom, one cannot enter the principle of non-arising; therefore, it is said that one calculates and clings to existence and non-existence.
What is supramundane wisdom? It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into the calculations of hope regarding self-characteristics and common characteristics."
[The commentary] says: "These are the partial wisdoms of emptiness belonging to the two vehicles. The Śrāvakas know suffering and sever its origin; they cultivate the path and realize cessation.

This involves the *dharmajñānakṣānti*, *dharmajñāna*, *anvayajñānakṣānti*, and *anvayajñāna*. Furthermore, the Pratyekabuddhas examine causes and scrutinize causes through the seventy-seven wisdoms. Thus, they perceive existence."

The three realms and the five aggregates of birth and death are objects of aversion; because one does not realize that they are mind-only, it is said that one "falls into self-characteristics and common characteristics.

Because one calculates that there is a nirvana to be realized, it is said that one "hopes for and clings to it. The reason for this clinging is that one has not yet departed from the nature of consciousness and has not realized the absence of ignorance.

What is the supramundane, most excellent wisdom? It refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who contemplate all dharmas as non-existent, seeing them as neither arising nor ceasing, and being free from the categories of existence and non-existence.
This is the stage of the Tathāgata, wherein the selflessness of persons and phenomena arises through personal realization.
The commentary states: "This is the supreme wisdom of the supramundane. The noble ones of the eighth stage realize signless *tathatā* and first attain this wisdom;
