They have become calloused and muddled. Yet the World-Honored One, who perceives and hears from afar, foresaw that listeners would likewise give rise to interpretations based on their words;
they would surely grasp at "non-arising" as being truly existent, establishing a fixed notion that there is a specific "non-arising" and giving rise to speculative views.
If it were thus, one would again fall into the heterodox views of the non-Buddhists. Therefore, at this critical juncture, [the Master] suddenly rebuked and warned them, saying:
"When I say that all dharmas are unarisen, my disciples should not establish this as a thesis.
For within this Dharma, the presence of even a hair’s breadth of conceptual opinion causes one to fall into the nesting place of birth and death. Thus...
Thus, one becomes an outsider within the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch said to Yongjia, "You have attained a state of non-arising that is full of intent.
Yongjia replied, "If there is no arising, how can there be intent? The Patriarch said, "If there is no intent, who would make distinctions? Yongjia replied:
Discrimination is also not the mind. The Patriarch said: "So it is, so it is. Why is this?
It is because the fundamental principle holds that all natures are non-natures, and because of the characteristics produced by their causes.
The commentary states: This interrogation and explanation address two kinds of fallacies in the non-arising thesis (*anutpāda-pakṣa*) established by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

That is to say, the calculations of the non-Buddhists do not transcend the two views of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) and eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*); therefore, there are two types of their non-arising thesis.
Namely, they falsely calculate that all phenomena (*dharma*) are utterly annihilated and thus constitute non-arising; hence it is said, "Because all natures are non-natures."
This is the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, they calculate that there exists a distinct and separate cause capable of producing all phenomena, which they call the "agent" (*kartṛ*).
This is like what Zhuang Zhou said in this land: "That which gives birth to birth does not itself undergo birth. This is because that which is unborn is able to produce the myriad phenomena;
it is exactly as stated in that other land, where the agent is unborn yet serves as the cause for production. That is to say, if...

Since that which is called "non-arising" serves as the cause for arising, this cause is itself the characteristic of arising. Therefore it is said, "and because that cause is the characteristic of arising.
This refers to the eternalist view (*śāśvatavāda*). This passage sets forth the essence of that school's position; what follows below reveals its faults.
If the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen were asserted, that very thesis would be undermined.
That thesis is undermined because the thesis itself arises dependently.
The Record states: This refers to the thesis established by those non-Buddhists; it contains the fault of the "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*).
The Buddha [points out] that regarding the thesis of "non-arising" established by those non-Buddhists, they themselves undermine the meaning of non-arising. Why?

Because according to their own school, arising occurs in dependence [upon conditions]. That is to say, both types of meanings of "non-arising" asserted by them are such only because they depend upon conditions.
Furthermore, the non-arising of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is dependent, because the meaning of non-arising is only manifested once all phenomena have ceased.
The non-arising of the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is also dependent, because non-arising is only manifested in relation to phenomena that arise.
Since both are dependent, how can they truly be non-arising? Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon [is empty]."
It is established that although [the entity] is called "unborn," it nonetheless becomes a phenomenon that is born. Therefore, that school's own position destroys its doctrine of non-arising;
this is also termed a contradiction with one's own teaching.
Furthermore, because that school does not admit the non-arising of all phenomena, and because it does not accept non-arising as their unconditioned characteristic,
the thesis that "all phenomena are unarisen" is undermined by its own assertions.
The commentary states: This serves to expose the faults inherent in that school and to distinguish them by means of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

Now, the reason that school is undermined is that its established position falls into the extremes of existence and non-existence, as well as eternalism and nihilism, regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).
For all phenomena are characterized by arising and ceasing, and are impermanent; yet that school relies upon [the duality of] existence and non-existence.
Regarding the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*): in reality, the dharmas have not yet arisen. Although their verbal expression does not arise, their meaning actually arises.

Therefore, this falls into the fault of contradicting one's own teachings (*sva-śāstra-viruddha-doṣa*). This is a contradiction of one's own school (*sva-siddhānta-virodha*). Thus it is said: "Because that school [asserts] non-arising enters into all dharmas.
If one examines this with the True Dharma (*saddharma*), however, my teaching takes the unimpaired characteristic (*akṣaya-lakṣaṇa*) as its basis.
Regarding arising: because arising is itself non-arising, they take the characteristic of destruction to be non-arising.

However, since the characteristic of destruction is impermanent, how could it truly be non-arising? Furthermore, as for that characteristic of destruction, they take its cessation and annihilation to be non-arising.
This is the subversion of the characteristic of arising. To claim that "the unarisen can give rise" is the subversion of the characteristic of non-arising.
Now, by using my teaching of the dharma of the indestructible characteristic to examine this, the thesis they have established—that all dharmas are unarisen—is refuted;
for their false conceptualization does not transcend the dharmas of existence and non-existence. Therefore, the following text brings this to light.
For this reason, Mahāmati, the thesis that neither existence nor non-existence arises enters into all natures, for the characteristics of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended therein.
The commentary states: "This explains the reason why that thesis is destroyed. It means that when I speak of that thesis, it is thereby destroyed."
Since they maintain that both existence and non-existence are unarisen, they establish their thesis based upon this.
However, all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing do not transcend existence and non-existence; thus, the thesis they have established is itself included within all phenomena.
Furthermore, all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, such that neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended. Since both existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended, they—
Upon what basis, then, could a thesis be established? Therefore, I say that such a thesis is undermined. Thus, the Tang translation states:
"In that thesis, both existence and non-existence are entirely unarisen; this thesis enters into all phenomena because the characteristics of existence and non-existence are likewise unarisen.
Furthermore, "unarisen" means that existence and non-existence are fundamentally non-existent from the outset.
Mahāmati, if that school were to establish its thesis by asserting that all natures are unarisen and do not arise, such a thesis would be undermined.

This is because there is no arising of the characteristics of existence or non-existence; therefore, a thesis should not be established. Furthermore, because the five-membered syllogism contains many fallacies, because the reasons are mutually dependent and possess distinct characteristics, and because it functions as a mere fabrication, the members of a thesis should not be established.
The commentary states: This uses the characteristics of the correct teaching as a reason to refute that heterodox school and thereby establish its faults;
it concludes that the proposed tenet cannot be maintained. "If" (*yadi*) functions here as a hypothetical concession. The Buddha says:

even if that school were to establish its tenet based on the existence of all natures (*sarva-bhāva*), then that very tenet would collapse of its own accord, because all phenomena possess both existent and non-existent natures and characteristics.
Because they are fundamentally unarisen. Since all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning, for what purpose would one establish a thesis (*pakṣa*) based upon them?

Therefore, one should not rely on them to establish a thesis. However, if the thesis thus established is examined through the correct teachings and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) of logic (*hetuvidyā*), it commits many fallacies; for its successive reasons (*hetu*) do not correspond with the thesis.

[They are] not joined, because they possess many dissimilar characteristics. It is not only that the reason is not joined with the thesis (*pakṣa*), but the very essence of the thesis itself is also unestablished.

Why? Because according to their [opponents'] reckoning, the agent is unborn. Therefore, I say that when teaching the disciples the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one should not further establish a formal thesis. Regarding the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vāda*) having many faults: the five members are—

There are five parts: first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*). Regarding the many fallacies:

the thesis has nine fallacies, the reason has fourteen fallacies, the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has five fallacies, and the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has five fallacies, totaling thirty-three fallacies.
As for the three members established by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), if they are examined and distinguished according to the True Dharma (*saddharma*), they possess only a single fallacy.
If [the reason] is not dispatched, it immediately belongs to the heterodox school (*tīrthika*), because the reason and the example serve only to establish the nature of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Therefore, since the reason does not apply and the example is inconsistent, both fail to establish the thesis. Thus, the various characteristics of the successive reasons and the fact that they are "produced" (*kṛtaka*) [are shown to be fallacious].
This would result in many fallacies; therefore, one should not establish such a thesis. The five-membered syllogism is fully contained in the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra*.
Because its meaning is extensive, I fear that a full reproduction would be too prolix. By understanding this, one will be able to determine the fundamental tenets of the Buddha-dharma.
It subdues and overcomes false views; those who observe it should investigate that treatise so as to grasp its essential meaning.
Namely: all phenomena are unarisen; likewise, all phenomena are empty; likewise, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
"One should not establish a thesis.
The commentary states: "This summarizes the preceding meaning. Previously it was said that [reality] is empty, unarisen, non-dual, and devoid of the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now it is said that since there is no arising, one should not establish a thesis; thus, whether it be 'emptiness' or 'lack of intrinsic nature,' neither should be established at all."
This is the core principle: because there are merely verbal expressions and no real meaning whatsoever, all that is conceptually discriminated is not known or seen as it truly is.
However, Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas speak of all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams, because they manifest both appearing and non-appearing characteristics.
Furthermore, because they perceive the faults of conceptual cognition, they declare that all phenomena are of the nature of illusions and dreams.

This is excepted only for the sake of providing a phrase to prevent fools from falling into terror; for, Mahāmati, fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence. Do not cause them to become terrified and thereby abandon the Mahāyāna.
The Record states: This is the manner in which the Tathāgata instructs all bodhisattvas to teach the Dharma. Question:
Since a bodhisattva should not establish a thesis regarding dharmas that are non-arising, what kind of dharma should they teach? Answer:
Indeed, a bodhisattva should teach that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams, because they appear and do not appear. Although illusions and dreams appear, in reality...
It is not manifest. This indicates that although all phenomena arise, in reality they are without arising. All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
that they appear to arise is not due to the arising of phenomena, but is rather the fault of the perception and cognition of sentient beings, who falsely perceive that there is arising.
Therefore, one should say that all phenomena have a nature like an illusion or a dream; it cannot be said that phenomena truly exist.
It is non-arising. Nevertheless, there are also those who speak of "non-arising"; this is merely for the sake of causing foolish people to depart from phrases that provoke terror.
Having no other choice, one employs the phrase "non-arising" simply to sever their view of arising. Since all dharmas are non-arising, there is no room for speech;
for as soon as one gives rise to thought or movement of mind, one falls into birth and death. However, it is for the sake of the foolish...

Regarding the teaching on non-arising: because foolish people are single-mindedly and stubbornly attached to the existence of real dharmas, they become terrified when it is suddenly said that all things are like illusions or dreams; thus, they distance themselves from the Mahāyāna and sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
If one does not guide them according to their capacities by means of the phrase "non-arising," they will be forever excluded from the Buddha-dharma, and the Bodhisattva likewise fails in his task.
Out of compassion, it is said that foolish people fall into the views of existence and non-existence; one must not cause them to be terrified and thereby lead them to abandon the Mahāyāna.
"Mahā" means "Great," and "Yāna" means "Vehicle. When a Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma in this manner, they attain the two characteristics of penetration.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without self-nature, without expression, without objective reality, and without continuity—these are the deluded imaginings of fools, like the evil perceptions of a corpse."

(As translated in the Tang Dynasty: "Evil perceptions are like corpses. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-arising; this is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Ultimately, there is nothing that arises;

they are accomplished through the nature of conditions. All phenomena are non-arising; the wise do not form conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) regarding them. Because their tenets arise from causes, the awakened ones have completely eradicated them.
The commentary states: This verse generally summarizes the five difficult points regarding emptiness, non-arising, and the lack of intrinsic nature.

It shows that [reality] is fundamentally free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects, thereby clarifying that non-Buddhists should not establish formal tenets.
Since there is no objective entity, it is empty; because all phenomena are fundamentally empty, there is no continuity. Yet, foolish people deludedly imagine the unreal to be real, as described here.
Evil conceptions are like a corpse that lacks consciousness; they merely increase defilement. These are thus empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), inconceivable, and non-arising.
How could one allow such a doctrine to be venerated as a school of thought by the false calculations of the outsiders?
For the "non-arising" established by them leads ultimately to annihilationism, wherein no phenomena arise, because they fail to comprehend dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Arising is without intrinsic nature; because that which lacks intrinsic nature arises through conditions, it is said that "ultimately there is nothing that arises.

In the phrase "that which is accomplished by means of nature and conditions," the character *xìng* (nature) from the lower clause should be read as carrying over into the upper clause. Furthermore, the character *suǒ* (that which) in "that which is accomplished" (*suǒ chéngjiù*) should be read as *bù* (not).
Therefore, the Tang translation states: "Because those things that arise are not established by conditions.

However, the meaning of the non-arising of all phenomena can only be realized through silent resonance by a wise person who has set aside the conceptual mind; one should not form mental constructs regarding it.
Moreover, since that school establishes [arising] based on the characteristic of arising, how could it truly be non-arising? Thus, the Awakened One completely eliminates it, for that...
It is not produced, yet it has the characteristic of being produced.
It is like one with cataracts seeing the appearance of falling hair; the nature of attachment is likewise so. It is the false conceptualization of the deluded.
In the three realms of existence, there is no intrinsic nature of things; yet one designates an intrinsic nature of things and gives rise to deluded thoughts through such contemplation.

By establishing verbal teachings based on signs and things, the mind becomes distracted and violently shaken. The Son of the Buddha is able to transcend this and remain far removed from all deluded thoughts.

The commentary states: This verse [teaches that] all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and exist only through deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), serving as a warning to the Buddha’s disciples not to give rise to views.

Just as there is fundamentally no floating hair before the eyes in empty space, yet it appears because of a cataract, this serves as a metaphor for how the various phenomena of the three realms are fundamentally non-existent within reality, yet are reckoned as such due to deluded conceptualization. The foolish merely cling to provisional names and are moved by them.
Those who possess right knowledge and vision should remain far removed from that which disturbs the mind-consciousness. Therefore, the Tang translation says:
"The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to dharmas. Based on these provisional designations, one engages in conceptualization and false discrimination.
These provisional names and various phenomenal marks agitate the mind-consciousness. The Sons of the Buddha completely transcend them and wander in non-conceptualization."
To perceive what is not water as water is a sensation born of craving; such is the delusion of the fool, but it is not so for the noble one.
The noble one perceives purity, which arises from the three liberations and samādhis; far removed from arising and ceasing, they wander in the realm of non-existence.
One practices the non-existence of all things, which is neither existence nor non-existence. From the equality of existence and non-existence, the fruits of the noble ones arise.
The commentary states: This verse clarifies that the characteristics of the three realms are not different; it is only the perceptions of the noble ones and the ordinary worldlings that differ.
However, the three realms originally lack any real dharmas; that foolish people delusively perceive them as truly existent is like a mirage.
To perceive water as water is born of craving; such is the case with the deluded. How could the noble wisdom be thus?
Because the noble one perceives purity, what is seen is the three realms as empty and devoid of substance;
this very state is the realization of the samādhi of liberation, far removed from arising and ceasing. The Tang translation says: "Constantly practicing within the realm of signlessness."

One practices the realm of signlessness, which is likewise neither existence nor non-existence; since existence and non-existence are entirely equal, one thereby gives rise to the fruits of sainthood.
Because of the distinctions perceived by ordinary beings, there is the continuity of karmic results;
because the sages perceive the three realms as no different [from nirvana], they give rise to the fruits of sainthood. Thus, a sutra says: "Do not view the three realms as the three realms."

What is nature and what is non-nature? What is equanimity? It is said that when the mind does not know and is utterly tossed about by internal and external [objects], if one can destroy that [state of agitation], the mind then perceives with equanimity.
The commentary states: This verse interrogates and explains the preceding meaning in order to clarify the equality of the noble and the ordinary.
It asks: Since the three realms are one, why do the ignorant perceive existence and non-existence? Why do the noble ones perceive equality?

Because those foolish people do not understand that the three realms are fundamentally empty, they falsely conceptualize the mind and its objects as truly existent; therefore, they are utterly adrift within the internal and external worlds.
Movement. If one can thoroughly understand this, then one should contemplate equality. Equality is another name for quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
That is to say, as long as one has not realized that objects are mind-only, various forms of discrimination arise; once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises.
The above section on dispelling the object of contemplation is concluded. △ Below follows the dispelling of the contemplating wisdom.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, when wisdom does not apprehend an object of perception, this is a conventional designation established by the measure of designation.

That which is grasped is non-existent in nature, and the act of grasping is also non-existent in nature. Because there is no grasping, wisdom does not arise; it is merely a conventional name. (The Tang translation says: "As the Buddha has taught, if...")

To know that objects of perception are merely provisional designations and are entirely unobtainable, one has nothing to grasp. Because there is nothing to grasp, there is also no grasper. Since both grasper and grasped are absent, conceptual discrimination does not arise; this is what is called wisdom.

The commentary states: Having already distinguished above that false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) lacks intrinsic nature, this [section] concerns the principle of the Great Wisdom (*mahāmati*), which was briefly discussed by the Buddha as the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
It is used to demonstrate that noble wisdom is "non-cognizing" (*ajñāna*). The Wei translation says:

"As the World-Honored One has taught, when wisdom observes, it cannot see the phenomena (*dharma*) of the preceding realm, up to and including the realization of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-avabodha*); there is no dharma that can be [perceived]."
There is grasping, yet there is no grasper. Therefore, wisdom (*jñāna*) likewise cannot differentiate and grasp; thus it is said that "wisdom does not arise.
However, the objects of attachment are the preceding realms—the various phenomena (*dharma*), which are what are called "characteristics" (*nimitta*).
It was stated previously that "not apprehending characteristics is wisdom. The reason wisdom does not apprehend characteristics is because all realms are merely...
This is a conceptual construction established through false imagination (*vikalpa*), for fundamentally there is no nature of either the grasped (*grāhya*) or the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Since there is no object to be grasped, even if true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) were present, from what could it differentiate and grasp? Therefore, it is said:
"Because there is nothing to be grasped, wisdom does not arise. Yet one fails to realize that the realm of false imagination is like darkness, while wisdom is like light.
When light comes, darkness naturally departs; it is not that there is a duality between darkness and light.
Therefore, when it is said that "sage-wisdom is without knowing," it is because there is no object to be known, and thus the wisdom that cognizes objects also ceases.
Since there are no marks of subject or object to be grasped, it is simply said that "no marks can be obtained. What is meant is that only the wisdom of suchness remains alone.
It is likely not that there is a total absence of cognition. Thus, it appears that Mahāmati does not understand the meaning of the non-apprehension of signs by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

He seems to think that because there is an object, there must be a corresponding subject; how then could there be no apprehension? He must believe that one can only be called "wisdom" if one cognizes an object.
Therefore, he raises this doubt by restating the preceding argument in order to pose a challenge. This restatement of the argument follows below.
He raised a doubt, saying:

"World-Honored One, is it because the nature of non-awakening—whether its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are different or not different—that wisdom does not apprehend it?
Or is it because the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of the specific and general characteristics are obscured that wisdom does not apprehend it? Or is it because of the mountains..."
Is it because of obstructions such as cliffs, rocks, walls, earth, water, fire, or wind that wisdom cannot perceive? Or is it because of being too far away or too close that wisdom cannot perceive?
Or is it because of being old, young, blind, or otherwise lacking in the sensory faculties that wisdom cannot perceive?
The commentary states: "This refers to the arising of doubt. 'Not perceiving' and so forth means being entirely unaware of that object.
'Self-characteristics being obscured' is a way of saying they are hidden and do not appear; it means there is no object at all to serve as a counterpart for cognition.
'Obstructed by mountain crags and the like' means that cognition does not penetrate through. 'Extremely distant' means it is beyond the reach of the eye."
"Proximate" means subtle and difficult to know. "Lacking the sense faculties" refers to being blind, dark, and ignorant.
"The aged and the young" refers to those who cannot know everything in its entirety. Mahāmati, one whose wisdom is doubtful cannot grasp the characteristics [of things];
is it not the case that these five factors prevent such attainment? Below, he presents a challenge.

World-Honored One, if one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different, and thus cognition is not attained, it should not be called "cognition";
rather, it should be called "non-cognition," because there is an object that is not apprehended.

The commentary states: This is one objection. It says that if one does not know an object at all, such that it cannot be apprehended, this would not be called "knowledge" (jñāna), but rather "lack of knowledge" (ajñāna), because there is an object which is not known.
Furthermore, if wisdom does not apprehend because the self-natures and mutual characteristics of various phenomena are obscured by their own intrinsic natures, that too is non-wisdom;

it is not wisdom, World-Honored One. Wisdom arises because there is such an appearance (*tathatā*); it is called wisdom because it accords with that appearance through the absence of intrinsic nature.

The commentary states: These are two difficulties. That is to say, if one were to claim that it is impossible to attain [realization] because there is no knowable object whatsoever to serve as its counterpart, this too is not wisdom. Why? Because wisdom arises precisely because there is an object known;
it is not the case that wisdom consists in the absence of a knowing nature encountering that knowable object. Therefore, the Tang translation says:
This, too, is not knowledge. It is called knowledge because it knows its object; it is not [knowledge] because of non-knowing.

O Jvalanā, that which is known—whether mountain crags, stone walls, earth, water, fire, or wind; whether extremely distant or extremely near; or by the old, the young, the blind, or those with impaired faculties—[is known].
That which is not obtained despite possessing wisdom is itself not wisdom; it must be a lack of wisdom, because there are objects that cannot be apprehended. The commentary states:

"This combines the third and fourth difficulties. This refers to things existing in the world, such as mountains, crags, stone walls, or the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which may be so distant that they do not reach the range of one's vision, or so near that they are obstructed by walls. Fourth.
There is great congestion and oppression; this indicates a lack of thorough penetration. Among sentient beings, there are those who are old, young, blind, or ignorant, possessing no discernment;
or there are those whose faculties are incomplete and thus cannot know exhaustively. If one were to claim that [the Dharma] is unattainable on account of such people, [it would be a mistake].
This, too, is not wisdom; it should rather be called non-wisdom, because there is an object that cannot be apprehended. The Tang translation states:
"That, too, is not wisdom, because although there is an objective sphere, wisdom is incomplete and thus fails to know it.

The intention of Mahāmati here seems to be that the failure to apprehend the preceding object constitutes non-wisdom, whereas only when one necessarily perceives the object does it constitute wisdom. Therefore, below...
[The opponent] refutes this.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not so. What is non-wisdom should be wisdom; it is not non-wisdom.
I do not speak of the objects of perception in such a concealed manner that wisdom would fail to attain them. This is an establishment based on the measure of conventional designation."
The commentary states: This refutes and answers the doubt that [the Buddha’s cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The Buddha’s intention was:
"Is it not the case that one lacks wisdom simply because one does not apprehend an external object? One should know that this so-called "lack of wisdom" is in fact wisdom; it is not a lack of wisdom.
However, when I say that wisdom does not apprehend characteristics, this is not to say that there are real external objects that mutually obscure one another.

It is said that wisdom does not apprehend [objects]. If one calculates that wisdom fails to apprehend because there are preceding objects that mutually obscure one another, this is merely a conceptual construction based on false imagination; it is not true wisdom. *Above is the refutation of error.
Below is the direct answer.*

One awakens to the fact that what appears to one’s own mind is merely a mental representation (*cittadṛśya-mātra*). One knows that external entities, whether existent or non-existent, lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); yet, despite this knowledge, one does not grasp at those objects. Because they are not grasped, cognition does not arise toward them;

thus it accords with the three gates of liberation. Even cognition itself is not grasped. For one who is free from false discrimination, there is no beginning to the nature or non-nature of things, which are but deceptive habitual tendencies.
To know in this way—that such knowing is itself a form of ignorance—is to be truly ignorant regarding external objects. Therefore, [one does not perceive] external things.
They are mutually grasped through conceptual attachment;

they do not sever the false imaginings regarding the characteristics, nature, and non-nature of locations. They establish [their views] based on the manifestations of their own minds and speak of "I" and "mine.
The commentary states: "This is the direct answer regarding the true meaning. The Buddha said: "That which I have taught cannot be apprehended by intellectual knowledge, because I..."
One awakens to the fact that all external phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are devoid of self-nature and are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
They are entirely empty and quiescent, for there is no objective realm to serve as a counterpart to cognition. Knowing things in this way, I say that cognition cannot apprehend them.
Thus it is said: "Awakening to the manifestations of one's own mind, one knows that external natures, whether existent or non-existent, are not real. Know this.
Yet the matter cannot be attained. "Yet" (ér) means it remains thus. Since there is no object that accords with the mind, the object is as-it-is (rú).
Likewise, since there is no mind that cognizes the object, the mind is as-it-is. When both mind and object are as-it-is, neither can be apprehended.
Because both mind and object cannot be apprehended, wisdom does not give rise to the "thus-flame" (ěr-yàn). "Thus-flame" refers to the objects of knowledge.

When objects cannot be apprehended, then objects do not arise. When the mind cannot be apprehended, then cognition does not arise. When neither mind nor objects arise, one accords with the three gates of liberation.
The three gates of liberation are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). "Accords with" means entering.
However, regarding the three liberations, it is not that wisdom does not enter them; rather, once they have entered, even the essence of wisdom is forgotten.
Therefore, it is said that "wisdom itself is not attained. This is what is meant by the "non-cognition of noble wisdom.

Yet, as for this state where wisdom is non-cognitive, it is certainly not something that deluded ordinary people—whose minds are conditioned by the habitual tendencies of beginningless false and frivolous conceptual proliferation—could possibly know through their own wisdom.
This is the knowledge of non-knowing; it is not that which is known by ordinary cognition. Therefore, it is said: "He knows, while they do not know.

Because they do not know this knowledge of non-knowing, they continue to engage in uninterrupted conceptualization and discrimination regarding the existence or non-existence of external objects and their forms.
Thus, the Wei translation states: "In order to depart from such a deluded mind, all dharmas are taught."

It is seen as nothing but one's own mind; because of the attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," it is said that they are established through the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind.
Thus, the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to self" are described as being grasped and clung to.
Failing to realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, they give rise to false conceptualization regarding the radiance of gnosis.
Because of this conceptualization, they fail to perceive external objects as being neither existent nor non-existent, and thus fall into the view of nihilism.
The commentary states: This rebuke is directed at Mahāmati for failing to know things as they truly are, thereby giving rise to the view of nihilistic cessation born of ignorance.

Because he does not realize that "self" and "what belongs to self," as well as all phenomena, are merely manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*), he gives rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding both wisdom and its objects.
Due to this false conceptualization, he investigates existence and non-existence but fails to attain the true meaning; consequently, regarding wisdom...
Objects arise based on views of annihilationism, giving rise to conceptual discrimination. These are all unwholesome and involve both [types of] supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Because they do not penetrate the true meaning, they falsely give rise to perverse wisdom. Therefore, the subsequent passage concludes by reprimanding them with reference to these two powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When there are objects of attachment, yet wisdom does not examine them, this is a lack of wisdom, not true wisdom; so say those who harbor false imaginings."

The commentary states: This verse in summary refutes doubt. It means that if there were truly an object of perception, yet one says that wisdom does not observe it, this is merely false discrimination;
to claim that the absence of wisdom constitutes non-wisdom is entirely the talk of deluded fools and is not the teaching of the wise.
When wisdom does not discern the nature of non-differentiation, nor [discern] obstacles, distance, or proximity, this is called false wisdom (*mithyājñāna*).
The commentary states: These three questions, combined with the preceding verse, collectively refute [such views] as false wisdom and incorrect vision (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The faculties of the old and the young are obscure, and thus wisdom does not arise; yet, in reality, such a flame exists. This too is called false wisdom (*mithyājñāna*).

The commentary states: "This verse addresses the fourth question. Combined with the preceding three questions, they all share the principle that only when there is an object of cognition can it be termed 'wisdom.
[The author] refutes them collectively, stating: 'This too constitutes false wisdom. However, if it were truly existent..."
"O Flame, this too is a false teaching; it is sufficient to know that the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is empty.

The two aforementioned attachments have now been shattered, the two hindrances have been purified, and the practice of wisdom has reached perfection. Below, the forgetting of words and sudden realization are elucidated to reveal that the ocean of fruition is free from conditions.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings are turned around by the delusive habitual tendencies of false imaginings from beginningless time.
While being thus turned around, they do not properly understand the thorough penetration of one's own school (*svaprakriyā-siddhānta*) or the thorough penetration of teaching (*deśanā-siddhānta*).

Because they are attached to external natures and characteristics manifested by their own minds, they cling to expedient teachings and fail to correctly discern the pure characteristics of the fourfold propositions (*cātuṣkoṭi*) within their own school.
The commentary states: This is a summary showing that the ocean of fruition is free from conditions.

Therefore, it rebukes Mahāmati for falsely giving rise to discrimination regarding the self-realized noble wisdom of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), for producing understanding based on mere words, for arbitrarily generating false attachments, and for erroneously interpreting the Buddha’s intent;
this is truly because he is not skilled in the two aspects of penetration. Self-realized noble wisdom is free from the marks of mental conditions and free from...
Regarding the characteristics of verbal expression: although there is no actual speech, it is not that there is no discourse.

Thus, when the Buddha speaks of "sage-wisdom being without cognition" and so forth, he intends for the listener to transcend words to contemplate the meaning and to forget cognition in order to accord with the mind.
Why is it that listeners still follow words and give rise to false interpretations? These are all the result of beginningless, false, delusory conceptualizations and evil habitual tendencies.

They revolve [in this way], yet regarding their own school’s teaching on the universal [truth], they lack thorough understanding; they merely cling to external objects as being substantially existent.
Consequently, they become attached to expedient verbal expressions and are unable to properly enter the realm of the pure true nature that transcends cognition.
The treatise says: "To posit a small object before one and claim it is the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something [grasped]..."
Because [the realization] has been attained, one does not yet truly abide in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), for the duality of object and cognition has not yet been forgotten.
When the World-Honored One, at this point, incidentally concludes his reproof by means of these two types of penetration (*abhijñā*), his intention is this:

"Previously, I have already instructed the practitioners of the three vehicles that they should skillfully understand the characteristics of these two penetrations and must not grasp the meaning according to the literal words. Thus, he intends to reprove Mahāmati as to why...
Failing to grasp the Buddha’s intent, you instead cling to words as mere provisional names and give rise to various kinds of false attachments.

Therefore, the teaching employs the forgetting of words to facilitate realization through direct契合 (qièzhèng). Such is the purport of this passage; hence, it concludes with a reprimand by means of the two types of penetration (pratisaṃvid).
Above, the two hindrances have been purified, the two attachments have been shattered, and the two deaths have been extinguished;

thus, he concludes with the admonition that realization is attained through the forgetting of words, thereby demonstrating the perfection of his own benefit (*svārtha*). △ Below this, he demonstrates the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha*), first providing a dual conclusion for both types of beneficial practice.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “It is indeed as Your Majesty has taught. I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, analyze and explain the *sūtra-vehicle* (the common teaching) and the *principle-vehicle* (the ultimate teaching).
May I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas become skilled in these two vehicles, so that in future ages ordinary people, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas shall not find fault with them.”

The commentary states: Because this Mahāmati, due to being rebuked by the Buddha for his improper conceptualization regarding the two supernormal powers (abhijñā), gave rise to false discrimination concerning noble wisdom (āryajñāna), he here reproaches himself and requests instruction on these two supernormal powers. Question: The two supernormal powers have already been elucidated previously.

"Why is it that you now request this again? He replied: "Previously, because non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles erroneously gave rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, they failed to understand that the realm of experience is merely the manifestation of mind-only.

Mahāmati specifically requested that the essence of the teaching be shown so that they might know it and open their eyes to right view. Thus the World-Honored One said: 'They are not only unskilled...'"

Regarding the characteristics of the ultimate penetration (*zongtong*) and the characteristics of the conventional penetration (*shetong*), because [the disciples] are not skilled in explaining the conventional penetration, they give rise to interpretations based merely on the words.
Therefore, I specifically explain the characteristics of these two penetrations so that those *tīrthikas* and *śrāvakas* may practice with ease, avoiding the fall into false views.
My intention lies in destroying the dualistic views of the *tīrthikas* and *śrāvakas*, so that they may come to know the practice that transcends words. This was prompted by Mahāmati’s inquiry.
The statement that "false conceptualization has no intrinsic nature" gives rise to five difficulties; the statement that "holy wisdom cannot be attained" gives rise to four doubts.
These all stem from a failure to understand that [all is] mind-only and a lack of comprehension regarding the provisional nature of conventional discourse.

Furthermore, by grasping at the literal meaning of words, they assume that real objects and cognitions can be found. Therefore, the Buddha rebukes them for their lack of skill in the two types of penetration and instructs them to act accordingly.

This is a vision. Therefore, Mahāmati specifically requested these two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) so that, by relying on the teachings to practice and preach the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings, he might sever the doubts of those of the Two Vehicles.
His intention lies in dispelling the duality of mind and object, and in emptying both object and wisdom; thus, through wondrous practice, he accords with the wondrous realm.
The character "xiang" (mark/aspect) appearing previously was intended to instruct others so they might know, thereby facilitating their own self-benefit. Now, in this...

The two [types of] penetration (abhijñā) are intended for certain practice and, moreover, for the benefit of others. Observers should understand this so that the meaning of the words may be grasped and no divergent views arise.
The former was the practice of "forgetting words"; this, however, is the actual realization beyond words.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharma-attainment:

namely, the attainment of the teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*) and the attainment of one's own realization (*svaprakriyā-prativedha*). As for the attainment of the teaching, it refers to that which accords with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings."
To preach various sūtras concerning the requisites for practice is called the "communication of teaching" (shetong).

The commentary states: "The intent of this communication of teaching is to benefit others. In the Sanskrit language, *sūtra*; in this [Chinese] language, it is translated as "契經" (*qijing*, "Sūtra that accords with reality").

This means that it accords with both principle and capacity. To accord with principle is to perfectly conform to the Middle Way; to accord with capacity is to skillfully apply [the teaching] to the three faculties.
Because a single sūtra contains many meanings, it is called the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (The Sūtra of All Equipments), meaning that there is no principle it does not encompass.
There are no capacities that are not encompassed.
As for the "thorough penetration of one’s own school," this refers to the practitioner who is free from the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind;

that is, they do not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither, and they transcend all mind, thought, and consciousness, realizing the sacred realm of self-awakening. (The Tang translation says: "Regarding...")

The realm of the noble self-realization is free from the characteristics of views produced by causes. (Both translations state: "It is free from all characteristics of views associated with causes and conditions.
It cannot be known by any heterodox teachers, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who fall into the two extremes. I declare this to be the Dharma of the ultimate penetration of our own school.
The Record states: "The meaning of this 'self-attainment' (svayam-prativedha) lies in self-benefit.

Because this self-attainment transcends the sphere of mind, intellect, and consciousness, it cannot be known by outsiders (tīrthikas) or those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). It is that which is free from views associated with causes and conditions."
This means that both mind and objects are transcended.
Mahāmati, these are called the characteristics of the penetration of one’s own school (*svapratyātma-gati*) and the penetration of teaching (*deśanā*).
You and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

I say there are two kinds of penetration: the penetration of the principle (*tongzong*) and the penetration of verbal expression (*yanshuo*). The verbal expression is for bestowing upon the ignorant; the principle is for those who practice cultivation. The Record states:
"The Bodhisattva possesses the merit of two kinds of benefit; therefore, through the penetration of speech, he teaches the Dharma according to the capacity of the recipient.

Thus it is said 'bestowing upon the ignorant,' meaning that ordinary people are as simple and foolish as children. The penetration of the principle is for one's own cultivation; this refers to practicing according to [the truth].
Because it is practiced. [The preceding section on the two practices of self and others is concluded. △ Below follows the exclusive request for the practice of benefiting others.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:

'Regarding the various dialectical treatises of the world, you must be careful not to study or associate with them. (In two other translations, 'the various treatises of the world' is rendered as *Lokāyata*, which is translated here as 'Left-World' and also as 'Evil Treatise'.)"

This refers to the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If one associates with them, one will embrace desire and not embrace the Dharma. (The Wei translation says: "That person merely embraces the food of desire.")
[Regarding] "not grasping at dharmas as food": Why did the World-Honored One speak thus?

The commentary states: This specifically concerns the practice of benefiting others. It appears that because the World-Honored One had previously severely rebuked his disciples for not permitting them to study the discourses of non-Buddhists, Mahāmati, upon hearing this discourse on benefiting others, [thought...]
That is to say, their own school is unwholesome; their doctrine is illogical and offers no benefit to others. Therefore, based on the World-Honored One’s previous words, a doubt arose:
"Since the World-Honored One has stated that his teachings are for the sake of benefiting the ignorant, why did he previously not permit the close study of the arguments of non-Buddhists?
For this reason, the question was raised. The World-Honored One replied: "As for the non-Buddhists..."
Discursive debate is established upon false views; if one associates with such [debate], it will destroy right knowledge and vision.

For those whose intent is to enter the realization of the ultimate nature of their own school (svayūthya-siddhānta), they should regard the abandonment of the habitual tendencies of names and words as the foremost task. Nevertheless, the three realms are fundamentally devoid of any real dharmas.

It takes the habitual tendencies of names and words as its essence. Among such names and words, the discourses of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are the most destructive to right view and the greatest destroyers of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, practitioners who seek to realize reality as it is must utterly reject them.

Thus, Mahāmati asked based on the "penetration of the teachings" (deśanā-praveśa), to which the World-Honored One subsequently responded based on the "penetration of one's own realization" (svaprativedha-praveśa).
Thus he replied. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Worldly discourse consists of various phrases and expressions, adorned by the collection of causes, conditions, and parables.
It seduces and deludes foolish ordinary people; it does not enter into the true self-realization, nor does one awaken to all phenomena through it—this is mere delusion."
With inverted perceptions, they fall into the two extremes; being foolish and deluded, they bring about their own destruction.

They continue through the various realms of existence and fail to attain liberation. (The Tang translation states: "The doctrines of the Lokāyata merely adorn their phrasing to deceive the foolish and ignorant. They follow worldly, false speech; they do not accord with reality nor conform to principle. They cannot enter the realm of truth, nor can they awaken to all phenomena.

They constantly fall into the two extremes, losing the right path for themselves and causing others to lose it as well. They transmigrate through the various realms, never attaining escape. They are unable to awaken.
Though one knows that [all things] are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one does not depart from the false conceptualization and attachment to the intrinsic nature of external objects.

Therefore, various worldly discourses and eloquent explanations do not free one from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; they are deceptive, delusive, and confusing.

The commentary states: This is an extreme statement regarding the faults of worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). It serves as a profound warning that those who practice according to reality (*yathābhūta*) must not associate with it.

The reason they must not associate with it is that such discourse does not lead to the realization of ultimate truth through self-attestation; it fails to awaken one to the fact that all is but the manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacitta-dṛśya-mātra*).
Relying instead upon birth-and-death delusions (*vikalpa*), one remains unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, and death, for it consists merely of empty words.

It is said that [these names] have no ultimate reality. Nevertheless, the World-Honored One specifically cautioned against the habitual tendencies of linguistic designations (*nāma-vāsanā*) in this sutra because, in the Sahā world, the Buddha-work is performed through sound.
This is because the sense-faculty of the ear is most acute among the sentient beings of this realm;
by means of sound entering the mind, they penetrate directly to the *dharmatā*, which is most profound. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* selected [this method].

In the *Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom*, the faculty of hearing is ranked first among the sense organs (*indriya*). In this scripture, for those who practice according to reality (*yathābhūta*), the names and words of the precepts (*śīla*) are ranked first.

This is because, for entering the Path in this world, there is nothing superior to the faculty of hearing as being most excellent, and for obstructing the Path, there is nothing superior to names and words as being most excellent.
As it is said: "The sense organ (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*) share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual."

Nevertheless, although ordinary beings generally form karmic bonds based on conventional names and expressions, there are occasionally those of sharp faculties who have long possessed the wisdom of *prajñā* through the熏 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) of hearing [the Dharma].

Such individuals are able to contemplate that the nature of language is empty and that sounds are unreal—like wind howling through a valley or an echo—and thus enter the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Conversely, as for the heterodox arguments of outside paths, once they enter the perfuming of hearing, they immediately become defiled.
The nature of phenomena destroys right knowledge and vision, demolishes the city of nirvana, and causes one to sink into samsara for eternal kalpas, severing the lineage of the Buddhas.

Even if such a person should encounter the appearance of a Buddha, they will be consumed by the fire of false views; their perverse wisdom will blaze ever more fiercely as they vainly oppose the True Dharma.

Although the Tathāgata, through his immeasurable skillful means, fourfold eloquence, and great compassion, dwells within them by merging his spirit with theirs, he is still unable to transform and lead them in.
Observe that since the World-Honored One appeared in the world and preached the Dharma for forty years, the followers of the six heretical teachers have remained as numerous as hemp or millet seeds;
yet those who have abandoned heterodoxy to return to the orthodox path include the three Kāśyapa brothers and others.
Śāriputra and the others numbered no more than one thousand two hundred and fifty people. Among them, even the most eminent were but those who kept their realization secret within.
If such was the case during the height of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), how much more so during the Final Dharma (*pāścāttya-dharma*)?

It was because our Buddha, the World-Honored One, foresaw five hundred years hence that this class of people would cause great destruction to the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*). For this reason, this sutra is specifically [addressed] by means of...
Refuting heterodoxy is its function; it was established for our time. Behold, what must the Sage’s heart of concern have been like!

How tragic it is that this scripture has entered China for nearly two thousand years, yet our own teachers and veteran scholars have struggled to read it, unable to construe even a single phrase, treating it as a bitter enemy.
How much more so when one seeks to grasp the intended meaning of these bequeathed words!
One who seals the mind-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs must uphold it to establish the fundamental principles;

only then can they administer rewards and punishments and truly shoulder the ancestral legacy of the Tathāgata. Because you do not understand this Dharma-gate, you have instead habitually followed worldly discourse, willingly accepting the Buddha’s rebukes as a wicked disciple. Thinking of this, I cannot help but shed tears.
"Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra was well-versed in many treatises and had himself composed a work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*).

A disciple of that worldly philosopher (*lokāyatika*), assuming the form of a dragon (the Tang translation says: 'manifesting in the form of a dragon'), went to the palace of Śakra to establish his own philosophical tenets.
He vowed to destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel; should he be defeated, he would cut off one head for each spoke as a penalty for his submission. Thus he spoke.
Having made this agreement, he then used the *śaila-dharma* (both translations state "the dharma of debate") to defeat Śakra. Śakra fell into defeat and immediately destroyed his chariot.

He returned to the human realm. Thus it is, Mahāmati: through worldly discourse adorned with causes and analogies, even down to the animal realm (the Wei translation says, "even manifesting in the form of an animal"), one can use various phrases and expressions to delude those gods and asuras.
Even a *rākṣasa* clings to views of arising and ceasing; how much more so a human being!

Therefore, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse, for it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering. Be careful not to associate with it. Mahāmati, proponents of worldly theories speak only of the body, perception, and their objects.
The Record states: This says, "Be extremely careful not to associate with those who study worldly doctrines.
This refers to the disciples of worldly doctrines who, even in the form of animals, are still able to subdue the various devas and asuras, let alone humans.
If my disciples of the Final Dharma lack the power of the Path and should happen to associate with them even once, would they not be destroyed by them? If...
Because it leads to destruction, it can bring about the causes for the arising of all sufferings; therefore, I warn you: be careful not to associate with it.

Since that worldly doctrine lacks a tenet of its own and speaks only of the body, sensations, and their objects, I say that it merely embraces craving and does not embrace the Dharma. This is my solemn vow.

Mahāmati, those proponents of worldly treatises number in the hundreds of thousands. However, in the future, during the final five hundred years, they shall destroy the collected teachings because the causes and views of evil awakening will flourish, and evil disciples will accept them.
The Record states: This was the World-Honored One’s prophetic prediction for the final dharma-age, a time when Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak.

Yet, as for that worldly discourse [the Lokāyata] which, five hundred years after my Dharma, will be able to destroy the communal recitation (saṃgīti), it is because the customs of the age will have become corrupt and diluted;
at that time, people will abound in evil perceptions and the fire of false views will blaze intensely. However, within my Dharma there is...
Disciples with evil views also receive that teaching; for this reason, they cause the destruction of the True Dharma.
Viewed in this light, those who destroy the Dharma are merely destroying themselves—how could it be through the power of another? Regarding "causes": "cause" refers to false causes. Regarding "view":
this refers to the five sharp-facultied afflictions (*kleśa*) among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Because they do not correctly understand the True Dharma, [they hold these views].
Therefore, it is called "evil discernment.
Thus, Mahāmati, the worldly treatises destroy the true compilation; they are adorned with various phrases, expressions, reasons, and analogies to expound the matters of the non-Buddhists.
They are attached to their own causal conditions and possess no independent realization.

The Record states: This explains the reason why the assembly was disrupted. However, the reason that those proponents of worldly treatises (*lokāyatika*) were able to destroy the True Dharma was because they adorned their various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies with the accounts of non-Buddhists;
they clung to the causes and conditions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and there was nothing among them but false views, for they lacked the penetration of the principle of no-intrinsic-nature.

If one knows [the danger] yet associates with them, it is like intentionally drinking another's toxic medicine; if one does not know [the danger] yet associates with them, it is what is called inadvertently taking a toxic medicine.
Mahāmati, those various non-Buddhists have no doctrine of their own; they extensively expound hundreds of thousands of infinite worldly treatises.
Regarding the gate of phenomena (*vastu-mukha*): there is no self-communication [of truth], nor do they recognize their own worldly discourse as ignorance.
The record states: "This formation establishes that dharma; the signs of the phenomena are transmitted one to another, yet they do not know it to be wrong.

Because those fundamental dharmas lack self-communication, the disciples who transmit them extensively explain hundreds of thousands of gates of phenomena, yet all of these likewise lack [self-communication]."
It is self-evident. Because there is no such self-evidence, those deluded people likewise never realize that they are merely engaged in the mundane discourse of ignorance;
these are those who have mistakenly ingested poison.

At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if the worldly discourses of the non-Buddhists—adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies, yet lacking any self-attained realization and characterized by attachment to their own particular objects—[are not the truth, then what is]?"
The commentary states: This passage from Mahāmati cites the Buddha’s previous words in order to pose a challenge.

[He asks: "Does the World-Honored One not also teach the worldly doctrines (*lokāyata*)? For the sake of the various assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras gathered from all directions, you have extensively expounded immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions;
is this not also your own system? Does it not also enter into the knowledge of all non-Buddhists?"
Mahāmati asked: "Is this a matter of verbal enumeration?

He recorded [the Buddha's response]: "Because Mahāmati heard the Buddha refute the worldly treatises of the non-Buddhists as lacking self-attestation, he followed up with a challenge to the Buddha, asking why the Buddha extensively taught various worldly dharmas for the sake of humans, devas, and asuras, yet these were not [self-attested]."
"The dharmas realized by wisdom are all merely worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). How could it be that the World-Honored One also lacks his own realization?
Would he not then fall among the ranks of the false conceptualizations and erroneous wisdom of all external paths? Thus did Mahāmati inquire based on worldly discourse.
The World-Honored One answered according to his own realization.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of worldly discourse; there is neither coming nor going. I speak only of that which neither comes nor goes.
Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to the gathering and arising [of phenomena], while 'going' refers to their dispersal and destruction. That which neither comes nor goes is that which is neither born nor..."
Cessation. The meaning I have explained does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or deluded conceptualization.

Why is this? It is because one does not cling to the existence or non-existence of external objects; rather, one abides in the manifestation of one's own mind, which cannot be overturned by the dualistic delusions of the two extremes.

Since the objective realm of marks lacks inherent existence, when one realizes that it is the manifestation of one's own mind, the delusions of mental manifestation no longer arise. When delusions do not arise, there is emptiness and non-existence...
The marks are non-active; entering the three gates of liberation is called "liberation. The commentary states:
This is the World-Honored One’s answer based on his own realization (*svapratyātma-gati*); the Dharma he teaches is not worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).

Worldly discourse refers to the phenomena of coming and going, arising and ceasing. As for "coming," it arises through the convergence of conditions; therefore, it is called "converging and gathering."
That which arises and departs ceases when conditions disperse; therefore, it is called "dispersal and destruction.

Because there is coming and going, arising and ceasing, it is termed "worldly discourse" (*loka-vāda*). However, that which I teach is the Dharma of no-coming and no-going, neither-arising nor ceasing.
How could it fall into the category of the deluded conceptualizations of worldly discourse? The reason it does not fall therein is that I do not cling to external objects.

Regarding existence and non-existence: because one has thoroughly realized that these are merely manifestations of mind-only, the false imaginings of existence and non-existence cannot turn them back.
This is because one has realized that objects have no intrinsic nature; thus it is said that "objective marks do not arise. This refers to the non-arising of objects.

When one awakens to the manifestations of one's own mind, the false imaginings of one's own mind do not arise; this refers to the non-arising of the mind. Since objects do not arise, there is no coming.

When the mind does not arise, there is neither arising nor ceasing. When the mind and its objects are without arising, this is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
To enter these three gates of liberation is what is called "liberation. My intention is that what I have taught is the Dharma of liberation.
It is not a phenomenon of birth and death; therefore, one does not fall [into it].
Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing brāhmaṇa came to where I was.
Without having been invited to do so, he immediately asked me: "Gautama, is everything created? I replied at that time:
"Brahmin, everything is created. This is the first worldly doctrine. He then asked again: "Is everything uncreated?"
I further replied: "All things are uncreated; this is the second worldly doctrine (*lokāyata*). The commentary states:
This World-Honored One, wishing to explain the worldly doctrines extensively, cites past events to briefly instruct the Bodhisattva on the methods for explaining and refuting such doctrines.
According to the old tradition, *brāhmaṇa* is fully called *brāhmaṇa-ma*.

*Na* (Nā). This is translated as "Pure Lineage" (*śuddhavaṃśa*) or "Pure Conduct" (*śuddhacaryā*). They claim that their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā; thus, they take the Brahmanical clan name.
The *brahmins* mentioned in various sūtras refer to this very class. This caste exists only within the five regions of India and is not found in other countries.
They possess their own distinct scriptures and have inherited them as their profession through the generations. They may either remain householders or renounce the world as monastics.
They all rely on their own arts and are haughty; they mostly esteem contentious debate. They are empty and idle, lacking self-awareness.

Because they take the creator Brahmā, as they conceive him, to be the divine self (*ātman*), it is said that they do not seek out those who dwell in emptiness and quietude, but instead question the creator regarding the arising of all phenomena.

Since their views do not transcend worldly discourse (*lokāyata*), as soon as they open their mouths, they fall into false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Therefore, [the Buddha] asked this one question.

The World-Honored One replied: "If one asks about one lifetime, it is called 'discourse on one lifetime. If one asks about two lifetimes, it is called 'discourse on two lifetimes,' and so on up to many lifetimes, it is called 'discourse on many lifetimes.
Therefore, he later rebuked them, saying: "Even the slightest movement of consciousness that discriminates external objects is all merely 'discourse on the world' (lokāyata)."
He asked me further: "Are all things eternal? Are all things impermanent? Are all things born? Are all things unborn? I replied to him:
"These are the six worldly doctrines (*ṣaḍ-laukika-vāda*). Mahāmati, he then asked me: "Are all things one? Are all things different?
Are all things both? Are all things neither? Do all things arise from various causes?"
"Is birth manifest? (The Tang translation says: "Do all beings arise through various causes and conditions? I then replied: "This is the eleventh worldly theory."
Mahāmati, he asked again: "Are all things indeterminate? Are all things determinate? Is there a self? Is there no self?
Does this world exist? Does this world not exist? Does another world exist? Does another world not exist?
Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary? Is it space? It was not...
"Is it cessation through calculation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), or is it nirvāṇa? Gautama, is it something produced (*kṛta*) or unproduced (*akṛta*)?
The response was: "This space... [The text continues: This asks whether the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are produced or unproduced. The Tang translation says: [as above].
Are space (*ākāśa*), nirvāṇa, and cessation not due to deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) created things, or are they uncreated?
Since non-Buddhists falsely imagine these three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) to all be created, the World-Honored One, after answering them, specifically instructed Mahāmati:
"Nirvāṇa, space, and cessation do not exist as three distinct entities; there are merely three enumerations. His intention was this:
Even these three dharmas cannot be apprehended; how much less can one calculate "action" and "non-action"?
Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or is there no intermediate state? Mahāmati, I then replied: "Brahmin, such assertions are all merely worldly discourse (*lokavāda*);
they are not what I teach. This is your worldly discourse. I teach only the beginningless false construction (*anādikāla-vikalpa*)."
The various evils of the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization are the causes of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualization and clings to external natures, as is the case with the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who claim that cognition arises from the conjunction of the self, the sense organs, and their objects.

"It is not so for me," [the Buddha said]. (The Tang translation states: "As the non-Buddhists claim that consciousness arises from the conjunction of the self, the sense organs, and the objects, it is not so for me. 'Consciousness' refers to *vijñāna*. O Brahmin, I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause;
I speak only of dependent origination as a conventional designation based on the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) within false conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

This is not something that you or others who have fallen into the perception of a self-continuum (*ātma-saṃtati*) are able to realize. (The Tang translation states: "I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause; I rely only upon false...")

The mind is described as dependent origination by way of the grasper and the grasped; it cannot be fathomed by you or others who are attached to a self. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not of three kinds;
there are only three enumerations.
The Record states: This is how the World-Honored One fully recounted the teachings he previously gave when addressing the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
It is said that the non-Buddhists, each clinging to their own views, questioned the Buddha one by one. The Buddha refuted them all collectively, saying:
"All of these are merely your worldly discourses (loka-vāda); they are not what I teach. However, what I do teach is solely the cause for all sentient beings.
From the beginningless habit-energies of conceptual proliferation, the appearances of the triple world arise.

Failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false imaginings, grasping at external phenomena through objective clinging; yet, in reality, nothing can be apprehended.
What I have taught is precisely this. As for the "self" (*ātman*) and the "faculties" (*indriya*) spoken of by the non-Buddhists—
As for the claim that consciousness arises from the conjunction of the three factors—the object, the sense-organ, and the cognition—this is your view as a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).

I do not hold such a view. Furthermore, you non-Buddhists assert that there is a distinct cause capable of producing all phenomena, or else you assert that all phenomena arise spontaneously without a cause;
these are your doctrines. My doctrine is not so. I teach only that it is through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that the grasper and the grasped are established.
Taking this up, I shall explain dependent origination. This teaching of mine cannot be understood by you non-Buddhists who cling to the delusive notion of a self.
The Buddha said that when non-Buddhists ask various questions, I simply answer them accordingly;

this is what is called "stopping debate" (*vāda-nigraha*), and it is also the explanation of the common characteristics [of phenomena]. However, all the questions posed by the non-Buddhists are merely those of their own...
As for those who falsely reckon the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) to be non-existent, they are engaging with the notions of self and dharmas;
fearing such confusion, the World-Honored One specifically told Mahāmati: "Those three unconditioned phenomena you asked about do not actually exist as three kinds;
there are merely three enumerations, but they are not substantially real. Therefore, the Tang translation says: "Space, nirvāṇa, and..."

As for non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it possesses only three numerical attributes; since it fundamentally lacks any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how much less can one speak of its being "non-existent" or "uncreated"?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time, the world-theorizing Brahmin again asked me: "Is it because of the causes of ignorance, craving, and karma..."
"Is there a third existence? Or is it without cause? I replied to him: "These two views are also merely worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*. He asked again:
"Do all natures enter into their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? I replied once more: "This too is worldly discourse, O Brāhmaṇa.

Even up to the point where the mind flows and falsely discriminates external objects (the Tang translation says: 'even down to the slightest movement of consciousness that discriminates external realms')."
All of these are worldly doctrines (*loka-vāda*).
The record states: "These non-Buddhists, having heard the Buddha’s teaching that false and evil habits are the cause of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), therefore asked in succession:
'Are those three realms of existence produced by causes—namely, ignorance, craving, and karma—or are they without cause? This was because..."

That mind insists that there is certainly no cause. The World-Honored One replied: "Not only is the conceptualization, discrimination, and verbal expression of what is falsely imagined called 'worldly discourse' (loka-vāda);
even the slightest movement of consciousness that discriminates external objects falls into the false views of non-Buddhists;
all such things are worldly discourse. Why? Because as soon as the mind is raised or a thought is stirred, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma."
To falsely perceive that there are phenomena external to the mind is to enter the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). While Master [Shan] was sitting, Yangshan entered;
the Master said, "Ji-zi, speak quickly! Do not enter the realms of the aggregates. Yangshan said, "Huiji believes even 'non-establishment' does not stand."
The Master said, "Do you establish yourself through faith, or do you not establish yourself through lack of faith? Yang said, "I am simply Huiji; whom else could I possibly believe in?
The Master said, "If it is so, then you are a śrāvaka of fixed nature. Yang said, "Huiji does not establish even a Buddha.
This is an example of how the mental consciousness of the ancients was not at all stagnant. Were it not for this, how could there be peace?
It is called a view that transcends Buddhas and surpasses patriarchs.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Lokāyatika Brahmin again asked me: "Is there anyone who is not a follower of the worldly discourse (*lokāyata*)?
I am the founder of all non-Buddhist schools; I teach various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables.
“Venerable one,” I replied, “there is, O Brahmin, that which is not yours; it is not an action, not a tenet, not a teaching, and not a non-teaching of various phrases and syllables;
nor is it without the adornment of causes and similes.”
