Mahāmati, as for 'Samyaksaṃbuddha' and 'Buddha,' these are free from all sense-faculties and means of valid cognition."
The commentary states: This is a general summary showing that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is beyond the realm of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).

From the initial inquiry of Mahāmati and the response of the World-Honored One, through the successive layers of cross-examination and debate, it is revealed solely that this [Dharma-body] is beyond the realm of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Not only in this assembly, but throughout the forty-nine years of the Buddha’s teaching—comprising over three hundred assemblies—[this same truth is maintained].
What has been explained in the assemblies does not go beyond manifesting this very point;

even that which is realized by all Buddhas of the three periods of time and transmitted by the patriarchs of successive generations is nothing other than this, and there is no other dharma. Therefore it is said: "Only this one thing is true;
the other two are not real. This is precisely what the ancient worthies meant by "the place where mind and consciousness do not reach. Thus it is.
That which is called "Buddha" is free from all sense faculties and their objects of cognition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Completely free from all sense faculties and their objects, Without phenomena and without causes, Already free from the perceiver and the perceived, And likewise free from characteristics and the characterized."

The commentary states: This verse summarizes how the Dharmakāya is free from all faults. The "faculties" (indriyas) and "measures" (pramāṇas) refer to the spheres of seeing, hearing, cognition, and knowledge.
Since the Dharmakāya is free from conceptualization, it is not a place where mental activity operates; therefore, it is entirely devoid of cause and effect, as well as subject and object.
The aggregates (*skandhas*) and conditions are the Perfectly Awakened One; neither identity nor difference can be perceived.
If there were nothing to be seen, how could one make distinctions? The commentary states: This verse [teaches] that the five aggregates and the Dharma-body are equal and non-dual.

When observed with the Right Eye (*samyag-cakṣus*), truth and delusion are equal; therefore, neither identity nor difference can be perceived. Since neither identity nor difference can be perceived, how could one...?
Is it a conceptual construction?

It is neither created nor uncreated; it is neither an effect nor a cause. It is not the aggregates (skandhas), nor does it reside within the aggregates, nor is there any other admixture, nor are there any inherent natures (dharmatās).
As it is seen through false imagination, one should know that it is likewise not non-existent. This dharma and its nature are also thus.
The commentary states: This verse describes the purity of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because the Dharma-body is pure, all things are "not" [as they appear].
Although it lacks all marks, it is not as if it were like those deluded perceptions; rather, the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is likewise not non-existent.
Since every phenomenon is truly real, it is said to be "also thus."

Because of existence there is non-existence; because of non-existence there is existence. If it were non-existent, one should not grasp at it; if it were existent, one should not conceptualize it. The commentary states:
This verse says that existence and non-existence arise in mutual dependence; one should not give rise to these two views.

That is to say, although the Dharmakāya is free from all marks, it does not fall into annihilationism; therefore, one must not cling to non-existence. One should know that the Dharmakāya is neither...

It is non-existent, yet it truly possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If one further forms a view of existence regarding the intrinsic nature of the *dharmakāya*, this too is a false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, it is said: "If it is non-existent, one should not accept it; if it exists, one should not conceptualize it. Thus, the Wei translation states:
Since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence likewise should not be asserted; this is what is meant by being entirely free from the measures of the sense faculties.
Those who linger in the discourse on self and non-self, sinking into the two extremes, destroy themselves and destroy the world.
"Being liberated from all faults and correctly observing the penetration of the self—this is called right contemplation. One does not disparage the Great Teacher.
The commentary states: "This generally reveals the departure from faults, concluding by returning to the mind of contemplation.

Previously, because ordinary beings falsely cling to a provisional self and non-Buddhists falsely calculate a divine self (*puruṣa*), the term 'non-self' was used to refute them. Yet, the followers of the Two Vehicles..."
One calculates that which is non-self to be a substantial dharma; therefore, this statement of the "true self" (ātman) of the Dharmakāya is made to refute it.
The intention is that both the aforementioned "self" and "non-self" are merely conventional designations (*vyavahāra-pramāṇa*).
Having already fallen into these two views, if one now regards the "true self" of the Dharmakāya as correct while again regarding the two previous types of self as incorrect, this too—
Falling into the domain of verbal expression, one remains attached to and sinks into the two extremes of existence and non-existence; this is ultimately not the final goal.

Not only does one destroy oneself, but one also destroys others. Why? Because there is only verbal expression and no real meaning at all, as all such things are mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one is liberated from all such faults as described above, one is able to correctly observe my teaching with mindfulness.
To thoroughly penetrate and transcend the realms of mind and consciousness is called right contemplation; only then does one refrain from slandering the True Dharma and disparaging the Teacher.

Any other view is entirely a false view. The above clarifies the fruit of Bodhi as the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), thereby manifesting the secret treasury of the three virtues of the Dharmakāya, thus concluding the return to the contemplation of the mind. Below, it reveals that the single mind of True Suchness is free from...
All characteristics are subsumed within and return to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). First, the departure from the characteristic of names.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has stated in the sūtras that [all things] are subsumed under non-arising and non-ceasing;
and furthermore, as the World-Honored One has stated that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata—how is this so?"
“World-Honored One, because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing. Is this not another name for the Tathāgata? (The Tang translation says:

“World-Honored One, as distinguished and grasped in the Buddha’s sūtras, non-arising and non-ceasing are said to be another name for the Tathāgata. World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain to me why non-arising and non-ceasing are called another name for the Tathāgata. If these are non-existent dharmas, how can they be called another name for the Tathāgata?

Furthermore, according to what the World-Honored One has taught—that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing—one should know that this falls into the view of existence and non-existence. The Buddha told Mahāmati: “I do not say that all dharmas are...”
"Birth is non-extinction; the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear.
The commentary states: "This difficulty clarifies that the single mind of quiescent extinction reveals the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as being free from the characteristics of names and marks.
Upon hearing that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished, Mahāmati consequently gave rise to doubt, saying: 'Furthermore, for instance...'"
That which is consistently taught throughout the sutras as being neither arising nor ceasing merely reveals the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Now, however, it is said that "neither arising nor ceasing" is an alternative name for the Tathāgata.

But since neither arising nor ceasing is the absence of intrinsic nature, and the absence of intrinsic nature transcends the characteristics of names and words, how can this be said to be an alternative name for the Tathāgata? Furthermore...
Non-arising is falling into the view of non-existence (*abhāva*); non-ceasing is falling into the view of existence (*bhāva*). Therefore, the Tang translation states:

"The World-Honored One taught that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing; one should know that this [otherwise] falls into the views of existence and non-existence. Thus, the World-Honored One replied:
"In my teaching of all phenomena, the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear. Why? Because that which does not arise does not exist, and that which does not cease..."

Thus, it is not non-existent; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Therefore, it does not belong to existence or non-existence, and it is said that the categories of existence and non-existence do not manifest.
In the Tang translation, there are questions regarding the two views of existence and non-existence but no answers; in this sutra, there are answers but no questions.
Thus, the two translations mutually elucidate one another.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-arising, then no dharma can be apprehended, because all dharmas are non-arising.
If there is indeed a dharma within names, I pray that you will explain it for me."

The commentary states: This passage, in which Mahāmati again raises a doubt regarding existence and non-existence, serves to clarify that the ultimate fruit of enlightenment is utterly free from the characteristics of names and signs.

The intent is as follows: since the World-Honored One has stated that the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear in the teaching of the Dharma, yet if they do not appear, there would be nothing to grasp; therefore, it is said that the "appropriation of dharmas" is unattainable. Since it is unattainable, then...
Among them, not even a single dharma is established, because all dharmas are non-arising.
Since not even a single dharma is established, who then is the one named "Tathāgata"? This would be a contradiction of one's own words.
If you say that the non-arising dharma is the name of the Tathāgata, it would seem as though there is still a dharma within this; it would not be transcendent.
"There is indeed [the distinction between] existence and non-existence. Therefore it is said: 'If there were a dharma within names. Here, 'if' (ruo) means 'as if' (si). What is the meaning of this?
I pray that you will explain it for me."
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it. I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "I do not say that the Tathāgata is without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Nor is it the case that all phenomena are subsumed under [the categories of] non-arising and non-ceasing because they do not depend on conditions. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
It is neither born nor extinguished, and it is not without meaning. Mahāmati, what I call the "mind-born Dharma-body" (manomaya-dharmakāya) is a name for the Tathāgata.
(The Tang translation states: "What I call 'non-arising' is precisely another name for the Tathāgata’s mind-born Dharma-body.

That which is non-arising is not within the realm of any heterodox teachers, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage (both translations state "seventh stage"). Mahāmati, that non-arising is the Tathāgata.

Regarding the alternative title, the commentary states: "This refutes Mahāmati’s erroneous calculations, which fail to grasp the Buddha’s intent; it is therefore answered with the correct principle of the Dharma-body.
This is because Mahāmati suspects that 'neither arising nor ceasing' implies annihilation, and further suspects that 'neither arising nor ceasing' [is a mere negation]."

This encompasses all phenomena of arising and ceasing. The underlying intent is that one must wait for the conditions of arising and ceasing to be exhausted before attaining non-arising and non-ceasing.
Therefore, this is refuted by saying: "It is neither devoid of nature, nor does it encompass all phenomena, nor does it depend on conditions.
Nevertheless, although everything is "not," it is not without meaning. Why? Because I speak of "all."
The Dharma should be understood as having the nature of non-arising; this is simply another name for the Tathāgata and nothing else exists apart from it.
However, the state of non-arising is that which Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage realize through direct experience and are able to clearly perceive as the true suchness of equality.
It is certainly not something that can be fathomed by those of external paths or the two vehicles, nor is it the domain of Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage.
Yongjia said: "If, in reality, there is neither birth nor non-birth, it is called the 'mind-made dharma-body' (manomayakāya) precisely because of this absence of birth and non-birth.
Once one realizes the equality of true suchness (tathatā), then every phenomenon is suchness; for all phenomena are without birth."
The essence of all things is fundamentally suchness; therefore, "non-arising" is another name for the Tathāgata.
Upon reaching this realm, there is not a single thing that does not broadcast the title of the Tathāgata, nor a single dharma that does not manifest the form of Vairocana.
Thus, the subsequent text explains this through many names. Zhaozhou said: "This old monk takes a blade of grass and treats it as a sixteen-foot golden body."
Regarding the function of the body: one takes the sixteen-foot golden body as a single blade of grass. The Buddha is affliction; affliction is the Buddha.
Were it not for one who has deeply realized the samādhi of non-arising, how else could one act in this way?
Mahāmati, it is like Indra, Śakra, and Purandara (Sanskrit: Śakradevendra; here translated as "Lord of the Gods," also called "Purandara" or "Kauśika"—all of which are alternative names for Śakra).
Such things as these each have many names, yet they do not possess multiple natures because of those many names, nor are they devoid of their own nature.
The commentary states: This analogy explains that although the Tathāgata has many names, he has no plurality of essences, thereby manifesting that there is only one reality.
The Tang translation says: "For example, regarding Śakra, the earth, and space, even down to hands and feet—each individual thing has various names;
yet it is not because of these many names that there are multiple essences, nor is it that there is no essence at all. By means of this...
All phenomena are true; thus, their names differ while their essence is identical. Only those who fully realize non-arising do not allow the difference in names to differentiate their essence.
It is only for those who pursue names that distinct views arise.

In this way, Mahāmati, in this Sahā world (formerly called Saha, also called Soka; here translated as "Endurance"), I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names (here translated as "innumerable").
Fools hear them all and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are alternative names for me, the Tathāgata.
(The Tang translation says: "Though all foolish people hear and speak of them, they do not know they are alternative names for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, there may be sentient beings...
Those who know me as the Tathāgata; those who know me as the Omniscient One; those who know me as the Buddha;
those who know me as the Savior of the World; those who know me as the Self-Awakened One; those who know me as the Guide; those who know me as the Broad Guide;
those who know me as the Guide of All; those who know me as the Rishi; those who know me as Brahmā; those who know me as Viṣṇu (here translated as "Great Power"); and those who know me as the Self...
As for those present here: some know him as the Victorious One (Jina); some know him as Kapila (the name of a city, so called because the Buddha was born in that city);
some know him as the Limit of Reality (Bhūtakoṭi); some know him as the Moon; some know him as the Sun; some know him as the King; some know him as the Unborn;
some know him as the Unceasing; some know him as Emptiness (Śūnyatā); some know him as Suchness (Tathatā); some know him as Truth (Satya); and some know him as Reality (Bhūta).
As for "limits" (or "boundaries"), there are those who know the dharma-nature, those who know nirvana, those who know permanence,
those who know equality, those who know non-duality, those who know signlessness, those who know liberation, and those who know the Way.

"O Mahāmati, there are those who know me as 'Mind-born' (*manomaya*). In this way, O Mahāmati, these three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names—neither more nor less—are known by me throughout this world and all other worlds, like the moon in water, neither emerging nor entering."
The Record states: "These manifest many names while their essence does not differ; this precisely reveals the transcendence of the marks of names and words.
Because their essence does not differ, they are like the moon in water—neither emerging nor entering. As it is said: 'The single moon universally appears in all waters;
the moon in every water is subsumed within the single moon. Because there is no coming or going, there is neither emergence nor entry. This is indeed the Dharma."
The body universally responds to sentient beings, manifesting with impartiality, yet without the characteristics of coming or going;
it is merely that they differ according to what each perceives and hears. The *Avataṃsaka* names state: "The Tathāgata has four hundred billion ten-thousand names."
The *Sūtra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma*, in the chapter on the Lifespan, states: "In other lands I act as a Buddha;
there are further different names, distinct lineages, and individual appellations. This is because the Dharmakāya is without birth, and thus there is nothing that is not born;
it is without name, and thus there is nothing that is not named. Because there is nothing that is not named, it cannot be named; because it cannot be named, it is called 'Name'."

"Word" (*akṣara*) means "separation. This is not something known by the ignorant. [End of the section on] being separated from the characteristic of names and words. [Now follows] being separated from the characteristic of verbal expression.
Those foolish people cannot know me because they fall into the two extremes; nevertheless, they all pay me respectful homage and offerings.

They do not skillfully understand the meaning and intent of words and phrases, nor do they discern their designations. Failing to understand self-realization, they become attached to various verbal expressions and textual passages.

They conceive of the unborn and undying as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and thus fail to know the distinctions among the Tathāgata’s names, such as Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā. They do not understand that these names converge in self-realization at the ultimate point.
Regarding all phenomena, one adheres to them according to how they are expressed.
The commentary states: "This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is free from the characteristics of verbal expression. However, names arise from verbal expression;
because those deluded worldlings do not realize that the nature of verbal expression is empty, they falsely conceptualize names as being distinct from one another. Up to this point...
Regarding the true dharmakāya, which is quiescent, unborn, and beyond all verbal designation, they are blind and possess no knowledge.

Because they do not know this, they falsely conceptualize existence and non-existence, falling into the views of the two extremes. Although such individuals may indeed make offerings to me, [they remain ignorant].
Yet they are unable to skillfully understand that within the meanings contained in names, phrases, and their underlying intent, many names may refer to a single essence.

Thus it is said that they do not differentiate names, but merely grasp at the characteristics of distinctions. Because they do not skillfully understand the self-communicating nature of the *dharmakāya*, they cling only to the literal teachings and remain oblivious to the true jewel, claiming that "non-arising and non-ceasing" implies a lack of intrinsic nature. This is utterly mistaken.
One should know that this very reality is the Dharmakāya, which pervades all places and serves as the various names and titles of the Tathāgata,
such as Indra and others. Because they do not understand that [reality] through self-communication and its ultimate convergence lies beyond verbal expression,
they merely cling to verbal designations regarding all phenomena.
"Mahāmati, those foolish people speak thus: 'The meaning is identical to the expression; there is no difference between the meaning and the expression. Why is this?
Because they claim that meaning has no body [of its own], and that apart from the expression there is no other meaning, it being merely the expression itself.
Mahāmati, those of corrupted intelligence do not know the self-nature of expression, nor do they know the arising and ceasing of expression; they do not understand that meaning does not arise."
It is extinguished. Mahāmati, all verbal expressions fall within the realm of letters, but the meaning does not; for it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Thus there is no taking birth, nor is there a body (the Tang translation says: because it is free from existence and free from non-existence, it is without birth and without substance).
The commentary states: This refers to those who calculate and rely on verbal expressions, failing to penetrate the true meaning.

Yet these deluded persons falsely claim that the meaning is identical to the verbal expression, and that the meaning is not distinct from the expression. If this were so, there would be only verbal expression without actual meaning.
Therefore, it is said that "the meaning has no essence," because such people do not understand the intrinsic nature of verbal expression. Taking...
It means that there is no meaning other than verbal expression; it merely rests upon verbal expression itself.

The reason for this is that those who are deluded and possess inferior wisdom do not understand that the intrinsic nature of verbal expression is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, whereas the meaning is not subject to arising and ceasing.
The reason why verbal expression arises and ceases while the meaning does not arise and cease is because of verbal expression.

One falls into words, but not into meaning, because meaning transcends words and is free from the marks of existence and non-existence, as it is without arising and without essence; therefore, it does not fall.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not teach a dharma that falls within the realm of words, because the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended.

With the exception of that which does not fall within words, Mahāmati, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls within words, this would be a false statement, for dharmas are beyond words. Therefore, Mahāmati, we Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas do not speak [of such things].
A single word; not answering with a single word. Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from words and letters. It is not that the teaching of the meaning does not benefit;
rather, verbal expression is merely the conceptual construction of sentient beings.
The commentary states: This clarifies that when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he does not fall into the mark of words and letters.

The reason he does not fall into them is that the Dharma is free from the marks of existence and non-existence. Apart from this non-falling into words and letters, both preaching and not preaching are clearly manifest.
If, beyond this, one were to claim that the Tathāgata has something to preach, that would be slandering the Buddha; hence it is said:
That would be a false teaching. Because the Dharma is free from words and letters, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach only the Dharma that is free from words and letters;
therefore, from beginning to end, they do not speak a single word nor answer a single word. Why? Because the Dharma is free from words and letters. Question:
If they do not speak a single word, how can they benefit sentient beings? Answer: It is not so.
This is spoken in the sense of being non-beneficial; it is merely spoken in reference to sentient beings as a means to shatter their delusory dreams.
It is certainly not a truly existent dharma that can be spoken of. Therefore, it is said: "That which is spoken is the delusion of sentient beings."

Mahāmati, if all dharmas were not taught, the teaching would perish. If the teaching perishes, then there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas. If these did not exist, who would speak and for whom?
The commentary states: This explains the objection. The objection says: "If phenomena are detached from words and letters, then there is no phenomenon that can be taught.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata further teach all phenomena? Therefore, this explanation says: "Because there is no phenomenon that can be taught..."
This is called the teaching of all dharmas; it is merely that their ineffability is being taught.

That is to say, although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to wordlessness. If one were to remain utterly silent and say nothing at all, the teachings would perish.
If the teachings perish, then there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas. If they were entirely non-existent...
If one were to destroy the characteristics of the *dharmadhātu*, who then would be the speaker of the Dharma, and for whom would the Dharma be spoken?
It is said that on the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single atom is established; yet at the gate of transformative manifestation, not a single dharma is abandoned.
This is to speak while having no speaking; how could it be that one must first cease all speaking before it can be considered "free from words"?
It is merely a designation.
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not be attached to verbal expressions.

One should extensively teach the Dharma through appropriate skillful means, because the aspirations and afflictions of sentient beings are not uniform; thus, I and all the Buddhas have [taught] various different [doctrines] for their sake.
He explains the various dharmas by liberating sentient beings, so that they may become detached from mind, thought, and consciousness.

It is not for the sake of attaining the state of the noble wisdom of self-realization that he says: "This explanation above—which speaks of 'not speaking'—is for the sake of those who are deluded, not for those who have already awakened. This means:

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, originally have no dharma to be taught. All those various dharmas they extensively expound are solely for the purpose of conforming to the diverse understandings and desires of sentient beings, in order to shatter their hopes and afflictions, and to cause them to transform their mind, thought, and consciousness.
That which is called the Buddha’s teaching of all dharmas is for the purpose of treating all minds; if there were no [minds], [there would be no teaching].
Mind. For what purpose would one need all dharmas? Therefore, it is said that [the teaching] is not for the sake of attaining the state of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
For this reason, O Mahāmati, let the Bodhisattva not cling to verbal expressions.
Regarding all dharmas as non-existent, he awakens to the manifestation of his own mind’s measure (svacittadṛśya-mātra) and is free from the two kinds of false conceptualization. All Bodhisattvas...
"O Mahāsattva, rely on the meaning, not on the words. The commentary states:

this explains the intention behind not teaching those who have not yet attained awakening. The reason for not teaching those who have attained self-awakened wisdom (*svapratyātmajñāna*) is that they have realized all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent and have understood them as the mere manifestation of their own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). They are well... [skilled].
They are free from the two false conceptual views of existence and non-existence; it is simply because these bodhisattvas rely solely on the meaning and do not cling to verbal expressions.
If good sons or good daughters rely upon the literal words, they will destroy the ultimate truth (paramārtha) for themselves and will be unable to awaken to it.

He has fallen into a continuous stream of wrong views and teaches them to the assembly; he does not properly understand all dharmas, all stages, or all characteristics, nor does he know the words and phrases.
The commentary states: "This means that those who are deluded cause harm to both themselves and others. The Tang translation says: "Those who rely on words fall into evil views;
clinging to their own tenets, they engage in verbal discourse and are unable to skillfully comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)."
As for literary expressions and phrases, they both corrupt themselves and corrupt others; they cannot cause the minds of people to attain understanding and realization.
If one is skilled in all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, and has mastered these phrases while being fully endowed with their essential meaning—then [he is a true teacher].
Thus, one is able to find personal delight in the true, signless bliss (*animitta-sukha*). One establishes sentient beings in the equality of the Mahāyāna. The commentary states:
"These words mean that the awakened one benefits both self and others. The Tang translation says: "One is also able to cause others to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding "the true, signless bliss," this refers to the excellent bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), distinguishing it from the two [vehicles].
This refers to riding upon the biased and deviant samādhis of non-Buddhists. To abide in the true bliss of signlessness (*animitta*) is precisely what is called embracing the Mahāyāna.
All the patriarchs of the past deeply realized this signless samādhi; therefore, they were able to establish sentient beings by means of the Dharma that transcends words and letters.
Mahāmati, to embrace the Mahāyāna is to embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
To embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas is to embrace all sentient beings. To embrace all sentient beings is to embrace the True Dharma.
To embrace the True Dharma is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed. The lineage of the Buddhas...

One who does not sever [the roots of goodness] is able to understand and attain the sublime spheres of rebirth (the Wei translation says "all superior and wondrous places of birth"; the Tang translation says "one attains the superior and wondrous state").
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who knows how to attain these sublime spheres of rebirth is always born through transformation and establishes the Mahāyāna.

By means of the ten powers of mastery, he manifests various forms and appearances; he penetrates the physical types, aspirations, and the characteristics of the afflictions of sentient beings, and teaches the Dharma according to reality.
"According to reality" means it is not different (the Tang translation says: "The true Dharma is without distinction or difference").

"According to reality" means it is characterized by neither coming nor going, wherein all fabrications cease; this is called "according to reality. Mahāmati, for good men and good women, [this is the case].
One should not grasp at or adhere to what is said according to conventional expression. As for "reality," it is because it is free from words.
The commentary states: This clarifies that one who well understands the Dharma as it truly is can fully possess all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
That is to say, one who thoroughly understands the Dharma of non-arising as it truly is can fully possess all mundane [dharmas].
The supramundane Dharma establishes the True Dharma and continues the Buddha’s life-force, enabling the lineage of the Buddhas to remain unbroken.
Thus, one is born into the family of the Buddhas; hence it is said that one attains a supreme and wondrous place of birth.

Having perfected the merit of self-benefit, one is likewise able to cause sentient beings to dwell securely in the Mahāyāna, manifesting physical bodies through the ten powers in accordance with the inclinations and understandings of sentient beings at the appropriate time.
One should teach the Dharma according to reality as it accords with the faculties [of beings], yet without any characteristic of coming or going.

This is the benefit for those who have thoroughly mastered the Dharma that is real and free from words. Therefore, practitioners must by no means cling to or follow the characteristics of verbal expressions.
Mahāmati, it is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool; the fool gazes at the finger and does not grasp the actual reality.

In this same way, fools follow the finger of verbal expression, grasping and becoming attached to it, never letting go until the very end, and thus they can never attain the ultimate, primary reality that transcends the finger of verbal expression.
The commentary states: "This is a metaphor for the error of ignorant people who cling to verbal expressions. A sutra says: 'The Dharma I have taught is like a finger pointing at the moon.
Only by letting go of the finger can one perceive the moon. If one clings to the finger as being the moon, then both are lost.'"

Therefore it is said: "To cling to the finger that points at words and never let go of it, one will ultimately be unable to attain the ultimate reality that transcends the finger of verbal expression.
Mahāmati, it is like an infant who should eat cooked food and not raw food; if they were to eat raw food, it would cause them harm.

They become deranged because they do not know the sequential methods for bringing [the mind] to maturity. Mahāmati, in this way, that which is neither arising nor ceasing is unwholesome if it is not cultivated through skillful means.
Therefore, you should cultivate skillful means well; do not follow mere words, like one who looks only at the tip of a finger.
The commentary states: This uses a metaphor to explain a metaphor in order to clarify the meaning of forgetting words to realize the truth.

However, the Way that transcends words is certainly not something that shallow intelligence can comprehend. If it were not pointed out through skillful means (*upāya*), one would ultimately remain in confusion and fail to enter.
It is like giving raw food to an infant; if one feeds them raw food, they will perish.
One will surely go mad. This is because the one who provides the food lacks skillful means (*upāya*). This dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing does not depend on skillful means;
it is like raw food. If one does not skillfully use the finger of the expedient of "leaving words behind," that person will likewise become frantic and delirious, failing to enter [the truth].
Thus Huangbo said: "Those who have only just emerged these days merely desire much..."
To claim that possessing extensive knowledge and seeking out the meanings of texts constitutes spiritual practice is a mistake; such "extensive knowledge" instead becomes a source of obstruction.

It is like giving a child only a great deal of butter and milk, yet remaining entirely ignorant of whether it has been digested or not. Those who study the path of the Three Vehicles are all of this same nature;
they are all said to have "undigested food. What is meant by "undigested food"? It refers to mere intellectual understanding.
All these are poisonous medicines; they are entirely subsumed under the realm of arising and ceasing.

Since such things do not exist within True Suchness (tathatā), what was previously called "the acceptance of the food of desire" is not the "acceptance of the food of Dharma. This is why Caoshan esteemed the food of right livelihood (samyag-ājīva);
these words of skillful means apply to both teacher and disciple. Therefore, he commanded that one should draw near to those of great virtue.
[He is] one of great learning.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should practice skillful means regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*). The true meaning is subtle, wondrous, and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvana.

Verbal expression, however, is conjoined with false discrimination (*vikalpa*). False discrimination is that which accumulates birth and death (*saṃsāra*). (The Tang translation says: "Verbal expression is [conjoined] with false discrimination...")
[The mind] conceives [them] as combined; thus it wanders through birth and death. Mahāmati, that which is the true meaning is obtained from those who have heard much.

Mahāmati, "those who have heard much" refers to those who are skilled in the meaning, not those skilled in verbal expression. One who is skilled in the meaning does not follow the sūtras or treatises of any heterodox schools;
they do not follow them themselves, nor do they cause others to follow them. This is what is called being a person of great virtue and great learning. Therefore, if one desires to seek the meaning—
One should draw near to those who are learned, that is, those who possess the true meaning; one should distance oneself from those who do the opposite, namely, those who are attached to mere words.
The commentary states: This teaching is the expedient means for cultivating the true reality. Without conduct that flows from the truth, there is no way [to attain it].
To accord with reality. However, the meaning of ultimate truth is a state of quiescence that transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness;
it is attained by those who have heard much and forgotten words, not by those who cling to names and characters.

What is called "having heard much" refers to being skillful at attaining the meaning beyond words, rather than being skillful in verbal expression. Being skillful in the meaning means attaining the locus of the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); then—
One does not follow the heterodox views and discourses of external paths oneself, nor does one cause others to follow them;

only in this way is one called a virtuous and learned person (*bhadanta-bahuśruta*). Therefore, those who seek the true meaning should draw near to the virtuous and learned, and distance themselves from those who are attached to mere verbal expression.
This is what is meant by the skillful means for cultivating the cultivation of the ultimate truth.

The preceding section has completed the manifestation of the single mind’s true thusness as being free from the characteristics of verbal expression. △ The following section distinguishes the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing in order to manifest that the single mind’s true thusness is free from the characteristics of mental objects and conditions.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about the World-Honored One’s demonstration of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? The causal principles of all externalists are likewise neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, you have also taught that space, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the realm of nirvāṇa are neither arising nor ceasing.”

“Extinction. World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) teach that causes give rise to all worlds. The World-Honored One also teaches that ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination serve as conditions for the arising of all worlds.
These causes and these conditions differ only in name. It is the same regarding external objects and their causes and conditions.
There is no difference between the World-Honored One’s discourse and that of the non-Buddhists concerning atoms, primordial matter (pradhāna), the Supreme Lord (īśvara), or the Self (puruṣa).”

The Lord and others [have taught] that these nine substances are neither born nor extinguished. The World-Honored One has also said that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The heterodox teachers also say that the four great elements are indestructible and that intrinsic nature is neither born nor extinguished.
"The four great elements are constant; these four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence, do not abandon their own nature.
What the World-Honored One has taught is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is nothing extraordinary about this. I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the distinction."

This is why [the Buddha] is extraordinary and surpasses all non-Buddhists. If there were no distinction, then all non-Buddhists would also be Buddhas, because they too are neither born nor extinguished.
Yet the World-Honored One has said that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system.
This is impossible. As previously stated, there would have to be many Buddhas in a single world-system because there is no distinction [between them].
The commentary states: This doubt arises because the Buddha’s teaching on non-arising and non-ceasing is thought to be no different from that of the non-Buddhists;

it seeks to challenge the clarification of the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the one mind as being free from the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, thereby correctly demonstrating its freedom from the characteristics of mental objects. Regarding this, there are four doubts.
First, it refers to the non-Buddhists who reckon a creator as the cause capable of producing all phenomena;
since all phenomena arise and perish while the creator neither arises nor perishes, they suspect this is no different from the three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) taught by the Buddha.
Second, it refers to the non-Buddhists who reckon the self (*ātman*) as the cause, such that the entire world flows forth from the self; hence it is said that "all worlds are produced."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has also taught that ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination act as conditions to give rise to all worlds.
These are merely different names for those causes and conditions. The same applies to the teaching that the external four great elements give rise to phenomena.

Third, there are the nine [factors] permitted by non-Buddhists: atoms, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), Maheśvara, the Lord of Beings (*Prajāpati*), time, direction, space, and the combination of the great elements.
The Dharma is neither born nor extinguished. The World-Honored One has also taught that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, for existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.

Fourth, there are those non-Buddhists who reckon that the four great elements do not perish and their self-nature is neither born nor extinguished, because the four great elements are eternal and circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their self-nature. Yet the World-Honored One has also spoken of the nature of the four great elements.
If true omnipresence pervades the Dharma-realm, then what the World-Honored One has taught would be no different from that of the non-Buddhists.

Therefore, I say that there is nothing extraordinary about the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One. I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain to me the point in which [the Buddha’s teaching] excels that of the non-Buddhists.
If the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is not distinct from that of the non-Buddhists, then all those non-Buddhists would likewise...
This is because that Buddha’s teaching is likewise neither arising nor ceasing. However, the World-Honored One previously stated that there are not many Buddhas in a single world-system.
If it were truly as described above, then there would be no distinction from the non-Buddhists;
consequently, multiple Buddhas would have to appear in a single world-system.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What I teach regarding non-arising and non-ceasing is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the outsiders (*tīrthika*). Why is this?
Those outsiders maintain that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which attains the characteristics of non-arising and immutability (the Tang translation says:

'That which I teach as non-arising and non-ceasing is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the outsiders; it is not a doctrine of the non-arising of impermanence. Why? Because what the outsiders speak of is a real nature and characteristic that does not arise and does not change'). I do not teach in such a manner."
They fall into the categories of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, my [teaching] is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing.

It is neither a nature nor a lack of nature. Because it appears like various illusions and dreams, it is not a lack of nature. Why is it not a lack of nature? Because form lacks the characteristic of self-nature;
it is because of its appearing and not appearing, and its being grasped and not being grasped. For this reason, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent.

Nature. (The Tang translation says: "The Dharma I teach is neither existent nor non-existent; it is free from arising and free from ceasing. Why is it not non-existent? Because various forms are seen like illusions and dreams. Why is it not existent? Because the self-nature of the characteristics of form is not existent; because they are seen and yet not seen, and grasped and yet not grasped.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. One merely awakens to the manifestation of one's own mind, and deluded thoughts do not arise.
Peaceful, secure, and blissful; worldly affairs are forever stilled. Such conceptual activities are the work of ignorant ordinary beings, not that of the noble sages.
The Record states: "These words were spoken by the Tathāgata; they speak of non-arising and non-ceasing while being detached from existence and non-existence, as well as arising and ceasing.

This is not comparable to the externalists who fall into views of existence and non-existence, giving rise to perceptions of arising and ceasing, for the externalists engage in false conceptualization."
All phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is neither produced nor subject to change. Yet, all phenomena are impermanent;
thus, that which you conceive as neither arising nor ceasing is itself merely a doctrine of impermanence, for it has not yet transcended the categories of existence and non-existence.
However, the reason my teaching transcends arising and ceasing is that these phenomena are fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent.
How is it not non-existent? It means that all phenomena are like illusory dreams and forms; although they are fundamentally non-existent, they do not prevent the manifestation of various appearances.
How is it not existent? Because the nature of those forms is fundamentally without self-essence and has never been existent from the beginning.
Just as those various things in illusions and dreams are merely what the ignorant see and grasp, while the wise do not.
Because one does not grasp at what is seen. Therefore, I observe all phenomena in this way; thus, I say they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Only those who fully realize that all is the manifestation of their own mind do not give rise to discrimination regarding those phenomena.
When discrimination does not arise, the ground of the mind is stilled. Because it is stilled, the pursuit of desire is forever severed. Since the pursuit of desire is severed, one dwells in peace.
Stable and joyful; from this point on, the affairs of the world shall forever cease. This is not for the foolish man;
therefore it is said that deluded ordinary people engage in activities through false imaginings, whereas this is not the case for the sages and worthies.
Unreal conceptualization is like a city of the Gandharvas and like magically conjured persons.

Mahāmati, just as in a city of the Gandharvas or among magically conjured persons, various beings and merchants enter and exit; yet foolish people, through their conceptualization, believe these to be real entries and exits.

In reality, however, there is no one who goes out or enters; it is merely due to their false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings give rise to the delusion of arising and ceasing.

Yet, for them, there is neither the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), just as when an illusory person is born—there is in fact neither arising nor ceasing, because both existence and non-existence are non-existent. All phenomena are likewise so.
It is free from arising and ceasing. Foolish ordinary beings fall into what is not as it truly is and give rise to the deluded conceptualization of arising and ceasing;

this is not the case for the noble sages. The commentary states: "This means that while the object is fundamentally without arising, the foolish person falsely gives rise to the view of arising and ceasing.

It is said that not only are phenomena fundamentally without arising, but the mind is also fundamentally quiescent and extinguished. When the mind is quiescent and extinguished, those deluded conceptualizations are likewise [extinguished].
They are utterly devoid of intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said that unreal conceptualization is like a city of the Gandharvas or a magically conjured person.
Now, although that city of the Gandharvas and those conjured persons may have various merchants coming and going, in reality there is no one who comes or goes.
Those who are deluded take them to be real; the wise do not. Thus, they are merely ignorant commoners.
As for the delusions that arise without birth or cessation, those very false imaginings are fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent.
They are like a phantom person being born; fundamentally, there is no birth. Because these delusions have no substance, it is said that in reality they neither arise nor cease.

Because both nature and lack of nature are non-existent, an ancient worthy was once asked: "When arising and ceasing do not stop, what should one do? The worthy replied: "Tsk! Who is it that arises and ceases?
This was because the ancients had thoroughly seen that delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) have no inherent nature; thus they spoke in this manner.
Therefore, if the mind is quiescent and extinguished, all phenomena are likewise quiescent and extinguished. This is what is meant by "one."

The mind does not arise; the myriad dharmas are without fault. It is only the ignorant, ordinary person who falls into unreal views and gives rise to the deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing themselves;
this is not the case for the sages and worthies.
It is not so for those who do not see things as they truly are. It is no different from the false imagination of the self-nature of phenomena (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).

If it were different from false imagination, one would be attached to all self-natures of phenomena and would not perceive tranquility. Because one does not perceive tranquility, one will never be free from false imagination.
The commentary states: This says that when the Sage perceives all phenomena as they truly are, he does not resemble the ordinary deluded person who falls into the false view of arising and ceasing;
therefore, it says "not so. Why? Because he perceives the very substance of all phenomena as suchness (*tathatā*), and thus does not give rise to discriminative or divergent views.
Therefore, it says: "The nature of reality and self-nature are not different from conceptual construction. However, all...
The Dharma has been, from its very origin, eternally characterized by quiescence; it does not admit the arising of views.
If one gives rise to various divergent views and discriminations, this constitutes clinging to the characteristics of all things as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The reason for such clinging is that one fails to see that all phenomena are originally tranquil. Indeed, if one does not see the tranquility of all phenomena...
Such a person will ultimately never be free from deluded thoughts. Why? Because the realm of the departure from thought can only be realized through direct correspondence with the truth.
The above section, which clarifies that the True Suchness of the One Mind is free from all marks, is now complete. Below is the conclusion regarding the ultimate One Mind.
Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of the signless is superior, not the vision of signs. The vision of signs is the cause for undergoing rebirth; therefore, it is not superior.
Mahāmati, that which is signless is the non-arising of false discrimination; being neither produced nor extinguished, I call this Nirvāṇa.
The Commentary states: This summarizes how the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the single mind, being free from all marks, accomplishes the ultimate fruit-virtue.
As the Sūtra says: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said that seeing through the absence of marks is superior.
It is not the view of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). Because non-Buddhists falsely perceive arising and ceasing within that which is unborn, they remain perpetually submerged in birth and death.

Thus, the view of characteristics is the cause for undergoing rebirth; therefore, it is inferior. If one can perceive the signless (*animitta*), then all discriminative false thoughts will not arise in this very moment.
Where there is no arising, there is no ceasing. Without arising or ceasing, [one attains liberation].
This is what is called Great Nirvāṇa. It means that the realization that false conceptualization has no inherent nature is itself Nirvāṇa;
it is not that there is a separate characteristic of Nirvāṇa existing apart from this.

Mahāmati, as for nirvāṇa: it is the vision of reality as it truly is; it is the attainment of the noble wisdom of self-realization of the Tathāgata, free from the previously existing conceptualizations of mind and mental factors. This, I call nirvāṇa.
The Record states: "This section indicates that the true nature of the single mind is the self-nature nirvana;

it is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening, which is free from mind, thought, and consciousness. The Treatise states: "The true suchness of the mind is the very essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the One Dharma-realm.
That is to say, the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. All dharmas depend solely upon delusion..."
There are distinctions based on mental recollection. If one is separated from mental recollection, then there are no signs of any objective realms.
Therefore, all dharmas have, from the very beginning, been free from the signs of names, free from the signs of verbal expression, and free from the signs of mental objects.
It is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible; it is solely this one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (Suchness).

Since all verbal expressions are merely provisional names lacking reality, following only deluded thoughts and being ultimately ungraspable, even that which is called *tathatā* is without characteristics.
It is the ultimate limit of verbal expression; by means of words, words are dispensed with. This is *tathatā*.
In its essence, there is nothing to be discarded, because all phenomena are entirely true.
Nor is there anything to be established, because all phenomena are identical to suchness (*tathatā*). One should know that all phenomena are ineffable and inconceivable;
therefore, they are called "true thusness. Question: If this is the meaning, how do sentient beings accord with it?

One is able to enter. The answer is: if one knows all phenomena such that, although it is said there is nothing that can speak or be spoken, and although there is mindfulness, there is likewise nothing that can mindfully attend or be mindfully attended to—this is called "conformity. If one is free from such mindfulness, this is called "attaining entry."

Therefore it is said: "As in the vision of the true meaning, having departed from the prior deluded thoughts and mental factors, one attains the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata’s self-realization; this I call nirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"To eliminate the doctrine of arising, I establish the principle of non-arising. I preach such a Dharma, Which the foolish are unable to understand.
All dharmas are unarisen, Lacking intrinsic nature and devoid of existence; Like a *gandharva-city*, a phantom, or a dream, They nevertheless appear to exist."
Nature is without cause; it does not arise and lacks intrinsic nature. Why should emptiness be explained? Because when separated from combination, the nature of cognition does not manifest;
therefore, emptiness is non-arising. I teach that there is no intrinsic nature.

The commentary states: From this point down to the end of the verse, it generally clarifies that True Suchness and the One Mind are free from the characteristics of arising, ceasing, causes, and conditions.
This means that although the Tathāgata originally has no dharma to preach, the reason he speaks of non-arising and the lack of self-nature is as follows.
This is intended to shatter their view of birth, for they cling to the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because those deluded worldlings do not know that all phenomena are unborn and fundamentally lack intrinsic nature, the Buddha speaks of Gandhāra cities, illusions, and dreams as metaphors for them.
However, that which they grasp as having intrinsic nature falls into the error of causelessness. Why, then, does the Tathāgata speak of non-arising and the absence of intrinsic nature?

Yes. Because all phenomena are empty, how could one speak of them based on emptiness? Those non-Buddhists falsely cling to the notion that all phenomena arise through the combination of their respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); now, this [teaching] departs from that.

Thus, because all phenomena are fundamentally empty and lack arising in their very essence, it is said that they have no intrinsic nature. This verse [thereby] transcends the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
That is to say, each individual combination appears as a nature yet does not exist. When analyzed, there is no combination; this is not like the views of the non-Buddhists.
Like dreams, illusions, falling hairs, mirages, and the city of the Gandharvas—various worldly phenomena appear with characteristics despite having no cause.
He subdues those who maintain theories of causality and proclaims the meaning of non-arising. To proclaim the meaning of non-arising is to ensure that the flow of the Dharma never ceases;
he blazes forth against those who maintain theories of no-cause, striking terror into all non-Buddhists.
The commentary states: This verse dispels the characteristics of causes and conditions.

Because non-Buddhists falsely imagine that there is a real productive cause through which phenomena arise from a combination [of factors], the World-Honored One said to me: "I merely analyze that combination;
although it appears, it does not exist. Therefore, he spoke of illusions, dreams, falling hairs, mirages, and the city of Gandharvas as metaphors to clarify that although all worldly phenomena...
It appears as if causeless, for it refutes the doctrine of causality and proclaims the meaning of non-arising.
Indeed, one who can proclaim the meaning of non-arising ensures that the flow of the Dharma will never be severed.

Furthermore, I ardently preach the doctrine of causelessness to destroy their [doctrine of] causality, so that those heterodox practitioners who hear it may give rise to trepidation. However, the Buddha—

This teaching of the doctrine of causelessness (ahetuvāda) is such that there is no cause for the arising of those [phenomena]; it is by no means comparable to the causeless theories of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Be aware of this. At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse:
"What is it? What is its cause? By what reason does it arise? In what place is it combined? Thus they propound the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

The commentary states: This is where Mahāmati raises a question by citing a verse from the Buddha’s inquiry into the causes of arising among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), in order to counter-argue and refute the meaning of the doctrine of causelessness. The Buddha asks the non-Buddhist: "How does your dharma of arising come into being?"
"Does it arise from a cause, or does it arise without a cause? He replied, "It arises from a cause. The Buddha asked again, "Since it arises from a cause, what is that cause?
He replied, "The atoms (*paramāṇu*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the primary qualities (*guṇa*) serve as its causes.
The Buddha asked again, "And for what reason do those atoms, the four great elements, and so forth [arise]?"
"Is it born? He replied, "It is born without cause. The Buddha said, "If those atoms and so forth are without cause, then that which lacks a cause is a non-existent phenomenon (*dharma*).
That which is a non-existent phenomenon has no location. That which has no location cannot undergo conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
That which does not undergo conjunction cannot be born. Since you claim it is without cause, at what location could there be a conjunction to establish your theory of causelessness?"

"Yes. Mahāmati raises this question to challenge [the teaching], because he has heard the Buddha above explain the absence of a cause (*ahetuka*) to refute those who maintain the existence of a cause.
Therefore, he doubts, saying: "Furthermore, the absence of a cause is what is imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); the Buddha has already used this to refute them."
Now, for what reason is it said again that there is no cause (*ahetu*) in order to refute those who hold to a cause (*sahetu*)? This leads to doubt, and thus the question is posed.

Since the causes of origination imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are themselves [claimed to be] without cause, the Buddha taught dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) precisely to refute that notion of no-cause.

Furthermore, the teaching of "no cause" is intended to refute their notion of a productive cause; its purpose lies in directly pointing to non-arising in order to still the views of arising and ceasing.
Therefore, the following section provides a clear response to this.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied in verse:
"Observing conditioned phenomena, one sees they do not exist without a cause, but possess a cause; thus, the views of those who debate arising and ceasing are extinguished."
The commentary states: The intent of this response is to clarify the departure from the characteristics of causes and conditions characterized by arising and ceasing.
That is to say, by being able to observe that all phenomena belong neither to having a cause nor to being causeless, one immediately and suddenly perceives non-arising;
thus, the views of arising and ceasing naturally subside. Nāgārjuna said: "When things arise from conditions, when things cease from conditions, [arising is merely...]"
Regarding all dependent origination: when conditions cease, only the conditions themselves cease. Thus one knows that when form arises, it is merely emptiness arising;
when form ceases, it is merely emptiness ceasing. Because emptiness does not belong to conditions, it simply does not arise.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke in verse, asking:
"What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature? Or is it that, having observed various conditions, there is a phenomenon called 'non-arising'?"
A name should not be without meaning; it is spoken solely for the sake of analytical explanation. The commentary states:

This inquiry concerns the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Since the Buddha above has explained that by departing from the dharmas of arising and ceasing he reveals non-arising, Mahāmati then asks:
"What is non-arising? Is it that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) that constitutes non-arising?"
"Is it that there is a distinct nature of birth which, upon observing various conditions, is called 'non-arising'?
Since the name 'non-arising' exists, there must necessarily be the meaning of non-arising. I pray that you will explain this to me."
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied in verse:

"It is not that there is no nature and thus no arising, nor is it that [arising] depends upon various conditions. It is not that there is a nature which is then designated by a name; yet the name is not without meaning."
All heterodox teachers, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas—these are not the domain of those in the seventh stage (the Wei translation reads "seventh ground").
This is called the mark of non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*). It is far removed from all causes and conditions and detached from all phenomena; there is only the abiding of the subtle mind.
When both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned, the body undergoes transformation accordingly; this I call non-arising.

The commentary states: This verse explains the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). By departing from all causes and conditions as well as an agent, one enters the dwelling of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*) and attains the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is the mind-made body of the Dharma (*manomayadharmakāya*); this is the true meaning of non-arising. Now, regarding this non-arising:
It is not non-existent, nor is it existent. Since this name exists, its meaning is likewise not non-existent;
however, this meaning of "non-arising" is the locus of abiding in reality as it is, realized from the eighth stage upward.

It is hardly the domain of the heterodox, the followers of the two vehicles, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage. This is because the views of those heterodox are erroneous, and the attachments of the two vehicles are partial. The seventh...
Bodhisattvas on the stages have not yet transcended the measure of mind (*cittamātra*) and still remain within the realm of arising and ceasing; they have not yet entered the subtle, true abode.
Because they have not yet forgotten the duality of mind and objects, this [state] is not what they can know. To be free from these various faults is true non-arising (*anutpāda*).
There is no external nature nor non-nature, nor is there any mental grasping; having severed all views, I declare this to be non-arising.

Thus, regarding the absence of intrinsic nature, emptiness and so forth should be distinguished: it is called "empty" not because of some emptiness, but because of non-arising that it is called empty.
The commentary states: This verse shows that both mind and objects are transcended, revealing the true meaning of non-arising through the empty reality of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since objects are free from existence and non-existence, and the mind is free from grasping, severing all views is itself the empty reality of the Dharma-body.
This is not an emptiness of annihilation; it is called "emptiness" because the mind and its objects are non-arising. [The preceding verse] eulogizes the meaning of non-arising.
[The following] generally eulogizes the departure from the characteristics of causes and conditions involving arising and ceasing.
When the collection of causal conditions comes together, there is arising and ceasing. Apart from the collection of causal conditions, there is no separate arising or ceasing.
Once one has abandoned the collection of causal conditions, there is no other distinct nature. To speak of identity or difference is the false conceptualization of the non-Buddhists.

That which has the nature of existence or non-existence is not born; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Apart from the transformation of numerical designations, none of these can be apprehended.
There are only conventional designations that link together like a chain; apart from that causal chain, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found.
The commentary states: This verse describes how the *tathatā* (true suchness) of the one mind is free from the characteristics of causes and conditions.

Causes and conditions are the root of arising and ceasing. Apart from these causes and conditions, there is no other dharma that arises. Therefore, Master Sengzhao said: "All dharmas arise through the convergence of conditions.
Since they arise through the convergence of conditions, they do not exist prior to arising. Because they do not exist [prior to arising], there is no arising. Thus it is said.

Apart from the various categories of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there is no separate arising or ceasing. Because phenomena arise through the transformation of the twelve links of dependent origination, they are called the "categories of causes and conditions.
If one abandons these, not only is there no arising, but moreover, all is perfectly equal and uniform, utterly devoid of any nature of unity or difference.
To speak of unity or difference herein is the view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Why is this so?

Since both existence and non-existence are entirely unarisen—because they are collectively not existent—and since nothing can be found apart from causes and conditions, that which arises dependently lacks intrinsic nature and is therefore empty. Being empty, it is unarisen;
being unarisen, the Dharma-body is equanimous and free from all marks. This is why, apart from causes and conditions, no further meaning of arising can be found.

Arising is without intrinsic nature and thus does not occur; it is free from the errors of all non-Buddhist schools (tīrthikas). It speaks only of the chain of conditions, yet the foolish and ignorant cannot comprehend it. The commentary states:
"This correctly demonstrates the meaning of dependent origination being without intrinsic nature. 'Nature' refers to causes and conditions.

This means that arising is fundamentally non-arising, for it necessarily arises in dependence upon conditions. Because that which arises dependently lacks intrinsic nature, arising is fundamentally non-existent. The Tang translation says:
Because arising is non-existent, there is no arising; thus, arising is itself non-arising. Consequently, one avoids the error of the non-Buddhists regarding the dharma of arising.
Since that which arises through conditions is itself non-arising, I speak only of causes and conditions while secretly revealing non-arising.
For this reason, the ignorant and foolish cannot understand it, falsely claiming that there is a nature of arising existing apart from causes and conditions.
If there were a nature of arising existing separately, apart from the chain of conditions, this would constitute a doctrine of causelessness that destroys the meaning of the causal chain.
Just as a lamp reveals various forms, if the manifestation of the causal chain were likewise [independent], then there would be various natures existing separately, apart from the causal chain.
The commentary states: This explains the meaning of the non-Buddhists' reckoning that there is a nature of arising distinct from and external to causes and conditions.
The Buddha said that if a fruit were to exist apart from causes and conditions with a separate nature of arising, it would fall into the doctrine of causelessness and sink into nihilism;
therefore, it is said that this "destroys the principle of the chain. The "chain" refers precisely to causes and conditions. For those outsiders...
The proponents of this [false] view falsely conceptualize that there is a distinct nature of arising which must depend upon causes and conditions to come into being.

They claim it is like various forms that exist beforehand, yet can only be seen after depending on the illumination of a lamp; thus, they hold that phenomena manifested through causes and conditions are just like the various forms revealed by a lamp.
Therefore, the Buddha refuted them, saying: "If this proponent were correct, it would mean that there is indeed an arising distinct from and external to causes and conditions."
Therefore, I say that they are proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).
There is no arising of that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), for its self-nature is like space. If one is free from the chain of causal links, the intellect has nothing to differentiate.

The commentary states: This rebukes the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) for failing to understand that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), and thus they give rise to false conceptualizations.
Because that which arises dependently lacks intrinsic nature, there is no arising. Where there is no arising, there is no intrinsic nature; its essence and characteristics are like empty space.
This is the Way that transcends conditions and severs all dualistic oppositions. Within this realm, the Buddhas of the three periods of time do not dare—
Observe this: who could possibly engage in discrimination regarding it? Therefore, it is said that wisdom is without discrimination.
Now, since they have given rise to discrimination outside of the realm of causes and conditions, it is clear enough that these are all merely false conceptualizations.

Furthermore, there is another aspect of non-arising, which is the dharma attained by the noble ones (*ārya*). That which is "arising and yet non-arising" is precisely the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

The commentary states: "This distinguishes the meaning of non-arising. It means that while the dharmas of arising postulated by those heterodox outsiders (*tīrthika*) are certainly false views, within our own Dharma there is yet another meaning of non-arising, which is what is attained by the noble ones of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*)."

It is not the ultimate reality. Because one must first exhaust all phenomena of birth before subsequently attaining non-arising, yet fails to understand that birth is fundamentally non-arising, it is not the ultimate reality.
Thus, what I call "birth is itself non-arising" is precisely the true *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), which is realized at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is not something known by the shallow wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If all those in the world were to observe the chain of causal links, they would all become free from such links and thereby attain samādhi. The commentary states:
"This distinguishes correct practice. It means that when non-Buddhists falsely speculate on a state apart from the law of dependent origination, they merely increase their wrong views;
it is not true liberation. If all people in the world could each observe that causes and conditions are without [inherent self-nature]..."
Regarding the nature: once one thoroughly understands the principle that there is no arising apart from conditions, one immediately attains the samādhi of non-arising, which is true concentration.
Below, the method for contemplation is shown.
Ignorance, craving, the various karmas, and so forth—these constitute the internal chain. The fire-drill, the lump of clay, the potter’s wheel, seeds, and the like are called external.
If these were to arise from causes and conditions while possessing an intrinsic nature other [than themselves], they would not fulfill the meaning of a "chain"; thus, they would be unestablished.

If that which arises lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for whom would it serve as a causal chain? Since they arise in mutual succession, one should understand the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The commentary states: "This demonstrates the method for contemplating dependent origination. Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), various karmas (*karma*), and so forth constitute the twelve links of dependent origination;

namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)."
The six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth;
and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. Thus they revolve through the three periods of time, entangling and binding without interruption;
therefore, they constitute the "inner chain. Just as drilling wood produces fire, a lump of clay forms a jar, or a seed gives rise to a sprout—these three are the "outer" [conditions].

All phenomena arise through internal and external causes and conditions. If one simply observes that these various dharmas are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, one immediately realizes non-arising.

Why, then, must one posit a "nature of other" (*parabhāva*) apart from this? If there were some separate "nature of other" existing outside of these that arose from causes and conditions, it would follow that it is causeless;
this would not only destroy the principle of causes and conditions, but would also contradict the very meaning of dependent origination.
Furthermore, those dharmas are not established, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) they postulate is without cause.
If one observes that produced dharmas fundamentally lack intrinsic nature, then causes and conditions are suddenly rendered empty. Moreover, who would serve as the link?
It is because there is a continuous succession of mutual production that the principle of causes and conditions is taught. The meaning is that if causes and conditions exist, [they necessarily...]
