There is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If one is apart from causes and conditions, there is simply non-arising. How could there be an intrinsic nature existing separately outside of causes and conditions?
Thus, one can contemplate that what arises through conditions is without intrinsic nature, and that what is without intrinsic nature arises through conditions;
thereby, one realizes that the essence of causes and conditions is empty and enters the meaning of true non-arising. The wise should practice such contemplation.

The dharmas of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion give rise to false conceptualizations in the ignorant. Apart from these enumerations, there is no distinct dharma; this is what is meant by "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The commentary states: This explains the reason why all dharmas lack intrinsic nature. It means that dharmas such as the four great elements are entirely empty in their very essence;
they originally possess no self-nature. They arise merely through the convergence of conditions, and there is no separate dharma apart from them. As for the non-Buddhists...
This is not understood. To recklessly calculate that the four great elements possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as the cause of arising is merely a false conceptualization;
it is not right view. Therefore, I say that dependent origination is without intrinsic nature, which is itself non-arising, in order to refute that calculation.
Apart from these enumerated factors, there is no other distinct phenomenon to be found; I am merely speaking of the absence of intrinsic nature.

Just as a physician treats various diseases without having multiple theories, but devises diverse remedies according to the distinctions among illnesses, so too do I destroy the afflictions of those sentient beings.
Knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I preach for them the gates of liberation.
It is not that there are various dharmas because the roots of affliction differ; rather, I preach only the Single Vehicle Dharma. This is [the meaning].
This constitutes the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states: "This concludes by returning to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in order to reveal the ultimate meaning of the True Suchness (Tathatā) of the One Mind.
This means that when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he speaks only of non-arising; yet, while non-arising is fundamentally beyond speech, there are many kinds of words [used to express it]."
Regarding the skillful means of verbal instruction: it is because [the Buddha] treats each according to their specific ailment.

Thus, just as a physician treats various illnesses where the ailments are many and the prescriptions likewise differ, so too does the Buddha preach the various dharma-gates of the *pāramitās* in order to eliminate the diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.

Since the roots of those ailments differ, he speaks of these various methods; yet the fundamental nature of this Dharma is not different—it is only that the capacities of the practitioners themselves vary. What is...
This means that there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for what the Buddha has taught as a skillful means.
He merely uses provisional names to guide sentient beings. Since entering the Mahāyāna is the fundamental principle, it is said that he teaches only the Single Vehicle Dharma.
This is precisely what constitutes the Mahāyāna. Previously, when revealing the ultimate point of principle, it was said: "My Mahāyāna is not a vehicle.
Now, having completed the explanation of the culmination of severance and realization, it is likewise concluded with the term "Mahāyāna.

The above section explaining that the True Suchness of the One Mind is free from all marks, thereby fully manifesting the virtues of ultimate Nirvāṇa and the True Self, is now complete. Below, the external [opponents] are refuted.
The seven kinds of impermanence in the Path are taught to reveal the true permanence of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence.
World-Honored One, you also say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and are subject to arising and ceasing. What is the meaning of this?"
"What is it? Is it false or is it correct? How many kinds of impermanence are there? The answer states:
This is because of the impermanence imagined by non-Buddhists; it is intended to reveal that Nirvāṇa is the ultimate, true nature of permanence.
Previously, the cause-and-condition of arising and ceasing was set aside to clarify the true self of the Dharmakāya; here, the state of impermanence is set aside.

Upon seeing this, one realizes that the Dharma-body is truly eternal. [The Master’s] intention was that since the Buddha also spoke of impermanence in the past, it was unclear which of the two—the Buddha’s teaching or that of the non-Buddhists—was erroneous and which was correct.
However, his purpose in asking how many kinds of impermanence the non-Buddhists allow for was to fully expose their calculations and refute them, so as to prevent them from falling into error.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All non-Buddhists maintain seven kinds of impermanence; these do not belong to my teaching.
What are the seven? Some of them assert that when something has been produced and is then abandoned, this is called impermanence."
The commentary states: This non-Buddhist school establishes the existence of a "Primal Nature" (*pradhāna*) as a creator capable of producing all four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and all phenomena.
Their current calculation, however, asserts that the produced four great elements are eternal, while their creator, having completed the act of creation, immediately relinquishes it.
"This is impermanent. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "It is apart from the impermanence of initial creation.
Some say that the destruction of shape and location is what is called impermanence.

The commentary says: This [view] calculates that both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are permanent and ultimately indestructible; it is merely [a matter of] division.
When length, shortness, and other such formal shapes (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) are analyzed, they cannot be apprehended. That is to say, the disintegration of the locus of form is impermanent.
Some say that form itself is impermanent. The commentary states:

This [view] maintains that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), which act as the creators, are permanent, while the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) they produce is impermanent. This is identical to the first [position].
The calculation of characteristics is reversed.
Some say that the interval during which matter undergoes transformation is called impermanence; it is the immediate disintegration of itself, as in the case of milk turning into curd.
This transformation occurs within an interval that is invisible; impermanence destroys all natures through such transformation.
The record states: This [view] maintains that both the primary creator and the derived products are eternal;

however, between these two types of form (rūpa), there exists a factor of impermanence that causes the derived form-dharmas to undergo continuous transformation and spontaneous destruction, as in the case of milk turning into curd.
Between the two forms, there is an impermanent dharma that effects this transformation, yet it is invisible. This...
"Impermanence can transform all natures. This contradicts the first two of the three aforementioned views.
Some say that nature itself is impermanent.
The commentary states: "This view holds that there is a self-nature of impermanence which is indestructible, yet it is capable of destroying all other phenomena. As for example...
Objects such as staffs, shards, and stones can destroy all things; this [view] is the opposite of the aforementioned position.
Some say that both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) are impermanent.

The commentary states: "This position holds that both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived elements (*bhautika*) are impermanent. 'Intrinsic nature' refers to the primary elements, while 'the absence of intrinsic nature' refers to the derived elements."
As for the derived [matter]: once the nature of the producer has finished producing matter, its own substance has already perished, and that which is derived likewise perishes accordingly;
therefore, both are impermanent. This contradicts the aforementioned position.
Some say that the non-arising of all phenomena is impermanence, and that it enters into all phenomena.
The commentary states: This view posits that there is a nature of non-arising which exists within all arising phenomena and undergoes destruction along with them;
this very non-arising is itself impermanence. The above lists the proposed views, while the following restates them.
One calculates and then destroys it.
Mahāmati, as for the impermanence of existence and non-existence, this refers to the destruction of the specific characteristics of the four great elements and their derivatives;
the self-nature of the four great elements is unattainable and does not arise.
The commentary states: This passage cites and refutes the sixth view, which holds that there is neither a nature nor a lack of nature in impermanence.

It refers to the calculation of those non-Buddhists who claim that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) can create all phenomena; however, they must first undergo the destruction of their own substance before they can produce anything, just as a seed must perish to produce a sprout.
Furthermore, that which is produced is not the original four great elements themselves. Therefore, both the creator and the created are destroyed, and on this basis—
"Impermanence. The Buddha refuted this, saying: "The intrinsic nature of those four great elements is fundamentally unobtainable.
Since that which creates them is fundamentally without substance, and being without substance it is fundamentally unborn; if it is unborn, there is neither subject nor object.
Since these two characteristics of subject and object are utterly unobtainable, by pointing to what dharma could one name 'impermanence'?"
That which is "unborn impermanence" is neither permanent nor impermanent. All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, do not arise;
even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom, they cannot be seen. This meaning of non-arising is not arising; this is called the characteristic of unborn impermanence.
If one does not awaken to this, one falls into the view of all external paths regarding the impermanence of arising.
The commentary states: This passage cites and refutes the seventh position, which holds that non-arising is impermanent.
However, those non-Buddhists falsely reckon that there exists a nature of non-arising that enters into all phenomena subject to arising;
because it perishes along with all phenomena, they claim this "non-arising" is impermanent. The Buddha said: "If one says that non-arising is impermanent, this is not so."
It is eternally neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why? If one says it is unarisen, then it is truly eternal; yet now it is said that it perishes along with all phenomena, and thus it is not eternal.
Therefore, it is called "neither eternal nor non-eternal. This points out its error, and he then refutes it, saying:
"Indeed, all phenomena such as existence and non-existence are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning; how could there be another [entity]?"
Does the nature of arising enter into those phenomena? If there were such a thing as the nature of arising that entered into those phenomena, it should be visible;
yet, when one analyzes all phenomena down to the finest atom, this meaning of non-arising is ultimately not to be seen.
Since it is not to be seen, it follows that the very basis for the arising of these phenomena is fundamentally non-arising. Furthermore, they are impermanent.
This is the nature of arising. Yet, I teach that the fundamental nature of the arising of all dharmas is non-arising.

Those who instead take non-arising to be arising are characterized by impermanence; therefore, it is said to be "not-arising. This is called the mark of the impermanence of non-arising. This is truly a perversity.
If my disciples do not awaken to this meaning—that this arising is fundamentally non-arising—they will fall into the ways of the outsiders (tīrthikas).
One perceives the impermanence of arising. Because that which they conceive as non-arising actually constitutes the dharma of arising, it is said that "arising has the meaning of impermanence.
Zhuang Zhou’s statement, "That which gives rise to arising does not arise," falls precisely into this [error].
Mahāmati, the impermanence of intrinsic nature is a conceptual construction of one's own mind; it is not a nature characterized by permanence or impermanence. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature of impermanence itself is indestructible. Mahāmati, this is the matter regarding the impermanence of the existence and non-existence of all natures.
Apart from impermanence, there is nothing else capable of causing the existence and non-existence of the natures of all dharmas—such as when a staff, a tile, or a stone destroys various things.
Regarding "things," the Record states: This passage refutes the fifth view, the calculation that there is impermanence as a nature.

The Buddha said that those non-Buddhists calculate that there exists a self-nature of impermanence which is indestructible, yet is capable of destroying all phenomena; this is merely their own [fabrication].
It is merely the mind’s conceptualization and false discrimination. Such a conception is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why?
Because that which is called "impermanence" has an indestructible intrinsic nature, yet it is capable of destroying all phenomena to accomplish the state of impermanence.
Thus, apart from this impermanence, there is nothing else that can destroy all phenomena.
However, impermanence can destroy those various phenomena, just as a staff, a tile, or a stone can destroy various objects.

If this were the case, impermanence would necessarily have to be distinct from the phenomena in order to be able to destroy them. Therefore, the following section refutes this by examining the relationship of identity and difference.

It is observed that each [entity] is not different [from its nature]; this nature is an impermanent thing (*vastu*). There is no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon. This is impermanence; this is the thing.
If there were no difference between the agent and the acted-upon, then all natures would be eternal and without cause. Mahāmati!
All natures are natureless; they have causes, yet they are not known by the ignorant and foolish.
The commentary states: This is an analysis based on identity and difference to refute the nature of impermanence.
That is to say, if impermanence were truly capable of destroying all phenomena, then the nature that destroys and the phenomenon destroyed must necessarily be two distinct entities.
Only then could it destroy them. Yet, as we observe now, each is not distinct from the other; one cannot separate the impermanent nature from the object that is destroyed.
Since the two aspects—the agent and the object—possess distinct essences, it is said that there is no difference between the act and the acted-upon.
The "act" is impermanence, and the "acted-upon" is the object that is destroyed. If the agent and the object were of different essences, then [it would follow that...]
One should be able to point it out, saying, "This is impermanence; this is the thing that is destroyed and ceases. Since it cannot be pointed out, it is not a separate entity from the thing itself.
If the capacity [to destroy] and the object [destroyed] were not distinct but constituted a single entity, then all phenomena would have to be permanent.
Furthermore, this falls into the error of causelessness (*ahetuka*). Why? Because according to their reckoning, the nature of impermanence is indestructible;
that which is indestructible is eternal. Now, since [impermanence] is of one essence with all phenomena, and since impermanence is thus eternal, all phenomena must likewise be eternal.
Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction, as all natures are eternal. Moreover, this is because they reckon the cause to be impermanent.
It is capable of causing all phenomena to perish. Now that they are of one essence, no cause can be seen that is able to cause all phenomena to perish;
this, moreover, falls into the fallacy of causelessness (*ahetuka*). Thus, that position is also not established, and it is therefore called "the nature of causelessness."
However, the disintegration and cessation of all phenomena do not occur without cause; therefore, the Tang translation states:
"The disintegration and cessation of all phenomena truly have causes, though they cannot be understood by the ignorant and foolish."
It does not arise from causes that are dissimilar. If it were to arise [from such], then all natures would be entirely impermanent; this would be a dissimilarity.
Furthermore, there would be no distinction between the agent and the object acted upon, yet we clearly perceive such distinctions.
The commentary states: Previously, it was refuted that impermanence can destroy all phenomena; here, it is further refuted that the nature of impermanence can produce all phenomena.

The Buddha said: "If they reckon that the nature of impermanence can produce all phenomena, then all produced phenomena would have causes and effects that correspond to one another, just as when planting beans or sesame seeds. It never happens that one plants beans and obtains sesame."
Therefore, it is said that things do not arise from causes that are dissimilar. If something dissimilar could produce [an effect], then a single cause would produce multiple effects.
Now, if all phenomena were produced by a single nature of impermanence, then all natures would be identical to that single impermanence.
Thus, it is said: "If they were produced, all natures would be entirely..."
If it were thus impermanent, then cause and effect would not be distinct and their categories would not be differentiated;
consequently, all dissimilar phenomena should arise simultaneously. This would be a case of the incongruous, wherein the producer and the produced could not be distinguished.
They blend together into one. Therefore, it is said that there is no distinction between the creator and the created.
Yet, as we currently observe, all phenomena each possess their own distinct differences; thus, it is not the case that impermanence can give rise to all phenomena.

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a causal factor (*kāraṇa-hetu*). If it were to fall [into that category], then all intrinsic natures would not be ultimate.

Since all intrinsic natures would fall into the characteristic of being causal factors, that which is itself impermanent would have to be impermanent; yet because the impermanent is impermanent, all intrinsic natures would not be impermanent, and thus they would have to be permanent.
The commentary states: This refutes the calculation that impermanence serves as the cause of arising; it cannot be considered permanent.

That is to say, if one insists that the nature of impermanence is a functional entity (*dharmin*) and acts as the cause of arising, then one falls into the fallacy of a "creator-cause" (*kartṛ-hetu*). Generally speaking, whatever is a creator—
Because all things are impermanent. If the cause that produces them already falls into impermanence, then all phenomena produced by it must also be impermanent.
Therefore it is said: "If they fall [into impermanence], then no nature is ultimate.
If the productive cause falls within the impermanent phenomena that are produced, then that cause, being itself impermanent, must likewise be impermanent.

Yet one cannot reckon that which is capable of producing as being permanent. Therefore it is said: "If all natures fall into the category of causal characteristics, they themselves are impermanent and should be impermanent.
If they are themselves impermanent—and since they are already impermanent—then all phenomena produced by them would not be impermanent;
they should instead be permanent. Why? Because [the producer], having abandoned its own permanence, enters into that [other]."

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*): if those phenomena were to possess the permanent nature of a self, then this [self] would itself be impermanent, and that which is produced would necessarily be permanent.
If that [self] were permanent, it could not be destroyed; yet, the notion that produced phenomena are subject to destruction would then be untenable.
Therefore, the Tang translation states: "If the nature of impermanence were a real entity (*bhāva*)."
That which [is thus] should be identical to what is produced. Since it is itself impermanent, and because it is itself impermanent, all dharmas that are impermanent should likewise be permanent.
If the impermanent were to enter into all natures, it would fall into the three periods of time. That past form is conjoined with destruction; it has not yet...
It does not arise from the future, because form does not arise. Present form is accompanied by the characteristic of disintegration.
The commentary states: "This refutes the nature of impermanence [as conceived by others] and demonstrates its entry into all phenomena.
However, non-Buddhists falsely imagine that impermanence enters into all phenomena while its own self-nature remains indestructible, yet it is able to destroy those phenomena. The Buddha said:

If it is claimed that impermanence enters into all natures, then it must fall within the three periods of time. Once it falls within the three periods of time, it follows that it undergoes destruction;
thus, its intrinsic nature cannot help but perish. Why is this? If it enters the past, the form of the past has already perished.
If it enters the future, the form of the future has not yet arisen. If it enters the present, the present [form does not exist]...

It abides; it perishes and changes moment by moment, yet impermanence itself also perishes along with it. Furthermore, since its own substance has already perished, how could it possibly cause those other phenomena to perish?

Form (*rūpa*) is a specific aggregation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements and their derivative form is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different [from them].

For all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the four great elements are indestructible. Within all three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), the four great elements and their derivative form exist as objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and undergo arising and ceasing. Apart from the four great elements and their derivative form, what could all non-Buddhists possibly conceive of?
"Only nature is impermanent; the four great elements do not arise, because their intrinsic characteristics are indestructible.
The commentary states: "This further refutes the view that the four great elements are permanent.

Because [the opponent] previously clung to the idea that impermanence does not destroy the nature [of things], which enters into all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), the Buddha refuted this, saying: 'All material phenomena of the three periods of time belong to...'"
It may be destroyed; yet there is no principle by which that which is impermanent is not subject to destruction. Therefore, this further obstructs their shifting argument, which claims:
"Because the impermanent [agent] that enters is indestructible, the four great elements (mahābhūta) that are entered must also be eternally abiding and indestructible.
To refute this, it is said: "Form (rūpa) is merely a specific nature produced by the accumulation of the four great elements; it is the created, while [the elements are] the creators."
The created and the creator do not possess two distinct natures. How could it be that when the created form-dharmas have perished, the four great elements that create them do not perish?
This is because the creator and the created are neither identical nor different. If they were not identical, their two natures would be separate;
if they were not different, both would belong to the category of the destructible. This is all the more so for all the creators and created within the three realms of existence.
Everyone knows that these are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. Furthermore, how could it be that while form perishes, the four great elements do not possess the principle of non-perishing?
Since both the subject and the object perish together, where else could one seek the nature of impermanence and indestructibility?
Therefore, the Tang translation states: "All non-Buddhists reckon that the essential nature of the four great elements is indestructible."

Form (*rūpa*) is precisely the derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by the differentiation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because it is neither different nor non-different [from them], its own-nature (*svabhāva*) likewise does not perish.
Mahāmati, within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), there is nothing among the primary and derivative elements that is not characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing.
How could there be any other separate nature of impermanence (*anityatā*) capable of producing things without itself perishing? For...
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) falsely speculate that the nature of impermanence is permanent, and that it acts as the sovereign cause of arising and ceasing.

Because this speculation lies hidden in the depths, it is refuted through successive stages. Thus, even Zhuang Zhou of our own land said: "That which gives birth to all things is itself unborn. He further said:

"That which undergoes decay and destruction is not truly subject to decay and destruction; that which constitutes the root and the branches is not truly the root and the branches. If one does not penetrate the truth of true non-arising, [one remains bound by such misconceptions].

I think that few do not fall into this category. Therefore, it was said previously: "If one does not awaken to this, then one falls into the view of all externalists who hold that birth is impermanent."
Regarding those who deny the impermanence of initial creation: they are not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor are there others distinct from the four great elements.

Because each has its own distinct characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), no differentiation can be found; they are without differentiation, and thus these do not undergo further creation. Through two means, they are not produced.
One should know that this is impermanent.

The commentary states: This reiterates the refutation of the first [position], which was the abandonment of the conception of impermanence. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceive that it is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are impermanent;
rather, there exists something distinct from the nature of the four great elements that is capable of initiating creation and then ceasing—this they name "impermanence."
This is because they hold that the derived four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal, while the primary creators are impermanent.
However, since they do not conceive of anything other than the three factors—mutuality, self-nature, and commonality—as being the creators, the Buddha refutes them by saying:
"The four great elements do not create one another, because each of the four great elements has distinct characteristics; nor do they create themselves, because there is no differentiation."
Because characteristics can be apprehended; yet, since no distinct characteristics can be apprehended, these [elements] are likewise not created anew in common.
This is because they are mutually separated and the two means of production do not operate. Since both locations are thus untenable, there is fundamentally no creator;
it is ultimately impermanent. Therefore, it is said: "One should know that this is impermanent. How could there be that which is impermanent...?
Can they produce those eternal dharmas? Therefore, the Tang translation states: "The primary elements do not mutually produce one another because they are distinct;
they do not produce themselves because they lack differentiation; nor do they produce them collectively because they are disjoined."

Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of form and location (*saṃsthāna*): it means that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) do not perish; they do not perish until the very end.

Mahāmati, "the end" refers to the point where, through analysis down to the subtlest atom (*paramāṇu*), one observes their destruction. One perceives the difference in the forms and locations of the four great elements and the derived matter;

length and shortness can no longer be apprehended. It is not that the four great elements themselves perish; rather, it is the manifestation of the destruction of their forms and locations that appears, falling within the realm of numerical reckoning.
The Commentary states: This cites and refutes the second [view], the calculation that shape and location are subject to impermanence through disintegration.

The non-Buddhists calculate that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which act as creators and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) they produce are ultimately indestructible; they analyze them down to the limit of the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*). However, [the text continues...]
One extinguishes the views of shapes, such as length and so forth, but one does not extinguish the substantial essence (*dravya*) of primary and derived matter (*bhūta-bhautika-rūpa*).

Therefore, that which does not destroy the substantial essence of matter is considered "permanent," while that which undergoes the transformation and destruction of shape and location is considered "impermanent. Thus it is said: "When there is a difference in shape and location, length and so forth cannot be apprehended;
this is not [the fault of] the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The Buddha refuted this, saying: "The four great elements do not perish; it is the shape and location that appear to perish."
This falls squarely within the Sāṃkhya system, because the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal.
As for the statement "form is impermanent," it means that form itself is impermanent; that [impermanence] refers to the impermanence of shape and location, not to the four great elements.
If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be what is conventionally designated by worldly discourse. If worldly discourse were not based on intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then...
They fall into the worldly theory (*lokāyata*). They see all natures as being nothing more than verbal designations;
they do not see the arising of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). The commentary states: This cites and refutes the third position, the view that form itself is impermanent.

The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that form is itself impermanent; however, since derived form (*bhautika-rūpa*) does not transcend shapes such as long or short, the Buddha said that what they [perceive]...

The calculation is as follows: the meaning is identical to the previous point regarding the impermanence of form and location. This is not because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are impermanent.

If the meaning of the impermanence of the four great elements were the case, it would belong to what is discussed in the orthodox teachings (*saddharma*). Therefore, it is said that this cannot be reached through conventional numerical discourse.
However, those who follow worldly treatises (*lokāyata*) who claim that derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is impermanent fall into the worldly view. Both translations use the term "Loka" (盧迦).
The view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is one of the four types of Vedic views; it refers to those who hold to the view of annihilation.

This is because they falsely perceive that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet this is merely a verbal assertion and entirely devoid of actual meaning, for they do not perceive the arising of any intrinsic characteristics.

Regarding impermanence as transformation (*pariṇāma-anityatā*): this refers to the manifestation of a different state of form (*rūpa*), not of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like gold being fashioned into an ornament;

it manifests through transformation, yet the nature of the gold is not destroyed—only the configuration of the ornament is destroyed. The same applies to the transformation of other natures and so forth.
It is also like this.
The commentary states: This passage cites the refutation of the fourth [view], namely that there is impermanence in the interval between the transformation of matter (*rūpa*).

The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon that both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*) are eternal; they merely hold that there is a certain quality of impermanence between these two types of matter which causes the derived matter [to change].
The continuity of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) undergoes transformation and naturally perishes, as in the case of milk turning into curd and so forth.

This statement refers to the manifestation of change in the nature of matter as "impermanence," rather than the impermanence of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves. Thus, it is like gold being fashioned into ornaments.
It manifests through transformation, yet the nature of the gold does not perish; it is merely the locus of the ornamental articles that perishes.
This is the case here, and the transformation of other phenomena is likewise. This shares the same underlying meaning as the two previous positions, though the phrasing differs.
This is the restatement of the position; the following text provides the refutation of that position.
When such various non-Buddhist views of impermanence are burned by the fire of false conceptualization, the primary elements do not burn their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If each of these specific characteristics were to perish, then the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) produced from the four great elements would necessarily be annihilated.
The Record states: This explains the basis for the aforementioned calculation. The Tang translation says:
"Various such non-Buddhists (tīrthika) falsely discriminate and perceive the nature of impermanence. They assert that fire cannot burn the intrinsic characteristics of the great elements;
rather, they merely disperse. If it were able to burn them, then both the primary elements and their derivatives would be utterly annihilated. Thus it is said.

These and other non-Buddhists falsely conceive of a view of permanence amidst impermanence, claiming that when the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are consumed by fire, only their shapes are destroyed while their intrinsic natures remain intact.
They argue that it is like a golden ornament: although its form may be destroyed, the nature of the gold remains undestroyed.

If the intrinsic natures of the four great elements were to be destroyed, then both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative matter (*bhautika*) would all cease to exist. This [view] posits a certain entity that undergoes destruction.
There is that which is indestructible; this is precisely what is called "one portion of Buddha-nature is permanent and one portion is impermanent.
In the Dharma-ending age, those who claim to have seen their nature mostly fall into this view. Generally speaking, the calculations of external paths do not go beyond permanence and impermanence.
Therefore, the subsequent passage refutes this by stating that it is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Mahāmati, in my teaching, arising is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? Because external objects are not determinate (as the Wei translation states:
"I do not say that external realms exist"). I speak only of the subtle mind within the three realms (as the Tang translation states: "The triple world is mind-only"), and I do not speak of seeds.

The various characteristics have arising and ceasing; they are the distinctions resulting from the conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as well as the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

Therefore, false imagination (*vikalpa*) consists of two kinds of things: the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) and the grasped object (*grāhya*). Knowing these two kinds of false imagination, one abandons the two views of external existence and non-existence.

(The Tang translation says: "Because the various characteristics are not spoken of; because the natures and locations of the great elements, in their various distinctions, neither arise nor cease; because there is no creator or created; and because the two natures of the grasper and the grasped all arise from discrimination. Just as...

Because one truly knows the nature of the two-fold grasping, one awakens to the fact that all things are the manifestation of one's own mind. What is called "deluded thought" (*vikalpa*) arises from mental activity; it does not arise without such activity.

Apart from the nature of the mind, there is no deluded thought characterized by having or lacking intrinsic nature. All phenomena—mundane, supramundane, and those superior to the supramundane—are neither eternal nor non-eternal.
The commentary states: This section clarifies the meaning of how *nirvāṇa* is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
It means that the reason those non-Buddhists fall into the views of annihilationism and eternalism is that they falsely perceive external objects as being substantially real;

failing to understand that these are merely manifestations of the mind alone, they speak of various phenomena having arising and ceasing, and falsely claim that the four great elements can create both the primary and the derived.

Therefore, through false views, there is the grasping of a grasper and a grasped; thus, one falls into the two views of existence and non-existence, and falsely gives rise to the notions of annihilation and permanence.
Both self and dharmas are entirely free from all such views, for they are thoroughly understood to be merely manifestations of one's own mind. As for those who harbor such deluded imaginings:
It arises solely from the activity of thought; it is not that there is no arising because there is no activity.

This "non-arising" of mine is free from the dualistic views of existence and non-existence regarding mind, intellect, and consciousness, and it thoroughly penetrates all the supreme dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
It is solely one's own mind; there is no other dharma whatsoever. Therefore, my teaching is neither annihilated nor eternal.

Failing to realize that what appears is the manifestation of one's own mind, one falls into the continuity of the evil views of the two extremes. All non-Buddhists fail to realize that these are their own deluded imaginings.
These ordinary worldlings lack any fundamental basis regarding the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane.
"Arising from the discourse on false discrimination; it is not realized by the ignorant.

The commentary states: "This verse reveals the error of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Because they do not understand that [all things] are mind-only, they fall into a continuous succession of evil views regarding the two extremes, failing to realize that everything arises from the false discrimination of one's own mind. This refers to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists."
Because they lack fundamental wisdom, they will also claim that the worldly, world-transcending,
and world-transcending-supreme teachings spoken by the Tathāgata likewise arise from the conceptual proliferation of verbal expression.
Not knowing that the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is beyond the sphere of mind, intellect, consciousness, and verbal expression, they thus give rise to inverted and deluded views.
"It is not so. However, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is not something that can be known by those ordinary and foolish people.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Separated from the created, and differing in shape and location; nature and form are impermanent—these are the deluded imaginings of the non-Buddhists.
The commentary states: This verse summarizes the seven kinds of impermanence postulated by the non-Buddhists, all of which are merely products of deluded conceptualization and discrimination.
These four are cited here; they may be understood according to the text.
The various natures are indestructible, abiding as the great self-nature. The non-Buddhists harbor notions of impermanence, submerged in various views.

The commentary states: This verse concerns the impermanence of transformation. It means that while the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is eternally abiding and devoid of movement or change, non-Buddhists fail to understand this and falsely conceive of impermanence; they are simply submerged in various erroneous views.

For those various non-Buddhists, there is neither arising nor ceasing; the nature of the Great Self is eternally constant. What, then, is meant by the perception of impermanence? All things are merely the measure of mind;
the two kinds of mind flow forth as the grasper and the grasped. There is no self, nor anything belonging to a self.

The commentary states: This verse refutes the heterodox views that "non-arising" is impermanent, that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are permanent, and that derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is impermanent.
It refers to the false calculations of non-Buddhists who claim that "non-arising" is impermanent and enters into all phenomena.

Since it is said to be "non-arising," and what does not arise cannot perish, how can it then be called "impermanent"? Furthermore, since it is said that the four great elements are... [the text continues].
[If it is] eternal, why do you further say that what is created is impermanent? Therefore, one knows that all dharmas are merely the direct manifestation (*pratyakṣa*) of the single mind.
Thus, the two views of existence and non-existence, the dual grasping of subject and object, and "self" and "what belongs to self" have never existed from the beginning;
these are all merely the false conceptualizations of one's own mind. The Chinese translation says: "Those various heterodox groups..."
All are said to be neither born nor extinguished; the nature of the great elements is itself eternal. What dharma, then, could be impermanent?
Brahmā is the root of the tree, and its branches extend everywhere. Thus have I taught: this is solely the measure of that mind.
The commentary states: This verse addresses the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). It is not merely the seven types of impermanence;
rather, all views of permanence—such as calculating that Brahmā is eternal, the lord of sentient beings, and capable of producing all things—are included among these false views.
Therefore, I say that these too are merely the measure of one’s own mind. Above, the impermanence conceived by the non-Buddhists was analyzed to reveal the true permanence of *nirvāṇa*.
This section analyzes only impermanence; the passage revealing true permanence has been misplaced after the chapter on *samādhi*.
Below, the *samādhis* of the three vehicles are analyzed to reveal the true bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skilled in the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of cessation-samādhi, nor fall into [the state of] one [who is not]."
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and followers of external paths are deluded;
thus it is recorded: "The preceding section clarified the heterodox views of external paths regarding impermanence, intending to reveal the ultimate, true permanence of nirvāṇa.
Before that text was concluded, this [section] distinguishes the bliss of the samādhi-gates attained by the three vehicles in order to reveal the true bliss of nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, this is to prevent error and delusion. Therefore, following this, I shall inquire into the sequential continuity of the states of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.

The intention is that if one can thoroughly understand the characteristics of these states of cessation, one will not mistakenly abandon the gate of the bliss of cessation within the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition.
"Abandon" here means "to lose. That is to say, if one knows that all three vehicles...

If it were not ultimate, one would falsely grasp at partiality and deviation, taking a little to be sufficient and thereby losing the gateway to the true meditative bliss of the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction.
Therefore, below, the World-Honored One enumerates in detail how the eight stages of the bodhisattva are not the ultimate reality.
The analogy of the dream-river is intended to urge you forward so that you do not mistakenly fall.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well, and I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain this for me. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as the Śrāvakas..."
Hearing that the Pratyekabuddhas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he recorded:
"This statement means that Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage and Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas alike sever the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of the three realms;

because they suffer from mental toil and anxiety, they extinguish the mind and enter meditative absorption. Nevertheless, they still possess the coming and going [of consciousness], and have not yet..."
It is able to enter the ears moment by moment because the marks of defilement and purity have not yet been forgotten.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the seventh stage enters meditative absorption (samāpatti) moment by moment; he enters the absorption that is free from all marks of intrinsic nature and self-nature.

This is not the case for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas fall into the perception of activity, and their grasping at the marks of the grasper and the grasped has not yet ceased.
"Right reception" (samāpatti). Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no "recollection" (smṛti) regarding right reception.

The commentary states: This means that the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage enters right reception in every thought-moment, which differs from the vehicles of the two [vehicles] who possess longing and aversion.
The reason why one enters it in every thought-moment at the seventh stage is that one does not perceive any birth-and-death to be loathed. It is not...
Because they perceive that there is a nirvana to be sought, it is said that [this state] is "the correct realization (samāpatti) that is free from all characteristics of intrinsic nature.

This is not something the two vehicles can reach. The reason the two vehicles do not reach the seventh stage is that, while they loathe the conditioned (saṃskṛta), they aspire to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);
yet they have not abandoned the objective realms of the grasper and the grasped. Therefore, the seventh stage is not within the domain of the two vehicles.

This refers to mindfulness of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Thus, the Wei translation states: "In the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in every thought-moment.
This is because all Bodhisattvas are able to remain far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation in every thought-moment, because they enter it by taking conditioned activities as their object."
Concentration falls within the sphere of the grasped and the grasper; therefore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the samādhi of momentary cessation within the seventh stage.
One attains the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena, which is not [yet] a portion [of the ultimate]; one attains various characteristics and natures;

and one awakens to the correct reception (*samāpatti*) of the wholesome and unwholesome characteristics and natures of all phenomena. For this reason, in the seventh stage, there is no correct reception of wholesome thought.

The commentary states: This clarifies why the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) cannot equal the seventh stage. Now, as for why the two vehicles cannot equal the seventh stage, the Wei translation says:

"Because they perceive the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena—existent phenomena and non-existent phenomena, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, as well as common and distinct characteristics—and thereby enter the samādhi of cessation; for this reason, the śrāvakas and..."
He awakens, yet he is unable to enter the moment-to-moment extinction samādhi within the seventh stage because he lacks the wisdom of skillful means.
In this context, "absence of wholesome thoughts" refers to the absence of those wholesome or unwholesome thoughts associated with the two vehicles.

"Mahāmati, for Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, as well as for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the conceptual characteristics of mind (citta), intellect (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna) are extinguished.

The commentary states: 'This refers to the mode of practice of the eighth stage. That is to say, Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage abide in the path of effortlessness (anābhoga-mārga) and are constantly in samādhi, without the characteristics of entering or emerging;
thus they are identical to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in their nirvāṇa, having extinguished the mind of conceptual construction."

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). However, while these names are the same, their meanings differ. Because the practitioners of the Two Vehicles extinguish the first six consciousnesses, their weary deliberations are forever severed, and they sink into a state of quiescent extinction;
thus, they lack even a single thought of saving sentient beings. As for the noble ones of the Eighth Ground, they relinquish the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
When the mind of arising and ceasing is extinguished, one sinks into quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) and fails to give rise to the vow to deliver sentient beings.

Although this quiescence is nominally the same [as that of the Bodhisattva], in reality there is a great difference. Why? Because those of the Two Vehicles take this very state to be *nirvāṇa* and do not proceed further;
whereas at the eighth stage, the Bodhisattva is sustained by the awakening of samādhi and receives the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.
Therefore, they do not grasp at the mark of nirvāṇa; this is the point of distinction. This will be clarified in the text below.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate the measure of the mind, thought, and consciousness within the triple world.

Having abandoned "I" and "mine," they practice by means of their own conceptualization. They fall into two kinds of delusions regarding external natures and various marks, which are actually subsumed within one's own mind.
It is subsumed under ignorance. One does not realize that one has been perfumed by the habitual tendencies of false and deceptive faults from beginningless time.
The commentary states: "This means that if one does not practice well prior to the seventh stage, one will fall into the heterodox views of external paths."
This refers to the contemplative practices cultivated from the first stage through the seventh stage.

Although these practices are able to observe that all within the three realms are nothing but mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and are originally intended to abandon the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," if one lacks the wisdom derived from extensive learning and relies instead on the views of one's own deluded imaginings—failing to practice skillfully—one will fall into the various false paths of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Such fools are caught in the extremes of existence and non-existence.
These two kinds of false views arise within one's own mind as the grasping of subject and object, which are taken to be real.
That is to say, the mind itself takes hold of the mind; what is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon.

This is simply a state of total ignorance, resulting from being permeated and transformed by the habitual tendencies of falsehood and the faults of beginningless time, of which one remains unaware. Even when Bodhisattvas reach this stage, they may still mistakenly fall [into these views].

Wrong views must certainly be guarded against with great care. The fifty grades of demonic obstacles (*māra*) described in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* all arise based on the investigation and inquiry into the observing mind;
there are even cases where one nearly reaches the stage of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) only to fall back into extinction. How much more so for those at the seventh stage?
Comparing this with that [situation], it corresponds precisely to the moment when the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is about to be broken but has not yet been broken.
Mahāmati, regarding the nirvāṇa of the eighth-stage Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas: the Bodhisattva is sustained by the realization of samādhi.
For this reason, they do not enter parinirvāṇa out of attachment to the bliss of the gateways of samādhi. If they were not so sustained, the stage of the Tathāgata would not be fulfilled;
because they would abandon all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings, the lineage of the Buddhas would consequently be severed. Thus say the Buddhas.
The World-Honored One reveals the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata;
yet the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, being led by the attachment to the bliss obtained through their gates of samādhi, form the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa.

The commentary states: This means that if one in the eighth stage does not receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, one will fall into the vehicle of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
It refers to what was stated above: the samādhis attained in the eighth stage and the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles, though their names are identical, [are distinct].

The realization attained is, however, different. Because they receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) of all Buddhas, they do not enter *nirvāṇa* within the gates of samādhi.

If they were not sustained by this empowerment, they would fail to transform and deliver all sentient beings, would be unable to fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata, and would likewise sever the lineage (*gotra*) of the Tathāgatas. For this reason, the Buddhas have taught the Tathāgata-...
Because of their inconceivable and great merits, they are made to ultimately not enter nirvana.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, however, become attached to the bliss of samādhi; for this reason, they conceive the notion of nirvana within that state.

Mahāmati, I have established the seven stages as follows: [the stage where one] skillfully cultivates the characteristics of mind, thought, and consciousness; skillfully cultivates the grasping of "I" and "mine"; [the stage of] the non-self of persons and phenomena;
[the stage of] birth and cessation, and specific and general characteristics; and [the stage of] the four analytical knowledges, the power of certainty, and the gates of samādhi.

The sequence of the stages (*bhūmi*) is established so that, by entering the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva may not fail to perceive their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), nor become unskilled in the seven stages and fall into the deviant paths of externalists. Therefore, the sequence of the stages is set forth.
The Record states: These words concern the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), which is the pivotal point for severing [afflictions] and realizing [the truth]. Therefore, one must apply effort (*prayoga*);
without such effort, one falls into the deviant paths of externalists (*tīrthika*). For this reason, the characteristics of the various stages are explained.

That is to say, from the first stage up to the seventh, following the path of true insight (*darśana-mārga*), one perceives skillful means (*upāya*) and is well able to observe the mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Far removed from the grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self," one attains the non-selfhood of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*).

Transcending the characteristics of arising and ceasing, as well as specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and being skillfully proficient in the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one then attains the gate of the definitive samādhi.

Upon reaching this stage of purely signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), one is able to gradually ascend through the eighth stage up to the tenth stage and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), entering the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and ultimately the ocean of fruition.
All of these are established based upon this seventh stage; this is truly the great crux of severance and realization. This is what is called the "perilous path.
Were it not for the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, one would mostly fall into the deviant paths of externalists.

The Buddha said: "I fear that these bodhisattvas may not skillfully understand specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and may not know the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*).
They might fall into the various evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Therefore, I shall explain for them the characteristics of the practices of the stages, so that they may know what should be abandoned and what should be traversed, and thus avoid falling back. This is the application of gradual progression within the absence of gradual progression."
Next, this is established out of necessity; it is not that there is anything truly taught.
Mahāmati, in reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is manifested by one's own mind.

That which is called the sequential succession of the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the various activities within the triple world, are not perceived by the ignorant. What is meant by "not perceived by the ignorant" is as follows:
I and all the Buddhas have taught the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) and have taught the various activities (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms (*tridhātu*).

It is recorded that these words mean: "The various activities of the three realms are fundamentally without arising or ceasing; the sequential arrangement of the stages is fundamentally without establishment.
There is only this single mind, and no other phenomena exist apart from it. It is merely because foolish people do not understand that it is 'mind-only' (*cittamātra*) that I [have spoken thus]."
Furthermore, the Buddhas establish such teachings as an antidote; in reality, there is nothing that can be said.
Ignorant people, lacking understanding, claim that I have indeed spoken something.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those in the eighth stage of the bodhisattvas are intoxicated by the intoxication of the bliss of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samādhi).

They are unskilled in the manifestation of their own minds as mere appearances (svacittadṛśyamātra), being obstructed by the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of self-characteristics and common characteristics.

They fall into the view of grasping at the non-existence of persons and phenomena (pudgala-dharmanairātmya), conceiving of a false nirvana through their discursive thoughts (vikalpa); this is not the awakening of the wisdom of true quiescence.
The commentary states: This refers to the fact that although the names "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha" are the same within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), what they realize is different.

Because those of the two vehicles become intoxicated by and attached to the samādhi of entry into cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they do not understand that self-characteristics and common characteristics are manifestations of their own minds.
Being obscured by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they fall into the category of the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*).
Because they perceive [phenomena], they give rise to the conceptualization of nirvana; this is not like the awakening to true, quiescent wisdom at the eighth stage.

When it is said that those of the Two Vehicles take the eighth stage to be nirvana, these are likely former practitioners of the great bodhisattva path who have regressed from their original vows, rather than those of fixed nature who are destined for quiescence. This is because they are fixed...
Their nature tends toward quiescence; they have attained the realization of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but not the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

They are still unable to know even the dharmas of the first stage (*bhūmi*), let alone those of the eighth. Therefore, this question is placed at the end of this chapter in the Wei translation, whereas it is absent from both the Song and Tang translations.

Mahāmati, as for the Bodhisattvas: though they perceive the bliss of the gate of the samādhi of cessation, they do not give rise to the conceptualization of nirvāṇa because they have accomplished great compassion through their original vows of pity and mercy, and because they know how to distinguish the ten inexhaustible phrases.

Since such conceptualization of nirvāṇa does not arise in them, they are free from the conceptualization of grasped and grasper; they realize that all is merely the manifestation of their own mind. (The Tang translation states: "Because by entering nirvāṇa, the fruit [of rebirth] is no longer produced. This is the first.

All dharmas are devoid of the arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). One does not fall into the mind, thought, or consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), nor into the false conceptualization that clings to the marks of external natures and self-natures.
It is not produced from the causes of non-Buddha-dharmas; rather, it arises in accordance with wisdom.

One attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, like a person who, while dreaming, uses skillful means to cross water, wakes up before having crossed, and upon waking reflects: "Was this real or was it false? It was not real."

It is not false. It is the manifestation of dreams within the mind, intellect, and consciousness, arising from various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), various forms and locations, and perceptions based on beginningless seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, which fall into the notions of existence and non-existence.

The commentary states: "This refers to the fact that although one enters the samādhi of cessation at the eighth stage, one does not realize [final] nirvāṇa, because one does not abandon the great vow to deliver sentient beings.
This bodhisattva has already entered nirvāṇa, yet does not give rise to the thought of nirvāṇa."

Therefore, it is said that in *nirvāṇa*, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise. Because one has thoroughly realized that there is only mind (*cittamātra*) and no external objects, one is free from the grasping of subject and object.
One does not give rise to discrimination regarding any phenomena, for one has deeply attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Consequently, one does not fall into the attachments to the nature and characteristics of the mind, intellect, consciousness, or external phenomena, because one has attained true knowledge.
Because of the power of vision, that which is not the true cause of the Buddha-dharma does not arise; it arises only in accordance with wisdom.

It is in this way that one attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening. Having long been submerged in the wearisome anxieties of birth and death, one now suddenly attains quiescent extinction;
its bliss is beyond comparison. Therefore, it is extremely difficult to emerge from this samādhi. When the Bodhisattva’s meritorious practice reaches—
Within this state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), few do not become intoxicated; most fall into the realm of quiescence of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Therefore, at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively exhort him with one voice, bestowing upon him the gateway to the arising of wisdom so as not to allow him to become attached to the bliss of this samādhi and fall into the stage of the two vehicles. For this reason, they grant him skillful means (*upāya*) to induce him to emerge from it.
Therefore, within this samādhi-dream, the bodhisattva exerts all his strength to wish to emerge. It is like dreaming of crossing a great river;
before having crossed, he awakens and reflects upon whether it was real or illusory. He further contemplates that such a phenomenon is neither real nor illusory;
it is seen solely due to the causes of beginningless false habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
The various colors, forms, and appearances are inverted; they do not depart from existence and non-existence.

They manifest merely within the dreams of the mind, thought, and consciousness through false imagination (*vikalpa*), yet in reality, they have never existed from the beginning. The old commentary states: "When one awakens from the dream-object, there is no water; thus the boat and raft are not 'correct.

When one sees water while dreaming, the boat and raft are not 'false. This is used as an analogy for the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where, having awakened, one realizes that birth and death were originally non-existent."

Therefore, the merits of the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) are neither correct nor false. Because one has not yet awakened on the seventh stage, the merits of the factors of the path are not erroneous;
rather, within the midst of deluded effort that has not yet reached transcendence, there is cultivation and realization, which is like constructing boats and rafts to cross a river in a dream.

Mahāmati, in this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reaches the eighth bodhisattva stage, they perceive the arising of conceptual construction (vikalpa)— the Wei translation says "they perceive the discriminating mind.
Having progressed from the first stage up to the seventh stage, and having perceived all dharmas as being like illusions through skillful means,

and having transcended the mental activity of conceptual construction regarding the grasped and the grasper, they employ the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma to cause those who have not yet attained it to attain it.

Mahāmati, this is the non-destructive skillful means of the bodhisattvas' nirvāṇa (the Wei translation says: "Nirvāṇa does not mean the extinction of all dharmas"; the Tang translation says: "The nirvāṇa attained is not a state of destruction").

It is the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by being free from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*). Mahāmati, in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no sequence or continuity;
it is taught as the quiescence of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the non-existence of things.
The commentary states: "This establishes the characteristics of the nirvāṇa-practice of the eighth stage. Regarding 'seeing the arising of deluded thoughts,' the Treatise says:
'When one realizes that the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic. Because it is far removed from subtle thought, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind.'"

The mind is eternally abiding; this is called ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). This Bodhisattva, by means of the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), manifests all dignified conducts (*īryāpatha*) without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
He diligently cultivates the Buddha-dharma and extensively performs the work of saving sentient beings.
That is to say, he brings all sentient beings to liberation without perceiving even a single sentient being who has been liberated. This is what is meant by "transcending the mind."
The consciousness attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Bodhisattva;

it is not like the Nirvāṇa of the Two Vehicles, which is a nirvāṇa consisting of the cessation and destruction of all apprehended phenomena. Nevertheless, although it is explained in this way, it is merely a provisional designation (*upāya-prajñapti*).
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), such a thing does not exist from the very beginning. Therefore, the Tang translation says: "The Ultimate Truth."
In the middle, there is no sequence, nor is there any continuity. It is far removed from all conceptualization regarding objective spheres;

this is what is called the dharma of quiescence (*śānti*). Because Mahāmati asked about the sequence and continuity of the cessation of meditative absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*), [the Buddha] concluded by showing that in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) there is neither sequence nor continuity, and taught that it is the quiescence of non-existent false discrimination (*parikalpita*).

Regarding the Dharma: In the Wei translation, at this point Mahāmati poses a question, which may be summarized as follows: "World-Honored One, you have now stated that the two vehicles attain the bliss of the gate of cessation in the eighth stage;
yet you have also stated that the two vehicles only realize the emptiness of persons and do not realize the emptiness of dharmas.
If this is so, then the two vehicles cannot even realize the dharmas of the first stage, let alone the bliss of the gate of cessation in the eighth stage."

The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of śrāvakas. Those now described as entering the bliss of the gate of cessation in the eighth stage are those who were originally practitioners of the bodhisattva path who fell into the level of a śrāvaka;
they have returned to cultivate the bodhisattva path according to their original resolve and thus likewise enter the bliss of the gate of cessation in the eighth stage.
They are not śrāvakas of cessation characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*), for the latter are incapable [of this]."

They enter the bodhisattva conduct; however, because they have not yet realized that the three realms are mind-only and have not yet been able to cultivate the various practices and dharmas of a bodhisattva, these śrāvakas who are fixed in their determination for nirvāṇa cannot realize the bliss of the gate of tranquility practiced by bodhisattvas.
As for the "three types," the first are those who conceal [their intent] within while manifesting it outwardly; the second are those who regress from the bodhisattva conduct.

Regarding those of the three fixed natures who possess the overweening pride of being destined for nirvana: while it was previously stated that those of the two vehicles attain Buddhahood, this present statement that they are "definitively unable" is intended to suppress and exalt, and to stimulate and encourage.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The measure of mind is non-existent; this is the stage of abiding and the Buddha-ground. The Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—all teach this."
The commentary states: This verse summarizes that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is fundamentally no sequential manifestation of the various stages (*bhūmi*) or the Buddha-stage.
This is the discourse on the final realization of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. "Abiding" (*vihāra*) is also a stage (*bhūmi*).
The reason they are non-existent is that [all things] are but mind-only (*cittamātra*). Therefore, the Tang translation says: "All abidings and the Buddha-stages are but mind, devoid of images."
This is what has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present:
the seventh stage is the Mind-Measure (cittamātra), the eighth is the Non-Existent (nirābhāsa); the two stages [the first and second] are called Abidings, and the Buddha-stage is the most supreme.
(The Tang translation says: "These two stages are called 'abiding'; the rest is what I have attained. "Self-realized wisdom and purity—this is my stage. The commentary states:
These verses refer to the seventh and eighth stages, which still belong to the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).
As for the purity of the noble self-realized wisdom and *nirvāṇa*, these belong to the ultimate fruit-ground realized by the Buddha. Nevertheless, although the seventh stage is indeed...

One practices because the measure of mind (*cittamātra*) has not yet been extinguished. Although the measure of mind is extinguished in the eighth stage, it is not yet ultimate and thus is not called the most excellent.
Only self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) is truly named the most excellent state.
The sovereign and most excellent place, pure and wondrously adorned, shines like a great blazing fire; its radiance reaches everywhere, and its fierce flames do not harm the eyes.

It manifests throughout the three realms of existence (triloka). (The Tang translation reads: "The supreme abode of Maheśvara, adorned as the pinnacle of form (Akaniṣṭha), is like a mass of great fire, emitting fierce and blazing flames.
It manifests within the three realms of existence, delightful and cool. Having manifested within the three realms of existence, some manifest beforehand, and therein they expound...
Regarding the teaching on the vehicles (*yāna*), all are the stage of the Tathāgata.

The commentary states: "These words establish the various vehicles and stages; they are all spoken by the two Buddhas of Reward (*nirmāṇa*) and Transformation (*saṃbhoga*), not by the Dharma-Buddha (*dharma-buddha*).

This refers to those who have attained the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*); [they reside] in the Palace of Jewel Flowers (*ratnapuṣpa-kūṭāgāra*) in the Heaven of the Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*)."
The Lord attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and manifests a vast and majestic body that radiates light, transforming throughout the three realms of existence;

this is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* Buddha. The treatise states: When the merits of this Bodhisattva have reached fulfillment, he manifests the highest and most magnificent body in the Akaniṣṭha heaven through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*), [thereby overcoming] ignorance...

To exhaust [all things] instantaneously is called the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Spontaneously, there exists inconceivable activity capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "transforming those currently in the three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*), the Chinese translation says: "Or there are those who manifest transformations."

There may be those who were transformed [in the past]; these are the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas. Only these *vipākakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas expound the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the various stages (*bhūmi*).

Although they teach the three vehicles, in reality, it is for the sake of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, it is said: "In that regard, the teaching of the various vehicles is entirely the stage of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, although there are various stages, in truth there is no characteristic of sequential progression. (Fervent)
However, that which does not impair the eyes refers to the fact that when a venomous dragon emits light, it immediately damages the human eye;
the Tathāgata’s radiance, by contrast, does not damage the human eye, being what is called pleasing and refreshing.
The tenth ground is the first; the first is the eighth. The ninth is the seventh; the seventh is likewise the eighth. The second is the third;
the fourth is the fifth. The third is the sixth. When there is nothing at all, what sequence can there be?
The commentary states: "In this verse, regarding the dharma of quiescence within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no sequential or continuous exposition.
This is intended to reveal that this sutra is spoken solely by the Dharma-Buddha as the dharma of quiescence; therefore, it lacks sequence.
This is what is meant by 'not traversing the path' and 'not falling into stages'—it is the supreme path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Nevertheless, within it..."

The frequent references to "stages" (bhūmi) are intended to show that the true cultivation of samādhi on the ground uses seals to shatter the biased and heterodox views of external paths and the two vehicles, ensuring they do not fall into wrong pride or overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
In reality, the underlying intent does not reside in the stages themselves; the wise understand this. *Above, the three vehicles' samādhis have been distinguished.*
The section on "Distinguishing Characteristics" to reveal the virtue of the true bliss of *nirvāṇa* and to prevent erroneous views has concluded.
△ The following text correctly demonstrates the virtue of the true permanence of *nirvāṇa*. This passage should properly belong after the preceding chapter on the seven types of impermanence.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, permanent or impermanent? [The Buddha] replied:
"This is because, having previously refuted the seven kinds of impermanence, the World-Honored One stated: 'In my teaching, arising does not [occur as impermanence].'"
