"Permanent and yet not impermanent. Therefore, Mahāmati took this opportunity to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:

"Is [the Tathāgata] ultimately permanent or impermanent? This was intended to reveal that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is free from both annihilation and permanence, and is thus the ultimate true permanence.
This passage is precisely the text that reveals the true permanence of Nirvāṇa; it should be placed within the section on the seven kinds of non-existence.
This passage appears at the end of the *Śāṅga* (Chapter on Permanence), but its misplaced insertion here is an error in the transmission and translation.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither permanent nor impermanent, for both [positions] entail faults.
If he were permanent, there would be the fault of being a creator; as for permanence, all non-Buddhists claim that the Creator is uncreated."
Therefore, the Tathāgata is both eternal and non-eternal; he is not an eternality produced by action, for that would entail faults.
It is recorded: "This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is neither eternal nor impermanent; it is for this reason that it is called true eternity."
Because both permanence and impermanence entail faults. Why is this? If one says that the Tathāgata is permanent, then one falls into the fault of attributing to him the status of a creator.
This is because all non-Buddhists assert that atoms, the principle of *pradhāna*, and so forth, are creators and are permanent;
yet the Tathāgata performs no action—how could he be the same as their "permanent" [entities]? Therefore, it is said:
Regarding the Tathāgata’s permanence that is not [ordinary] permanence: it is certainly not the permanence of a creator, for such a permanence of a creator entails logical fallacies.

If the Tathāgata were impermanent, there would be the fallacy of being something produced. Since the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas) lack intrinsic nature, when the aggregates perish, [the Tathāgata likewise ceases].
It should be severed, yet the Tathāgata does not sever it.

It is recorded [in the scriptures] that this statement means the Tathāgata is not impermanent. If one were to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, then one falls into the error of attributing something produced to him.
If one speaks of what is produced, then he would be identical to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Now, the five aggregates are merely [conventional] characteristics.

As for that which is characterized, these characteristics ultimately do not exist. If the Tathāgata were identical to the five aggregates (*skandhas*), then when the aggregates perish, the Tathāgata would likewise be annihilated.
However, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and uninterrupted;
how could it be identical to the conditioned aggregates? Since they are not identical, he is not impermanent.
"Mahāmati, all that is produced is impermanent, such as jars, garments, and so forth; thus, everything would fall into the error of impermanence.
Furthermore, the skillful means of the equipment for omniscience would be rendered meaningless because they are produced.
Moreover, all that is produced would necessarily be the Tathāgata, since there would be no cause for distinction. Therefore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent."
The commentary states: This further clarifies that all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are impermanent, summarizing the meaning of being free from faults.
That is to say, all conditioned things—such as jars, garments, and the like—are impermanent. If the Tathāgata were likewise a conditioned thing, he would incur the fault of impermanence.
If the Tathāgata were impermanent, then the primary causes cultivated by those possessing all-knowledge, such as merit...
The adornment of wisdom, the myriad practices of the six perfections, and all the various skillful means—all these are empty and of no benefit, for they share the same nature as conditioned things:
impermanence. How much more so the Tathāgata, whose merit flows through ten thousand generations yet remains eternally present, and whose Way penetrates hundreds of kalpas and becomes ever more firm;
how could he be impermanent? If the Tathāgata were indeed the same as conditioned things, then all things in the world would likewise [be impermanent].
All that is created would necessarily be the Tathāgata, because there is no other cause. Therefore, the Tathāgata is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not eternal in the manner that space is eternal. If he were eternal like space, then the noble wisdom of self-realization—
There is the fault that all things would be rendered purposeless.
The commentary states: This statement that the Tathāgata is eternal does not mean he is eternal in the same way as empty space is.

This is because empty space is inert and devoid of cognition, whereas the Tathāgata possesses true wisdom and spiritual discernment. If one were to say that he is eternal in the same manner as empty space, then...

If one were to claim that the nature of the noble self-realized wisdom, which is inherently endowed with merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is entirely empty and useless, one would fall into the error of nihilism and ignorance. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a permanence like empty space.

Fearing that foolish people, upon hearing the teaching that the Dharmakāya is truly eternal, might consequently give rise to a view of vacuous emptiness, the World-Honored One preemptively refuted such [notions].
In this regard, Mahāmati, it is like space: it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is free from the faults of permanence and impermanence, as well as oneness, difference, both, and neither;
because it cannot be described, the Tathāgata is not permanent.

The commentary states: "Regarding the previous statement that [the Tathāgata] is 'not like empty space,' this means that the Tathāgata possesses the merit of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and thus cannot be compared to empty space, which is insentient and devoid of cognition.
This statement that he is 'like empty space' means that the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of empty space is serene and unchanging;
it does not fall within the categories of existence or non-existence, unity or difference, conjunction or disjunction, nor any other such numerical or quantitative distinctions."
Because of these faults, it cannot be said that the Tathāgata is either eternal or non-eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an unarisen eternity, he would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse;
because he would be an unarisen eternity, there would be no purpose for skillful means (*upāya*). Due to the fault of being an unarisen eternity, the Tathāgata is not eternal.
The commentary states: These words clarify that the Tathāgata does not take non-arising as his permanence.

Since it was previously stated that "non-arising" is a synonym for the Tathāgata, there is a fear that one might falsely cling to the notion that ultimate non-arising constitutes the permanence of the Tathāgata; therefore, this [passage] refutes such a view.

If the Tathāgata were eternal by virtue of being unarisen, then the Tathāgata would be identical to the horns of a rabbit or a horse, since they are ultimately unarisen; thus, the Tathāgata would fall into the error of non-existence.
If the Tathāgata were non-existent, then all the myriad practices and skillful means cultivated by the bodhisattvas would have nothing to be realized, and would all be empty and useless. And...
In the fruit of the Tathāgata, there is likewise an absolute absence of the utility of vast beneficial things.

Because this [utility] is absolutely absent, if one were to claim that the Tathāgata is eternal by virtue of being unarisen, one would fall into this great error. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not eternal through non-arising.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another reason for knowing that the Tathāgata is eternal. Why is this? It is because the wisdom attained without interruption is eternal;
therefore, the Tathāgata is eternal. Mahāmati, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the Dharma remains fixed and certain.
Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddha-Tathāgatas abide in this uninterrupted state; it does not abide in empty space, nor is it something for the ignorant.
Regarding what the Noble Ones perceive and know, the Record states: "This refers to the Tathāgata’s truly existent, true, and eternal Dharma, which is not something known by foolish ordinary beings.
It is said that the eternal Dharma of the Tathāgata is the principle of true eternity realized by the uninterrupted noble wisdom."
All Buddhas and Tathāgatas share the same dharma-nature, abide in the same dharma, and occupy the same dharma-position.
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, this dharma remains eternally constant, unchanging, and immutable.

This dharma exists even within the uninterrupted nature (anantara-dharmatā) wherein all followers of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists abide; it is not a void nothingness. Yet, it cannot be known by the foolish and ignorant.

Mahāmati, the wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is perfumed by *prajñā*; it is not perfumed by the mind, the intellect, the consciousness, nor by those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
Mahāmati, all that exists within the three realms of being is produced from unreal conceptualization;
the Tathāgata is not born from unreal, false conceptualization. Mahāmati, it is because of duality that there is permanence and impermanence; it is not [due to such duality].
Non-duality. Non-duality is quiescence, because all phenomena lack the characteristic of dualistic arising.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Mahāmati, as long as verbal conceptualization arises, there will be the faults of eternity and non-eternity.
For one whose conceptualizing awareness has ceased, these are transcended; the foolish, however, hold views of eternity and non-eternity and do not attain quiescence.
The wise are forever free from permanence and impermanence, and are not perfumed by permanence or impermanence.
The commentary states: This explains the reason for the Tathāgata’s true permanence. That is to say, it clarifies why the Tathāgata is truly permanent.

As for why sentient beings are impermanent: it is because that which the Tathāgata has attained—holy wisdom—is permeated by the true wisdom of *prajñā*, and not permeated by the delusions of mind, intellect, consciousness, the aggregates (*skandhas*), the elements (*dhātus*), or the sense bases (*āyatanas*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is named "Eternal. As for why all sentient beings within the three realms of existence are impermanent, it is because they...
All these are perfumed by unreal conceptualization; therefore, they are called impermanent. Yet the Tathāgata does not arise from such conceptualization.
Furthermore, how could the mental activities of those ordinary, ignorant beings ever know the eternal Dharma of the Tathāgata?
Because they perceive the true and the false as two distinct things, they regard nirvāṇa and saṃsāra as dual, and thus there arises the discourse of permanence and impermanence.
This is not the dharma of non-dual quiescence. If both truth and falsehood are forgotten, then quiescence is non-dual;
thus all dharmas are entirely equal, without duality or distinction, without arising or origination.
Because the Tathāgata has realized this dharma of non-dual quiescence, it cannot be said to be either permanent or impermanent. This is because of quiescence.

Within the non-dual dharma, the paths of speech and thought are cut off. Even the mere arising of a thought or a mental movement involves verbal expression and the birth of discriminative consciousness, whereby one falls into the errors of permanence and impermanence; how much more so for various kinds of false conceptualizations?
Only when discriminative delusions are extinguished can one suddenly transcend those errors, such as the views of permanence and impermanence held by outsiders and foolish commoners.
Therefore, it is not quiescent. One who is free from these two views is called a person of great wisdom.
Because the wise have forever abandoned the view of non-quiescence, they are not perfumed by the false views of permanence and impermanence;
rather, they are perfumed by true and eternal wisdom. This means that those who lack wisdom are such that their mind-consciousness undergoes even slight fluctuations.
Movement! Birth and extinction have not yet been forgotten, and few remain unaffected by their habitual perfuming.
This is why the Tathāgata’s profound compassion provides such rigorous protection and offers such deep admonition; how can one fail to recognize this?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"For those who lack the necessary means, there arise the faults of permanence and impermanence. If one possesses non-conceptual awareness, one is forever free from permanence and impermanence."

The commentary states: At the beginning of both translations of the verses, there is one verse each. The Tang version says: "Far removed from permanence and impermanence, yet manifesting permanence and impermanence;
One who constantly contemplates the Buddha in this way will not give rise to wrong views. If one were to speak of permanence or impermanence, all that is accumulated would be of no benefit.
To eliminate discriminative cognition, he does not speak of permanence or impermanence. This refers to "all requisites."
These are precisely the various evil views—such as permanence, impermanence, identity, and difference—imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
It is said that all such views are entirely without benefit; they are merely false conceptualizations and discriminations that give rise to the faults of permanence and impermanence.
If the mind of discrimination ceases, all views will suddenly come to rest, and one will then forever be free from the faults of permanence and impermanence.

According to the tenets established by others, there are many diverse and conflicting meanings; yet when one observes that all is but the measure of one's own mind (*cittamātra*), verbal expression becomes unattainable.
The commentary states: "If these words were derived from the self-tenets established by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there would be many diverse and confused views and understandings.
However, if one realizes that all is a manifestation of Mind-only (*cittamātra-pratyakṣa*), then the path of speech and thought is cut off, and even verbal expression does not [apply]."
This can be understood; how much more so when one seeks the true meaning by relying on those heterodox teachings? These words contain various meanings derived from the established thesis.
It is sufficient to know that the argumentative cause (*hetu*) elucidates the meaning of the Tathāgata’s true permanence through the seven kinds of impermanence.
The text and its meaning are inherently interconnected; the observer should understand this. [The preceding section] connects to the discussion of the seven kinds.
The section on impermanence, which elucidates the true constant nature of *nirvāṇa*, is hereby concluded.
△ Below, the self-nature purity of the *tathāgatagarbha* is shown to elucidate the true pure nature of *nirvāṇa*.
Record of the Contemplation on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Seven;
Record of the Contemplation on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Shi Deqing of Haiyin at Jianye during the Ming Dynasty.

This concludes the fourth section, "The Essence of All Buddha-Speech," following the preceding discussion on the seven kinds of impermanence to reveal the true and constant nature of Nirvāṇa. △ Below.
By demonstrating that the *tathāgatagarbha* is pure by nature, he reveals the truly pure virtue of *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that the World-Honored One will further explain for me the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Since they lack a self (*ātman*), who is it that arises and who is it that ceases? Fools rely upon this arising and ceasing."
They do not perceive the exhaustion of suffering, nor do they recognize nirvāṇa.
The commentary states: "This is intended to demonstrate that the self-nature of the tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure, thereby revealing the true and pure virtues of the dharmakāya."
Therefore, this question is raised. As for the statement, "Furthermore, speak to me of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus),
and sense-bases (āyatanas)," it is because at the beginning of the first two fascicles, where the ultimate point of revealing the principle was shown, it was already asked how the Tathāgatagarbha—
pure by nature and possessing the thirty-two marks— enters the bodies of all sentient beings, yet is enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

Defiled by the dust of afflictions—the unreal imaginings of greed, desire, and delusion—they further suspect that the World-Honored One’s teaching on the *tathāgatagarbha* is identical to the "self" (*ātman*) of the non-Buddhists.
The World-Honored One has already resolved this, saying: "What I teach as the *tathāgatagarbha* is not the same as the 'self' of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, at times I speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), suchness (*tathatā*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the Dharma.

Having spoken of the *tathāgatagarbha* through such terms as "nature," "dharma-kāya," "nirvāṇa," "freedom from self-nature," "neither arising nor ceasing," "primordially quiescent," and "naturally in a state of nirvāṇa," it is nevertheless used solely to reveal the ultimate principle and thereby manifest the selflessness of the dharma-kāya,
in order to refute the heterodox views of a personal self (*ātman*). For this reason, the *tathāgatagarbha* is specifically cited.

By means of this inquiry: "Now that the karma of realization and abandonment has been brought to completion, one intends to reveal that the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally pure, yet merely defiled by the adventitious dust of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

Desiring directly to purify those defilements in order to manifest the pure virtues of *nirvāṇa*, [the interlocutor] specifically raises the subject of the defiled meanings—such as the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—to be remedied, thereby intending to address the World-Honored One."
The discourse on the intrinsically pure nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is intended to reveal the true, pure qualities of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said:

"Furthermore, speak to me concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)"; herein, Mahāmati asks from the perspective of defilement, to which the World-Honored One subsequently replies from the perspective of the intrinsically pure nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The Buddha said, "Excellent! Listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is capable of universally producing all realms of existence and births."

It is like an actor who manifests various realms of existence; though devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self," because they do not perceive this, birth occurs through the expedient means of the conjunction of three conditions.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), failing to perceive this, falsely imagine a creator. Perfumed by beginningless, false, and evil habitual tendencies, this is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
It gives rise to the ground where ignorance dwells and coexists with the seven consciousnesses, like the body of ocean waves, arising eternally.
It is uninterrupted; it is free from the fault of impermanence; it is free from the doctrine of a self; its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure.
The commentary states: "These words reveal that the Tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure, thereby manifesting the true and pure virtues of the Dharmakāya."
The *tathāgatagarbha* is the name for the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*) while it is still enmeshed in bondage. Mahāmati raised a doubt, saying:
"If the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are without self (*anātman*), then who is it that is born and who is it that perishes? Who knows the exhaustion of suffering?

Who realizes *nirvāṇa*? The Buddha said: "Although the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*) are without self, there exists the *tathāgatagarbha*, which serves as the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) of sentient beings."
This very nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* can serve as the cause for both mundane and supramundane wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.

It can universally produce the forms, colors, and defiled dharmas of the cycle of birth and death within the six realms, much like an actor manifesting various roles; yet fundamentally, it is devoid of self or what belongs to a self.
Furthermore, it can also accomplish the pure supramundane dharmas. This is because those of the two vehicles do not understand this *tathāgatagarbha*.

The nature (*prakṛti*) is the cause of birth and death; it is said that the three conditions—the sense organs, objects, and consciousness—combine through expedient means to serve as the cause of birth.
Non-Buddhists do not understand this *tathāgatagarbha* nature, and instead falsely conceive of a "self" (*ātman*) as an agent to be the cause of birth.
However, this *garbha* nature has been defiled and transformed by beginningless false and evil habits, thereby losing [its original state].
The name of this *tathāgatagarbha* is merely a designation for the *vijñānagarbha*. Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha taught that the *tathāgatagarbha* is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*.

Based on this *garbha*-consciousness, the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) arises, and the waves of the preceding seven consciousnesses are transformed and produced, arising and ceasing without cessation.
Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* also follows the seven consciousnesses in transmigrating through birth and death, just as when the ocean waves subside.
Because wind gives rise to waves, birth and death continue in succession, remaining uninterrupted for long kalpas.
In reality, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally and eternally abiding; it is free from the two vehicles' view of impermanence. It is fundamentally without self;
it is free from the non-Buddhists' discourse on a divine self (*ātman*). Although it exists within the midst of entanglement, slumber, and defilement, its essential nature is actually stainless.
It is ultimately pure. This is what is meant by being deluded regarding this nature, which results in birth and death;
and awakening to this nature, which results in nirvana. Because this *tathāgatagarbha* nature cannot be destroyed by impermanence, it is true permanence.
Because it cannot be invaded by manifold sufferings, it is true bliss. Because it cannot be constrained by birth and death, it is the true self. Because it cannot be defiled by afflictions—
Therefore, it is truly pure. This is why it constitutes the true fruit-body of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
All other consciousnesses undergo arising and ceasing; the manas and the mental consciousness, among others, consist of seven [consciousnesses] at every moment.

Due to unreal conceptualization (*parikalpita*), they grasp at various objects and diverse forms and locations, reckoning upon names and characteristics, and fail to realize that these are manifestations of their own minds.

Regarding the marks (*nimitta*): not perceiving suffering or pleasure, one does not reach liberation; these are called the various entanglements of marks. Greed arises, and greed is produced. The commentary states:
"This says that the *ālayavijñāna* is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, whereas the seven consciousnesses do arise and cease;

this clarifies that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of the defilement of birth-and-death. Mahāmati asked: "If the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are all without self (*anātman*), who is it that gives rise [to them]?"
"Who is it that ceases? Why, then, does that foolish person not know the exhaustion of suffering and not know liberation? The Buddha’s intended meaning in his reply was this:
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha; they are neither born nor do they perish.

Although they are currently enmeshed in defilements and are called the *ālayavijñāna*, their essence is fundamentally true and likewise neither born nor perishing. That which undergoes birth and death is not the *ālayavijñāna*, but rather...

The preceding seven consciousnesses merely undergo arising and ceasing. Thus, the Tang translation states: "The remaining seven consciousnesses—the manas and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—arise and cease from moment to moment.
However, the reason those seven consciousnesses arise and cease is specifically because they take false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as their cause.
Taking objective spheres as conditions, they arise through conjunction; they then calculate and cling to names and signs as being truly existent.
This is because they do not understand that these objective spheres—the dharmas such as form and so forth—are merely manifestations of one's own mind. Because they do not understand this...
Attachment to names and signs, and to objects that are either favorable or adverse, gives rise to feelings of aversion and affection, which in turn produce sensations of suffering and pleasure.
Bound by these names and signs, sentient beings—having arisen from craving and further generating craving through these causes and conditions—follow the stream of birth and death.
They do not know the exhaustion of suffering and do not seek liberation; it is for this reason that the Tathāgatagarbha undergoes transformation.
The manifestation of the six destinies serves as the defiled cause of birth and death.

Whether as the cause or as the object-condition (*ālambana*), when those various faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*) cease and do not arise in succession, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the fourth dhyāna, and the liberation through the realization of the true reality (*satya*). Therein, the practitioner no longer perceives pleasure or pain through the false imaginings of their own mind.

One should form the conception of liberation. That which is neither separated from nor subject to transformation is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. (The Tang translation states: "If causes and objects of perception, as well as the roots of grasping, are extinguished and do not arise in succession...")

Those who, through their own wisdom, discriminate between painful and pleasant sensations, may attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or attain the four dhyānas, or further skillfully enter the liberations of the [Four] Truths; they then falsely give rise to the notion that they have attained liberation. Yet, in reality, they have not yet abandoned or transformed the name "consciousness-store" (*vijñānālaya*) within the Tathāgatagarbha.

This consciousness-store is the seventh consciousness, which continues to flow and does not cease. (The Tang translation states: "If there were no store-consciousness, the seven consciousnesses would then cease. Why is this so?
Because those consciousnesses arise by taking that as their object of attachment, this is not the sphere of practice for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Failing to realize non-self, they grasp at self-characteristics and common characteristics, whereby the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases arise.
The Record states: This refers to the Tathāgatagarbha serving as the cause for the non-Buddhist practitioners of the "Thoughtless" school and for those of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding "cause" and "object-condition": it was stated above that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the cause and objective phenomena (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*) are the condition.

Here, "conceptual construction" refers to the first seven consciousnesses, which constitute the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; "objective phenomena" refers to the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. Now, it says:

Regarding the sequential non-arising of the various faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*) upon their cessation: this refers to the fact that when the first six consciousnesses do not grasp at objects, the seventh consciousness naturally does not arise.

This is because both those of external paths and those *anāgāmins* of dull faculty are able to extinguish the six consciousnesses like ashes, yet they fail to realize "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*), lack the wisdom born of extensive learning, and rely merely on the false discrimination of their own minds.

In sum, they loathe suffering and seek pleasure; some enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and dwell in the five *anāgāmin* heavens, while others fall into the state of non-perception and enter the four dhyānas as non-Buddhist outsiders.

Even if there are arhats of sharp faculties who skillfully cultivate the Four Noble Truths, transcend the triple world, attain liberation through the true truths, and realize the principle of partial emptiness, in reality they have not yet attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
They then falsely give rise to the notion of extinction and liberation. This is merely the exhaustion of birth and death which they mistake for liberation;
in reality, they have not attained all-encompassing liberation, because they have not yet abandoned or transformed the name "consciousness-store" (*vijñānagarbha*) within the Tathāgatagarbha.
As for the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the seven consciousnesses continuing to flow and not being extinguished, this refers to those external...

The reason why the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) do not attain true cessation is that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has not yet been transformed; therefore, the seven consciousnesses continue to flow and do not cease.
Why is this? Because they depend upon it for their transformation and take it as their object, mutually functioning as the conditions for one another’s arising. Thus, the Tang translation states:
If the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were absent, the seven consciousnesses would cease. Why? Because they arise dependent upon it and their respective objects.

This means that when the storehouse consciousness is transformed, the seven consciousnesses also cease accordingly. Therefore, prior to the seventh stage, one has not yet relinquished the storehouse consciousness;
one merely practices based on one's own deluded conceptualizations, and thus the mind and its objects do not accord with reality.

Because they seek the Dharma outside of the mind, they frequently fall into false views. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this, they fall into the views of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
This is because within their impure *ālayavijñāna* lie the beginningless, false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Therefore, the Tang translation states:
However, this is not a realm known by any non-Buddhists, followers of the two vehicles, or other practitioners.
This is because they only realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), as they grasp at the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.

Furthermore, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is also called the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the *ādāna-vijñāna*; the latter is translated here as the "non-extinguishing consciousness" (*amuta-vijñāna*).
Because it remains within the flow of birth and death without sinking, the verse says: "The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle;
the habitual tendencies and seeds form a torrential stream. I do not reveal it to the foolish and the ignorant, for fear they would conceptually grasp it as a self;
therefore, it is not their domain."
Upon seeing the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the self-nature (*svabhāva*), and the non-self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*) are extinguished.

One proceeds through the stages (*bhūmi*) in successive succession, and cannot be shaken by the views of other outsiders (*tīrthika*). (The Tang translation states: "If one sees the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the non-self of all phenomena, they gradually turn toward extinction according to the sequence of the stages, and are not moved by the evil views of outsiders.
This is called abiding in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*Acalā-bhūmi*), wherein one attains the bliss of the thirteen gates of samādhi.
Sustained by the power of samādhi and upheld by all Buddhas, one contemplates the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas.
By the force of one's own original vows, one does not abide in the bliss of the samādhi-gate nor in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Turning toward the noble path of self-realization, which is not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those who practice the paths of the various non-Buddhists, one attains it.
The ten paths of the noble ones' lineage, as well as the body, wisdom, and mind-born [bodies], are free from the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who desires to seek superior progress should purify the Tathāgatagarbha and that which is named the Ālayavijñāna.
The commentary states: This means that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the supramundane pure cause.

It is said that by transforming the name of the *ālayavijñāna*, one perceives the *tathāgatagarbha* and immediately attains the effortless path (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), at which point one realizes the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*). The verse says:
"Before the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), one merely abandons the *garbha*. By abandoning this defiled name of the *ālayavijñāna*, it is precisely [the realization of] the *tathāgata*.
This is the coming to the treasury of purity; it is not that there is anything else to be attained.

What is called "attachment to dharmas" refers to the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and all phenomena of both the true and the false used as antidotes.

Because the seven consciousnesses have not yet been extinguished when the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) has not yet been transformed, they all possess attachment, grasping [these things] as a self. Now...

Once the ālayavijñāna has been transformed, the seven vijñānas are extinguished. When the seven vijñānas are extinguished, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the non-self of persons and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished, because these five dharmas and so forth all depend upon the ālayavijñāna for their establishment.
Now that the consciousness has been transformed, they too are extinguished; as the saying goes, "If the bark no longer exists, where can the hair attach? This is what constitutes attainment.

One advances to the eighth stage through the non-selfhood of dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*). Upon reaching this stage, both arising and ceasing have ceased, and even the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) have vanished;
since there is no effort that can be applied, it is called the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*).

Since there is no longer any effort, having attained the non-selfhood of dharmas, one cannot be shaken by any of the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); therefore, it is named the Stage of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*). Having dwelt in this stage, immediately—

One attains the bliss of ten kinds of samādhi gates. Previously, this bodhisattva was immersed in the toil and anxiety of arising and ceasing, and their consciousness was agitated by discursive thought;
thus, they had not yet attained true bliss. Now that arising and ceasing have been extinguished and quiescent extinction has manifested before them, their bliss is beyond all analogy.
Consequently, they would become attached to samādhi and fail to give rise to the thought of liberating sentient beings.
Were they not sustained and drawn forth by the empowerment of the Buddhas' power, they would fall into the stage of the two vehicles.

Therefore, they are sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas' samādhi and spiritual powers, and further supported by the force of their original vows; thus, although they have realized nirvana, [they do not abide therein].
He does not abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nor does he grasp at the bliss of samādhi.

Therefore, by means of the illusion-like samādhi, he manifests a mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) to benefit sentient beings and to proceed toward the ultimate fruit of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
This is why his path of practice differs from that of the non-Buddhists and the followers of the two vehicles. For this reason, the Bodhisattva cultivates the suchness (*yathābhūta*).
Those who practice in search of the supreme Dharma should purify the name of the *vijñānagarbha* within the *tathāgatagarbha*; this is all there is.
Beyond this, there is nothing else to be realized. The above concludes the correct exposition of the truly pure virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
The following text clarifies doubts and exhorts to practice.

Mahāmati, if there were no storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) called the Tathāgatagarbha, then there would be neither arising nor ceasing. Mahāmati, yet all ordinary beings and sages alike possess arising and ceasing;
however, for the practitioner, the noble wisdom of self-realization abides in the bliss of the present dharma, never abandoning skillful means.

The Record states: This is the resolution of a doubt. The question asks: "Since you have changed the name of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) to the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store), does the *tathāgatagarbha* also undergo arising and ceasing, given that the *vijñānagarbha* (consciousness-store) does? The answer says: "If the name 'consciousness-store' did not exist..."

The Tathāgatagarbha, however, is without arising or ceasing. Again, it was asked: "Since all ordinary, ignorant beings have not yet transformed the ālayavijñāna, their minds undergo arising and ceasing.
When all sages have already transformed the ālayavijñāna, does their mind also undergo arising and ceasing? He replied:

"From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) downward, although they have transformed the ālayavijñāna, there may still be arising and ceasing, because they are still proceeding toward self-awakening."
The noble wisdom abides in the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), yet it does not abandon the courageous application of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) for the sake of the work of arising.

Furthermore, as long as the maturation (*vipāka*) is not yet empty, there remains the subtle mark of birth and the ignorance that has not been exhausted—namely, the so-called "true and constant flow" (*tathatā-pravāha*).
Therefore, there is still arising and ceasing. Thus it is said: "Yet all ordinary beings and sages alike possess arising and ceasing; the practitioner..."

The noble realization of self-awareness is the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), wherein one does not abandon skillful means. Question: It is said that what arises and ceases is the seven consciousnesses.

Above it was stated that if the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were absent, the seven consciousnesses would cease. Since the seven consciousnesses have ceased, and the noble ones have already transformed the *tathāgatagarbha*, how can there still be arising and ceasing?
Answer: This is because only the conventional designation (*nāman*) has been transformed; there is no reality [to arise or cease].
Because of its nature. The sutra below states: "The seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvana.
As for the *tathāgatagarbha*, it experiences suffering and pleasure, and is conjoined with their causes; it arises and perishes.

Observing this, that which previously [was said to] arise and perish is not the seven consciousnesses, but rather the *tathāgatagarbha*. Why? Because the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses the capacity for conformity (*anuvṛtti*).
The meaning of "conditions" (pratyaya) is the meaning of "non-alteration. Thus, that which is neither arising nor ceasing refers to the meaning of non-alteration;

whereas that which arises and ceases refers to the meaning of following conditions. By following defiled conditions, it becomes the cause of birth and death, and sentient beings undergo arising and ceasing from moment to moment.
By committing various evil karmas, they sink and wander within birth and death; this is the arising and ceasing of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If, however, they follow pure conditions, these become the causes for *nirvāṇa*. Thus, while Bodhisattvas are in every thought-moment without arising, they give rise to the function of great wisdom to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings, thereby realizing and proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*;
this is the arising and ceasing of noble ones (*ārya*). Therefore, both ordinary beings and noble ones possess arising and ceasing.
Extinction. Because birth is non-birth and non-birth is birth, ordinary beings and sages are equal. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Buddha-nature is impermanent. He also said:
"If the Dharma-body were quiescent extinction, it would be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and stones; who then would experience bliss? Furthermore, he said:
"The Dharma-nature is the essence of arising and ceasing; the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing. They are one essence."

Because the five functions arise and cease, they are considered "constant. This is not the profound realization of non-arising for one who has attained penetration into the dependent origination of the dharma-nature.
Why would this be so? Mahāmati, this Tathāgata-garbha, which is the ālayavijñāna, is what is perceived by the mental conceptions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; although it is [inherently]...
The nature is pure; because it is covered by adventitious defilements, it appears as if impure. It is not so for the Tathāgatas, Mahāmati.
For the Tathāgata, the manifest realm is like looking at an *āmala* fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
The commentary states: This explains the resolution of the objection. It asks:

Since it is said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is pure by nature and that ordinary beings and sages are equal, why is there a distinction between sages and ordinary beings? It answers: Because their perceptions differ.
The Tang translation says: "This Tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna, is pure by nature; it becomes impure when defiled by adventitious dust.
All followers of the two vehicles and the various non-Buddhists speculate upon it and give rise to views, yet they cannot realize it through direct perception.
The Tathāgata perceives this clearly and directly, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand. Because ordinary beings..."

Because it is a [limited] awakening, it is impure. The deluded awakening of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the partial awakening of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) both belong to the category of inference (*anumāna*) rather than the two [valid] cognitions (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, what they perceive is impure. Bodhisattvas possess a partial awakening; when Bodhisattvas of the ten stages contemplate the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), it is like seeing the moon through a grain of rice—thus it still belongs to inference and has not yet reached ultimate purity. Only the realm directly present before the Tathāgata is truly pure.
Regarding the realms, one views the Tathāgatagarbha as clearly as observing a fruit in the palm of one's hand; only then does it become the ultimate purity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, this sutra values the direct perception of the manifestation of Mind-only, wherein the meaning of the sudden vision of Buddha-nature is revealed herein.

"Mahāmati, regarding this meaning, I have established it through my supernormal power so that Queen Śrīmālā and those bodhisattvas who are endowed with sharp intelligence may proclaim and expound upon the names 'Tathāgatagarbha' and 'Ālayavijñāna,' [explaining] that the seven consciousnesses arise simultaneously."
The Śrāvakas are attached to [their views], seeing only the selflessness of persons and phenomena (though the Tang translation says: "causing all Śrāvakas to see the selflessness of phenomena").
Therefore, Lady Śrīmālā, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke of the realm of the Tathāgata, which is not the realm of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.
The Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna are the realm of wisdom belonging only to the Buddhas and those Bodhisattvas of superior intelligence who rely upon the meaning. For this reason:
"You and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train yourselves in the Tathāgatagarbha, the ālayavijñāna.
Do not merely hear or perceive it and consider that sufficient.
This record states: this reveals the ultimate purity and virtue of nirvāṇa; since it reaches its limit here, it concludes with an exhortation to practice.

The Tang translation says: "For the sake of Queen Śrīmālā and other bodhisattvas of profound, wondrous, and pure wisdom, I have taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is called the *ālayavijñāna*, which arises simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses, enabling all śrāvakas to perceive the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Mahāmati, this realm of the Buddha was taught for the sake of Queen Śrīmālā; it is not the realm of non-Buddhists or of those of the two vehicles."
Wisdom. This Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna is the realm of the Buddhas and the sphere of activity for you, O Bodhisattvas of Pure Wisdom, who accord with the true meaning;
it is not the sphere of activity for any of those non-Buddhists who cling to words or for the followers of the Two Vehicles.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and arrogant..."
Because they are able to believe in this Dharma, it is not a domain for those whose wisdom is not yet purified. Furthermore, it says:
"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, who are gentle and of sharp faculties; who, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, have practiced the profound and wondrous Path.
For the sake of these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra; therefore, for those of sharp and fulfilled wisdom, I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha."

This refers to the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness), which arises simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses. The reason for speaking of this is precisely to urge on those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) so that they may realize the non-self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
As for what is called "pure wisdom" (jñāna), it means relying on the meaning and not relying on the words. *Baoming* says:
"Anything that takes the form of literary patterns belongs to defilement. Baizhang said: "Originally there are no names or titles; we call it 'Buddha'."

This is defilement; this is what is called "Dharma. Alas! To call this the Buddha-Dharma is itself defilement, let alone greed, anger, and delusion, as well as various false views, memories, and conceptual calculations.

This is why those who do not possess profound, wondrous, and pure wisdom cannot enter it. Therefore, I urge you: do not merely hear or perceive it and imagine that you have attained sufficient knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The profoundly deep Tathāgatagarbha Coexists with the seven consciousnesses; Born from the two kinds of appropriation, The wise one remains far removed from them."
The commentary states: "This verse refers to the intrinsic purity of the *tathāgatagarbha*. It means that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally pure from the beginning;

however, because it is perfumed by beginningless evil habits, it becomes the *ālayavijñāna*. Therein arises the ignorance of the ground (*mūlavijñāna-avidyā*), which coexists with the seven consciousnesses.
Thus, the causes and conditions for both defilement and purity are established based upon it; hence it is said: 'The two kinds of appropriation arise.'"

Because this *tathāgatagarbha* is neither defiled nor pure, and because the mental afflictions of both the noble and the ordinary are exhausted, it is said that "the wise remain far removed from the two kinds of grasping," namely the grasper and the grasped—these being the two divisions of the seeing and the seen. These arise because of the existence of mind and objects;
when these are forgotten, they do not arise.
"The mind manifests like a reflection in a mirror, perfumed by habitual tendencies since beginningless time. For one who observes according to reality, all phenomena are entirely without substance.
The commentary states: This verse explains the meaning of "separation" mentioned above.

All dharmas—whether mundane or supramundane, pertaining to birth-and-death or nirvana—are like reflections appearing in a mirror within the *tathāgatagarbha*; they have never existed from the very beginning, yet they arise solely through [habitual tendencies] since beginningless time.

Because it is perfumed by the two tendencies of defilement and purity, yet within the Tathāgatagarbha, one cannot find even the slightest trace of coming or going, delusion or awakening, birth or death;
therefore it is said that for one who observes according to reality, all phenomena are entirely without phenomena. An ancient master said:
"Throughout the entire earth, one cannot find a single person who is 'without affairs' (wu-shi). How true this is!
It is like a fool who, seeing a finger pointing at the moon, looks at the finger and not at the moon; those who are attached to names and words do not see my true reality.
The commentary states: "This verse shows that fools, by clinging to conventional designations, fail to attain the true meaning. As stated previously:
"The Dharma I teach is like a finger pointing at the moon."

The mind is like a stage performer; the intellect is like the assistant performer; the five consciousnesses are the companions; and deluded thoughts are the audience watching the performance. The commentary states:
"This verse describes how the ignorant follow after consciousness rather than wisdom. Yongjia said:

"The depletion of the Dharma-treasure and the destruction of merit—none of these do not arise from this mind, intellect, and consciousness. Here, "mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses, which are capable of transformation and manifestation.
Therefore, they are like performers; the "mind" (manas) refers to the seven consciousnesses, which rely on causes and depend on conditions, thus being like the master of the troupe.

The five consciousnesses arise in clusters, thus acting as the companions. The sixth consciousness performs discrimination, thus acting as the spectator. Fundamentally non-existent and unreal like a magical illusion, they are compared to a performance;
this is why the contemplation of reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*) is so highly esteemed. This is as Wang Wen Gong did when observing actors.

The verse says: Among the various performers in the theater, one is noble and another is lowly; yet the mind knows they are fundamentally the same from the start, and thus there is neither joy nor resentment.
Master Jiyin remarked that this old man’s entire body is eyes, and he cannot be deceived for a single moment.

This section begins from the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Self-Nature" in the first fascicle and concludes here with the refutation of names, marks, and false conceptualizations. This is the general overview.

Having completed the analysis of the characteristics of false and correct causes and effects by means of the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness, [the following section] clarifies the ultimate distinctions among these five dharmas, three natures, eight consciousnesses, and two selflessnesses.
This is divided into two parts. First, a general clarification of the causes and bases of delusion and awakening. △ First, the question:

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self—[the two translations both say:

'the characteristics of their distinctions']—so that I and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may, throughout all stages in continuous succession, discern these dharmas and enter into all Buddha-dharmas, entering into the One."
Regarding "all Buddha-dharmas," up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening,
it is recorded that this question clarifies the ultimate distinctions among the five dharmas and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This is because all previously mentioned worldly and transworldly,
mundane and sagely, heterodox and orthodox causes and effects are entirely dependent upon these five dharmas and the three natures.
The establishment of the eight consciousnesses as self-nature and the two kinds of non-self has been completed;

however, the specific characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the various aspects of non-self—which constitute the agent of this establishment—have not yet been clarified.
Therefore, I ask this question, hoping that the Buddha will discern and explain them clearly, so that practitioners may understand them thoroughly and without doubt. Thus it may be.
By relying on this, one discerns without error and enters into all Buddha-dharmas, even unto the ultimate stage of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
○ Next, in the response, first there is a general clarification of the causes and bases of delusion and awakening;
second, there is a detailed exposition of the inclusion through the four gates. △ First:
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “The five dharmas, the three self-natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and the characteristics of the various modes of discrimination are as follows:
namely, name, appearance, conceptualization, right knowledge, and suchness. If a practitioner practices and enters the noble realization of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening...”

They proceed by being free from views such as annihilationism, eternalism, existence, and non-existence; they dwell in the present with the manifestation of the blissful meditative attainment (*sukha-samāpatti*) of the present life.

Yet, Mahāmati, they do not realize that those five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and external objects are merely manifestations of one's own mind—the false imaginings of ordinary people.
This is not the view of the various noble sages.
The commentary states: "This passage generally clarifies the causal basis for both the delusion and awakening of the true and the false.

The meaning is that if a practitioner, through observation, clearly perceives without error the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses, and selflessness, then regarding the Tathāgata...

When one realizes this state, one is free from views such as annihilationism, eternalism, existence, or non-existence, and attains the profound samādhi of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
If ordinary fools do not understand this dharma, they falsely perceive that phenomena truly exist externally to the mind;
they give rise to false discrimination and grasping, and thus wander through birth and death. Thus, both delusion and awakening, as well as the noble and the ordinary, all depend upon this.

This is the Dharma. Second, the specific explanation of the inclusion within the four gates is divided into five parts. First, a general clarification of the distinct characteristics of the five dharmas is divided into two.
△ First, the explanation of the dharmas that are distinct.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, how is it that the deluded imaginings of foolish commoners arise, while those of the noble sages do not?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Foolish commoners are attached to conventional designations, names, and marks. They follow after these as their minds flow and disperse.

Once they have so dispersed, they fall into various appearances and forms, and into the views and aspirations of ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self. They become attached to exquisite colors and forms. Having become attached, they are shrouded and obstructed by ignorance.”

Therefore, they give rise to defiled attachment. Once attached, they accumulate karma born of greed, hatred, and delusion. Having accumulated it, they entangle themselves with false imaginings, like a silkworm spinning its cocoon.
They fall into the ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the various realms of existence, like a waterwheel drawing from a well.

Because of their ignorance, they cannot understand that things are by nature like illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water—devoid of "I" and "mine"—and thus they give rise to [the notion of] oneness.
All unreal conceptualizations are devoid of both the characteristic and that which is characterized, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing; they arise from the conceptualization of one’s own mind.
They do not arise from Īśvara, time, atoms, or primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Foolish worldlings merely follow along with names and signs.

The commentary states: This is a general statement regarding the causes for the arising of distinctions among the names and characteristics within the five dharmas, as well as the basis for the false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists.
The Tang translation says: "Ordinary fools do not know that names are merely provisional designations;

their minds follow after them in movement, perceiving various characteristics, conceiving of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and becoming defiled and attached to form, thereby obscuring noble wisdom and giving rise to [delusion]."
Driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, one creates various karmas, like a silkworm spinning its cocoon;

thus, through false conceptualization, one binds oneself and falls into the great ocean of birth and death across the various realms of existence, circling incessantly like a waterwheel drawing from a well.

Failing to realize that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, and like the moon reflected in water—merely what is seen by one’s own mind arising from false discrimination—one remains bound by the duality of subject and object and the cycle of birth.
Abiding in cessation: this refers to that which arises from the Lord, time, atoms, or primordial nature (*pradhāna*), following the flow of names and signs.
This is said because ordinary beings do not know that names and signs are false and unreal; thus, they falsely grasp at them as "self" and "what belongs to the self.
Relying on these, they perform various karmas, incessantly taking upon themselves the bitter fruits of birth and death. Furthermore, externally...
The Way is not known through names or characteristics; it is a manifestation of one's own mind alone.

It arises based on the causes and conditions of birth and extinction produced by the false discrimination of subject and object, thereby giving rise to divergent views. These views claim that [the world] arises from a creator god (*īśvara*), time, atoms (*paramāṇu*), or primordial nature (*pradhāna*).

Thus, names and characteristics are fundamentally non-existent; they merely arise through dependent origination (*paratantra*) and exist only due to pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Below...
This correctly explains the distinctions among the five dharmas.

Mahāmati, as for those "characteristics" (*nimitta*): that which is illuminated by visual consciousness is called "form" (*rūpa*); that which is illuminated by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called "sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena" (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma*). These are what are called "characteristics."
The commentary states: This explains "name" and "mark" among the five dharmas. "Name" and "mark" refer to form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Consciousness and mental factors (*nāma*) constitute "name.
The five sense organs and the six sense objects are collectively termed "mark. Furthermore, since each mark has its own name, they are also called "name and mark.

Thus it is said that what is illuminated by visual consciousness is termed "form," and so forth. Generally, that which is confronted by the five sense organs constitutes actual form (*dravya-rūpa*), whereas that which is confronted by the mental organ...

The objective condition (ālambana) of mental objects (dharmas) is a provisional form (rūpa). However, in reality, it is visible and resistant; as a provisional construct, it is invisible and non-resistant.

This is clearly elucidated in the *Vijñaptimātra-śata-dharma* (The Hundred Dharmas of Consciousness-only); here, however, it is treated merely for the sake of establishing its designation and characteristics.
Mahāmati, those who engage in conceptual construction (vikalpa) establish various names and manifest various characteristics; it is thus, and not otherwise (the Tang translation says:
"This matter is thus, certainly not otherwise"). Names such as elephant, horse, chariot, infantry, man, woman, and so forth—these are called conceptual construction.

The commentary states: This explains the deluded discrimination (*vikalpa*) among the five dharmas. Regarding "establishing various names and manifesting various characteristics," it means that names are established based on characteristics, and characteristics arise following names.
Since names and characteristics are fundamentally non-existent and exist only in dependence upon conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), they are called "deluded discrimination."
Mahāmati, as for right knowledge: its names and marks cannot be apprehended; it is like a passing guest. The various consciousnesses do not arise;
it is neither annihilated nor eternal, and it does not fall into the stages of any externalists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.

The commentary states: This explains "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*) among the five dharmas. "Not abiding" means being like a guest; because it does not abide in names and marks (*nāma-nimitta*), it is unobtainable.
Because it is unobtainable, the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) do not arise. Now, since consciousness does not arise, what is it other than wisdom?
When one observes all phenomena with wisdom, one does not engage in discrimination, nor does one fall into error; one avoids the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Then one will not fall into the stages of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Because one does not fall into partiality or deviation, it is called "right knowledge" (samyag-jñāna).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by means of this right knowledge, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not establish names and signs, yet it is not that they do not establish them.
Regarding "name and appearance" (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*): by abandoning the two views of establishment and denial, one knows that name and appearance do not arise;

this is called *tathatā* (suchness). The commentary states: This refers to *tathatā* among the five dharmas. If one perceives through consciousness (*vijñāna*), then name and appearance arise adventitiously;
if one contemplates with correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), then name and appearance are not established. This is precisely the fundamental suchness of name and appearance.
It is not that there exists a "suchness" (tathatā) separate from and external to names and appearances;

rather, it is simply that one does not give rise to the two views of existence and non-existence regarding names and appearances, thereby avoiding both affirmation and denial. Because one knows that names and appearances are fundamentally unborn from the beginning, they are called "suchness.
Therefore, it is said that it is not the case that names and appearances are not established. What is meant is that only the wisdom of suchness alone remains, yet names and appearances do not arise.
The objective realm is suchness (*tathatā*). That which allows one to know that names and characteristics do not arise is the mind that is suchness.
Since the mind and the objective realm are both suchness, not a single dharma is established. *Above, the differentiated dharmas were clarified; below, the person who abides in suchness is revealed.*
Mahāmati, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in suchness (*tathatā*), they attain the realm of non-existence and thereby attain the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Having attained the Stage of Joy, they are forever separated from all external paths and evil destinies, and correctly abide in the supramundane path.
Their realization of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) matures, and they personally realize the nature of all phenomena as being like an illusion and so forth.
[The] marks. Departing from all deluded thoughts, one perceives the distinct marks of the nature [of reality].
The commentary states: These words refer to the actual realization of one who abides in suchness (*tathatā*). This is the attainment of the realm of non-existence.
Because it is solely suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the maturation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):

because one is not bound by signs (*nimitta*), one attains the path of the Dharma through self-awakening (*pratyātma-jñāna*) and is thus free from all deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). Because one attains the function of true suchness, one perceives the distinct characteristics of the nature;
that is to say, by eliminating ignorance (*avidyā*), one beholds the fundamental Dharmakāya. Through its own cessation, there arises inconceivable activity in its various forms.
Its function is such that it is equal to True Suchness (tathatā) and pervades all places; this refers to the characteristics of the stages from the first bhūmi up to the ninth.
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one realizes ten types of True Suchness upon entering the stages, as that text emphasizes superior qualities.
Here, however, there is only one True Suchness and no second, as this is based on actual realization.
Proceeding in succession up to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), within that interval, the power of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) blossom forth.

(The Wei translation states: "Having entered the stage of the Cloud of Dharma, one next uses the power of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal knowledges to adorn the ground of the Tathāgata with various flowers.

Having attained the ground of the Tathāgata, one manifests various transformations through perfect illumination to bring sentient beings to maturity, like the moon reflected in water, and thus skillfully brings the ten [perfections] to ultimate fulfillment.

This is the inexhaustible phrase. For the sake of sentient beings with various inclinations and understandings, he expounds the Dharma through analytical teaching. The Dharma-body is free from mental constructs;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained through suchness.

The commentary states: This clarifies the characteristics of attaining the fruit through the perfection of practice. Because the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is transformed, it receives the name *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store).
Therefore, it is said that the *dharmakāya* is free from mental constructions. This is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into the state of suchness (*tathatā*). As the treatise says:
Regarding the essential nature of *tathatā*: from the very beginning, its self-nature has been fully endowed with all meritorious qualities.
That is to say, its essence possesses the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom; the meaning of universally illuminating the *dharmadhātu*;
the meaning of true and authentic cognition; the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind; the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the meaning of coolness.

Because it has the meaning of being immutable and sovereign, and because it is fully endowed with such Buddha-dharmas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—which are inseparable, uninterrupted, non-distinct, and inconceivable, and because it is fulfilled to the point that nothing is lacking, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and also the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*.
It continues, saying: "Such pure dharmas consist of immeasurable merits."
This is precisely the single mind, wherein there is nothing further to be contemplated. For this reason, it is fulfilled and is called the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body.
It is only through the absence of contemplation that fulfillment is attained; therefore, it is said that the Dharma-body is free from the activities of the intellect.
This is called entering into suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the ultimate stage, such functional activity is naturally possessed as a matter of course.
The above concludes the explanation of the distinct characteristics of the five dharmas. Below is the explanation of how the three gates enter into the five dharmas, which is divided into two parts.
First: How the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) enter into the five dharmas.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it?

Do the three natures enter into the five dharmas, or do they each have their own distinct characteristics and categories? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The three natures, as well as the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness, are all included within the five dharmas."

The Record states: This question clarifies how the four gates mutually encompass one another, thereby manifesting the fusion of defilement and purity within the True Suchness of the One Mind, and revealing the wondrous inclusiveness of the Tathāgatagarbha nature. The old commentary says:
Previously, Mahāmati raised four gates as questions, yet the Tathāgata answered by means of only the single gate of the five dharmas; therefore, he asks this again.
"Do the three natures enter into the five dharmas? Or is there a separate school that maintains the existence of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
The Buddha replied: "The other three gates are all included within the five dharmas; by practicing even a single gate, all gates are fully encompassed. The same applies to the remaining three.
The reason they mutually include and complete one another is that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is interpenetrating and harmonious. Following this...
"Because of the transformation of conditions, Mahāmati, those names and characteristics are the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The commentary states: "This refers to the entry of the nature of false imagination into the five dharmas as name and characteristic (*nāma-nimitta*). Because there are names and characteristics..."
Therefore, discrimination arises. If names and signs did not exist, from what would discrimination arise? Thus, this false imagination is subsumed within those names and signs.
Mahāmati, if the mind and mental factors arise based on that false imagination, they arise simultaneously, like sunlight and its seeds.
The distinct apprehension of various characteristics is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The commentary states: "This refers to the entry of the dependent nature into the five dharmas as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That is to say, among those five dharmas, conceptual construction is termed 'characteristic' (*nimitta*);
these arise in mutual dependence. This is because when conceptual construction gives rise to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), [the characteristic arises]."
Thus, the provisional names of all phenomena arise based upon this, like the sun and its light; that is to say, because the mind and its objects are not separate from one another.
Since there are various names, there are various appearances, and further, various conceptual discriminations arise, mutually supporting one another.
This is what is meant by: "When the mind arises, various phenomena arise," for the mind and its objects serve as mutual conditions for arising.
This dependent origination-nature is subsumed under the category of "conceptualization" within those five dharmas.
Mahāmati, because right knowledge and suchness are indestructible, they are called the perfected nature.
The commentary states: This refers to the accomplishment of self-nature as it enters into the five dharmas, namely correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).

That is to say, correct wisdom and suchness are the wondrous nature that is innate; they are not something produced by artificial effort, and therefore they cannot be destroyed. Because they cannot be destroyed...

Therefore, it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected; this is termed the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The above concludes the explanation of how the three natures enter into the five dharmas.
Below, the explanation of how the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness enter into the five dharmas follows.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the eightfold discrimination of the false imagination manifested from one's own mind consists of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
These characteristics are unreal because they are products of false imagination; thus, the grasping of the two—self and what belongs to self—is extinguished, and the two kinds of selflessness arise.
The commentary states: This means that the eight consciousnesses and the two types of selflessness are included within the five dharmas.

That is to say, the delusive phenomena manifested within one's own mind constitute "name" and "characteristic"; the arising of attachment to these gives rise to the eight consciousnesses, which is precisely "discrimination."
If one realizes that these delusive appearances are all unreal, then conceptual discrimination will not arise; this is precisely right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).

These eight consciousnesses are thus included within the five dharmas. If one falsely discriminates within the mind and its objects that there is a real self and what belongs to the self, this constitutes name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) and false imagination (*parikalpita*).
If one realizes that the mind and its objects are unreal, the two types of grasping (*parigraha*) are extinguished. The two...
The absence of self-arising is precisely correct wisdom and suchness. These two types of selflessness are included within the five dharmas.
△ Third, the explanation of how the four gates encompass all phenomena.

Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas encompass the stages of the self-realized noble wisdom of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas, as well as their continuous succession through the various grounds;
all the teachings of the Buddha are entirely contained within them.
The commentary states: "This refers to how the four gates encompass all dharmas. That is to say, it is not merely that the five dharmas encompass the other three gates;
rather, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—whether cause or fruit—all dharmas whatsoever, are entirely contained within them.
4. Explaining the ultimate convergence into suchness to demonstrate right contemplation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are: appearance (*nimitta*), name (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*).

Mahāmati, as for "appearance," it refers to that wherein locations, forms, colors, images, and so forth manifest; this is called appearance. (The Tang translation states: "In this context, 'appearance' refers to the distinct shapes of the forms and other objects that are perceived.")

This is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*). If something possesses such characteristics, it is called a "vase" and so forth; that which is precisely this and nothing else is called a "name" (*nāman*). (The Tang translation says:

"Based on those various characteristics, one establishes names such as 'vase. That it is thus, and not otherwise, is called 'name'"). To apply various names in order to manifest the characteristics of vases and other mental states and mental factors is called "conceptual construction" (*parikalpita*).
Those names and those characteristics are ultimately unobtainable; from beginning to end, they do not exist.

Awakening. To be without successive conceptualization regarding all phenomena and to be free from unreal妄想 (vikalpa) is called *tathatā* (suchness). (The Tang translation states: "Those names and those marks ultimately do not exist;

they are merely the successive conceptualizations of the deluded mind. Observing in this way until awakening ceases is called *tathatā*. True, definitive, and ultimate self-nature is unobtainable; that is the mark of *tathatā*.
It is the point of entry where I and all Buddhas accord with and enter it, universally for the sake of sentient beings as suchness.

It is truly the thorough exposition, designation, and manifestation; it enters into that through right awakening, being neither annihilated nor eternal, and free from the arising of false conceptualization.
It accords with the noble path of self-realized wisdom, a characteristic unattainable by any outsiders, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
This is called right knowledge.
The commentary states: These words refer to the skillful means for practicing the five dharmas. It was previously stated that the five dharmas exist in mutual dependence:
