namely, that names exist in dependence on mental constructions (*vikalpa*), and mental constructions exist in dependence on names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*).

Furthermore, those names and signs are generally discussed in terms of the mutual dependence between mind and objects; therefore, they are subsumed within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This [present passage], however, speaks of them individually.
All phenomena are collectively termed "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). Each characteristic has its own name; the conceptual differentiation of these names is called "discursive thought" (*vikalpa*).

These names, characteristics, and discursive thoughts are fundamentally *tathatā* (suchness). One who can thoroughly comprehend this characteristic of *tathatā* and further manifest it for the sake of sentient beings is said to possess "right knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*), which is precisely what is meant by the "noble wisdom of self-awakening" (*svasaṃvedya-āryajñāna*).
Therefore, while the sequence of the five dharmas mentioned earlier and later differs, their underlying intent is distinct.
That which is ultimately unobtainable as name and appearance is the fundamental suchness (*tathatā*) of the object.

That there is no awakening from beginning to end means that since there is no object known, there is likewise no knowing mind; thus, the mind is fundamentally suchness. Because both mind and object are suchness, they are in a state of *tathatā*.
Regarding all phenomena, there is no successive arising and ceasing, and one is thus free from unreal conceptualization.
This is the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness). Because it is without characteristics, its true, definitive, ultimate self-nature cannot be apprehended.
This is the point of realization and entry for myself and all Buddhas; and as for why I universally reveal and explain this to sentient beings, it is also [for their benefit].

I have explained this suchness as it truly is, manifesting it for them so that those sentient beings may follow and enter into it, thereby avoiding the extremes of nihilism and eternalism, not giving rise to false conceptualization, and entering the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which transcends the spheres of all non-Buddhists and the two vehicles.
Only in this way is it called right knowledge; this is precisely what I have realized and what I have taught.
It is nothing more than this. That which sentient beings realize is likewise nothing more than this. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Below, he concludes by exhorting [the reader] to practice and study.
"Mahāmati, these are called the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
All the Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should study them through your own skillful means and also teach others; do not follow after others."

The commentary states: This is a summary exhortation to practice. The Tang translation says: "Within this Dharma, you should skillfully penetrate it through your own wisdom, and you should also exhort others to penetrate it.
Once you have penetrated this, your mind will become resolute and will no longer follow after others.
However, it is only when one penetrates suchness that the mind finally becomes resolute and no longer follows after others."
This is why those in the seventh stage have not yet transcended mind and consciousness, and thus still fear falling into the deviant paths of externalists.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—these entirely encompass the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states: "This verse in summary encapsulates all the teachings of the Mahāyāna Buddha-dharma within the four preceding sections.
The Sanskrit term *mahāyāna* is translated here as 'Great Vehicle' (*dàchéng*)."
Name, mark, false discrimination, the two kinds of self-nature, correct wisdom, and suchness—these constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The commentary states: "This verse subsumes the three natures within the five dharmas.

The preceding section, which demonstrated the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two non-selves to clarify the ultimate characteristics of differentiation, is now complete. The following section clarifies the permanence of the *dharmakāya*.
Abiding therein, he demonstrates the mark of the equality of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa. This is divided into two parts. △ First, clarifying that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, regarding the phrases spoken by the World-Honored One—that the Buddhas of the past are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise those of the future and the present—how is it, World-Honored One, that they are so?”
"I have spoken thus, yet there is further meaning to be received. I pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will explain it.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept it merely as it was spoken. The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like the sands of the Ganges. Why is this?
Because they transcend worldly perception and cannot be illustrated by worldly analogies."

The commentary states: The preceding section generally and comprehensively revealed the ultimate truth regarding the causes and effects of the true and the false within the dharma-realm, ultimately converging upon suchness (*tathatā*).
This section, however, intends to demonstrate the permanence of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) in order to manifest the equality of the dharma-realm as suchness;
therefore, the analogy of the sands of the Ganges is raised for inquiry. Generally, when expressing a vast number, the sands of the Ganges are used as a metaphor.
Mahāmati thought to himself: "Does 'fruit' refer to the Buddhas of the three periods of time being as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
Therefore, it is said, 'one receives according to what was taught. Or does it have some other distinct meaning? The Buddha said:

"It cannot be said that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why? Because the Tathāgata is most supreme, transcending all worlds, and there is none equal to him."
This cannot be sought through measurement; therefore, it is said to transcend worldly expectations and is beyond the scope of analogy. As the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena within the three realms, whether existent or non-existent, cannot serve as metaphors for the Buddha."

Because ordinary fools and non-Buddhists falsely imagine permanence—(the Tang translation says: "I [teach] that ordinary fools and various non-Buddhists constantly cling with their minds to permanence and impermanence")—they nourish evil views, resulting in an endless cycle of birth and death.
It is in order to cause them to become weary of and detached from this wheel of saṃsāra, so that they may apply themselves with diligence and progress toward excellence.
For their sake, he says: "The Buddhas are easy to see; they are not like the udumbara flower, which is difficult to encounter. Thus, he causes them to cease their expedient seeking.
At other times, however, observing those who are to be transformed, he makes this statement: "A Buddha is difficult to meet, like the udumbara flower.
As for the udumbara flower, there has never been one seen, nor is one seen now, nor will one ever be seen. Such is the Tathāgata in the world."
It is seen, not because it is established through one's own conventional understanding. Therefore, it is said that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is like the udumbara flower.
Mahāmati, those who establish their own conventions and understandings based on worldly expectations cannot believe in this;
it is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, for which no analogy exists. The true Tathāgata transcends what is perceived by the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Its characteristics cannot be illustrated by analogy.
The Record states: "This refers to the eternally abiding Dharma-body, which cannot be sought through verbal expression, mental measurement, or metaphor."
However, the Dharmakāya transcends words and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories; how could it be sought through comparison with numbers and quantities?

That the Buddha is likened to the sands of the Ganges for ease of understanding is intended solely to exhort indolent sentient beings, to shatter their attachments and their fear of the distant goal, and to cause them to weary of and renounce birth and death, thereby giving rise to a mind of diligent effort. Therefore...
For their sake, he explains that the Buddhas are as easy to see as the sands of the Ganges, rather than being like the udumbara flower;
it is as if saying, "The place of jewels is near. If he were to say that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, they would surely become discouraged and timid, thinking him hard to behold.
Because they were unwilling to advance and seek [the truth], I used words that are easy to perceive to inspire them; these were not words of ultimate reality.
If there were those whose faculties were mature and capable of receiving transformation, I feared they might become indolent;

wishing to cause them to apply themselves with diligence and swiftly hasten toward Bodhi, I therefore said that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the Udumbara flower, so as to cause them to give rise to longing and yearning.
This is because of the mind that yearns [for the Buddha]. This, too, is a parable; it is not a literal reality.
Furthermore, as for the udumbara flower, there is no one who has seen it in the past, sees it now, or will see it in the future. Yet the Tathāgata, appearing in the world, knows and sees all.
How, then, can the udumbara flower be compared to the Tathāgata? Thus, those who use the udumbara flower as a metaphor for the Buddha are speaking of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
This is merely a skillful means to entice sentient beings; it is not the establishment of the Dharma-body’s own realm of self-communication.

Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is like the udumbara flower. However, the Dharma of self-establishment and self-communication is the realm of the Dharma-body realized through internal, noble wisdom, which is peerless in the world;
hence it is said to transcend worldly expectations. To those ordinary and ignorant people, however—
One cannot believe in or accept the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), as it is beyond all analogy.

Yet, people falsely claim that it can be known through metaphors. They fail to realize that the true *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by the mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); it cannot be sought by establishing analogies within it. Therefore, the *Prajñā*...
It is said: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, however, when I speak of the Buddha being like the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault in this.

The commentary states: This is a resolution of a doubt. The doubt is as follows: "If the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is such that nothing can be used as a simile for it, yet the Buddha is nevertheless compared to the sands of the Ganges River, does this not fall into the fault of self-contradiction? Therefore, the commentary provides this explanation.
However, when I occasionally speak of the Buddha being like the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault of contradiction. Why?
Because what I mean by "the sands of the Ganges" does not refer to a mere abundance; it is because there is a profound meaning.
Therefore, the following seven kinds of profound meanings are used to explain it.

“Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges. Even if all fish, turtles, crocodiles (*śiśumāra*), lions, elephants, horses, humans, and beasts were to trample upon them, the sands do not think, ‘They are disturbing me,’ nor do they give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Their intrinsic nature is pure and free from all defilement.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the Ganges of the noble wisdom of self-realization.”

Even if all the non-Buddhists, humans, animals, and others were to cause every kind of disturbance—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—the Tathāgata would not give rise to deluded thoughts in response. The Tathāgata is tranquil and free from conceptualization.
Because the Tathāgata’s original vow is to establish sentient beings in the bliss of samādhi, there is no disturbance; it is no different from the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore,
Because of the severing of greed and hatred, the commentary states:
"This metaphor reveals that the Dharmakāya is free from conceptual thought (*niṣprapañca*). The Tathāgata’s own realization of noble wisdom and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are like a river;
the great powers, supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), and masteries are like the sands of the Ganges. Although they are trampled upon, [they do not perish]."

Even when various non-Buddhists and celestial Māras give rise to thoughts of disturbance and affliction toward the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata remains serene and does not produce even a single thought of aversion or abandonment.

This is because he is sustained by the power of the samādhi of his original vow to benefit sentient beings, and because he has severed the habitual tendencies of greed, anger, attachment, and hatred from time immemorial. By means of this—
The wisdom that is free from conceptual thought is thus like the sands of the Ganges; it is hardly a matter of mere abundance.
Because it takes sentient beings suffering as its object of focus through the objective condition of bodhi, it is called the "bliss of the samādhi of the original vow."

It is like the sands of the Ganges, which are the very nature of the earth element. When the kalpa ends and all is consumed by fire, that fire burns all the earth, yet the earth element does not abandon its own nature because it arises simultaneously with the fire element.
Other deluded beings form the perception that the earth is burning, but the earth is not actually burned, for fire is merely its cause.
In this same way, Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible, like the sands of the Ganges.
The commentary states: This metaphor reveals that the Dharma-body is indestructible.

The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is called "Dharma-nature" when residing in insentient things, and "Buddha-nature" when residing in sentient beings. Thus, it is like sand being the intrinsic nature of the earth;

while the insentient world undergoes the eight phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, and sentient beings undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death, [the Dharma-body remains]. Although these are the eight phases, [it is not destroyed].
Though there is the flux of conditioned existence and the fire of the three poisons of ignorance burns and seethes, the *dharmakāya* remains serene, never undergoing increase or decrease therein.
Why? Because both are unborn and non-dual. Thus, it is like the great earth being burned while the sand does not lose its own nature;
for the sand and the fire are co-arisen, yet the deluded person says that the earth is being burned.
Yet the earth is not actually burned. Since the earth takes fire as its cause, and fire is able to produce soil, fire is thus the cause of the earth.
By analogy, a fool might think that the fire of the three poisons will burn and destroy the *dharmakāya*;
yet the *dharmakāya* is in fact indestructible. Why? Because the afflictions of the three poisons are themselves the cause of the *dharmakāya*.
Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too is the radiance of the Tathāgata without limit.
For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, it universally illumines all the assemblies of Buddhas.
The Record states: "This metaphor illustrates that the Dharma-body is without limit. The Treatise says:

"It is because its essential nature possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light; it is because it universally illumines the Dharma-realm. It further states: "Because the nature of wisdom is itself form."
It is taught that the Dharmakāya pervades all places, and the forms it manifests have no spatial limits.

According to the mind, it can display the worlds of the ten directions, with immeasurable Bodhisattvas, immeasurable Reward-bodies (Sambhogakāyas), and immeasurable adornments, each distinct from the others;
yet all are without limits and do not obstruct one another. This cannot be known through the discrimination of the mind and consciousness, because...
Because it signifies the sovereign function of *tathatā* (suchness), it is said that "the radiance is without limit," and so forth.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges: one can never find separate grains of sand that are different from them.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has no birth or death within saṃsāra, because the causes and conditions [for such birth] have been severed.

The commentary states: This metaphor illustrates the single characteristic of the Dharmakāya. It means that the Dharmakāya is far removed from arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, because it has eternally severed the causes of birth and death within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). The treatise says: "Originally equal, for they are of one and the same awakening. Therefore, it is said:
"For example, if one seeks a sand grain different from the sands of the Ganges, it can never be found."
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, whose increase or decrease cannot be perceived.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s wisdom matures sentient beings without increasing or decreasing, because it is not a physical phenomenon (*kāyadharma*). Physical phenomena are subject to destruction, but the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata is not a physical phenomenon.
The Record states: "This metaphor illustrates that the Dharma-body is free from the faults of increase and decrease. The Treatise says:

"First is the Greatness of Essence (tǐ-dà), meaning that the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena is equal and neither increases nor decreases. That which is called the Tathāgata’s wisdom is spoken of in terms of maturing sentient beings.
As for "neither increasing nor decreasing," this refers to the provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna) that benefits others; it is [the wisdom] throughout the ten directions that is...
All sentient beings may take up the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata does not diminish; all may accord with the Buddha-mind, yet there is no increase.
This is what is meant by: "The more one gives to others, the more one has; the more one bestows upon others, the more one possesses.
Why is this? Because the Dharma-body is not a physical body. Thus, the Tang translation says: "It is like the sands of the Ganges; even if one takes them away..."

One knows of decrease, yet upon examination finds no increase. The Buddhas are likewise: through the wisdom of skillful means, they bring sentient beings to maturity without decrease and without increase.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body has no physical body.
Just as when pressing the sands of the Ganges, no oil can be obtained— (both translations include the four characters "Mahāmati, for example")— in this same way,
although all these beings in extreme suffering oppress the Tathāgata, until those beings have attained *nirvāṇa*, he does not relinquish his own samādhi, vows,
and aspirations within the *dharmadhātu*, because of his great compassion.
The commentary states: This metaphor reveals the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the same essence (*samatā*).
Since the karmic nature of sentient beings is entirely the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, when sentient beings undergo extreme suffering, it is as if they are afflicting the Tathāgata.
Therefore, as long as sentient beings have not yet attained final nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata likewise cannot possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Thus, even unto...
Not even a single minute sentient being fails to enter nirvana;

yet the Tathāgata does not abandon the activity of delivering beings through his own samādhi and vows within the dharmadhātu, for he is sustained by great compassion of identical essence. Oil serves as a metaphor for the mind of anger.
The Wei translation states: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot harbor anger even when oppressed by the sufferings of sentient beings.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges which flow along with the water; they do not exist without the water.
In the same way, Mahāmati, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata flow toward Nirvāṇa. For this reason, it is said that they are like the sands of the Ganges. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
One does not follow the flow of various goings, for "going" has the meaning of destruction. Mahāmati, the original limit of birth and death is unknowable;
because it is unknowable, how can one speak of "going"? Mahāmati, "going" has the meaning of cessation, yet the foolish do not understand this.
The commentary states: This metaphor speaks of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Sand represents all phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
water represents the Dharma of the Dharma-body’s *nirvāṇa*. Yet, when the Dharma-body flows through the five destinies, it is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*).

If sentient beings, by means of the karma-consciousness of ignorance, speak of the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*, then that Dharma of *nirvāṇa* follows along with the flow of birth and death. Thus it is like...
Now, by means of the noble wisdom of self-realization, one explains the phenomena of birth and death; yet these phenomena of birth and death all flow toward nirvāṇa.
It is not only the phenomena explained that follow nirvāṇa, but the speech itself is also nirvāṇa, because the characteristics of verbal expression are quiescent.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he does not follow the flow of various migrations. For this reason, he does not follow [them].
Regarding "transmigration": because one does not perceive the existence of dharmas of birth and death, it is said that the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of birth and death cannot be known.
Since the original limit of birth and death itself cannot be known, how could I say that birth and death have the sense of "going away"?
Furthermore, "going away" has the meaning of "cessation. However, the original limit of birth and death is precisely the eternally abiding *nirvāṇa*. Moreover—
It is said that this is severed; however, this is not something known by ordinary people. The above clarifies that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding.
Below, it clarifies the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the original limit of sentient beings' birth and death cannot be known, how is it..."

Liberation can be understood thus. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "When the causes—the beginningless habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false views, faults, and delusive conceptualization—are extinguished, one realizes that external objects are manifestations of one's own mind. This transformation of the basis of conceptualization is liberation;
it is not annihilation. Therefore, it is boundless and not a state of total non-existence, for it serves as the ground for those [who have been] conceptually constructed."
Through various names such as "the infinite" and so forth, one observes the internal and external, becoming free from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

There is no separate sentient being; both cognition (*jñāna*) and its objective field (*jñeya*)—all phenomena (*dharma*)—are entirely quiescent. (The Tang translation states: "Free from the discriminating mind, there is no distinct sentient being. By observing all internal and external phenomena with wisdom, one knows that both the knower and the known are utterly extinguished.
Because one does not recognize that false conceptualization is a manifestation of one's own mind, conceptualization arises; if one recognizes it, it is extinguished.

The commentary states: "This clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal, thereby manifesting that the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Buddha-realm and the suchness of sentient beings are one single suchness, not two different suchnesses.
The Tang translation says: "If the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of birth-and-death cannot be known..."
"How do sentient beings attain liberation while within birth and death? Mahāmati meant that one seeks liberation separately from outside of birth and death.
The Buddha said: "The original limit of birth and death is itself nirvāṇa. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this original limit, they undergo birth and death;
therefore, there exist beginningless falsehoods, faults, evils, and the habitual tendencies of discursive thought."
This is why one falsely perceives that there are real dharmas existing outside the mind.
Now, by merely extinguishing those habitual tendencies of deluded thought, one is able to realize that there are no dharmas outside the mind; this very deluded thought is itself nirvana.

It is not that nirvana exists separately apart from this deluded thought. Therefore it is said: "When the body of deluded thought is transformed, liberation is attained without its being extinguished."

Therefore, "boundlessness" is not a state of absolute nothingness. Since the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is entirely constituted by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), this very conceptualization is merely another name for the primordial limit.
Thus, the Wei translation states: "The primordial limit is the discriminating mind."

They are different names for the same essence. Apart from the conceptualizing mind, there are no sentient beings. Thus, the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is itself delusive thought (*vikalpa*), and delusive thought is itself sentient beings.
Therefore, as the ultimate limit is suchness (*tathatā*), so too are sentient beings suchness. Because they are all suchness, [there is no distinction].
Observing all internal and external phenomena with wisdom, one knows that both the knower and the known are entirely quiescent.

It is only because of a failure to understand that deluded thoughts arise from the mind itself that such thoughts are produced. If one understands that there is only mind, then deluded thoughts are immediately extinguished.
Viewed in this light, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are fundamentally not two different things; they differ only between delusion and awakening.
All are merely transformations of one's own mind; how could there be anything else?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Observe all the Teachers, who are like the sands of the Ganges: They are neither destroyed nor do they depart, And yet they are not ultimately [existent]."
This is what constitutes equality.
The commentary states: "This verse refers to the equality of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Yet it is neither destroyed nor departed, nor is it ultimately annihilated;
this is why it is called the equality of suchness (*tathatā*)."
Contemplating all Tathāgatas, who are like the sands of the Ganges, entirely free from all faults, whose nature remains constant even as they flow along—
this is the perfect awakening of the Buddha.

The commentary states: "This verse [shows] that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding. Because its nature remains constant even as it follows along with the flow [of phenomena], this is what is called 'true and real eternal abiding.
The above section concludes by clarifying the eternal abiding of the Dharma-body to reveal the mark of equality between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
From here below, the self-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* (the hidden mind) is shown to reveal the mark of equality between the true and the false, and between arising and ceasing."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all dharmas.
World-Honored One, in what sense are all dharmas momentary?"

The commentary states: This is intended to reveal the suchness (*tathatā*) of sentient beings; therefore, he asks about phenomena that arise and perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇa*). The Wei translation says:
"Explain to me the characteristics of the arising and perishing of all phenomena. Why does the Tathāgata say that all phenomena do not abide for even a single thought-moment?
Furthermore, 'all phenomena,' when spoken of in their ultimate sense, refers to both mundane and supramundane [phenomena], including the holy ones..."
The general principle of all phenomena is such that nothing is excluded; to speak briefly, they are simply the phenomena of the five aggregates of sentient beings' body and mind.
Taken as a whole, they all belong to the realm of arising and ceasing, and for this reason they are called "sentient beings.
If one discriminates with a deluded mind, they are all phenomena of arising and ceasing—namely, the one hundred and eight phrases initially inquired about by Mahāmati.

This being so, when Mahāmati previously posed his questions, the World-Honored One rejected them all by saying "no," intending to reveal that within the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), such phenomena fundamentally do not exist.

Now, for the time being, he provides a detailed exposition within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), clarifying each point—such as the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and non-self—until the ultimate identity of the true and the false is fully realized. Having reached this consummation, he is about to...

This clarifies that the nature of arising and ceasing is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), thereby demonstrating that it is not only the realm of the Buddhas that is suchness, but the realm of sentient beings is likewise suchness.
Thus, although Mahāmati has already heard that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding, he specifically raises the question regarding the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Since the phenomena of the true and the delusive do not transcend the single mind, the World-Honored One subsumes them within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
He raised [the question].
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. I shall explain it for you. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All dharmas refer to those that are wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate, conditioned, unconditioned, mundane, supramundane, and existent..."

Faulty and faultless; with outflows and without outflows; grasped and ungrasped. (The Wei translation says "internal dharmas and external dharmas"; the Tang translation says "dharmas that are grasped and dharmas that are not grasped. Mahāmati!

Briefly stated, the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the consciousness (*vijñāna*), along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), are the causes of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

It is by these—the mind, the intellect, and the consciousness—that the habitual tendencies are nourished and increased. (The Tang translation states: "To state the essentials: the phenomena of the five aggregates of clinging take the habitual tendencies of the mind, intellect, and consciousness as their cause, thereby attaining growth.

O Mahāmati, the false conceptualizations of the ignorant regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome, the cultivation of the bliss of samādhi, and the dwelling in the happiness of the present life through the correct attainment of samādhi—these are called the noble ones (*ārya*).

Wholesome and untainted (*kuśalānāsrava*; the Tang translation states: "Ordinary fools give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding this, calling it wholesome or unwholesome; the noble ones directly realize and dwell in the bliss of samādhi—this is what is called the wholesome and untainted dharma").

The commentary states: This clarifies that the dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms, as well as those of ordinary beings and sages, all exist in dependence upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of body and mind.

That is to say, all dharmas, for the most part, do not exceed the categories of the mundane and supramundane, the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, as well as the mental states of existence and non-existence, and the dharmas that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*). All such dharmas are universally comprised within the five [aggregates].
The aggregates (skandhas) take the body and mind as their cause. However, ordinary fools grasp these five aggregates as being substantially real;
therefore, based upon them, they perform worldly actions—wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—that result in faults and tainted karma.

Because non-Buddhists do not understand that the five aggregates are without self, they falsely grasp them as a divine self (ātman), giving rise to the two views of existence and non-existence. Therefore, it is said:
Arising and ceasing. World-transcending sages, by the power of samādhi, contemplate these five aggregates—the body and mind—as being like illusions and transformations.
Abiding in the present experience of the Dharma-joy, they accomplish wholesome, outflow-free dharmas; therefore, this is called non-arising and non-ceasing.

Fundamentally, all share the same single body and mind of the five aggregates. It is simply because their perceptions differ that the distinction between ordinary beings and sages exists. Based on this...

To speak in truth, all things without exception are not apart from arising and ceasing; this is what is called a *kṣaṇa*. Why? Because they have not yet transcended mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
What is called the "arising of the bodhicitta" and the "ceasing of the mind of arising and ceasing" is itself still arising and ceasing.

As long as there remains the mind that grasps at existence, everything is arising and ceasing; how much more so for those who engage in false conceptualization and discrimination? Yet, this arising...
The nature of cessation is fundamentally non-arising. Why is this? Because all phenomena do not depart from the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is fundamentally no coming or going, nor delusion, awakening, birth, or death; how then could those various phenomena undergo arising and ceasing?
Thus we know that "momentariness" (*kṣaṇa*) is a false perception.

Mahāmati, as for the wholesome and the unwholesome, they refer to the eight consciousnesses. What are these eight? They are the Tathāgatagarbha, which is called the ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness), along with the manas, the manovijñāna, and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses. These are not as described by the non-Buddhists.

The Commentary states: This statement that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome is intended to reveal that although there are phenomena of arising and ceasing, their fundamental nature is neither arising nor ceasing.

However, while it was previously stated that all phenomena of arising and ceasing do not transcend the wholesome and the unwholesome, it is now said that these two dharmas—good and evil—are both the eight consciousnesses, and the eight consciousnesses are themselves the *tathāgatagarbha*. Yet, the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally non-arising.
Cessation. Although these eight consciousnesses are subject to arising and ceasing, they are also neither arising nor ceasing. Why?

Because the *tathāgatagarbha* undergoes transformation through being perfumed by conditions of both defilement and purity. If ignorance perfumes the *tathatā*, the *tathāgatagarbha* follows along with defiled conditions and arises;
it is then termed the eight consciousnesses and possesses arising and ceasing. If the *tathatā* perfumes [ignorance], [the *tathāgatagarbha*]... [follows along with pure conditions].
It is clear that while the Tathāgatagarbha arises in accordance with pure conditions, those very eight consciousnesses are called the Tathāgatagarbha and are neither born nor extinguished.

Thus, while defilement and purity arise and cease according to conditions, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains profoundly still and eternally abiding, entirely devoid of the characteristics of birth and extinction, good and evil, or coming and going. This is not something known by the non-Buddhists.
Therefore, the Treatise states: "The consciousnesses arising from the perfuming of ignorance cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can they be realized by the wisdom of the two vehicles;
even Bodhisattvas on the ultimate stage cannot know them exhaustively; only a Buddha thoroughly understands them.
Why is this? Because this mind, from its very origin, is pure by nature, yet possesses ignorance."
Being defiled by ignorance, there is a defiled mind; yet although there is this defiled mind, it is eternally constant and unchanging.
Therefore, this meaning can be known only by a Buddha. Furthermore, it is said that there are two kinds of the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*):

first, fundamental perfuming, because it is capable of accomplishing the meaning of the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*); second, the perfuming of views and craving (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā*) which arises [therefrom]. Because...
Because it is able to accomplish the meaning of the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness), it is here said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is named the *ālayavijñāna*.
[It includes] the mind (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), and the five bodies of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Now, although it was stated at the beginning that "arising and ceasing" refers to the various consciousnesses, what is now stated as "non-arising and non-ceasing" likewise refers to the various consciousnesses, because the *ālayavijñāna* is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Mahāmati, as for the five bodies of consciousness, they are conjoined with the mind (manas), the intellect (manovijñāna), and the mental consciousness (vijñāna). Their characteristics of good and evil undergo successive transformation and destruction;

they flow in a continuous stream, giving rise to what appears to be an indestructible body. They arise and they perish—(the Tang translation says: "they arise without a distinct substance, and having arisen, they immediately perish")—failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind.
As they successively cease, other consciousnesses arise, grasping at the distinctions of forms and appearances.
The commentary states: These words describe the manner of arising and ceasing of the first five consciousnesses.

"Accompanied by mind, thought, and mental consciousness" means that when the first five consciousnesses arise, they each lack self-nature and necessarily depend upon the sixth, simultaneous mental consciousness to arise.

However, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) must necessarily rely on the seven-consciousness mind-faculty (manas-indriya). These seven consciousnesses, in turn, evolve through internal and external gates.

When they evolve through the external gate in the same manner as the six consciousnesses, they must internally rely upon the eighth consciousness as their fundamental support (*mūlāśraya*), because the seventh consciousness lacks its own substantial entity.
Therefore, it is said that when the five consciousnesses arise, they must be simultaneous with the mind, the thought, and the mental consciousness.
They revolve; thus, performing good and performing evil, they undergo successive transformation and destruction. They flow in a continuous stream, arising and ceasing without pause.

Nevertheless, because they do not depart from the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, although each cognizes its own respective object, no distinct entity arises.
Therefore, it is said that they are born with an indestructible body. Since there is no birth of a distinct entity, although there is birth, there is no birth;
thus it is said that "having been born, they immediately perish," meaning that at the very moment of arising, they perish. As the following verse states: "When a thing arises, it has cessation.

This reveals the meaning of the true non-arising of phenomena. It is only because of the failure to realize that appearances are the manifestation of one's own mind that one falsely perceives the distinctions of arising and ceasing.
Do not hold a separate grasping; in reality, they are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning. As for the successive cessation and the arising of other consciousnesses:
when the five consciousnesses first grasp an object in a single moment, there is no discrimination; this is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By the second moment, when one discriminates between the beautiful and the foul, the preceding five have already ceased, and it then belongs to the sixth [consciousness], the *manovijñāna*.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises and discriminates by distinguishing between forms—whether beautiful or ugly—and thereby generates grasping and attachment;
hence it is said that they "cease successively" as other consciousnesses arise.
The mental consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses arise together in association; because they do not abide for even a single moment, this is termed a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: These words describe the manner in which the six consciousnesses arise and perish. However, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise independently;
it necessarily arises simultaneously in conjunction with the five sensory consciousnesses at the time they perceive their respective objects. Therefore, the Tang translation says:
Co-arising with those five consciousnesses, they grasp various distinct forms and characteristics; they do not abide for even a single moment.
I call these "momentary dharmas. Viewed in this light, the five, seven, and eight consciousnesses are all fundamentally unarisen.
That which undergoes arising and ceasing is merely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, the "Chapter on Nirvāṇa" in the first two fascicles states:
"The cessation of deluded conceptualization and consciousness is called nirvāṇa. By comparing this with the preceding text, one will naturally come to clearly understand its profound meaning.

Mahāmati, "moment" (kṣaṇa) refers to the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is the Tathāgatagarbha. (The Wei translation says: "The ālayavijñāna is named Tathāgatagarbha. The Tang translation says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is named storehouse-consciousness.

It is the momentary habit-energy of the co-nascent mental consciousness; the untainted habit-energy is not momentary. This is not perceived by ordinary, ignorant people because they are attached to the doctrine of momentariness.
Failing to realize that all phenomena are both momentary and non-momentary, they fall into the view of annihilationism.

This refutes the notion of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The commentary states: "This precisely reveals that what appears as arising and ceasing is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; it clarifies the principle that 'the immutable follows conditions' and 'following conditions is the immutable.
The intended meaning is that what is called 'momentary' is none other than the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Furthermore, regarding consciousness...
The "store" (ālaya) is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha. Since the Tathāgatagarbha is not momentary, how could the consciousness-store (vijñānālaya) possibly be momentary?
Thus, being both momentary and non-momentary, one can know that arising and ceasing are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing.

However, that which undergoes arising and ceasing is likely not the *ālayavijñāna*. It is rather the six consciousnesses that arise simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses, which are perfumed by the defiled, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) habitual tendencies they have grasped. Does that [consciousness] itself arise and cease?

If so, then its arising is from conditions and its ceasing is from conditions; it has no connection whatsoever with the essence of my *ālaya*. Therefore, it is called the "consciousness co-arising with the manas."

Regarding the momentariness of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): if they are perfumed by untainted (*anāsrava*) habitual tendencies, then even that which arises and ceases would itself be neither arising nor ceasing.
Therefore, it is said that untainted habitual tendencies are not momentary; however, this is not something known by the foolish and ordinary.

Because they are attached to the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*), and because they do not know that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally non-momentary, they falsely conceptualize that even unconditioned *tathatā* perishes just like other phenomena; thus, they fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding this "moment" (*kṣaṇa*), although the Chinese translation from the Wei dynasty is stylistically inconsistent, its meaning is more explicit; it renders it as *chani*.

"Ka" signifies emptiness. The *ālayavijñāna* is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is called "empty" because it is not permeated by the mental formations (*vāsanā*) of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
It is called "not empty" because it is fully endowed with the dharmas of untainted permeation (*anāsrava-vāsanā*).
This corresponds precisely to the first two of the four meanings concerning the essential nature and characteristics of awakening (*bodhi*) discussed in the treatise. The treatise states:
"The essential nature and characteristics of awakening consist of four kinds of great meanings, which are equal to space and like a pure mirror. What are these four?"
First is the mirror of emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā-ādarśa*). It is far removed from all marks of the realms of mind and consciousness;

no phenomena can appear therein, for it does not possess the sense of cognitive illumination. Second is the mirror of causal perfuming (*hetu-vāsana-ādarśa*). This refers to that which is "not empty" as it truly is;
all realms of the mundane world appear within it, neither emerging nor entering, neither being lost nor destroyed, eternally abiding within the one mind.
Because all phenomena are of the nature of ultimate reality (*tathatā*), they cannot be defiled by any defiled dharmas;

the essence of wisdom is immovable, as it is fully endowed with untainted [seeds] that permeate sentient beings. However, the Wei translation lacks the phrase "permeation by the evolving consciousnesses of common intention.
This refers to the state of being far removed from all mental objects and characteristics; by comparing these two versions, one can sufficiently understand the arising [of the seeds].
Cessation is fundamentally non-arising, and thus there is no cessation.
Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure, is accompanied by their causes, and undergoes both arising and ceasing; it is intoxicated by the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance-dwelling.
Ordinary, deluded people do not realize this; they perceive [reality] in moments, and their minds are perfumed by false conceptualization.
The commentary states: "This explains the meaning of 'originally non-arising' (anutpāda) mentioned above.

Conventionally, it is said that the seven consciousnesses arise and perish in a cycle of flux, thereby bringing about birth and death. This statement that the seven consciousnesses do not flow [in such a cycle] precisely reveals the profound depth of non-arising."
This is the meaning. The reason the seventh consciousness does not undergo transmigration is that it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

For while the phenomena of birth and death, good and evil, suffering and pleasure, and so forth, are produced by the first six consciousnesses, it is the eighth consciousness that receives the perfuming, maintains the seeds, and brings about future results.
However, since the seventh consciousness neither produces nor receives [these], it cannot [act as the basis for transmigration].
Since it is not even the cause of birth and death—let alone that which arises and immediately perishes—it does not transmigrate; it cannot even serve as the cause for birth and death.
Furthermore, how could it possibly act as the cause for nirvāṇa? Since it cannot serve as the cause for either defilement or purity, it is clear that it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If intrinsic nature itself does not exist, who is there to undergo arising and ceasing? Nevertheless, the *tathāgatagarbha* is intrinsically pure by nature. Fundamentally...
It is neither born nor extinguished; it does not experience suffering or pleasure, nor is it the cause of birth and death.
If one now says that it experiences suffering and pleasure, arising and ceasing together with their causes, this is likely not the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Rather, it is due to the four abiding afflictions and the absence of causal conditions, being intoxicated by them, that there is suffering and pleasure coexisting with birth and death, and the false arising and ceasing. However...

The essence of this *tathāgatagarbha* is eternally pure, profoundly still, and permanently abiding. How, then, could it ever possess the characteristics of birth and death, suffering and pleasure, or arising and ceasing?
Thus, when one observes with thorough discernment both internally and externally, there is ultimately no such thing as arising or ceasing.

Yet ordinary, deluded beings do not awaken to this truth; they falsely give rise to the view of momentariness. This is because their minds are perfumed by false conceptualization, rather than by clarity.
This is wisdom. The following uses analogies to clarify it.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, just as gold, diamond, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary qualities and are never destroyed, so it is with Mahāmati:

if there were moments (kṣaṇa) in the attainment of the unintermittent [Dharma]—as the Wei translation says, "the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata," and the Tang translation says, "if one attains the realized Dharma"—then the noble ones would not be noble.
Yet the Sage has never ceased to be the Sage; he is like gold or a diamond, which does not diminish in weight or measure even after passing through kalpas.
Why, then, do the foolish and ignorant, being unskilled in my teaching of hidden intent, conceive the notion of momentariness regarding all internal and external phenomena?
The commentary states: This uses a metaphor to establish the characteristic of ultimate quiescence. That is to say, the *tathāgatagarbha* is by nature pure and firm;
although it exists within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), its essence is eternally indestructible, like the diamond-like bone of a Buddha.
Because it has attained such extraordinary qualities, this is realized by all Buddhas as their own awakened noble wisdom (*svasaṃvedya-āryajñāna*).
The ultimate Nirvana is that which all sentient beings attain as their own mind-nature; it is the Dharma of the equality and non-interruption between the holy and the ordinary.
If sentient beings were to possess this nature of non-interruption and yet undergo birth and death, [it would be a contradiction].
Furthermore, when a sage attains it, he does not thereby become something other than a sage.
Now, since a sage who has attained it has never ceased to be a sage, how could an ordinary person who attains it truly remain an ordinary person? Moreover, this nature is like a diamond;
even after passing through kalpas and being weighed, it does not diminish. How could it increase in a sage, or [decrease] in an ordinary person?
Is it that they are diminished? Since the holy and the ordinary are equal, how could there still be arising and ceasing within all phenomena?
Therefore it is said: "Why do foolish people, being unskilled in my hidden and concealed teaching, conceive the notion of momentariness regarding all internal and external phenomena?
This sutra points directly to the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*) of sentient beings and suddenly reveals the *Tathāgatagarbha*. Thus...

Beginning from the "Chapter on Arising and Ceasing" in the first fascicle, what has been discussed thus far—discerning and clarifying the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox—all relies upon the eight consciousnesses (*vijñānas*) established through delusion and enlightenment.

Now that the principles, practices, causes, and effects revealed herein have reached their ultimate limit, the text returns once more to the *tathāgatagarbha* as the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Here, it is clarified that the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, thereby demonstrating equality as suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, by means of this [explanation], it is shown that one enters the gate of True Suchness from the gate of Arising and Ceasing, converging back into the One Mind as the ultimate goal;

this is the general purport of the entire work. Therefore, what follows clarifies that the cultivation of the fundamental nature involves neither cultivation nor attainment, demonstrating that the Dharmakāya is free from all faults, thereby concluding the discourse. The subsequent verses on Emptiness, Impermanence, and Momentariness should...
This belongs here; it was merely a scribal error in the translation. May readers kindly take this into account, for the underlying principle will then become even more manifest.

The above concludes the section on the manifestation of the equality of arising and ceasing. Below follows the extensive elucidation of the six perfections to demonstrate the characteristic of wondrous practice being without cultivation.

The Bodhisattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that one attains perfect enlightenment by fulfilling the six pāramitās, what are these six?
(Both translations include this; [the second asks] 'How are they fulfilled?')"

The commentary states: This extensively clarifies the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) to demonstrate that wondrous practice is without cultivation and without attainment, thereby establishing the aforementioned meaning of equality.
Based on what was previously stated, one who merely realizes the manifestation of their own mind and realizes the noble wisdom of self-awakening is called a Buddha;
thus, there would be no need for the arduous, extensive cultivation of the six perfections over many eons. How so? Worldly...
In other sūtras, the World-Honored One has consistently taught that one attains Buddhahood only upon the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
This [your current position] contradicts the sacred teachings. We simply do not know which six perfections you refer to; how, then, can one attain Buddhahood according to what you now say?
Therefore, this question was raised. Below, the World-Honored One answers with three kinds of six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

That which is here called "fulfillment" refers to sudden cultivation in a single thought-moment, rather than traversing many kalpas; it is intended to clarify that there is neither cultivation nor attainment.
This is to demonstrate the ultimate wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*).
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the *pāramitās*: namely, the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane."
The commentary states: Mahāmati asked about which six perfections [were meant], and the World-Honored One answered with the names of three types.
"Worldly" refers to the practices of humans and devas; "supramundane" refers to the practices of the two vehicles; and "supremely supramundane" refers to the practice of the One Vehicle.
Mahāmati, as for the worldly pāramitās: they consist of being attached to the grasping of "self" and "what belongs to self," and of grasping at the two extremes.

For the sake of seeking various places of rebirth and delighting in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, one fulfills the dāna-pāramitā (the perfection of giving). [The Tang translation says:

"That is to say, all foolish commoners are attached to 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' cling to the two extremes, seek bodies within the realms of existence, and crave objects such as form; thus they practice the pāramitā of giving. [Likewise for] śīla (morality), kṣānti (patience), vīrya (diligence), and dhyāna (meditative concentration).

Wisdom is also like this. Regarding the supernatural powers of ordinary beings and their rebirth in the Brahma heavens, it is recorded that these refer to the six perfections with outflows (*sāsrava*) within the world.
That is to say, foolish ordinary people, being attached to signs, practice giving while calculating "I am the one who gives" and calculating that there is an object to be given;
they act based on the two views of existence and non-existence in order to seek what has not yet been attained.
Coming to receive rebirth in the superior realms of humans and devas, one practices giving while fully possessing the sensory objects of the six dusts and the five desires;
the same applies to the other five perfections, such as ethical discipline. Because these are outflowing causes (*āsrava-hetu*), they induce outflowing fruits (*āsrava-phala*);

thus, one is born in the Brahma heavens and attains the five mundane superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) of ordinary beings, never departing from birth and death. Therefore, it is called "the worldly. — Yongjia.
It is said: "Giving while dwelling upon signs produces the merit of rebirth in the heavens, which is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void.
When its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down; thus one incurs an unfavorable rebirth in the future. This is why it is so."

Mahāmati, as for the supramundane pāramitās: because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the grasping of nirvāṇa, they practice the six pāramitās while delighting in their own personal nirvāṇic bliss.

The Record states: This refers to the two vehicles and the six perfections. It means that those of the two vehicles, out of weariness with and desire to abandon birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and out of longing for and approaching *nirvāṇa*, seek their own deliverance and practice six kinds of inferior, untainted (*anāsrava*) conduct;
therefore, they cannot become Buddhas, because they are attached to the marks of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the supramundane, supreme *pāramitā*: because one realizes that the objects of grasping are merely the measure of the false imaginings manifested by one's own mind, and because of the duality within one's own mind, false imaginings do not arise.

Since one does not grasp at the various realms of existence as being real, and does not cling to the forms and characteristics of one's own mind, one gives rise to the *dāna-pāramitā* for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, employing the most supreme skillful means.
The Record states: These words refer to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the foremost practice of the Supreme Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

It means that a Great Bodhisattva, having realized that all is a manifestation of mind-only (*cittamātra*) and performing the contemplation of reality (*yathābhūta-pratyavekṣā*), perceives that both internal and external phenomena within their own mind are merely manifestations of false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Thus, in the giving they perform, they skillfully penetrate the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*) and do not give rise to the delusion of a giver.
One forms the perception [of giving] without generating attachment to the recipient, nor grasping at the color or form of the object being given in between;

rather, one constantly practices generosity solely for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings. Therefore, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) takes the nature of relinquishment as its antidote.
The Treatise says: Within the dharma of *tathatā*, profound understanding manifests; that which is cultivated is free from marks.
Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) in accordance with it.

Yet, among the six perfections, giving is preeminent. The Treatise states: "The meaning of giving encompasses the six: the gift of material goods, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma. Among these, one, two, and three [respectively correspond to them]."
This is called the stage of dwelling in practice; therefore, it is termed the "supreme-upon-supreme" skillful means.
The precept wherein conceptualization does not arise with respect to those very objects is the *śīla-pāramitā*.

The commentary states: "This is the perfection of morality (*śīla*). In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *śīla*; here [in Chinese] it is translated as 'coolness' (*qingliang*), and also as 'stopping' (*zhi*)."

It is so. "Precept" (*śīla*) is the direct translation. This precept spoken of here does not possess the characteristic of being maintained through volitional effort; rather, it is a natural precept (*dharmatā-śīla*).

All the perfections (*pāramitā*) are likewise so. That which is called "the precept wherein delusive thoughts do not arise regarding those conditions" means that when delusive thoughts do not arise regarding the conditions of all objects—whether defiled or pure, whether giving or receiving—one's own nature is pure, and the characteristic of the precept is like space.

What constitutes upholding or violating? Taking intrinsic purity as the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). The Treatise states: "Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is undefiled and is free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) in accordance with this."
This is the patience of the non-arising of those very deluded thoughts; knowing the grasped and the grasper is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

The commentary states: "This is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*). In the Sanskrit language it is *kṣānti*; here it is translated as 'peaceful endurance' (*an-ru*) or 'patience through forbearance' (*nin-yuk*).

It is called 'patience through forbearance' because the mind is able to peacefully endure external objects that cause insult. This refers to [the state] regarding those very instances of upholding or violating precepts within delusion..."
One conceives that [phenomena] do not arise. To accept this dharma of non-arising within the mind is what constitutes "patience with the non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

it does not refer to the conventional meaning of forbearance. However, non-arising is not something that can be "endured" as an object; rather, one is called "patient" because one knows that the nature of both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) is empty and quiescent.

It is by virtue of this that it is designated as the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). As the treatise states: "Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without suffering."
Because he is free from anger and affliction, he practices in accordance with the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.

During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he applies himself diligently through skillful means; practicing in accordance with these skillful means so that false conceptualizations do not arise is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
The Record states: "This is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). In Sanskrit it is *vīrya*, which here means 'vigor.

Because one practices in accordance with reality, and regarding the skillful means of practice, does not even give rise to the thought of 'skillful means,' the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the sudden abandonment of the two attachments;
this is true vigor. Therefore, this is established as the perfection of vigor. The Treatise says: "By knowing the nature of phenomena..."
Being without the marks of body or mind, because of being free from indolence, one practices in accordance with the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
When all false conceptualizations are extinguished, one does not fall into the grasping for the nirvana of the śrāvakas; this is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

The commentary states: This is the perfection of dhyāna. In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *dhyāna*; here it is translated as "cultivation through contemplation" (*sīwéishōu*), and its direct equivalent is "calm contemplation" (*jìnglǜ*).
This means that while the deluded thoughts of mind, thought, and consciousness are entirely extinguished, one uses great compassion and great vows to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
Although one attains nirvāṇa, one does not take its realization as a final goal; therefore, one does not fall into the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas. By these two...
Because there is grasping in the practice of dhyāna, this takes non-attachment to nirvāṇa as the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*). The treatise states:
"Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally settled and its essence is without distraction, one practices the perfection of dhyāna in accordance with this."
The false imaginings of one’s own mind are without intrinsic nature; when observed with wisdom, one does not fall into the two extremes.
Thus, the preceding body is transformed into something superior and indestructible, attaining the noble path of self-realization—this is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The record states: This is the *Prajñāpāramitā*. In Sanskrit it is called *prajñā*, which here is translated as "wisdom.

It means to clearly understand that the characteristics of the triple world manifest from the deluded thoughts of one's own mind and do not truly exist. By observing with wisdom, one does not fall into the two views of existence and non-existence;
thus the Dharma-body becomes increasingly sublime, and one realizes its indestructibility through the absence of arising and ceasing, thereby attaining entry.
The realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gati*) constitutes what is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). The treatise states:

"Because the essence of the *dharmatā* is luminous and free from ignorance, one practices in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*. Thus, these six perfections are all cultivated in relation to the [ultimate] nature (*dharmatā*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "When the mind is never in harmony with worldly minds, this is called diligence (*vīrya*). Compassion...

The custom of the people of Chile is not associated with consciousness; this is termed "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*). Having already realized the Buddha-fruit and the world-transcending sublime wisdom, this is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Because both are cultivated in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*), there is no characteristic of cultivation within cultivation.
This is what is called "fulfilling unsurpassed bodhi in a single thought-moment. Therefore, it is said to be the characteristic of non-attainment. For this reason, it is the practice of suchness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Emptiness, impermanence, and momentariness—these are constructed by the deluded thoughts of fools. Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they conceive of them as being momentary."
In a single kṣaṇa, agitation ceases; it is quiescent and free from activity. All phenomena are non-arising—this is what I call the meaning of *kṣaṇa*.
When a thing arises, it simultaneously perishes (the Wei translation says: "at the very moment of arising, there is perishing"). This is not taught for the sake of the ignorant.
The commentary states: This verse explains the meaning of the preceding chapter on moments (*kṣaṇa*). The translator has misplaced this passage here.
It means that foolish people, through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), discriminate among all phenomena as being substantially existent and reckon them to be permanent;
therefore, the World-Honored One taught emptiness, impermanence, and momentariness—likening them to a river, a lamp flame, and a seed—as they swiftly pass away from moment to moment.

It does not abide, for that [abiding] is refuted by the destruction of such conceptualizations. Yet, because foolish people do not understand the hidden intention, they again cling to verbal expressions as being real and fixate upon the notion of "momentariness.
They fail to realize that the nature of momentary phenomena is fundamentally not momentary;
it is quiescent within its own essence, tranquil, and free from all conditioned activity. It is only through delusion that one fabricates the notions of arising and ceasing.
This is my view. Because all dharmas are fundamentally unborn from the very beginning, I speak only of the meaning of the *kṣaṇa* (moment).

Yet, the place where all dharmas arise is precisely where they cease; in their very substance, they are unborn. How could this meaning of non-arising be explained to the ignorant? Therefore it is said:
"That which arises at the outset is simultaneously subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

They arise at the very place they appear and perish at the very place they are; they are illusory and false, designated as "characteristics," yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity.
How could this be easily explained to the ignorant?
The nature of uninterrupted continuity is perfumed by false conceptualization; with ignorance as its cause, the mind arises from it.

Until form has yet arisen, what interval exists in between? (The Wei translation says: "If ignorance is the cause that can produce all minds, until form has yet arisen, upon what does it depend during this interval?
As the continuity perishes in successive order, (the Wei translation says: "as soon as it arises, it immediately ceases"), another mind arises following it, not abiding in form.
At that time, from what object-condition (*ālambana*) does it arise? Since it arises from that [object], it arises from a cause that is not as it truly is (*ayathābhūta*).

How can it be established as non-existent while being known to perish momentarily? (The Tang translation says: "If the mind arises conditioned by that, its cause is false; since the essence is unestablished due to the falsity of the cause, how can it be momentary destruction?")
The commentary states: This verse successively elucidates that the mind and its objects are unborn, thereby explaining the meaning of "momentary" and "non-momentary.

It means that throughout the six realms of existence—whether above or below within the triple world—their abiding and coming have been fundamentally empty and devoid of substance from the very beginning.
Their essence is eternally present, entirely lacking even the slightest mark of arising or ceasing. If one were to speak of the continuous arising and ceasing of the six realms...

Regarding the characteristic [of the mind]: if it is claimed that the mind undergoes arising and ceasing based on an object due to ignorance (*avidyā*) perfumed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), this is also not the case.
Why? If there were a material object (*rūpārtha*) existing as a condition for the mind, one could say that the mind arises from it.
However, when the material object has not yet arisen, upon what dharma does this mind rely to abide and give rise to discrimination?
Therefore, it is said: "As long as form has not yet arisen, upon what does the intermediate state depend? This implies that the view that the mind arises from an object is erroneous.
Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "One should not abide in form when generating the mind. Yet, if one does not abide in form when generating the mind, there is fundamentally no arising.
If one were to claim that all phenomena arise and perish in a continuous succession, and that other minds and...
Furthermore, the claim that [consciousness] arises following the transformation and cessation of its respective object is also incorrect. Why?

If those material objects were to exist as persisting entities, one could say that [consciousness] arises following them. However, those phenomena arise at their respective locations and perish at their respective locations;
their own essence is quiescent, and they are entirely devoid of any characteristic of arising. Thus, matter is fundamentally without persistence.
Since form has no abiding, what dharma could there be that serves as an object for the mind to perceive and thereby arise? Therefore, it is said:
"When one does not abide in form, what is there to be perceived for it to arise? Thus, those who calculate that objects have arising and ceasing are deluded.

Since form has no abiding, the object is fundamentally non-arising. If one claims that the mind arises from that non-arising object, then such a cause is like the son of a barren woman; it is likewise a mere fabrication. Therefore, it is said:

"Because it arises from that [object], it does not arise from a cause that is in accordance with reality. Since the cause is a fabrication, the essence of that which is produced cannot be established.
How can one falsely perceive the existence of dharmas that arise and perish in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), when in reality nothing is established?
Observing this through successive and thorough investigation, the mind and its objects become tranquil; one realizes there is absolutely no arising or perishing.
This is why I speak of the "moment. That which is without arising or perishing exists because the mind and its objects do not reach one another. Thus, the Great Sūtra says:
It is said: "For example, like the waters in a river, rushing and competing to flow away; so too are all phenomena, each unaware of the others.
The meditative absorption of the practitioner, the diamond-like relics of the Buddha, the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and the indestructible things of the world [are likewise]."
Abiding in the True Dharma, one attains it; the Tathāgata is fully endowed with wisdom. A bhikṣu attains equanimity. How can one perceive moments?
Gandharvas, illusions, and the like—form has no such moments. Regarding unreal forms and the like, one views them as if they were real.
The Record states: These words declare that all dharmas are unarisen; they can only be clearly seen by the eye of wisdom, and cannot be known through deluded thoughts or false views.

This means that for one who practices according to reality, within right concentration, they observe that all worldly dharmas are truly eternal and, in their very essence, as firm and solid as a vajra, a śarīra relic, or the celestial palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven—permanently abiding.
It is indestructible, for the waters and fires of the Ābhāsvara Heaven cannot reach it. If even for a practitioner who observes with a concentrated mind the result is already such as this,
how much more so for a bhikṣu who dwells in the True Dharma as an eighth-stage bodhisattva,
who has attained the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom and realized the equality of true thusness— how could he perceive that all phenomena still exist?
Is it the characteristic of arising and ceasing moment by moment? Furthermore, all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are fundamentally unreal, like a city of the *gandharvas* or a magical illusion;
they do not undergo arising and ceasing moment by moment because they lack reality.

How can deluded beings falsely regard what is unreal as real, calculating the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to be the creators of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)? Since the great elements themselves are unreal, how...
Why, then, is it said that they can create? All of this is the false vision of the ignorant. The above verse-text should be examined in conjunction with the chapter on moments (*kṣaṇa*);
its meaning will then become clear of itself. The preceding explanation of the characteristic of non-cultivation in sublime conduct is hereby concluded.
△ Below, the extensive refutation of various doubts generally reveals that the Dharmakāya is free from faults.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, being no different from all Bodhisattvas. All sentient beings...”
"Those subject to birth do not enter nirvāṇa; who then attains the Buddha-way?
The commentary states: "This extensively explains the doubts of the multitude and generally reveals that the Dharmakāya is free from faults.

Mahāmati, because the World-Honored One’s initial statement seemed somewhat contradictory, he feared that future generations would not properly understand the Tathāgata’s hidden and esoteric teachings.
The mind, thereupon, gives rise to doubt; for this reason, each point is raised and examined to clarify that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternally free from all faults.

However, while the ancient commentary divides these questions and answers into ten sections, upon carefully examining the flow of the discourse and considering the intent of the responses—when compared with those two translations—it is clear that the first six should be combined into two. Therefore, there are only [seven sections].

Sixth, regarding doubt: these are merely successive elaborations of the intended meaning. Nevertheless, when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he responds to sentient beings through the three wheels of body, speech, and mind, remaining forever free from all faults.
Within the present six questions, the accounts of bestowing predictions, explaining consciousness, and establishing the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) pertain to the karma of speech.
The descriptions of Vajrapāṇi’s protection and the retribution suffered by those encountering Māra pertain to the karma of the body. [The text] does not mention a single... [omission].
"Characteristics" refers to constant concentration, being without deliberation (*vitarka*) or investigation (*vicāra*), which constitutes mental action (*manas-karman*).
Because the three types of action are thus purified, the body does not manifest itself; there is no teaching, yet it teaches. It responds without deliberation and knows without investigation.
